variables.name: Susceptible population
variables.documentation: The population that has not yet been exposed to COVID-19 and is susceptible to infection.

variables.name: Exposed population
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are still in the incubation period and not yet infectious.

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People who have recovered from COVID-19 and currently have immunity.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible people become exposed through contact with infectious individuals.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The rate at which exposed people complete incubation and become presymptomatic infectious. This is the fraction that will eventually develop symptoms.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: The rate at which symptomatic infectious people recover.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: The initial number of susceptible people at the start of the simulation, representing a country-sized population.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: The probability that a random contact is with a susceptible person, based on the fraction of the population that is susceptible.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: The probability that a contact between an infectious person and a susceptible person results in transmission.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: The total living population, used as the denominator for contact probability calculations. Note: this excludes cumulative deaths, so the population shrinks as people die.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: The average time from exposure to becoming infectious, measured in days. Typical COVID-19 incubation is 2-5 days.

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: People who have completed incubation and are infectious but have not yet developed symptoms.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious and showing symptoms of COVID-19.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious but never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: The rate at which presymptomatic infectious people develop symptoms. This is a third-order pipeline delay of the Incubation inflow, delayed by the presymptomatic period. The input to the delay should be the inflow to the stock (Incubation), not the stock divided by a residence time, because DELAY3 is a pipeline (conveyor) delay that conserves material.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: The rate at which asymptomatic infectious people recover. This is a third-order pipeline delay of the Asymptomatic incubation inflow, delayed by the average period of asymptomatic infections.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The rate at which exposed people complete incubation and become asymptomatic infectious. This is the fraction that will never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: The fraction of infections that are asymptomatic, estimated between 25% and 80%.

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: The total rate of people completing incubation, implemented as a third-order pipeline delay of the Infection rate. This represents the biological incubation process.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: An exogenous inflow of presymptomatic infectious people arriving from abroad, representing imported cases. Defined as a graphical function of time.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: The average duration of infectiousness for asymptomatic cases, measured in days.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The rate at which symptomatic infectious people die from COVID-19.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: The fraction of symptomatic COVID-19 cases that result in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: The average duration of the presymptomatic infectious period before symptoms develop, measured in days.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: The rate at which recovered people lose immunity and become susceptible again. Implemented as a third-order pipeline delay of total recoveries.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: The average duration of immunity after recovery, approximately one year.

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: The average duration of the symptomatic infectious period before recovery or death.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: The total number of currently infectious people, including symptomatic, presymptomatic, and asymptomatic cases.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: The effective number of contacts per person per week, reduced by social distancing measures.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: The fraction of normal contacts that are prevented by social distancing policies. Defined as a graphical function of time representing policy changes over the simulation period.

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: The cumulative total number of deaths from COVID-19 over the simulation period.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: The baseline number of contacts per person per week in the absence of social distancing.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant: 7 days per week.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: The total rate of people exiting the symptomatic infectious stage (through either recovery or death). Implemented as a third-order pipeline delay of the Developing symptoms inflow.

errorExplanations.name: recovery_without_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Asymptomatic incubation' flow as input, not the 'Asymptomatic infectious' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Formulation Error Analysis and Fixes

I identified one formulation error in the original model:

Error 1: "Recovery without symptoms" — Incorrect DELAY3 formulation

What was wrong: The original equation was:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week, Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

This is a fundamental misuse of the DELAY3 pipeline delay. Throughout the rest of the model, pipeline delays are used consistently: the input to the delay is the inflow to the corresponding stock, and the delay time is the residence time. For example:

  • Total incubation = DELAY3(Infection, ...) — the input is the inflow to Exposed population
  • Developing symptoms = DELAY3(Incubation + Influx..., ...) — the input is the inflow to Presymptomatic infectious
  • Total exiting symptomatic infectious = DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, ...) — the input is the inflow to Symptomatic infectious
  • Losing immunity = DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, ...) — the input is the inflow to Recovered population

However, "Recovery without symptoms" used Asymptomatic_infectious / Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections / Days_per_week as its input — this is an exponential decay formulation (stock divided by residence time) being fed into a pipeline delay, which is conceptually inconsistent and produces incorrect units (People·Weeks/Days²). The correct input should be Asymptomatic_incubation, which is the inflow to the Asymptomatic infectious stock, consistent with the pipeline delay pattern used everywhere else in the model.

How it was fixed: Changed the equation to:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

This makes "Recovery without symptoms" follow the exact same pipeline delay pattern as all other transition flows in the model: the input to the DELAY3 is the inflow to the upstream stock, and the delay time is the average residence time converted from days to weeks.
supportingInfo.title: Fixed Recovery Without Symptoms Pipeline Delay

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People who have recovered from COVID-19 and currently have immunity.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible people become exposed through contact with infectious individuals. Calculated as the product of infectious population, contact rate, infection probability per contact, and the fraction of contacts that are with susceptible people.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The flow of exposed people who complete incubation and become presymptomatic infectious. This is the symptomatic fraction of total incubation completions.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: The rate at which symptomatic infectious people recover, based on the complement of the case fatality rate applied to total exits from the symptomatic infectious compartment.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: The initial number of susceptible people at the start of the simulation, representing the total population of the modeled region.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: The probability that any given contact is with a susceptible person, calculated as the fraction of the total population that is susceptible.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: The probability that a contact between an infectious person and a susceptible person results in transmission of the virus.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: The total living population, summing all compartments except cumulative deaths. Used as the denominator for calculating contact probabilities.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: The average number of days from exposure to becoming infectious, approximately 3 days for COVID-19.

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: People who have completed incubation and are infectious but have not yet developed symptoms. This is a pipeline delay stage before symptom onset.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious and showing symptoms of COVID-19. They will either recover or die.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious but never develop symptoms. They will recover without showing symptoms.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: The rate at which presymptomatic infectious people develop symptoms, modeled as a third-order pipeline delay of the inflow to the presymptomatic compartment with the presymptomatic period as the delay time.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: The rate at which asymptomatic infectious people recover, modeled as a third-order pipeline delay of the inflow to the asymptomatic infectious compartment with the average asymptomatic infection period as the delay time. This is consistent with the pipeline delay pattern used throughout the model.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The flow of exposed people who complete incubation and become asymptomatic infectious. This is the asymptomatic fraction of total incubation completions.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: The fraction of infections that are asymptomatic, estimated between 25% and 80%. Set to 50% as a central estimate.

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: The total rate of people completing incubation, modeled as a third-order pipeline delay of infections with the average incubation time as the delay.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: An exogenous inflow of presymptomatic infectious people arriving from abroad, represented as a time-based graphical function capturing waves of imported cases.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: The average duration of infectiousness for asymptomatic cases, approximately 6 days.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The rate at which symptomatic infectious people die from COVID-19, based on the case fatality rate applied to total exits from the symptomatic infectious compartment.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: The fraction of symptomatic COVID-19 cases that result in death, set at 1%.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: The average number of days a person is infectious before developing symptoms.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: The rate at which recovered people lose immunity and become susceptible again, modeled as a third-order pipeline delay of recovery flows with the average immunity period as the delay time.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: The average duration of immunity after recovery from COVID-19, approximately one year (52 weeks).

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: The average duration of the symptomatic infectious period, approximately 1 week.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: The total number of currently infectious people, including symptomatic, presymptomatic, and asymptomatic infectious individuals.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: The effective number of contacts per person per week after accounting for social distancing measures that reduce contacts.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: A time-based graphical function representing the intensity of social distancing measures over time, ranging from 0 (no measures) to 1 (complete isolation). Captures the phased introduction and relaxation of restrictions.

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: The cumulative total number of deaths from COVID-19 since the start of the simulation.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: The baseline number of contacts per person per week in the absence of any social distancing measures.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: A unit conversion constant: 7 days per week, used to convert delay times from days to weeks.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: The total rate of people exiting the symptomatic infectious compartment, modeled as a third-order pipeline delay of the inflow to the symptomatic compartment with the average symptomatic period as the delay time.

errorExplanations.name: influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad
errorExplanations.problem: The graphical function should use TIME as an input, not DT (DT).

supportingInfo.explanation:
After careful analysis of the model, I found no formulation errors. Here is my detailed review:

  1. Pipeline delay consistency: The model consistently uses DELAY3 (third-order pipeline delays) throughout for all disease progression stages — incubation (Total incubation), presymptomatic-to-symptomatic (Developing symptoms), asymptomatic recovery (Recovery without symptoms), symptomatic exit (Total exiting symptomatic infectious), and immunity loss (Losing immunity). This is internally consistent and appropriate for epidemiological modeling where pipeline delays better represent the distribution of residence times in each compartment.

  2. Unit conversions: Parameters specified in days (Average COVID incubation time = 3 days, Presymptomatic period = 3 days, Average period of asymptomatic infections = 6 days) are correctly converted to weeks by dividing by Days_per_week (7 days/week) before being used as delay times in the DELAY3 functions, which operate in the model's time unit of weeks.

  3. Stock-flow conservation: The Exposed population stock correctly has Infection as its inflow and Incubation + Asymptomatic incubation as its outflows. The split between symptomatic and asymptomatic pathways using Share_of_asymptomatic_infections applied to Total_incubation correctly ensures all people leaving exposure are accounted for. The Symptomatic infectious stock has Developing symptoms as inflow and Recovery + Dying of COVID as outflows, with the split governed by Case_fatality_rate_of_COVID_patients applied to Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious.

  4. Total population: Correctly computed as an auxiliary (not a stock) summing all living compartments, excluding Cumulative COVID deaths. This is correct — it's an algebraic sum, not an accumulation.

  5. Infection rate formulation: Infectious_population * Contacts_per_person_per_week * Infection_rate_per_contact * Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person is a standard mass-action-like formulation appropriate for this type of compartmental model.

  6. Graphical functions: Social distancing measures and Influx from abroad are both time-based graphical functions, which is appropriate for exogenous policy and seeding inputs.

The model is structurally sound with no formulation errors detected. All equations, variable types, and delay structures are internally consistent and epidemiologically appropriate.

errorExplanations.name: social_distancing_measures
errorExplanations.problem: The graphical function should use TIME as an input, not DT (DT).

supportingInfo.explanation:
After careful analysis of the model formulations, I found no formulation errors in this COVID-19 epidemiological model. Here is my detailed review:

Pipeline Delay Consistency: The model consistently uses DELAY3 (third-order pipeline delays) throughout all compartment transitions — Total incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious, and Losing immunity. This is appropriate and internally consistent. Pipeline delays (DELAY3) are the correct choice for epidemiological models because they produce a more realistic distribution of residence times compared to first-order exponential delays.

Unit Conversions: All day-to-week conversions are handled correctly using the Days_per_week constant (7 Day/Week). For example, Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week correctly converts 3 days into 3/7 weeks for the delay duration.

Stock-Flow Structure: All stocks have appropriate inflows and outflows. The Exposed population stock correctly accumulates Infection and is drained by both Incubation and Asymptomatic incubation. The splitting of flows using Share_of_asymptomatic_infections is correctly formulated.

Infection Rate: The infection formulation Infectious_population * Contacts_per_person_per_week * Infection_rate_per_contact * Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person correctly implements standard mass-action mixing with frequency-dependent transmission.

Total Population: Correctly computed as the sum of all living compartments (excluding Cumulative COVID deaths), which means it properly shrinks as people die.

Death and Recovery Split: The Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious variable correctly uses DELAY3 on Developing_symptoms with Average_length_of_symptomatic_period, and is then split into Recovery and Dying of COVID using the case fatality rate and its complement.

Social Distancing: The graphical function input correctly uses TIME, and the formulation (1 - Social_distancing_measures) * Normal_number_of_contacts_per_week correctly reduces contacts.

The model is well-formulated with no errors requiring correction.

errorExplanations.name: total_population
errorExplanations.problem: Total population should be an auxiliary/converter variable that sums the population stocks, not a stock.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I identified and corrected two formulation errors in the original model:

Error 1: Total Population was a Stock with a Flow — Should be an Auxiliary

Variable: Total population (was type stock with inflow Total population net flow)

Why it was wrong: Total population is defined as the sum of all compartments (Susceptible + Exposed + Asymptomatic infectious + Presymptomatic infectious + Symptomatic infectious + Recovered). This is a simple algebraic aggregation, not an accumulation over time. Making it a stock with a flow that sets its value to the sum of compartments each timestep is a classic variable type error — it conflates algebraic sums with integrations. The flow Total population net flow was computing the sum of all compartments (in units of Person) but was typed as a flow (Person/Week), creating a dimensional inconsistency. The stock would not correctly track the population because it would integrate the sum rather than equal it.

How I fixed it: Changed Total population from a stock to an auxiliary variable (type variable) with the equation Susceptible_population+Exposed_population+Asymptomatic_infectious+Presymptomatic_infectious+Symptomatic_infectious+Recovered_population. This correctly computes the total as an algebraic identity at each timestep. The Total population net flow variable was removed as it is no longer needed (it served no valid purpose).

Error 2: Total population net flow removed

Variable: Total population net flow (was type flow)

Why it was wrong: This flow had units of Person/Week but its equation computed a sum of populations in units of Person. It existed solely to feed the erroneously-typed stock. With Total population corrected to an auxiliary, this flow is unnecessary and dimensionally incorrect.

How I fixed it: Removed this variable entirely from the model.

All other formulations were reviewed and found to be consistent. The model correctly uses DELAY3 (third-order pipeline delays) throughout for incubation, symptom development, recovery, and immunity loss, which is appropriate for epidemiological compartment models where the distribution of residence times matters.
supportingInfo.title: Fixed Total Population Type and Flow Errors

supportingInfo.explanation:
Formulation Errors Found and Fixed

Error 1: Infectious population was incorrectly formulated as a stock with a flow

What was wrong: Infectious population was defined as a stock with an inflow called Infectious population net flow. However, the infectious population is simply the algebraic sum of three stocks: Symptomatic infectious + Presymptomatic infectious + Asymptomatic infectious. It is not an accumulation via flows — it is a simple aggregation. Modeling it as a stock with a flow that equals the sum of the three compartments is structurally incorrect because:

  1. The flow Infectious population net flow had the equation Symptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Asymptomatic_infectious, which has units of Person, not Person/Week as required for a flow. This is a dimensional error.
  2. Integrating the levels of three stocks would produce a completely wrong result — it would accumulate person-weeks, not track the current infectious population.
  3. The stock would drift away from the true infectious population over time.

How it was fixed: Infectious population was changed from a stock to a variable (auxiliary) with the equation Symptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Asymptomatic_infectious. The erroneous flow Infectious population net flow was removed entirely. The relationships were updated so that the three infectious compartments feed directly into Infectious population as algebraic inputs.

Summary

The single critical error was a variable type error for an aggregation — a common formulation mistake where a simple sum is incorrectly modeled as a stock. The fix converts it to an auxiliary variable that correctly computes the sum at each time step. All other formulations (DELAY3 pipeline delays, unit conversions, split flows) were reviewed and found to be correct.
supportingInfo.title: Fixed Infectious Population Aggregation Stock Error

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the escalating dynamics that led to the American Revolution through two reinforcing feedback loops and one balancing loop.

The Escalation of Grievances Loop (R1): British taxation and military presence generated colonial grievances. These grievances accumulated because Britain rarely offered concessions, viewing them as weakness. The French and Indian War debt was the initial trigger—Parliament needed revenue and looked to the colonies, imposing the Stamp Act and subsequent taxes. Each new tax added to colonial resentment, particularly because colonists had no Parliamentary representation.

The Resistance-Repression Spiral (R2): As grievances accumulated, colonists organized resistance—boycotts, protests, and dramatic acts like the Boston Tea Party. Britain responded by deploying more troops (the Intolerable Acts included military enforcement). However, military presence created new grievances (the Boston Massacre being the most inflammatory example), which fueled more resistance, triggering more military deployment. This is a classic escalation archetype where each side's response amplifies the other's.

The Identity Reinforcement Loop (R3): Shared grievances strengthened colonial identity. As colonists from Massachusetts to Virginia faced common British policies, they developed a sense of being "Americans" rather than separate colonial subjects. This stronger identity made collective resistance easier to organize, which generated more shared experiences, further strengthening identity.

The Weak Balancing Loop (B1): Theoretically, British concessions could have resolved grievances and broken the escalation cycle. However, Parliament's unwillingness to compromise meant this balancing mechanism was essentially inactive, allowing the reinforcing loops to dominate.

The probability of armed conflict increased as both resistance and military presence grew, creating the volatile conditions that erupted at Lexington and Concord in 1775.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Grievances Drove Revolutionary Conflict

variables.name: Colonial Grievances
variables.documentation: The accumulated sense of injustice and resentment felt by American colonists toward British rule. This stock represents the buildup of complaints over taxation without representation, restrictions on trade, and perceived violations of colonial rights. It accumulates through new grievances and depletes only when the British address colonial concerns.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures three interconnected reinforcing feedback loops that explain how road rage incidents can escalate over time:

The Congestion-Frustration Loop (R1): Road rage incidents cause traffic slowdowns and rubbernecking, which increases traffic congestion. Higher congestion increases driver frustration and impatience, which in turn leads to more road rage incidents. This creates a vicious cycle where incidents breed more incidents through their impact on traffic flow.

The Social Learning Loop (R2): As road rage incidents accumulate, more drivers observe aggressive behavior on the roads. Through observational learning, this aggressive behavior becomes increasingly normalized in society. When aggressive driving is seen as normal or acceptable, drivers are more likely to engage in road rage themselves, creating more incidents and further normalizing the behavior.

The Stress Amplification Loop (R3): Driver stress is amplified by multiple factors including sleep deprivation and perceived provocations from distracted drivers. However, if the reinforcing loops dominate, the system can spiral toward increasing road rage. The key leverage points for intervention include reducing distracted driving, improving sleep habits, and actively working to denormalize aggressive driving through awareness campaigns.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the reinforcing feedback loop that escalated tensions toward revolution. Colonial Grievances accumulate as Britain imposes oppressive policies like the Stamp Act and responds to colonial defiance. These grievances fuel Colonial Resistance through protests and acts like the Boston Tea Party. Critically, this resistance provokes even harsher British Oppressive Actions (the Intolerable Acts), which further accelerates grievance accumulation. This creates a classic escalation archetype where each side's response amplifies the other's, making conflict increasingly inevitable. The model shows how initial taxation disputes spiraled into revolution through this self-reinforcing cycle of grievance, resistance, and retaliation.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Grievances Drove Revolutionary Conflict

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures a reinforcing feedback loop that explains how road rage can escalate in society. The core dynamic works as follows:

The Road Rage Spiral (Reinforcing Loop R1): Road Rage Incidents → Effect of Incidents on Stress → Driver Stress Level → Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents

When road rage incidents increase, drivers become more stressed through learned behavior (observing aggression normalizes it), heightened anxiety, and defensive driving that paradoxically increases aggression. This elevated stress makes drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions, which generates more incidents, completing the reinforcing loop.

The Balancing Force (Loop B1): Road Rage Incidents → Incident Decay Rate → Road Rage Incidents

Incidents naturally decay over time as they are resolved, forgotten, or processed. This provides a stabilizing force against unlimited growth.

Future Trajectory: The system's behavior depends on the relative strength of these loops. If the reinforcing loop dominates, road rage will escalate exponentially until some external intervention occurs. If the balancing loop is stronger, the system will stabilize at an equilibrium level. The graphical function captures the nonlinear relationship where high incident levels create disproportionately stressful environments, potentially tipping the system toward escalation.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model explains the American Revolution through four interconnected feedback loops:

Loop 1: The Escalation Spiral (Reinforcing) Colonial Grievances → Colonial Resistance → British Repression → Effect of Punitive Acts → Colonial Grievances

This is the central engine driving toward revolution. British taxation created grievances, which sparked resistance (boycotts, the Boston Tea Party). Britain responded with repression (troops, the Intolerable Acts), which created more grievances. Each side's response amplified the other's, making conflict increasingly inevitable.

Loop 2: The Identity Amplifier (Reinforcing) Colonial Resistance → Colonial Identity → Colonial Identity Multiplier → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance

Shared resistance experiences built a common American identity. As colonists boycotted together, protested together, and formed the Continental Congress, they stopped seeing themselves as Virginians or Bostonians and started seeing themselves as Americans. This stronger identity made resistance more unified and effective, which created more shared experiences.

Loop 3: Grievance Accumulation (Reinforcing) Colonial Grievances → Effect of Grievances on Resistance → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance → British Repression → Effect of Punitive Acts → Grievance Accumulation Rate → Colonial Grievances

This extended loop shows how grievances compound. The more grievances accumulated, the more resistance grew, which provoked more British repression, which created even more grievances. The Boston Massacre and Intolerable Acts exemplify how British responses backfired.

Loop 4: Resistance Fatigue (Balancing) Colonial Resistance → Resistance Decline Rate → Colonial Resistance (negative)

This weak balancing loop represents natural resistance fatigue. However, the reinforcing loops overwhelmed it because British escalation continuously renewed colonial anger.

The model shows that armed conflict became likely when both grievances and repression reached critical levels. Britain's choice to punish rather than accommodate transformed tax disputes into revolution.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model reveals how road rage can become self-perpetuating through interconnected feedback loops:

Loop 1: The Stress-Rage Spiral (Reinforcing) Driver Stress Level → Effect of Stress on Incidents → Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Effect of Incidents on Stress → Stress Accumulation Rate → Driver Stress Level

When drivers are stressed, they're more likely to react aggressively to provocations, creating incidents. These incidents then increase anxiety and normalize aggressive behavior among other drivers, further elevating stress levels. This vicious cycle can cause road rage to escalate rapidly.

Loop 2: The Traffic Congestion Amplifier (Reinforcing) Road Rage Incidents → Effect of Incidents on Traffic → Traffic Congestion → Effect of Traffic on Stress → Stress Accumulation Rate → Driver Stress Level → Effect of Stress on Incidents → Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents

Road rage incidents cause accidents, police responses, and rubbernecking that worsen traffic congestion. This congestion frustrates drivers, building stress that makes future incidents more likely—a secondary reinforcing mechanism.

Loop 3: Stress Recovery (Balancing) Driver Stress Level → Stress Relief Rate → Driver Stress Level

This natural balancing loop represents how drivers recover from stress through rest and time away from driving, providing a counterforce to stress accumulation.

Loop 4: Incident Memory Decay (Balancing) Road Rage Incidents → Incident Decay Rate → Road Rage Incidents

As time passes, incidents fade from collective memory, reducing their influence on traffic and stress—a stabilizing force against runaway escalation.

The system's future trajectory depends on the relative strength of reinforcing versus balancing loops. If stress accumulation outpaces relief, road rage can spiral upward until some intervention breaks the cycle.
supportingInfo.title: Road Rage Escalates Through Stress Feedback Loops

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The American Revolution emerged from a reinforcing escalation loop that drove colonial grievances to the breaking point.

The Escalation Spiral (R1): British Oppressive Actions → Colonial Grievances → Colonial Resistance → British Oppressive Actions

This classic escalation archetype explains how the conflict spiraled out of control. When Britain imposed taxes like the Stamp Act to recover French and Indian War costs, colonists accumulated grievances because they lacked parliamentary representation. These grievances fueled resistance through boycotts and protests. Britain responded with harsher measures—the Boston Massacre, then the Intolerable Acts after the Tea Party—which only deepened grievances further.

The model captures why reconciliation failed: each British attempt to reassert control backfired by adding fuel to colonial resentment. The developing American identity (represented by Grievance Sensitivity) meant colonists interpreted British actions through a lens of tyranny rather than legitimate governance. Once this reinforcing loop gained momentum, it became self-sustaining until hostilities erupted.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model explains the American Revolution through six interconnected reinforcing feedback loops that created an escalating spiral toward armed conflict:

Loop 1: The Taxation-Grievance-Resistance Loop British taxation increases colonial grievances, which fuel resistance. Resistance increases British enforcement costs, raising revenue needs, which leads to more taxation. This is the classic "taxation without representation" cycle that began with the Stamp Act.

Loop 2: The Resistance-Repression Loop Colonial resistance triggers British military buildup. However, military repression galvanizes rather than suppresses opposition—the presence of troops in Boston inflamed tensions rather than calming them. This reduces resistance decline, allowing resistance to grow faster.

Loop 3: The Punitive Acts Escalation Loop Resistance (like the Boston Tea Party) triggers punitive legislation (the Intolerable Acts), which generates grievances, which fuel more resistance. Each act of defiance met with harsh punishment only strengthened colonial resolve.

Loop 4: The Violent Incidents Loop Military presence combined with resistance creates violent incidents like the Boston Massacre. These incidents generate grievances and serve as powerful propaganda, fueling more resistance, which brings more military presence.

Loop 5: The Identity Formation Loop Shared grievances and shared resistance strengthen American identity. Stronger identity enables more unified resistance, which creates more shared experiences, further strengthening identity. The colonies transformed from separate entities into a unified "American" people.

Loop 6: The Grievance-Identity-Resistance Loop Grievances strengthen identity, identity enables resistance, resistance triggers punitive responses that create more grievances. This triple-reinforcing structure made de-escalation nearly impossible.

The French and Indian War debt provided the initial push—Britain needed revenue and expected colonies to pay. But the system's feedback structure meant that each British attempt to assert control strengthened the forces opposing it. The revolution emerged not from any single cause but from these interlocking cycles that transformed manageable tensions into irreconcilable conflict.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and at least 8 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model reveals six interconnected feedback loops that explain how road rage incidents might change over time:

Reinforcing Loop 1: Stress-Incident Spiral Road rage incidents → increased traffic congestion → higher driver stress → more incidents. This vicious cycle shows how incidents create conditions that breed more incidents.

Reinforcing Loop 2: Congestion-Provocation Amplifier Traffic congestion → more perceived provocations → higher stress accumulation → more incidents → more congestion. Congested conditions create provocative situations that fuel the cycle.

Reinforcing Loop 3: Social Learning Trap Road rage incidents → increased aggressive driving normalization → higher incident rate → more incidents. As people observe aggressive driving, it becomes socially acceptable, encouraging more aggressive behavior.

Reinforcing Loop 4: Normalization-Provocation Cascade Aggressive driving normalization → more perceived provocations → higher stress → more incidents → further normalization. Normalized aggression creates more provocative situations.

Balancing Loop 5: Public Awareness Response Road rage incidents → increased public awareness → faster denormalization of aggressive driving → fewer incidents. Society responds to high incident levels with campaigns that discourage aggressive driving.

Balancing Loop 6: Infrastructure Investment Response Road rage incidents → infrastructure investment → faster congestion reduction → lower stress → fewer incidents. Governments respond to problems by improving roads.

The model suggests road rage can exhibit explosive growth through multiple reinforcing loops, but balancing mechanisms eventually activate. The key insight is that normalization of aggressive driving creates a particularly dangerous reinforcing dynamic that may require deliberate intervention to break.
supportingInfo.title: Road Rage Feedback Dynamics Model

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and at least 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The American Revolution emerged from four interconnected feedback loops that drove escalating conflict:

Loop 1: The Grievance-Resistance Spiral (Reinforcing) Colonial Grievances → Resistance Growth → British Oppression → Grievance Accumulation → Colonial Grievances. This is the core escalation engine. British policies like the Stamp Act created grievances, which sparked resistance like boycotts, which triggered harsher British responses like the Intolerable Acts, which created more grievances. This vicious cycle made conflict increasingly inevitable.

Loop 2: The Identity-Resistance Amplifier (Reinforcing) Colonial Resistance → Identity Formation → Resistance Growth → Colonial Resistance. Shared resistance experiences like the Boston Tea Party forged a distinct American identity, which in turn made colonists more willing to resist. This self-reinforcing loop transformed scattered protests into a unified independence movement.

Loop 3: The Diplomatic Erosion Loop (Reinforcing) Colonial Resistance → Diplomatic Efforts (decreasing) → Grievance Resolution (decreasing) → Colonial Grievances (increasing) → Resistance Growth → Colonial Resistance. As resistance grew, colonists abandoned negotiation, which meant grievances went unresolved, which fueled more resistance. This closed off peaceful resolution paths.

Loop 4: The Suppression Backfire (Balancing but Weak) Colonial Resistance → British Oppression → Resistance Suppression → Colonial Resistance. Britain attempted to suppress resistance through force, but this balancing loop was overwhelmed by the reinforcing loops because oppression generated far more grievances than it suppressed resistance.

The model shows how initial tensions from French and Indian War debts triggered these feedback loops, creating an escalating spiral that made the outbreak of hostilities nearly inevitable once set in motion.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Feedback Loops Ignited Revolutionary War

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and at least 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures four interconnected feedback loops that explain how road rage incidents might change over time:

Loop 1: Stress-Incident Reinforcing Loop (R1) Road rage incidents → Traffic congestion → Driver stress → More incidents. When incidents occur, they slow traffic and create congestion. This congestion frustrates drivers and increases stress levels. Stressed drivers are more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions, leading to more road rage incidents. This is a reinforcing loop that can cause escalating road rage.

Loop 2: Congestion-Incident Reinforcing Loop (R2) Road rage incidents → Traffic congestion → Driver stress → More incidents → More congestion. This extends the first loop by showing how incidents directly contribute to congestion (accidents block lanes, aggressive maneuvers slow traffic), which feeds back through stress to create more incidents.

Loop 3: Social Normalization Reinforcing Loop (R3) Road rage incidents → Normalized aggressive behavior → More incidents. As people observe more road rage, aggressive driving becomes normalized as acceptable behavior. This learned behavior makes drivers more likely to engage in road rage themselves, creating more incidents. This is a particularly dangerous reinforcing loop because social norms change slowly but persistently.

Loop 4: Natural Decay Balancing Loops (B1, B2, B3) Each stock has a balancing loop through its outflow: incidents decay over time, stress recovers naturally, congestion dissipates, and normalized behavior slowly returns to baseline. These balancing loops provide stability but may be overwhelmed by the reinforcing loops during periods of high stress.

The model suggests road rage can exhibit "tipping point" behavior: below a threshold, the balancing loops dominate and incidents remain stable. Above the threshold, the reinforcing loops dominate, causing escalating road rage that becomes self-sustaining through stress, congestion, and social normalization.
supportingInfo.title: Road Rage Escalation Through Stress and Social Norms

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures six reinforcing feedback loops that drove the American Revolution:

Loop 1: Grievance-Resistance Spiral (R1) Colonial Grievances → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance → British Military Response → Perceived Tyranny → Grievance Accumulation Rate → Colonial Grievances. This is the core escalation dynamic where British responses to resistance created more grievances, fueling more resistance.

Loop 2: Taxation-Grievance Loop (R2) British Taxation Pressure → Grievance Accumulation Rate → Colonial Grievances → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance → British Military Response → Perceived Tyranny → Grievance Accumulation Rate. The Stamp Act and Townshend Acts created grievances that spiraled into resistance.

Loop 3: Identity Amplification Loop (R3) Colonial Resistance → Identity Formation Rate → Colonial Identity → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance. Shared resistance experiences like the Boston Tea Party strengthened American identity, which made future resistance more likely.

Loop 4: Tyranny-Resistance Loop (R4) Perceived Tyranny → Grievance Accumulation Rate → Colonial Grievances → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance → British Military Response → Perceived Tyranny. Events like the Boston Massacre became propaganda tools that intensified anti-British sentiment.

Loop 5: Suppression Backfire Loop (R5) Colonial Resistance → British Military Response → Resistance Suppression Rate (attempting to reduce resistance) BUT Colonial Resistance → Suppression Effectiveness (negative), meaning suppression became less effective as resistance organized.

Loop 6: Identity-Grievance Amplification (R6) Colonial Identity → Resistance Growth Rate → Colonial Resistance → British Military Response → Perceived Tyranny → Grievance Accumulation Rate → Colonial Grievances → Resistance Growth Rate (amplified by identity). Identity made grievances more potent.

The model shows how British war debt initiated taxation, which triggered a cascade of reinforcing loops. The Intolerable Acts (closing Boston's port) exemplify how British responses backfired, strengthening rather than weakening colonial resolve.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Grievances Ignited Revolutionary Resistance Loops

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model reveals how road rage incidents can become self-perpetuating through six interconnected feedback loops:

Reinforcing Loop 1 - The Stress Spiral: Road rage incidents increase driver stress levels, and stressed drivers are more likely to engage in aggressive behavior, creating more incidents. This classic "Limits to Growth" dynamic shows how initial incidents can cascade.

Reinforcing Loop 2 - The Congestion Trap: Incidents cause traffic slowdowns, increasing congestion. Higher congestion frustrates drivers and creates more opportunities for conflict, leading to more incidents. This represents a "Success to the Successful" archetype where problems compound.

Reinforcing Loop 3 - The Normalization Cycle: Frequent road rage incidents normalize aggressive driving behavior in society. When aggression is seen as acceptable, more drivers engage in it, creating more incidents. This is a dangerous social contagion dynamic.

Reinforcing Loop 4 - Congestion-Stress Amplification: Traffic congestion increases driver stress, which increases incidents, which increases congestion further. This creates a compound reinforcing effect linking two problem areas.

Balancing Loop 5 - Stress Recovery: Driver stress naturally dissipates over time as people recover, providing a counterbalance to stress accumulation.

Balancing Loop 6 - Social Pushback: As aggressive driving becomes too normalized, society pushes back through social disapproval, education, and enforcement, gradually denormalizing the behavior.

The model suggests that without intervention, road rage can enter a vicious cycle where incidents breed more incidents through multiple pathways. However, the balancing loops indicate that natural recovery mechanisms exist, and targeted interventions addressing stress, congestion, or social norms could break the reinforcing cycles.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include the variables "Taxation", "Anti-British Sentiment" and "Colonial Identity".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the escalating feedback dynamics that drove the American Revolution through two reinforcing loops:

The Escalation Loop: British taxation without representation created grievances that built Anti-British Sentiment. This sentiment, combined with growing Colonial Identity, produced Colonial Resistance (like the Boston Tea Party). Britain responded with Punitive Measures (the Intolerable Acts), which backfired by further increasing sentiment and military presence, leading to Violent Incidents (the Boston Massacre). Each British crackdown intensified colonial opposition rather than suppressing it.

The Identity Formation Loop: As Anti-British Sentiment grew, colonists developed shared grievances. Their collective resistance actions reinforced a distinct Colonial Identity separate from British identity. This stronger identity made colonists more willing to resist, which created more shared experiences, further strengthening identity—a classic "success to the successful" archetype.

The model shows how these loops interconnected: stronger identity amplified the effect of sentiment on resistance, while resistance strengthened identity. The British faced a "fixes that fail" archetype—their punitive responses temporarily addressed resistance but ultimately accelerated the revolutionary momentum they sought to prevent.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Feedback Loops Drove Revolutionary Momentum

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include the variables "Traffic Congestion", "Driver Stress" and "Accidents".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model reveals how road rage emerges from and reinforces a dangerous Reinforcing Loop structure that can spiral out of control.

The Core Vicious Cycle: The central dynamic is a reinforcing feedback loop connecting Traffic Congestion → Driver Stress → Road Rage Incidents → Accidents → back to Traffic Congestion. When congestion increases, drivers experience more frustration and stress. Elevated stress reduces impulse control, making road rage incidents more likely. These aggressive driving behaviors cause more accidents, which block lanes and create even more congestion—completing the cycle.

The Provocation Amplifier: A secondary reinforcing loop accelerates this dynamic: Road Rage Incidents → Perceived Provocations → Driver Stress → Road Rage Incidents. When road rage is prevalent, aggressive driving behaviors (tailgating, cutting off, honking) are perceived as provocations by other drivers, increasing their stress and making them more likely to engage in road rage themselves. This creates a contagion effect where road rage spreads through the driving population.

Balancing Forces: The model includes natural balancing mechanisms through stress relief and incident resolution. However, these operate on relatively slow timescales compared to the rapid escalation of the reinforcing loops. This asymmetry means the system can quickly spiral upward but recovers slowly.

Key Leverage Points: The model suggests interventions at several points: increasing road capacity reduces the congestion trigger, reducing time pressure decreases stress buildup, and addressing aggressive personality traits through education could reduce the population susceptible to road rage. The nonlinear graphical functions capture how stress has a disproportionate effect on road rage—small increases in stress at high levels produce dramatic increases in aggressive incidents.
supportingInfo.title: Road Rage Escalation Through Reinforcing Feedback Loops

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contact rate

supportingInfo.explanation:
This SEIR (Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered) model captures the fundamental dynamics of infectious disease spread. The model contains four stocks representing disease compartments through which individuals progress.

The core feedback loop is a reinforcing loop driving epidemic growth: more infectious people create more infections, which after incubation creates more infectious people. This is the classic epidemic amplification mechanism.

This reinforcing loop is eventually counteracted by a balancing loop representing herd immunity: as susceptibles become infected and recover, the pool of potential new infections shrinks, reducing the effective reproduction number below 1 and causing the epidemic to decline.

The reproduction number (R0 = 3.5 with these parameters) determines epidemic potential. When R0 > 1, each infectious person generates more than one new infection on average, and the epidemic grows. The effective reproduction number adjusts for current immunity levels.

The incubation time creates a delay between infection and infectiousness, which affects epidemic timing but not final size. The infectious duration affects both how long individuals can spread disease and the recovery rate.

This structure explains why epidemics follow characteristic S-shaped cumulative curves and bell-shaped incidence curves, with rapid initial growth followed by peak and decline as susceptibles are depleted.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the key dynamics of healthcare system capacity during a health crisis through several interconnected feedback loops:

Capacity Constraint Loop (Balancing): When patients exceed available beds, the capacity availability effect reduces admissions, preventing unlimited patient accumulation. This represents patients being turned away when the system is full.

Workload-Quality Loop (Reinforcing): High patient loads increase workload, which degrades care quality. Poor care quality slows discharges (patients stay longer) and increases deaths. Slower discharges keep patients in the system longer, maintaining high workload - a vicious cycle during crises.

Burnout-Capacity Loop (Reinforcing): High workload accelerates burnout accumulation. Burnout reduces worker productivity, which decreases effective capacity, which increases workload further. This creates a downward spiral where overworked staff become less effective.

Burnout-Turnover Loop (Reinforcing): High burnout increases departure rates while simultaneously making hiring less effective (reputation effects). This depletes the workforce, reducing capacity and increasing workload on remaining staff.

Workforce Adjustment Loop (Balancing): When patients exceed workforce capacity, the workforce gap triggers hiring to restore balance. However, the time delays in hiring (4 weeks) and the burnout effects on hiring effectiveness can cause this loop to lag behind rapidly changing demand.

Bed Capacity Adjustment Loop (Balancing): Similar to workforce, bed capacity adjusts to patient demand but with delays (3 weeks to add beds). This surge capacity helps but cannot respond instantly to crisis waves.

The crisis intensity varies cyclically, creating waves of demand that stress these feedback structures and reveal system vulnerabilities.
