additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Additions

New Stocks Added

Four new stocks were introduced as described:

  • Outrances (initial: 150): gains a constant 20/hour, loses 40% and 10% of its current level per hour — two separate balancing loops driving it toward equilibrium.
  • Illigents (initial: 30): gains 40% of current outrances per hour (cross-stock coupling), loses a constant 5/hour.
  • Yelbs (initial: 65): gains 10% of current outrances per hour, loses 12% of current trazes per hour — a cross-stock drain creating a dependency between trazes and yelbs.
  • Trazes (initial: 85): gains a constant 15/hour, loses 18% of its current level per hour — a classic balancing loop.

Key Feedback Structures

  • Outrances has two simultaneous balancing (negative) feedback loops via its two fractional outflows, both driven by its own level.
  • Trazes has a single balancing loop via its 18% fractional outflow.
  • Outrances → Illigents: A reinforcing cross-link where outrances drive illigents inflow, creating a dependency chain.
  • Outrances → Yelbs and Trazes → Yelbs: Yelbs is influenced by two separate stocks — outrances feeds it while trazes drains it, creating an interesting cross-stock interaction.

Constants Separated

All numerical constants (rates and fixed flows) were given their own named variable nodes per modeling best practices, ensuring no embedded constants in equations with other variables.

testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
In my business, we start the period with one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever existing_store_lambdas are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever existing_store_mus are currently available.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Chained Inventory System with Feedback Loops

The existing model (with existing_store_lambda and existing_store_mu) was preserved intact, with only the supply_mu flow corrected to be driven by 3% of maxabizers (as specified) rather than a constant.

New Stocks Added

Five new stocks were introduced: whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers. Each follows a standard stock-and-flow structure with a proportional inflow and a separate outflow.

Causal Chain

The system forms a reinforcing chain threading through all inventories:

  • whatajigs grows from itself (5%) and feeds balacks
  • balacks grows from whatajigs (5%) and is depleted by existing_store_lambda (3%)
  • whoziewhats grows from balacks (5%) and depletes itself (3%)
  • funkados grows from whoziewhats (5%) and is depleted by maxabizers (3%)
  • maxabizers grows from funkados (5%) and is depleted by existing_store_mu (3%)

Feedback Loop Closure

Two key feedback loops are closed:

  1. Maxabizers → supply_mu → existing_store_mu → maxabizers_outflow → maxabizers: A balancing loop where maxabizers build up mu, which then drains maxabizers.
  2. existing_store_lambda → balacks_outflow → balacks: Lambda stock acts as a drain on balacks, linking the original model into the new chain.

All rate constants were extracted as named auxiliary variables to comply with modeling best practices.
supportingInfo.title: Chained Inventory System with Closing Feedback Loops

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the exponential growth dynamics of frimbulator inventory. The structure represents a reinforcing feedback loop (R1): Frimbulators → Daily Growth → Frimbulators. This is a classic "Success to the Successful" or exponential growth archetype where the stock reinforces its own growth. The current inventory level determines the absolute amount of daily growth (2% of current inventory), which then adds back to the inventory, creating compound growth. I separated the growth rate (0.02) into its own variable rather than embedding it directly in the flow equation, following best practices for constant handling. This structure will produce exponential growth behavior where the inventory grows increasingly faster over time as the base (current inventory) increases.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

This model captures a Balancing Process with Exponential Growth archetype. The frimulator inventory is a stock that experiences two simultaneous processes: percentage-based growth and constant reduction.

Key Causal Relationships

Reinforcing Loop (R1): Frimbulators → Incoming_Frimbulators → Frimbulators. This creates exponential growth because the incoming flow is proportional to the current stock size. As inventory grows, the 5% growth produces increasingly larger absolute additions.

Balancing Process: The Constant_Reduction creates a steady drain of 5 frimbulators per week through Outgoing_Frimbulators, which opposes the growth.

Model Behavior

Initially, the 5% growth on 100 frimbulators produces 5 units per week, exactly balancing the 5-unit constant reduction. As inventory grows beyond 100, the percentage-based incoming flow exceeds the constant outgoing flow, causing net accumulation. The reinforcing loop dominates over time, leading to exponential growth despite the constant reduction.
supportingInfo.title: Frimulator Inventory Growth with Constant Reduction

This model captures a two-stock system with mutual interdependence between whatajigs and balacks inventories.

Whatajigs Stock Dynamics:

  • Whatajigs grows through self-reinforcement: the stock drives its own 5% annual growth (reinforcing loop)
  • Whatajigs is depleted by balacks at a 300% rate, creating a negative feedback connection from balacks to whatajigs

Balacks Stock Dynamics:

  • Balacks grows based on whatajigs at a 5% rate, creating a positive feedback connection from whatajigs to balacks
  • Balacks experiences self-limiting decay at 3% annually (balancing loop)

Cross-Stock Feedback Structure:

  • A reinforcing loop exists: whatajigs increases balacks growth, which increases balacks, which increases whatajigs reduction, which decreases whatajigs
  • This creates oscillatory potential as the two stocks influence each other in opposing ways

Constants Separated

All numerical constants (growth rates and multipliers) are extracted as separate variables to follow best practices and enable easy parameter adjustment.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Discovery Model

This model captures all cause-and-effect relationships described in the background information across three independent inventory systems.

Marticatenes System

I created a stock-and-flow structure with marticatenes as the central stock starting at 50 units. The stock has two flows: a constant inflow of 10 units per month and an outflow equal to 20% of current inventory. This creates a balancing feedback loop where higher marticatenes levels increase the outflow, which then reduces the stock.

Refluppers System

I modeled refluppers as a stock starting at 75 units with two flows. The critical causal link is that refluppers inflow depends on marticatenes count (20% of current marticatenes), creating a cross-system causal relationship. The outflow is constant at 8 units per month. This means marticatenes directly influences refluppers accumulation.

Exemintes System

I structured exemintes as an independent stock starting at 120 units. It has a constant inflow of 8 units per month and an outflow of 10% of current inventory, creating another balancing feedback loop similar to marticatenes.

Key Causal Relationships

Each system exhibits internal balancing feedback where the stock level influences its own outflow. The unique cross-system causality is marticatenes driving refluppers inflow. All constants are separated into distinct variables to make causal relationships explicit and modifiable.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Structure Extraction

This model captures all cause-and-effect relationships from the provided information through three interconnected inventory systems:

Three-Stock Chain Structure: The system forms a causal chain: dominitoxings → povals → auspongs. Each stock influences the next through fractional inflows.

Dominitoxings System:

  • Receives constant daily additions (12 units)
  • Experiences fractional outflow (30% daily)
  • Drives inflow to povals through positive causal link

Povals System:

  • Receives fractional inflow from dominitoxings (30% of dominitoxings)
  • Experiences fractional outflow (20% of itself)
  • Drives inflow to auspongs through positive causal link

Auspongs System:

  • Receives fractional inflow from povals (20% of povals)
  • Experiences constant outflow (12 units daily)

Key Causal Relationships: All fractional rates create positive polarity relationships (stock increases → flow increases). All flows create their expected stock relationships: inflows add positively, outflows subtract negatively. Constants influence their respective flows with positive polarity.

This structure represents a cascading inventory system where upstream stocks causally influence downstream accumulations.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, we begin with one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock loses a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we start the period with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

I created a complete stock-and-flow model capturing all causal relationships described in the background information. The model contains three independent subsystems, each representing a distinct inventory with its own dynamics.

Pablanksills Subsystem

The pablanksills stock begins at 110 units and has two flows: a reinforcing growth loop (6% quarterly growth) and a constant depletion (18 units per quarter). The growth creates a positive feedback where larger inventory generates more growth. Following the mandatory constant handling rule, I separated the 6% rate into growth_rate_pablanksills and the 18-unit depletion into constant_depletion_pablanksills as distinct variables.

Posistorathers Subsystem

The posistorathers stock starts at 70 units with constant additions (25 units per quarter) and fractional outflow (35% per quarter). This creates a balancing structure where the stock seeks equilibrium between constant inflow and proportional outflow. I extracted constant_addition_posistorathers and outflow_rate_posistorathers as separate variables per the constant handling requirement.

Crypterals Subsystem

The crypterals stock (initial value 95) has the most complex structure with three flows: constant additions (18 per quarter), contributions from posistorathers (35% of posistorathers stock), and fractional depletion (22% of crypterals). This creates a cross-subsystem linkage where posistorathers directly influences crypterals accumulation. All constants were separated into distinct variables: constant_addition_crypterals, contribution_rate_posistorathers, and depletion_rate_crypterals.

Causal Relationships

Every cause-and-effect relationship is explicitly captured with correct polarity. Stocks positively influence their proportional flows (reinforcing). Flows positively influence their destination stocks (inflows) or negatively influence them (outflows). Rate constants positively influence their respective flows. The model contains 18 causal relationships total, forming two reinforcing loops (pablanksills growth, crypterals self-reinforcement) and multiple balancing loops (all outflows).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Structure Extraction

I created a comprehensive stock and flow model capturing all causal relationships from the provided information. The model contains four interconnected inventory systems:

Primary Stock-Flow Structures:

  • Ocs inventory: Starts at 25, gains from proptimatires (15% weekly), loses constant 3 units weekly
  • Proptimatires inventory: Starts at 40, gains constant 5 units weekly, loses 25% of itself weekly
  • Priaries inventory: Starts at 80, gains from proptimatires (10% weekly), loses based on houtals (5% weekly)
  • Houtals inventory: Starts at 60, gains constant 7 units weekly, loses 8% of itself weekly

Key Cross-Stock Causal Relationships:

  1. Proptimatires drives ocs inflow (positive feedback)
  2. Proptimatires drives priaries inflow (positive feedback)
  3. Houtals drives priaries outflow (creates depletion pressure)

Structural Decisions: All numerical constants were separated into distinct variables following best practices. Each flow has explicit rate variables, enabling clear causal tracing. The model captures both self-regulating loops (stocks affecting their own outflows) and cross-system dependencies (proptimatires affecting multiple other stocks, houtals affecting priaries).

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gains from exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gains from 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

This model captures four interconnected inventory systems with their respective accumulation and depletion processes.

Stock-Flow Structures

Outrances System: A stock with constant inflow (20 per hour) and two fractional outflows (40% and 10% per hour). This creates a balancing feedback loop where higher outrances lead to greater depletion.

Illigents System: A stock that gains from outrances (40% conversion rate) and depletes at a constant rate (5 per hour). This creates a reinforcing connection from outrances to illigents.

Yelbs System: A stock that gains from outrances (10% conversion rate) and is reduced based on trazes (12% conversion rate). This creates two cross-system dependencies.

Trazes System: A stock with constant inflow (15 per hour) and fractional outflow (18% per hour). This creates a balancing feedback loop.

Key Causal Relationships

The model exhibits a cascade structure where outrances serves as a source for both illigents and yelbs. Additionally, trazes influences yelbs through its reduction effect, creating an inter-system dependency. Each stock has its own balancing loop through fractional depletion, while the constant inflows provide steady replenishment.

Constant Separation

All numerical constants have been extracted into separate named variables following best practices, ensuring model transparency and ease of modification.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, our records indicate one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures a cascade system with five interconnected inventory stocks. Each stock has growth and depletion flows with specific causal relationships:

Whatajigs forms the foundation, growing from its own stock (5% self-reinforcing growth) while depleting at a constant rate. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where whatajigs drives its own growth.

Balacks receives inflow from whatajigs (5% of whatajigs) and depletes proportionally to itself (3%). This creates a cross-stock cascade where whatajigs influences balacks growth.

Whoziewhats receives inflow from balacks (5% of balacks) and depletes proportionally to itself (3%). This extends the cascade chain further.

Funkados and Maxabizers form a mutual interdependency: funkados grows from whoziewhats but depletes based on maxabizers, while maxabizers grows from funkados but depletes based on whoziewhats. This creates two balancing feedback loops that couple these final two stocks together.

The model reveals a complex causal structure: a linear cascade (whatajigs → balacks → whoziewhats) feeding into a circular interdependency (funkados ⇄ maxabizers via whoziewhats). All constants are extracted as separate variables to make relationships explicit and enable sensitivity analysis.
supportingInfo.title: Cascading Inventory System with Circular Interdependency

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added Frimbulator Inventory System

I added a new stock called frimbulators with an initial value of 20 units, representing the organization's inventory. This stock accumulates through a single inflow called frimbulator_incoming.

The incoming flow is calculated as 2% of the current existing_stock_a count, creating a causal link between the existing stock and the frimbulator inventory growth. I created a separate constant variable frimbulator_growth_rate (0.02) to represent this 2% rate, following the best practice of never embedding numerical constants directly in equations.

This creates a reinforcing feedback loop: as existing_stock_a grows through its own growth_flow, it drives higher frimbulator_incoming, which accumulates in the frimbulators stock. The structure captures the dependency where frimbulator inventory growth is tied to the existing_stock_a level rather than being independent.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Updates: Closing Feedback Loops

Initial Inventory Correction: Changed existing_inventory initial value from 75 to 100 frimbulators as specified.

New Reinforcing Loop (R1): Added enhancement_flow (5% of existing_inventory weekly) as a new inflow to existing_inventory. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop: existing_inventory → enhancement_flow → existing_inventory. As inventory grows, enhancement grows proportionally, accelerating inventory growth. Created enhancement_rate constant (0.05) following best practices.

New Balancing Loop (B1): Added buffer_depletion_flow (3% of existing_buffer weekly) as a new outflow from existing_inventory. This creates a balancing feedback loop connecting the two stocks: existing_buffer → buffer_depletion_flow → existing_inventory. Higher buffer levels increase inventory depletion. Created buffer_depletion_rate constant (0.03).

Constant Extraction: Following XMILE best practices, extracted all numerical rates into separate named variables (consumption_rate, enhancement_rate, buffer_depletion_rate) rather than embedding them directly in flow equations.

Feedback Structure: The model now contains one reinforcing loop (inventory self-enhancement) and two balancing loops (consumption and buffer-driven depletion), creating dynamic tension between growth and depletion forces.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Warehouse Inventory System

I've extended the original two-pool model by adding three new warehouse inventory stocks (marticatenes, refluppers, and exemintes) that create feedback loops connecting back to the original pools.

New Feedback Loops Created:

  1. existing_pool_alpha → marticatenes → refluppers → existing_pool_beta loop: This creates an indirect connection where existing_pool_alpha feeds marticatenes (15% monthly), which then feeds refluppers (20% monthly), which finally depletes based on existing_pool_beta (10% monthly). This closes a feedback path between the two original pools.

  2. existing_pool_beta → refluppers outflow: The existing_pool_beta now has a second outflow (refluppers_outflow) in addition to its original feed_beta inflow, creating a balancing effect on the refluppers inventory.

Structural Changes:

  • Separated all constant values into named variables (feed_alpha_rate, drain_alpha_fraction, etc.) following best practices
  • Added marticatenes stock with fractional inflow from existing_pool_alpha and fractional outflow from itself
  • Added refluppers stock with fractional inflow from marticatenes and fractional outflow driven by existing_pool_beta
  • Added exemintes stock with constant inflow and fractional outflow from itself (independent subsystem)

System Behavior:

The model now exhibits cascading dynamics where changes in existing_pool_alpha propagate through marticatenes to refluppers, which then affects existing_pool_beta through depletion. This creates interdependencies across all warehouse inventories and the original pools.
supportingInfo.title: Warehouse Inventory Feedback Loop Integration

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Three New Inventory Systems

I added three new stock-and-flow structures to represent the inventory systems described:

Pablanksills System (Reinforcing Loop R1): Created a stock starting at 110 units with proportional growth (6% per quarter) and constant depletion (18 units per quarter). This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where higher inventory leads to higher growth, which further increases inventory.

Posistorathers System (Balancing Loop B1): Created a stock starting at 70 units with constant additions (25 units per quarter) and proportional depletion (35% per quarter). The proportional outflow creates a balancing loop that limits growth as the stock increases.

Crypterals System (Mixed Dynamics): Created a stock starting at 95 units with two inflows and one outflow. The constant replenishment (18 units) and proportional enhancement from posistorathers (35% of posistorathers level) add to the stock, while proportional depletion (22% of crypterals) removes from it. This creates a cross-stock linkage where posistorathers directly influences crypterals growth.

Key Structural Pattern: All three systems follow the classic stock-flow archetype with separate variables for all constants, ensuring model transparency and ease of parameter adjustment. The posistorathers-to-crypterals connection represents an inter-system dependency.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Expansion: Adding Four New Stock-Flow Chains

I expanded the original two-stock model by adding four new interconnected stock-flow structures that create multiple feedback loops.

New Stocks Added:

  • ocs (initial: 25 units): Receives inflow from proptimatires (15% weekly) and has outflow driven by existing_chamber_eta (4% weekly)
  • proptimatires (initial: 40 units): Receives inflow from existing_chamber_theta (9% weekly) and has outflow proportional to itself (25% weekly)
  • priaries (initial: 80 units): Receives inflow from proptimatires (10% weekly) and has outflow driven by houtals (5% weekly)
  • houtals (initial: 60 units): Receives constant inflow (7 units weekly) and has outflow proportional to itself (8% weekly)

Feedback Loops Created:

  1. existing_chamber_theta → proptimatires → ocs → existing_chamber_eta: This creates a reinforcing connection where theta influences eta through intermediate stocks

  2. proptimatires → priaries → houtals: A cascade where proptimatires drives priaries growth, which is then constrained by houtals

  3. proptimatires self-regulation: The 25% outflow creates a balancing loop limiting proptimatires accumulation

  4. houtals self-regulation: The 8% outflow creates a balancing loop limiting houtals accumulation

All constants were extracted as separate variables following best practices, and all causal relationships were documented with appropriate positive polarities since all relationships involve variables moving in the same direction.
supportingInfo.title: Four Interconnected Stock Flow Chains with Feedback

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Five Interconnected Inventory Chains

I added five new inventory stocks (whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers) that form a complex chain of interdependencies with the existing model.

New Feedback Loops Created:

  1. Whatajigs → Balacks → Whoziewhats → Funkados → Maxabizers Chain: Each inventory feeds forward to enhance the next inventory at 5% annually, creating a cascading positive reinforcement structure.

  2. Existing Store Lambda → Balacks Feedback: The original existing_store_lambda now influences balacks reduction (3% drain), connecting the original model to the new chain.

  3. Existing Store Mu → Maxabizers Feedback: The original existing_store_mu drains maxabizers at 3%, creating another connection point that closes the loop back to the original model.

  4. Maxabizers → Funkados Negative Loop: Maxabizers reduces funkados, while funkados enhances maxabizers, creating a balancing feedback loop between these two stocks.

Structural Pattern: This represents a "Limits to Growth" archetype where growth-promoting processes (5% enhancements) are constrained by draining processes (3% reductions), with cross-connections to the original lambda and mu stores creating system-wide interdependencies. Each stock has both self-reinforcing growth and external draining mechanisms, preventing unlimited accumulation.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, we start the period with twenty frimbulators. Every day, this inventory gets replenished by 2% growth relative to its current size.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Variables identified from the text

  • Frimbulator Inventory — a stock, because it is an accumulation at the facility that changes only through its flow. Its initial value is the stated starting level.
  • Initial frimbulator inventory — the stated starting level (twenty), abstracted into its own named constant rather than hard-coded inside the stock.
  • Frimbulator Replenishment — a flow (inflow to the stock), because it is the daily rate at which units are added. Marked as one-directional since replenishment can only add units.
  • Fractional replenishment rate — the stated 2% per day, abstracted into a named constant so the equation reads plainly as "inventory times the daily fractional rate."

Causal relationships extracted

  1. Initial inventory → Inventory (+): sets the starting point.
  2. Inventory → Replenishment (+): growth is relative to current size, so the stock drives its own inflow.
  3. Fractional rate → Replenishment (+): a bigger percentage means a bigger daily addition.
  4. Replenishment → Inventory (+): the inflow accumulates into the stock.

Relationships 2 and 4 together form a reinforcing (exponential growth) loop — the classic compounding archetype. Because each day's addition is proportional to the current level, inventory grows exponentially rather than linearly.

Structural checks applied

  • No outflows were invented; the text describes only replenishment.
  • The replenishment flow appears only as an inflow, never simultaneously as an outflow.
  • No numeric constants appear inside equations; both the 20 and the 0.02 are named variables.
  • Time is measured in days and the step is small enough to approximate the daily compounding smoothly.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure identified

  • Frimbulators is the only accumulation, so it is modeled as a stock with an initial value of 100 (initial value only, no integral expression).
  • Growth is an inflow, computed as the stock multiplied by a Fractional Growth Rate. This closes a reinforcing (exponential growth) loop: more frimbulators → more growth → more frimbulators.
  • Depletion is an outflow set equal to a constant Depletion Rate. Because it does not depend on the stock, it is not a balancing feedback loop — it is an exogenous constant drain that only subtracts.

Formulation choices

  • The 5% and the 5 units per week were abstracted into named constants (Fractional Growth Rate, Depletion Rate) rather than hard-coded inside the flow equations.
  • Both flows are marked one-directional, since neither an addition nor a loss can physically run backwards here.
  • Growth and Depletion are separate flows — no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow.

Behavior

Since the initial reinforcing inflow (100 × 0.05 = 5 per week) exactly equals the constant drain of 5 per week, the system starts at an unstable equilibrium. Any upward disturbance sends it into runaway exponential growth; any downward disturbance sends it into accelerating collapse.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, there are initially one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure identified

Two accumulations were found, each with one inflow and one outflow:

  • Whatajigs (initial value 100): grows by a fraction of itself (whatajigs growth) and is drained by a flow proportional to the balacks stock (whatajigs reduction).
  • Balacks (initial value 200): receives a fraction of the whatajigs stock (balacks additions) and loses a fraction of itself (balacks losses).

Rates abstracted into named constants

Every percentage in the description was pulled out of the flow equations into its own named parameter — whatajigs growth rate (5%), whatajigs reduction rate (300%), balacks addition rate (5%), and balacks loss rate (3%) — so no arbitrary numeric constants appear inside equations.

Feedback loops

  • A reinforcing loop: whatajigs → growth → more whatajigs (exponential growth engine).
  • A balancing loop coupling the two stocks: more whatajigs → more balacks additions → more balacks → larger whatajigs reduction → fewer whatajigs. This predator–prey-like coupling, with a very strong 300% reduction coefficient, dominates and drives the whatajigs stock down quickly.
  • A balancing loop within balacks: more balacks → more losses → fewer balacks.

Modeling choices

All four flows are marked one-directional since they represent physical gains and drains that cannot run backwards. The stocks hold only initial values, with all change expressed through their flows. RK4 integration with a small time step is used because the coupled loops can produce oscillatory behavior.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, there are initially fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory is enhanced by exactly ten new marticatenes. Simultaneously, each month the stock gets diminished by 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory gains from 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock suffers depletion of a constant eight refluppers.  Meanwhile, we begin with one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory gets replenished by exactly eight new exemintes. Simultaneously, each month the stock has outgoing 10% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three inventories are represented as stocks, each with one inflow and one outflow, and every stated numeric value is abstracted into its own named parameter rather than hard-coded inside an equation.

Marticatenes — starts at 50, gains a constant 10 per month, and loses 20% of its current level. Because the loss depends on the stock itself, this creates a balancing (goal-seeking) loop that drives the stock toward equilibrium at 50 units (10 ÷ 0.2).

Refluppers — starts at 75, gains 20% of the current marticatene level (the one cross-inventory coupling in the description), and loses a constant 8 per month. Its outflow does not depend on its own level, so there is no balancing loop here; its behavior is driven entirely by the marticatene stock.

Exemintes — starts at 120, gains a constant 8 per month, and loses 10% of its current level. Again a balancing loop, seeking equilibrium at 80 units (8 ÷ 0.1).

Causal relationships captured

  • Each initial-value parameter causes its stock's starting level.
  • Each constant rate parameter causes its respective flow.
  • Each percentage fraction, together with the stock it applies to, causes the corresponding proportional flow.
  • Marticatenes causes reflupper additions (the inter-inventory link).
  • Inflows raise their stocks (positive); outflows lower their stocks (negative).

Modeling choices

  • All flows representing physical additions or removals are marked one-directional so they can never run backwards.
  • Stocks hold only initial values in their equations, with accumulation handled by the flow connections.
  • No conditional logic or embedded constants were used; the two proportional-loss fractions and the 20% conversion fraction are explicit parameters so they can be tested independently.
supportingInfo.title: Three Coupled Inventories With Balancing Loops

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, the baseline inventory shows thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory is enhanced by 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock experiences losses of 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory gains from exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock decreases by 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three accumulations were identified, each with its own inflow and outflow:

  • Povals (initial 35): fed by 30% of the dominitoxings count, drained by 20% of itself per day.
  • Auspongs (initial 90): fed by 20% of the poval count, drained by a constant twelve per day.
  • Dominitoxings (initial 45): fed by a constant twelve per day, drained by 30% of itself per day.

Modeling choices

  • Each inventory is a stock because it accumulates over time and can only change through its flows; all rates of change are flows.
  • Every numeric coefficient (0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 12, 12, 0.3) was pulled out into a clearly named constant so no arbitrary numbers are buried inside equations.
  • The proportional outflows on povals and dominitoxings form balancing (goal-seeking) loops — the bigger the stock, the faster it drains — so each of those inventories settles toward an equilibrium. The dominitoxings stock is self-contained and converges to forty units, which then drives povals, which in turn drives auspongs, forming a one-way causal chain.
  • The auspong outflow is a fixed drain rather than proportional, so it exerts no balancing feedback; auspongs are governed entirely by the upstream chain.
  • All flows are marked one-directional since additions and losses cannot run backwards.
supportingInfo.title: Three Chained Inventories With Proportional Balancing Flows

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we have on hand one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we start the period with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory receives new additions of exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock gets diminished by 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three accumulations were identified, each with its own explicit flows:

  • Pablanksills (starts at 110): a proportional growth inflow (6% of the current stock — a reinforcing loop) and a fixed depletion outflow of 18 per quarter. Because growth compounds while the loss is constant, this stock accelerates upward once growth exceeds 18 units.
  • Posistorathers (starts at 70): a constant additions inflow of 25 per quarter and a proportional transfer outflow of 35% of the stock (a balancing loop that drives the stock toward an equilibrium near 71).
  • Crypterals (starts at 95): a constant additions inflow of 18 per quarter, plus the transfer arriving from posistorathers, and a proportional loss outflow of 22% of the stock (another balancing loop).

Key modeling choices

  • The 35% drain on posistorathers and the 35%-of-posistorathers enhancement of crypterals are the same physical movement, so a single flow serves as the outflow of one stock and the inflow of the other. This makes the cross-stock cause-and-effect link explicit rather than duplicating it.
  • All rates and constants (6%, 18, 25, 35%, 18, 22%) were pulled out of the flow equations into clearly named constant variables, so no arbitrary numbers appear inside equations.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since none of these processes can physically run backwards.
  • Stocks hold only initial values; no sums were represented as stocks, and no delay functions were used.
supportingInfo.title: Three Linked Stocks With Proportional And Constant Flows

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, our records indicate twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory gains from exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock gets diminished by 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory gains from exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four accumulations were identified, each with exactly one inflow and one outflow:

  • Ocs (starts at 25): grows by a fraction of the proptimatires level, drains at a fixed three per week.
  • Proptimatires (starts at 40): grows by a fixed five per week, drains by a fraction of its own level — a self-balancing (goal-seeking) structure that settles where arrivals equal losses.
  • Priaries (starts at 80): grows by a fraction of the proptimatires level, drains by a fraction of the houtals level. Its flows are driven entirely by other stocks, so it has no internal feedback.
  • Houtals (starts at 60): grows by a fixed seven per week, drains by a fraction of its own level — again a self-balancing structure.

Causal links captured

Every percentage and constant in the description was abstracted into its own named parameter (growth fractions, decay fractions, fixed arrival and loss rates) so no bare numbers appear inside flow equations. This makes each cause explicit: parameters cause flows, flows cause stock changes, and cross-stock drivers are shown as separate causal links.

Cross-stock (non-feedback) drivers:

  • Proptimatires → ocs inflow
  • Proptimatires → priaries inflow
  • Houtals → priaries outflow

Self-referencing (balancing loop) drivers:

  • Proptimatires → its own outflow → Proptimatires (negative loop)
  • Houtals → its own outflow → Houtals (negative loop)

Modeling choices

  • All four accumulations are true stocks (not sums), since each changes only through its flows.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since each represents a physical addition or removal that cannot reverse.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • Weekly time unit with a quarter-week time step for numerical accuracy of the proportional drains.
supportingInfo.title: Four Interlinked Weekly Stock Flow Structures

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, there are initially one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, there are initially sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory receives new additions of 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four accumulations were identified, each with its own explicit initial value and its own inflow/outflow pair:

  • Outrances (starts at 150): one constant inflow (20 per hour) and two separate proportional outflows — a 40% per hour loss and a 10% per hour depletion. These were kept as distinct flows because the text describes two independent draining processes; each forms its own balancing loop with the stock.
  • Illigents (starts at 30): inflow driven by 40% of the outrances stock, outflow a constant 5 per hour.
  • Yelbs (starts at 65): inflow driven by 10% of the outrances stock, outflow driven by 12% of the trazes stock — note this drain does not depend on yelbs themselves, so yelbs have no internal balancing loop.
  • Trazes (starts at 85): constant inflow of 15 per hour and a 18% per hour proportional outflow (its own balancing loop).

Causal couplings across stocks

Outrances act as a driver for both illigents and yelbs, and trazes act as a driver for the yelb drain. These cross-stock links are one-directional, so the system is a cascade: outrances and trazes behave as independent first-order systems that goal-seek toward equilibrium, and illigents and yelbs are driven by them.

Modeling conventions applied

  • Every numeric rate and percentage was abstracted into a clearly named constant (arrival rates, loss fractions, depletion fraction, conversion fractions) rather than embedded in equations.
  • Stock equations contain only initial values; accumulation is expressed through inflow/outflow assignment.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • All physical flows (arrivals, losses, depletion) are marked one-directional so they can never run backwards.
  • A time step of 0.25 hour is used so the proportional flows (up to 50% per hour on outrances) integrate accurately.
supportingInfo.title: Four Coupled Stocks With Explicit Causal Links

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Five accumulations were identified — whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers — each with exactly one inflow and one outflow, so every stock changes only through its flows.

Chain of causation (a cascading pipeline):

  • Whatajigs feed themselves (a reinforcing self-growth loop at five percent) and lose a fixed three units per year, which is a constant drain rather than a proportional one.
  • Whatajigs drive additions to balacks; balacks drive additions to whoziewhats; whoziewhats drive additions to funkados; funkados drive additions to maxabizers.
  • Balacks and whoziewhats each drain proportionally to themselves (balancing loops that pull them toward equilibrium).
  • Funkados and maxabizers are cross-coupled at the tail: funkados drain in proportion to maxabizers, while maxabizers drain in proportion to whoziewhats. This creates an additional cross-link back from the whoziewhat level into the maxabizer level.

Formulation choices

  • No hard-coded numbers appear in flow equations. The repeated five percent and three percent rates were abstracted into named constants (growth fraction and decline fraction), and the fixed whatajig loss was abstracted into its own named constant.
  • Stock equations carry only initial values (100, 200, 200, 12, 88), never integration expressions.
  • All ten flows are marked one-directional, since each represents a strictly additive or strictly subtractive annual process; this prevents any outflow from reversing direction if a driving stock were to go negative.
  • No conditional logic or averaging functions were needed, and no simple sums were mistakenly represented as stocks.
supportingInfo.title: Cascading Five Stock Chain With Cross Coupling

testParams.name: Epidemic spread model with key epidemiological processes
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is a classic SEIR compartmental structure with four population stocks — susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered — plus a cumulative deceased stock. People move through them only via flows, which is the correct use of stocks.

Flows

  • infecting: susceptible → exposed, driven by contacts times infectivity.
  • incubating: exposed → infectious after the incubation delay.
  • recovering: infectious → recovered (survivor share of cases).
  • dying: infectious → deceased (fatal share of cases).
  • vaccination: susceptible → recovered directly, capturing the public health intervention.
  • quarantining: exposed → removed, capturing contact tracing that pulls latent cases out before they become infectious.

All of these are one-directional processes, so each is constrained to be non-negative.

Key feedback loops

  • Reinforcing contagion loop: more infectious → more contacts → more infecting → more exposed → more infectious. This produces the exponential take-off.
  • Balancing depletion loop: more infecting → fewer susceptible → fewer susceptible-infectious contacts → less infecting. This is what eventually turns the epidemic curve over (herd immunity), and it is why contacts is scaled by the susceptible share of total population.
  • Balancing recovery loop: more infectious → more recovering/dying → fewer infectious.

Policy levers (kept as separate named parameters, no hidden constants)

  • social distancing effect multiplies normal contact rate to give the effective contact rate; set below 1 to represent distancing.
  • vaccination rate shifts susceptibles directly to immune, weakening the contagion loop.
  • quarantine effectiveness drains the exposed pool before it can feed the infectious pool.

reproduction number (R0 = contact rate × infectivity × illness duration) is included as a diagnostic auxiliary so you can see immediately how each intervention pushes transmission above or below the epidemic threshold of one.

total population is a simple algebraic sum, so it is modelled as an auxiliary rather than a stock. The daily time step and 200-day horizon match the epidemiological timescale described.
supportingInfo.title: SEIR Model With Vaccination And Quarantine Levers

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model represents the crisis as three interacting resource systems, all on a weekly clock over one year.

Patient flow (constraint chain). An exogenous crisis wave (new cases) fills a queue of untreated patients. Admissions move people into the patients stock, but only up to capacity headroom, which is the tighter of empty available beds and the unused portion of staff capacity. People who wait too long leave through unmet care exits — the "turned away" pathway. Discharges occur via recoveries, driven by an average length of stay that stretches when staff are overloaded.

Bed resources. Available beds are consumed by admissions and released by recoveries, so beds recirculate. Bed opening is a surge program that closes the gap between desired total beds and total beds, but only after a multi-week bed surge delay.

Workforce. Healthcare workers are drained by staff turnover and worker sickness (into a sick workers stock, from which they return) and replenished by hiring, which also lags by weeks. Workload is patients per worker relative to a normal caseload, and burnout is a slowly-adjusting exhaustion index driven by workload.

Key feedback loops

  • Burnout death spiral (reinforcing): high workload → burnout → turnover → fewer workers → higher workload. Burnout also cuts productivity, shrinking staff capacity and raising workload again.
  • Contagion drain (reinforcing): high workload → more staff exposure and illness → fewer available workers → higher workload.
  • Care-quality erosion (reinforcing): overload → longer length of stay → beds stay occupied → queue grows → more pressure.
  • Balancing loops: admissions are capped by capacity (self-limiting), and both hiring and bed surge are gap-closing loops — but their long delays mean relief typically arrives after the peak, the classic delayed-correction pattern that produces overshoot and lingering staff losses.

Formulation choices

  • Total beds is a simple sum of occupied and empty beds, so it is an auxiliary, not a stock.
  • All non-time graphical effects (length of stay multiplier, indicated burnout, turnover multiplier from burnout, productivity multiplier, exposure multiplier) pass through the point (1, 1) so that normal conditions produce normal behavior and deviations read in both directions.
  • Burnout adjustment is the only bidirectional flow, since exhaustion can both build and recede; every other flow is one-directional.
  • No hard-coded numbers appear inside equations — delays, fractions, and standards are all named constants.
  • Workload uses safe division to remain defined if the workforce collapses toward zero.
supportingInfo.title: Capacity-constrained hospital with burnout-driven workforce erosion

variables.name: untreated patients
variables.documentation: The queue of people who need hospital care but have not yet been admitted. It accumulates when new cases arrive faster than the hospital can admit them, representing the delays and turn-aways described in the background.

variables.name: new cases
variables.documentation: Exogenous arrival of people needing care, shaped as a health-crisis wave over the year. This is the external driver that stresses the system; it is a time-based graphical function so no normalization through (1,1) is required.

variables.name: admissions
variables.documentation: Patients moved from the waiting queue into hospital care. Admissions are the smaller of the people waiting and the free capacity (beds and staff), spread over the admission processing time. This is the core capacity constraint of the system.

variables.name: admission time
variables.documentation: Average time it takes to process and place an admission, which limits how fast free capacity can be filled.

variables.name: unmet care exits
variables.documentation: People who leave the queue without being treated because they waited too long, they were turned away, or their condition resolved or worsened outside the hospital.

variables.name: waiting tolerance time
variables.documentation: Average time a person will remain in the queue before leaving without hospital treatment.

variables.name: patients
variables.documentation: Patients currently occupying a bed and being cared for. It rises with admissions and falls as patients recover and are discharged.

variables.name: recoveries
variables.documentation: Discharge of treated patients, modeled as a first-order outflow set by the average length of stay. Slower care under strain lengthens stay and slows this flow.

variables.name: average length of stay
variables.documentation: Effective time a patient occupies a bed. It equals the normal stay stretched by a multiplier that grows when staff are overloaded and care quality degrades.

variables.name: base length of stay
variables.documentation: Normal hospital stay when the system is operating at normal workload.

variables.name: length of stay multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of workload on how long patients stay. Normalized so that normal workload (1) gives a multiplier of 1; overloaded staff give less attention per patient, so recovery takes longer.

variables.name: available beds
variables.documentation: Staffed beds that are currently empty and ready for a patient. Each admission consumes one, each discharge frees one, and surge programs add new ones.

variables.name: total beds
variables.documentation: All beds in the hospital, occupied plus empty. Used to judge whether more surge capacity is needed. This is a simple sum, so it is an auxiliary rather than a stock.

variables.name: desired total beds
variables.documentation: Bed count management would like to have, covering current patients and the waiting queue while keeping a planned occupancy buffer.

variables.name: target occupancy
variables.documentation: Fraction of beds the hospital aims to have filled, leaving headroom for new arrivals.

variables.name: bed opening
variables.documentation: Rate at which surge beds are brought online to close the gap between desired and existing beds. The surge delay captures the time needed to physically open and equip beds.

variables.name: bed surge delay
variables.documentation: Time required to open additional beds, creating the lag between recognizing a shortage and relieving it.

variables.name: capacity headroom
variables.documentation: How many more patients can actually be taken in right now. It is the tighter of the two constraints: empty beds and the remaining patient load the current workforce can handle.

variables.name: staff capacity
variables.documentation: Number of patients the present workforce can care for, equal to headcount times the normal caseload per worker, adjusted for how burnout erodes productivity.

variables.name: patients per worker normal
variables.documentation: Caseload one healthcare worker can handle at normal, sustainable effort.

variables.name: productivity multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of burnout on how much work each staff member can do. Normalized so normal burnout (1) yields normal productivity (1); exhausted staff deliver less care.

variables.name: healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Healthy staff available to treat patients. This is the key resource: it is depleted by quitting and by workers falling ill, and replenished by hiring and by recovered workers returning.

variables.name: desired healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Workforce needed to cover current patients and the waiting queue at the normal caseload per worker.

variables.name: hiring
variables.documentation: Recruitment of temporary and permanent staff to close the workforce gap. The hiring delay represents recruiting, credentialing and onboarding time.

variables.name: hiring delay
variables.documentation: Average time to bring an additional worker on board, the lag that makes surge staffing slow relative to a crisis wave.

variables.name: staff turnover
variables.documentation: Workers permanently leaving the hospital. Turnover rises sharply as burnout accumulates, which is the reinforcing loop that can hollow out capacity.

variables.name: normal turnover fraction
variables.documentation: Baseline weekly fraction of staff who quit under normal working conditions.

variables.name: turnover multiplier from burnout
variables.documentation: Effect of burnout on quit rates. Normalized so normal burnout (1) gives normal turnover (1); severe burnout multiplies departures several-fold.

variables.name: worker sickness
variables.documentation: Staff who fall ill and temporarily leave the workforce. Illness rises with exposure and strain, so treating more patients per worker directly erodes available capacity.

variables.name: baseline sickness fraction
variables.documentation: Weekly fraction of staff falling ill under normal workload and exposure.

variables.name: exposure multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of workload on staff infection risk. Normalized so normal workload (1) gives normal sickness (1); heavier caseloads mean more contact, fatigue and infection.

variables.name: sick workers
variables.documentation: Staff currently off work because they are ill. They are temporarily unavailable but return after recovering.

variables.name: worker return
variables.documentation: Recovered staff coming back to duty, restoring part of the lost capacity.

variables.name: worker illness duration
variables.documentation: Average time a sick worker is away from work.

variables.name: workload
variables.documentation: Ratio of patients being cared for to what the current healthy workforce can normally handle. A value of 1 is normal pressure; above 1 the staff are stretched. Safe division protects against a zero workforce.

variables.name: burnout
variables.documentation: Accumulated exhaustion of the workforce, indexed so 1 is the normal level. It builds gradually when workload is high and recedes only slowly when pressure eases, which is why it drives turnover long after a peak.

variables.name: burnout adjustment
variables.documentation: Gradual movement of burnout toward the level implied by current workload. It is bidirectional because burnout can build up or recover depending on conditions.

variables.name: indicated burnout
variables.documentation: Burnout level that current workload would eventually produce. Normalized so normal workload (1) sustains normal burnout (1); pressure above normal drives burnout up more than proportionally.

variables.name: burnout adjustment time
variables.documentation: Time it takes for staff exhaustion to catch up with current working conditions, creating persistence in burnout.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two accumulations drive the behavior:

  • Road capacity grows through construction and shrinks through depreciation. Construction is triggered by congestion itself, so it is a problem-driven investment policy.
  • Travelers accumulates through a net adjustment flow that closes the gap between actual traffic and the traffic people would choose given current travel times. This flow is deliberately slow (a two-year adjustment time) because switching routes, departure times, modes, or deciding to make a trip at all takes time — this delay is what makes the initial improvement look like a success before it erodes.

The two feedback loops

  1. Intended balancing loop (build your way out): congestion → pressure to build → road capacity → congestion falls.
  2. Induced-demand balancing loop (the fix that fails): more capacity → lower congestion → shorter travel time → driving becomes more attractive → latent trips convert into real trips → travelers rise → congestion returns.

Because the second loop draws on a large pool of potential travel demand (trips currently suppressed or taken by other routes, times and modes), congestion returns toward its original level after each expansion. This is the classic fixes that fail archetype, and because construction responds to the very congestion it recreates, the system also shows addiction to the fix: capacity keeps growing while congestion does not improve.

Nonlinearities

  • The congestion delay multiplier is the speed–flow curve: delay barely moves at low volumes and explodes near saturation. This is why small volume increases can wipe out large capacity gains.
  • The effect of travel time on demand captures behavioral elasticity: faster trips induce extra travel, slower trips suppress it.
  • Both graphical functions are normalized to pass through (1, 1), so normal conditions produce normal behavior and the curves express deviations in both directions.

Externalities

Pollution rises both with the number of trips and with congestion (stop-and-go driving pollutes more per trip), and feeds a quality-of-life index. It is modeled as an outcome indicator rather than a driver, matching the description in which externalities affect wellbeing but do not currently restrain traffic growth.

Formulation notes

  • Congestion, travel time, desired travelers and pollution are auxiliaries, not stocks — they are algebraic consequences, not accumulations.
  • The traveler adjustment flow is bidirectional (drivers can leave as conditions worsen); construction and depreciation are one-directional.
  • All numeric parameters are named variables rather than embedded constants.

variables.name: initial road capacity
variables.documentation: Starting size of the road network.

variables.name: road construction
variables.documentation: Rate at which new lane capacity is added. Planners expand the network in proportion to its current size, accelerating when congestion is above normal. Construction can never be negative.

variables.name: effect of congestion on construction

variables.name: road depreciation
variables.documentation: Loss of effective capacity as pavement and structures wear out over their service life.
variables.units: vehicle trips per hour per year

variables.name: road lifetime
variables.documentation: Average service life of road infrastructure before it must be replaced.

variables.name: travelers
variables.documentation: The stock of drivers actually using the road network per hour. It accumulates gradually because changing route, departure time, mode or whether to travel at all takes time.

variables.name: initial travelers
variables.documentation: Starting traffic volume on the network.

variables.name: traveler adjustment
variables.documentation: Net rate at which drivers enter or leave the road network as actual usage moves toward the level people want given current travel times. It is bidirectional because worsening conditions push travelers back out of the system.
variables.units: vehicle trips per hour per year

variables.name: travel behavior adjustment time
variables.documentation: Average number of years it takes for travel choices, and eventually land use and car ownership, to respond fully to a change in travel time.

variables.name: desired travelers
variables.documentation: The traffic volume people would choose if they could adjust instantly, equal to the latent pool of potential trips scaled by how attractive driving currently is.

variables.name: potential travel demand
variables.documentation: The full pool of latent trips available from other routes, other times of day, other modes and suppressed trips at normal travel time.

variables.name: effect of travel time on demand
variables.documentation: Attractiveness of driving as a function of travel time relative to normal. Normalized so normal travel time (input 1) gives normal demand (output 1); faster trips induce extra demand, slower trips suppress it.

variables.name: congestion
variables.documentation: The classic volume to capacity ratio: how much traffic is present relative to how much the roads can carry.

variables.name: normal congestion
variables.documentation: Reference volume to capacity ratio considered acceptable service, used to normalize congestion effects.

variables.name: relative congestion
variables.documentation: Congestion expressed as a multiple of the normal acceptable level, so that a value of one means normal conditions.

variables.name: travel time
variables.documentation: Average door to door trip time, equal to the normal trip time stretched by congestion delay.

variables.name: normal travel time
variables.documentation: Trip time experienced when congestion is at its normal reference level.

variables.name: congestion delay multiplier
variables.documentation: Nonlinear speed flow relationship: travel time rises slowly at low volumes and explodes as the network saturates. Normalized so normal relative congestion (input 1) gives normal travel time (output 1).

variables.name: relative travel time
variables.documentation: Travel time expressed as a multiple of the normal trip time; the signal drivers respond to when deciding whether to drive.

variables.name: pollution
variables.documentation: Air pollution and noise generated by traffic. It rises with the number of vehicle trips and rises further when trips are slower, because stop and go driving emits more per trip.

variables.name: emissions per vehicle trip
variables.documentation: Pollution and noise produced by one vehicle trip under free flowing conditions.

variables.name: reference pollution
variables.documentation: Pollution level regarded as normal, used to normalize the quality of life effect.

variables.name: effect of pollution on quality of life
variables.documentation: How pollution and noise degrade livability. Normalized so normal pollution (input 1) gives normal quality of life (output 1).

variables.name: reference quality of life
variables.documentation: Quality of life index at normal pollution levels.

variables.name: quality of life
variables.documentation: Livability index that captures the negative externalities of traffic. It is an outcome indicator rather than a driver of behavior in this model.

testParams.name: Add a single stock with one flow
testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
At the facility, the baseline inventory shows twenty frimbulators. Every day, this inventory benefits from 2% of the current existing_stock_a count.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

  • frimbulator_inventory (stock, starts at the stated baseline of twenty) — the facility's accumulation of frimbulators.
  • baseline_frimbulator_inventory — the stated value of twenty, kept as a named parameter rather than a bare number inside the stock's initial value.
  • frimbulator_accumulation (inflow) — the daily addition, computed as the two percent share of the current existing_stock_a count. It is one-directional since frimbulators can only be added by this process.
  • frimbulator_gain_fraction — the two percent, named explicitly.

Corrections to the prior structure

  • Hard-coded numbers were pulled out of the flow equations into named parameters: growth_fraction (was 0.1 inside growth_flow), drain_fraction (was 0.05 inside drain_flow), and input_rate (was 5 inside input_flow). The flow equations now reference these names.
  • All flows were marked one-directional, since growth, input, and drain each move material in a single direction.
  • Missing causal links were added so every equation term appears as a relationship, including the stock-to-flow links that complete the reinforcing loop around existing_stock_a and the balancing loop around existing_stock_b.

On feedback

The new inventory sits downstream of existing_stock_a: it is driven by that stock but the description gives no evidence that frimbulators feed anything back. Because the source is described as a benefit rather than a transfer, existing_stock_a is not depleted by it. The inventory therefore inherits the reinforcing growth already present in existing_stock_a — inventory rises at an accelerating pace — rather than forming a loop of its own. Adding a return link would require evidence the text does not supply.

testParams.name: Add a single stock with two flows
testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
In my business, there are initially one hundred frimbulators. Every week, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current existing_inventory count. Simultaneously, each week the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever existing_buffer are currently available.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Additions

  • frimbulators (stock, initial 100): the new accumulation you described.
  • frimbulator_acquisition (inflow) = existing_inventory × frimbulator_growth_fraction (0.05): the weekly five percent gain driven by current inventory.
  • frimbulator_depletion (outflow) = existing_buffer × frimbulator_depletion_fraction (0.03): the weekly three percent drawdown driven by the available buffer.
  • Both flows are one-directional (they cannot run backwards).

Closing the feedback loop

As given, frimbulators were a pure "sink" — inventory and buffer drove them, but nothing came back. Since frimbulators are the business's productive assets, they were connected back to supply:

  • reference_frimbulators and frimbulator_adequacy express the fleet relative to normal (equals 1 at start).
  • effect_of_frimbulators_on_supply is a graphical multiplier passing through (1, 1), rising with diminishing returns and collapsing to zero if the fleet is wiped out.
  • supply_flow is now base_supply_rate × that multiplier.

This creates a reinforcing loop (inventory → frimbulator acquisition → frimbulators → supply capability → inventory) that is held in check by two balancing loops: consumption draining inventory, and the ever-growing buffer depleting frimbulators — a classic "limits to growth" structure.

Formulation cleanups

  • consumption_flow had the bare number 0.02 embedded; it now references the named constant consumption_fraction.
  • replenish_flow had the bare number 3; it now references buffer_replenish_rate.
  • base_supply_rate was split out of supply_flow so the constant is named rather than hard-coded.
  • All stocks keep initial values only (no INTEG), and no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
supportingInfo.title: Frimbulator Stock Added With Supply Feedback Loop
