testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
Throughout the process, there are initially one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current base_stock_x count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever base_stock_y are currently available.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added inventories

  • whatajigs (stock, starts at 100) with inflow whatajig_growth and outflow whatajig_loss.
  • balacks (stock, starts at 200) with inflow balack_growth and outflow balack_loss.

Closed feedback loop The description contains a complete circuit: whatajigs create balacks (5 percent of whatajigs per year) and balacks destroy whatajigs (300 percent of balacks per year). Adding both flows closes a balancing loop between the two inventories: more whatajigs → more balacks → greater whatajig losses → fewer whatajigs. Because the destruction gain is very strong relative to the creation gain, this loop behaves like a fast-acting corrective loop and can oscillate, so the run settings use RK4 integration.

Cross links from the original structure

  • base_stock_x now drives whatajig_growth (5 percent of X per year).
  • base_stock_y now drives balack_loss (3 percent of Y per year). These are open (non-feedback) drivers; nothing in the text supports whatajigs or balacks feeding back into X or Y, so no such links were invented.

Formulation corrections to the existing model

  • output_x: the hard-coded 0.03 was replaced by the named constant output_x_fraction.
  • input_y: the hard-coded 0.1 was replaced by the named constant input_y_fraction.
  • All new rate parameters were likewise abstracted into named constants (whatajig_growth_fraction, whatajig_loss_fraction, balack_growth_fraction, balack_loss_fraction).
  • All four new flows are one-directional (uniflow) since creation and destruction processes cannot run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock, and no existing variable names were changed.

Please add the following to my model...
During operations, there are initially fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory benefits from 15% of the current existing_pool_alpha count. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory receives new additions of 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock has outgoing 10% of whatever existing_pool_beta are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory increases due to exactly eight new exemintes. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 10% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added three new accumulations and their flows

  • marticatenes (starts at 50): gains fifteen percent of the alpha pool each month and loses twenty percent of itself each month. The self drain forms a balancing loop that pulls the inventory toward the level supported by the alpha pool.
  • refluppers (starts at 75): gains twenty percent of the marticatenes count each month and loses ten percent of the beta pool each month. This links the two previously separate chains: the alpha side feeds refluppers through marticatenes, while the beta side (which grows in a reinforcing loop) drives an escalating outflow — a classic drifting drain that will eventually overwhelm the inflow.
  • exemintes (starts at 120): gains a constant eight per month and loses ten percent of itself per month. The proportional drain closes a balancing loop that drives the stock toward its goal level of eighty.

Loop closure

Each new stock whose drain depends on its own level now has an explicit balancing feedback loop drawn back from the outflow to the stock. The two original loops (the balancing drain on the alpha pool and the reinforcing growth of the beta pool) are also now made explicit in the causal structure.

Formulation cleanups

  • Hard coded fractional rates were abstracted into named constants: alpha_drain_fraction, beta_feed_fraction, marticatenes_gain_fraction, marticatenes_loss_fraction, refluppers_gain_fraction, refluppers_loss_fraction, exemintes_loss_fraction, and exemintes_addition_rate. No existing variable names were changed.
  • All new flows are marked one directional since they represent physical arrivals and departures that cannot run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

In the system, there are initially thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory gets replenished by 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory increases due to 20% of the current povals count. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
New structure added

  • dominitoxings (stock, starts at 45) is filled by dominitoxing_inflow, which is 8% of the existing delta depot, and emptied by dominitoxing_outflow, which is 30% of its own level. The self-draining outflow forms a balancing loop that gives this stock a goal-seeking approach toward the level set by its inflow.
  • povals (stock, starts at 35) is filled by poval_inflow, 30% of the current dominitoxings, and emptied by poval_outflow, 20% of its own level — another balancing (stock-adjustment) loop.
  • auspongs (stock, starts at 90) is filled by auspong_inflow, 20% of the current povals, and emptied by a constant twelve per day. Because the drain is constant and not proportional to the stock, there is no balancing loop on this stock; it simply integrates the net difference and can trend up or down indefinitely.

Chain of causality linking old and new structure: the delta depot's reinforcing growth loop (delta stock → input → delta stock) drives dominitoxings, which drives povals, which drives auspongs. The reinforcing growth in the delta depot therefore eventually propagates exponential growth down the whole cascade.

Formulation cleanups (no variable renamed)

  • Hard-coded numbers inside flow equations were abstracted into named constants: gamma_supply_rate, gamma_output_fraction, delta_input_fraction, delta_drain_rate, plus new poval_inflow_fraction, poval_loss_fraction, auspong_inflow_fraction, auspong_drain_rate, dominitoxing_inflow_fraction, dominitoxing_loss_fraction. Behavior is unchanged; the parameters are now visible and testable.
  • All flows were marked one-directional, since each represents a physical addition or removal that cannot legitimately reverse.
  • Each new stock is a true accumulation changed only by its flows; no aggregation was mis-typed as a stock, and no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

Please add the following to my model...
During operations, the baseline inventory shows one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock is reduced through a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock is reduced through 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from exactly eighteen new crypterals. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Additions to the existing model

  • Pablanksills chain: Added the stock pablanksills (starting at the baseline of 110) with a proportional inflow pablanksills_growth (6% of the current stock) and a constant outflow pablanksills_decline (18 per quarter). The growth flow depends on the stock it fills, which closes a reinforcing (growth) loop; the constant drain is an unlinked leak, so it cannot balance that loop.

  • Posistorathers chain: Added the stock posistorathers (starting at 70) with the constant inflow posistorathers_arrival (25 per quarter) and the proportional outflow posistorathers_transfer (35% of current stock). Because the outflow is driven by the stock level, this closes a balancing loop that drives the stock toward equilibrium.

  • Crypterals chain and the coupling: Added the stock crypterals (starting at 95) with the constant inflow crypterals_arrival (18 per quarter) and the proportional outflow crypterals_depletion (22% of current stock), which closes a second balancing loop. The described "35% of the current posistorathers" entering crypterals is exactly the posistorathers outflow, so it is modeled as one conserved transfer flow that is simultaneously an outflow of posistorathers and an inflow to crypterals, creating a clear material chain from posistorathers to crypterals.

  • Constants abstracted: Every stated percentage and fixed amount was pulled out into its own named parameter (pablanksills_growth_fraction, pablanksills_decline_rate, posistorathers_arrival_rate, posistorathers_transfer_fraction, crypterals_arrival_rate, crypterals_depletion_fraction) and each initial level into a named baseline variable, so no arbitrary numbers appear inside a flow equation.

  • Existing structure preserved: No previously supplied variable was renamed or restructured; the epsilon tank's reinforcing refill loop and the zeta tank's constant pump remain as given, and their flow-to-stock links were made explicit in the relationship list.

testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
During operations, there are initially twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory grows through incoming 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 4% of whatever existing_chamber_eta are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory benefits from 9% of the current existing_chamber_theta count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 8% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

Four new inventories (stocks), each with its own inflow and outflow:

  • ocs (starts at 25): gains 15% of the proptimatires count each week and loses an amount equal to 4% of chamber eta's contents. This makes the ocs inventory a downstream consequence of both the proptimatires chain and the eta chamber.
  • proptimatires (starts at 40): gains 9% of chamber theta's contents each week and loses 25% of itself. Because the loss depends on its own level, this closes a balancing loop that pulls the inventory toward an equilibrium set by the theta feed.
  • priaries (starts at 80): gains 10% of the proptimatires count and is reduced by 5% of the current houtals count.
  • houtals (starts at 60): gains a fixed seven per week and loses 8% of itself, another balancing loop driving it toward a steady state of about 87.5.

Feedback loops now present

  • The original reinforcing loop on chamber eta (its level drives its own injection) is preserved and now propagates outward: a rising eta level increases ocs losses.
  • Two new balancing (self-correcting) loops were closed, on proptimatires and on houtals, since each stock's outflow is proportional to the stock itself.
  • A cascade chain now connects chamber theta → proptimatires → ocs and priaries, and houtals → priaries, so upstream chambers propagate through the whole operation.

Formulation corrections applied

  • Hard-coded constants abstracted. Every embedded number in a rate expression was moved into a clearly named variable: injection_eta_fraction (0.07), extraction_eta_rate (8), feed_theta_rate (6), plus new fractions for each new flow (ocs_inflow_fraction, ocs_depletion_fraction, proptimatires_inflow_fraction, proptimatires_depletion_fraction, priaries_inflow_fraction, priaries_depletion_fraction, houtals_replenishment_rate, houtals_depletion_fraction). Only stock initial values remain as plain numbers, which is correct.
  • Uniflow settings. All physical additions and depletions were marked one-directional so no inventory can be drained by a negative flow or filled by a negative depletion.
  • Missing relationships supplied. Every flow-to-stock link (inflow positive, outflow negative) and every parameter-to-flow link is now explicitly represented, so no equation references a variable that lacks a documented causal link.
  • Complete specification added. Simulation now runs 0–52 weeks with a quarter-week step using Euler integration, matching the weekly language of the description.

testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
During operations, we begin with one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory receives new additions of exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 18% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added chain of four coupled stocks

  • Outrances (starts at 150) gains a constant 20 per hour and drains through two proportional streams.
  • The described 40% hourly loss of outrances is numerically identical to the hourly replenishment of illigents, so it is represented as one connecting flow (outrance_to_illigent) that leaves outrances and enters illigents. The same logic applies to the 10% loss, represented by outrance_to_yelb feeding yelbs. This makes the causal transfer explicit rather than two disconnected coincidences.
  • Illigents (starts at 30) receives that transfer and loses a constant 5 per hour.
  • Yelbs (starts at 65) receives the 10% transfer and loses 12% of the traze stock each hour, which couples trazes to yelbs.
  • Trazes (starts at 85) gains a constant 15 per hour and loses 18% of itself.

Feedback loops closed

  • Outrances → 40% transfer → reduces outrances (balancing).
  • Outrances → 10% transfer → reduces outrances (balancing).
  • Trazes → traze loss → reduces trazes (balancing).
  • Vessel iota → charging → raises vessel iota (reinforcing, already present) against its constant discharge.

Formulation cleanups to the prior model

  • Hard-coded numbers were pulled out of flow equations into named parameters: iota_charging_fraction (0.09) for charging_iota, iota_discharge_rate (11) for discharge_iota, and kappa_loading_rate (5) for loading_kappa. Behavior is unchanged; the structure is now self-documenting.
  • All new constants (outrance_arrival_rate, illigent_conversion_fraction, yelb_conversion_fraction, illigent_departure_rate, yelb_loss_fraction, traze_arrival_rate, traze_loss_fraction) are separate auxiliaries for the same reason.
  • Every flow representing a one-directional physical process is marked as non-negative so stocks cannot be filled by a reversed loss stream.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock; the two transfer flows are outflows of outrances and inflows of the receiving stocks only.

Please add the following to my model...
At the warehouse, we start the period with one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-eight maxabizers. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

Five new inventory stocks were chained onto the existing lambda and mu stores, each with its own inflow and outflow:

  • whatajigs (starts at 100): grows by a fraction of itself and loses a fixed quantity each year.
  • balacks (starts at 200): fed by a share of whatajigs, drained by a share of the existing lambda store.
  • whoziewhats (starts at 200): fed by a share of balacks, drained by a share of itself.
  • funkados (starts at 12): fed by a share of whoziewhats, drained by a share of maxabizers.
  • maxabizers (starts at 88): fed by a share of funkados, drained by a share of the existing mu store.

Feedback structure

  • Reinforcing loop (whatajigs): the stock drives its own proportional growth, mirroring the existing reinforcing loop on the lambda store — exponential growth unless the fixed removal dominates.
  • Balancing loop (whoziewhats): the stock drives its own proportional depletion, so it seeks an equilibrium set by the balacks inflow.
  • Balancing loop (funkados ↔ maxabizers): funkados feed maxabizers, and maxabizers in turn drain funkados. This two-variable loop was closed exactly as described and acts as a self-limiting exchange between the pair.
  • Cross-links to the original model: the lambda store now drains balacks and the mu store drains maxabizers, so the pre-existing dynamics propagate into the new chain.

Formulation choices

  • Every percentage and fixed quantity was pulled out into a named fraction or rate variable rather than being buried inside an equation, so each assumption is visible and adjustable.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since growth, replenishment, removal and depletion of physical inventory cannot run backwards.
  • total_warehouse_inventory was added as an auxiliary (not a stock), because a sum across stocks is an algebraic aggregation, not an accumulation with its own flows.
  • Stock initial values are stated as plain starting levels; the accumulation itself is expressed through the inflow/outflow structure.
supportingInfo.title: Chained inventory stocks with reinforcing and balancing loops

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains the outbreak of war

The model treats the Revolution not as a list of grievances but as a set of interlocking feedback loops that escalated between 1763 and 1775.

The origin: a debt-driven balancing loop that failed. The French and Indian War loaded Britain with debt (British War Debt accumulating War Spending). Parliament tried to close that gap by taxing America (Tax Burden on Colonies → Tax Revenue Collected → Debt Repayment). This is a classic balancing loop intended to fix the problem — but its fix produced side effects that undermined it.

Reinforcing loop 1 — Taxation and resentment ("fixes that fail"). Because the colonies had no members in Parliament, the tax was felt as unconstitutional (Representation Deficit amplifying Grievance from Taxation). Grievance accumulated in Colonial Resentment, which built Colonial Resistance Organization — Sons of Liberty, non-importation associations, committees of correspondence. That organization destroyed Tax Compliance, so the taxes raised little money, the debt stayed high, and Parliament pressed harder. The attempted fix made the fiscal problem worse.

Reinforcing loop 2 — Defiance and coercion ("escalation"). Organized, angry colonists produced Acts of Defiance such as the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered with Punitive British Legislation — the Intolerable Acts and the closing of Boston's port — which added directly to resentment, which produced more organization and more defiance. Each side read the other's response as proof it must escalate.

Reinforcing loop 3 — Troops, blood and propaganda. Coercive laws required British Troop Presence to enforce them. Soldiers among a hostile population generated Violent Incidents — the Boston Massacre — which the patriot press magnified (Propaganda Effect) into empire-wide grievance, deepening resentment and provoking more defiance and more troops.

Reinforcing loop 4 — Cost of coercion. Enforcement Spending on the army flows straight back into the war debt, so coercion recreated the very fiscal pressure that started the taxation, tightening the whole system.

The slow variable — identity. American Colonial Identity is a stock with an inflow and no outflow: shared suffering and joint action built a permanent sense of being one people. Because it never decays, each round of the crisis started from a higher base, which is why the calm after the Stamp Act repeal did not restore the old relationship.

The trigger. Resentment plus organization plus a visible army produced Militia Mobilization and a stock of Colonial Military Readiness. Once armed minutemen and British regulars occupied the same countryside, Outbreak of Hostilities followed almost mechanically — Gage's march to seize the Concord stores lit a fuse that the loops had been laying for twelve years.

Formulation notes

  • Anger, identity, organization, troops and armed readiness are modeled as stocks, because each accumulated over years and did not reset; taxes, defiance, coercive laws and incidents are rates or auxiliaries.
  • Aggregations such as Tax Revenue Collected and Outbreak of Hostilities are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are algebraic each year.
  • Every numeric parameter is named (for example Propaganda Amplification, British Coercion Propensity) rather than buried inside an equation.
  • All one-directional processes (spending, deployment, decay, mobilization) are constrained so they cannot run backwards.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated British public debt, swollen by the French and Indian War (1754-63) and by the cost of garrisoning and policing America. It is the ultimate driver of the ministry's search for colonial revenue.

variables.name: War Spending
variables.documentation: Military expenditure during the French and Indian War that added to the debt Britain later asked the colonies to help retire.

variables.name: War Period Indicator
variables.documentation: Time-based switch that turns war expenditure on during 1754-1763 (the French and Indian War) and off afterwards.

variables.name: Annual War Cost
variables.documentation: Yearly cost of prosecuting the French and Indian War.

variables.name: Enforcement Spending
variables.documentation: Cost of keeping regiments in America to enforce the acts. Coercion is expensive, so it feeds back into the debt that motivated taxation in the first place.

variables.name: Cost per Troop Year
variables.documentation: Annual cost of maintaining one unit of troop presence in the colonies.
variables.units: debt index per troop index per Year

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected from the colonies that reduces the debt.

variables.name: Tax Revenue Collected
variables.documentation: Revenue actually received: the tax levied multiplied by the fraction the colonists are willing to pay. Smuggling, non-importation and intimidation of stamp agents cut this sharply.

variables.name: Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Fraction of levied taxes that is actually paid. Organized resistance (Sons of Liberty, non-importation associations, committees of correspondence) drives it toward zero.

variables.name: Resistance for Full Noncompliance
variables.documentation: Level of organized resistance at which collection of colonial taxes becomes impossible.

variables.name: Tax Burden on Colonies
variables.documentation: New duties laid on America (Sugar, Stamp, Townshend, Tea Acts). The larger the debt, the harder Parliament presses the colonies for revenue.

variables.name: Tax Pressure Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly Parliament converts outstanding debt into new colonial taxation.

variables.name: Grievance from Taxation
variables.documentation: The felt injustice of taxation. Because the colonies had no members in Parliament, every shilling taxed was experienced as an unconstitutional imposition: no taxation without representation.

variables.name: Representation Deficit
variables.documentation: The complete absence of colonial representation in Parliament, which magnifies the political meaning of any tax.

variables.name: Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: Accumulated anger and distrust toward British authority. It is a stock because grievances were remembered and compounded from 1765 onward rather than forgotten each year.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: Background level of colonial irritation with imperial regulation before the new taxes.

variables.name: Resentment Growth
variables.documentation: New anger generated each year by taxes, by coercive laws such as the Intolerable Acts, and by publicized bloodshed such as the Boston Massacre.

variables.name: Resentment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How much resentment each unit of provocation creates.

variables.name: Resentment Decay
variables.documentation: Cooling of anger when provocations stop, as happened briefly after the repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties.

variables.name: Resentment Memory Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which a grievance fades if it is not renewed.

variables.name: American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulating sense of being American rather than British subjects of thirteen separate provinces. Shared grievance and inter-colonial cooperation built it steadily and it did not erode.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak pre-1763 sense of a common American interest.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Shared suffering under imperial policy and joint action through congresses and committees forged a common American identity.

variables.name: Identity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which shared grievance and joint organizing convert into a common identity.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance Organization
variables.documentation: Institutional capacity to resist: Sons of Liberty, non-importation associations, committees of correspondence, provincial conventions and the Continental Congress.

variables.name: Initial Resistance Organization
variables.documentation: Minimal formal resistance structure existing before 1765.

variables.name: Organizing Rate
variables.documentation: Angry colonists who see themselves as one people build shared institutions of resistance.

variables.name: Organizing Effectiveness
variables.documentation: Rate at which grievance plus identity is converted into durable organization.

variables.name: Organization Decay
variables.documentation: Committees and associations lapse when the crisis quiets, as they largely did between 1770 and 1773.

variables.name: Organization Decay Time
variables.documentation: Average life of a resistance body that is no longer being provoked.

variables.name: Acts of Defiance
variables.documentation: Public acts of resistance such as stamp riots, the burning of the Gaspee and the Boston Tea Party. They require both anger and the organization to act on it.

variables.name: Defiance Propensity
variables.documentation: Willingness of organized, angry colonists to move from petition to open defiance.

variables.name: Punitive British Legislation
variables.documentation: Parliament's coercive answer to defiance: the Declaratory Act, the Coercive or Intolerable Acts, and the closing of the port of Boston until the destroyed tea was paid for.

variables.name: British Coercion Propensity
variables.documentation: Parliament's disposition to answer challenges to its sovereignty with punishment rather than concession.

variables.name: British Troop Presence
variables.documentation: Redcoats stationed in the colonies, especially the occupation of Boston from 1768 and the army under Gage after 1774.

variables.name: Initial Troop Presence
variables.documentation: Garrison left in America at the close of the French and Indian War.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Soldiers sent to enforce coercive laws and protect customs officials.

variables.name: Troops per Coercive Act
variables.documentation: Military force accompanying each unit of coercive legislation.

variables.name: Troop Withdrawal
variables.documentation: Redeployment or removal of regiments, as after the Boston Massacre when troops were pulled to Castle Island.

variables.name: Troop Rotation Time
variables.documentation: Average time a deployed force stays before being withdrawn absent new orders.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Clashes between soldiers and civilians, above all the Boston Massacre of 1770. Armed troops quartered among an already hostile population make bloodshed nearly inevitable.

variables.name: Incident Propensity
variables.documentation: Chance that troops and an angry crowd produce violence.

variables.name: Propaganda Effect
variables.documentation: Patriot printers and engravers, such as Revere's print of the Massacre, magnified each incident far beyond its local scale and spread it through the committees of correspondence.

variables.name: Propaganda Amplification
variables.documentation: Multiplier by which publicity turns a local clash into an empire-wide grievance.

variables.name: Colonial Military Readiness
variables.documentation: Armed capacity of the colonists: trained militia, minutemen, and stockpiled powder and arms at places like Concord.

variables.name: Initial Militia Readiness
variables.documentation: Ordinary colonial militia capacity before the crisis.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Provincial congresses arm and drill the militia in response to anger and to the visible threat of the army.

variables.name: Mobilization Effectiveness
variables.documentation: Rate at which organization and threat are converted into armed readiness.

variables.name: Demobilization

variables.name: Demobilization Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which armed readiness decays without renewed threat.

variables.name: Outbreak of Hostilities
variables.documentation: The likelihood of open fighting. Armed militia and a standing army in the same countryside produced Lexington and Concord when Gage marched to seize the colonists' stores.

variables.name: Confrontation Propensity
variables.documentation: Chance that armed colonists and British regulars in contact exchange fire.

variables.documentation: British debt already outstanding when the French and Indian War began.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says about the future of road rage

Road rage is not a simple chain of causes; it is generated by a set of interlocking loops around four accumulations — Traffic Congestion, Driver Stress, the Aggressive Driving Norm, and the current level of Road Rage Incidents — plus one balancing accumulation, Enforcement and Awareness.

Reinforcing loops (the engines of growth)

  1. Congestion → stress → frustration → incidents → congestion. Incidents block lanes (Incident Congestion Effect), which adds to congestion formation, which raises stress loading and perceived delay, which raises frustration and aggression propensity, which produces more incidents. This is a classic vicious cycle that turns a modest rise in traffic into a much larger rise in aggression.
  2. Incidents → learned norm → provocations → incidents. Every witnessed act of aggression reinforces the Aggressive Driving Norm. A stronger norm means drivers are cut off, tailgated and honked at more often (Provocation Frequency), which produces more incidents. Because norms accumulate slowly, this loop is the reason road rage can drift upward for years and then be hard to reverse.
  3. Stress → frustration → incidents → congestion → stress. Stress is a stock, so it carries over between trips; escalation today makes tomorrow's driver less tolerant.

Balancing loop (the brake, and why it arrives late)

Rising incidents eventually attract policing, penalties and awareness campaigns. Enforcement both deters escalation directly (Deterrence Effect) and erodes the aggressive norm. But this loop works through a long institutional delay and then decays as attention fades — the shifting the burden / eroding goals pattern in which the brake is applied only after the problem is visible and is released too early. This delay is what produces overshoot-and-oscillation in incidents rather than smooth control.

External pressures

Traffic Volume is set to rise over the simulated decade, and Road Design Quality, Weather Severity, Fatigue Level, Distracted Driving Prevalence, Hostile Personality Share and Schedule Pressure enter as leverage points that scale capacity, stress loading, provocations or propensity. Poor road design and bad weather act by cutting effective capacity, so they amplify congestion rather than causing rage directly.

Modeling choices worth noting

  • Congestion, stress, norms, incidents and enforcement are stocks because each persists and adjusts with its own time constant; frustration, impatience, provocation frequency and aggression propensity are auxiliaries because they are instantaneous algebraic products, not accumulations.
  • All effects of one variable on another are expressed through normalized graphical functions that pass through the point (1, 1), so that normal conditions reproduce today's behavior and every driver of change can be read as a deviation from normal.
  • No arbitrary constants are buried in equations; every rate, delay and pressure is a named variable that can be tested as a policy lever.
  • Baseline parameters put the system in equilibrium, so the future trajectory is generated purely by the growth in traffic interacting with the loops — the clearest way to see which feedback dominates.

Implication: because two reinforcing loops (congestion-frustration and norm learning) are faster and more direct than the single delayed balancing loop, incidents are likely to grow faster than traffic itself. The highest-leverage interventions are the ones that break loops rather than treat symptoms: expanding effective capacity through road design, cutting distraction and fatigue, and sustaining enforcement and awareness before incidents spike rather than after.

variables.name: Congestion Formation

variables.name: Congestion Clearance

variables.name: Congestion Clearance Time
variables.documentation: Average time for congestion conditions to relax once pressure is removed.

variables.name: Traffic Volume

variables.name: Road Design Quality

variables.name: Weather Severity

variables.name: Weather Capacity Effect
variables.documentation: Graphical function showing how bad weather reduces usable road capacity. Normal weather (input 1) yields a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Effective Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Capacity actually available to traffic, degraded by poor road design and adverse weather.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress and arousal carried by the average driver. Modeled as a stock because stress builds up over repeated exposure and takes time to unwind.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions load stress onto drivers: worse congestion, worse weather and more fatigue all raise it.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Rate at which drivers unwind through rest, calm driving and time away from the road.

variables.name: Stress Recovery Time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated driver stress to dissipate.

variables.name: Normal Stress Load
variables.documentation: Baseline stress imposed by everyday driving under normal conditions.

variables.name: Congestion Stress Effect
variables.documentation: Graphical function translating congestion into extra stress loading. Normal congestion (input 1) gives multiplier 1.

variables.name: Weather Stress Effect
variables.documentation: Graphical function translating adverse weather into extra stress from harder, riskier driving.

variables.name: Fatigue Level
variables.documentation: Driver fatigue and sleep deprivation relative to normal. Fatigue raises stress loading and impairs judgment.

variables.name: Congestion Delay Effect
variables.documentation: Graphical function showing how congestion-driven lateness raises the sense of being blocked and running behind schedule.

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: How tightly drivers' schedules are packed, relative to normal. Tight schedules lower tolerance for delay.

variables.name: Impatience

variables.name: Frustration

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement

variables.name: Norm Erosion

variables.name: Norm Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for social learning and unlearning of driving norms.

variables.name: Distracted Driving Prevalence

variables.name: Provocation Frequency

variables.name: Hostile Personality Share
variables.documentation: Share of the driving population with impulsive, hostile or competitive traits, relative to normal.

variables.name: Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Graphical function showing how enforcement and public awareness suppress the willingness to act out aggressively. Normal enforcement (input 1) gives multiplier 1.

variables.name: Aggression Propensity
variables.documentation: Likelihood that a provoked driver reacts aggressively: personality and frustration raise it, deterrence lowers it.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents

variables.name: Incident Onset
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage episodes start: provocations must meet a driver willing to escalate.

variables.name: Incident Deescalation

variables.name: Incident Duration
variables.documentation: Average persistence of an aggressive driving episode and its visible aftermath.

variables.name: Normal Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Baseline rate of incident onset under normal provocation and normal propensity.

variables.name: Incident Congestion Effect

variables.name: Enforcement and Awareness

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The story as feedback, not a list of causes

The events listed (Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Tea Party, Intolerable Acts) are not independent causes; they are successive turns of the same two reinforcing loops.

R1 – Coercion and grievance spiral (the escalation archetype). War debt from the French and Indian War pushed Britain to tax the colonies. Taxation without representation raised Colonial Resentment, which produced Colonial Defiance (stamp riots, boycotts, the Tea Party). Defiance provoked British Coercion (troops in Boston, the Intolerable Acts closing the port), which poured straight back into resentment. Each side's corrective action was read by the other as an attack, so the loop tightened rather than settled.

R2 – Resistance builds identity, identity builds resistance. Acting together forged American Identity, and a stronger shared identity converted the same grievance into larger, better-coordinated resistance. Identity is modelled as an accumulation fed by defiance itself, so the colonies could not simply return to 1763 once the loop had turned a few times.

Where the shooting comes from. Armed Hostilities is the product of defiance and coercion: violence needed both an armed, organised colonial movement and a British resolve to enforce obedience. That is why Lexington and Concord happened only after a decade of loop turns, not at the Stamp Act.

Structural choices. Resentment and identity are stocks because outrage and self-conception accumulate and persist; coercion and defiance are one-directional rate flows (a government cannot un-issue an insult, so they are constrained to be non-negative); hostilities is an algebraic index, not an accumulation, because it measures current conflict intensity.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Loops Between Coercion, Defiance, Identity

variables.name: Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: The accumulated stock of colonial grievance against Crown and Parliament. It begins at a nonzero level because the debts of the French and Indian War (1754-63) led Britain to impose revenue measures such as the Stamp Act of 1765 on colonists who had no representation in Parliament. Resentment is a stock because outrage from each episode (Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Intolerable Acts) did not evaporate; it piled up in memory, pamphlets and committees of correspondence.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: The rate at which Britain adds new taxes, troops and punitive laws. It is driven by colonial defiance: smuggling and riots brought the Townshend duties and the quartering of soldiers (leading to the Boston Massacre of 1770), and the destruction of the tea in 1773 brought the Intolerable Acts closing the port of Boston. Each coercive act adds directly to the accumulated stock of resentment.

variables.name: Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: Acts of open resistance: non-importation boycotts, tarring of stamp distributors, the Boston Tea Party, the Continental Congress, and the arming of militias. Defiance rises with accumulated resentment and is amplified by the sense of being a distinct American people. It is modelled as the flow that builds American Identity, because acting together against Britain is what made colonists think of themselves as Americans.

variables.name: American Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulated sense of a shared American people separate from Britain. It is a stock because it was built up episode by episode through joint boycotts, intercolonial congresses and shared propaganda about events like the Boston Massacre. A higher identity converts the same amount of grievance into far more organised and confident resistance.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: The risk of actual shooting, realised at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. Violence requires both sides at once: armed, organised colonial resistance and a British determination to enforce obedience by force. It is the product of the two, so hostilities explode only when defiance and coercion are both high.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains road rage

I built the smallest possible feedback structure that still explains why road rage can grow on its own rather than staying at a fixed level.

The one accumulation. Only one thing in this story genuinely accumulates: the Aggressive Driving Norm — the learned, copied, socially tolerated script for how to behave when blocked or provoked. Individual incidents are events, not accumulations, so Road Rage Incidents is an auxiliary calculation, not a stock. Congestion, weather, fatigue and personality are all folded into the Driver Stress multiplier to stay inside the five-variable limit.

The reinforcing (escalation) loop — the engine of the problem. Aggressive norm → more incidents → more drivers witness aggression and more victims retaliate (Norm Reinforcement) → an even stronger norm. This is the classic escalation/reinforcing archetype: road rage is largely self-caused. A second, nested reinforcing loop runs through stress: aggression creates crashes, stop-and-go waves and perceived provocations, which raise frustration and impatience, which lower everyone's threshold for aggression.

The balancing loops that decide the future. Norm Erosion drains the norm through driver turnover, enforcement, education and calmer role models. A second balancing effect is built into the stress curve: at very high aggression levels, stress bends back down because drivers withdraw — driving defensively, avoiding peak hours, or not driving at all.

What the model predicts. Because the stress curve passes through (1,1), the historical normal is a tipping point, not a resting place. Starting the norm just 10% above normal, the reinforcing loop dominates and incidents grow rapidly; growth then slows and settles at a much higher plateau (roughly 2.5 times normal) where withdrawal and norm erosion finally match reinforcement. In other words, society does not drift back to calm on its own — it locks into a new, more hostile equilibrium.

Leverage. The two intervention points are the strength of the imitation link (visible enforcement, not glamorizing aggression, de-escalation training) and the erosion rate. Reducing congestion or improving road design shifts the stress curve down and can pull the tipping point back above the current norm.

Formulation checks applied. Incidents are an auxiliary product, not a stock; reinforcement and erosion are separate one-directional flows so no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow; the stock's equation is an initial value only; the graphical function is normalized through (1,1); and no arbitrary numeric constants are buried in the equations.
supportingInfo.title: Reinforcing Normalization Loop Drives Road Rage Escalation

relationships.polarityReasoning: An inflow adds to its stock, so a faster inflow raises the norm.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The accumulated stock of learned, socially normalized aggressive driving behavior in the driving population, expressed as an index where 1 equals the historical normal level. It is a stock because norms are not created or destroyed instantly: they build up as drivers repeatedly witness and imitate aggression, and they fade only gradually as calmer driving is observed and older habits are unlearned. It starts slightly above normal (1.1) to represent a mild present-day disturbance whose future consequences we want to trace.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: The rate at which aggressive driving becomes normalized through learned behavior. Every road rage incident is witnessed by other drivers, who see tailgating, cutting off, and honking as ordinary or even necessary, and who are provoked into retaliating. The rate is therefore set equal to the current level of incidents: the more aggression that is displayed on the road, the faster it is copied. It can only add to the norm, so it is one-directional.

variables.name: Norm Erosion
variables.documentation: The rate at which normalized aggression fades away through driver turnover, calmer role models, enforcement, education and simple forgetting. It is proportional to the norm itself, so the larger the stock of learned aggression, the more of it decays each year. This is the balancing side of the norm and gives the system a characteristic adjustment time of one year.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: A multiplier capturing the psychological and situational pressure the average driver is under: frustration, impatience, anxiety, fatigue and the felt provocation of being cut off or tailgated, all amplified by the congestion, poor road design and bad weather that aggressive driving itself creates through crashes and stop-and-go waves. It is a graphical function of the aggressive driving norm and passes through (1,1) so that a normal norm produces normal stress. Stress rises steeply as aggression spreads, but the curve bends back down at very high levels because drivers eventually withdraw, slow down, drive defensively, avoid peak hours or stop driving altogether, which relieves congestion and exposure.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The rate of road rage incidents per year, indexed to 1 at historical normal. It is the product of how normal aggressive driving has become (the propensity or learned script) and how stressed, frustrated and provoked drivers currently feel (the trigger). Both must be present: a calm driver in a hostile culture and a stressed driver with no aggressive script both produce fewer incidents than a stressed driver in a culture where aggression is expected.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.

The Boston Tea Party

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the Revolution built itself: a feedback story

The model treats 1763–1783 as a set of interlocking loops rather than a chain of events. Four "slow" stocks — Colonial Grievance, Colonial Identity, Intercolonial Coordination, and Loyalty To Crown — remember what happened and convert isolated episodes into a trajectory toward war. British War Debt, Coercive Legislation, British Troops In Colonies, Revolutionary Propaganda, Colonial Militia Strength, and Open Hostilities complete the structure.

Reinforcing loops (the engine of escalation)

R1 – Tax the ones who won't pay (fiscal trap). War debt → tax burden → grievance → resistance → collapse of tax compliance → less revenue → debt stays high → more taxes. Trying to make the colonies pay for the French and Indian War produced exactly the resistance that made them unpayable.

R2 – Defiance and punishment (escalation / "attack and counterattack"). Resistance → acts of defiance (the Tea Party) → punitive legislation (the Intolerable Acts) → grievance → more resistance. Each side reads the other's move as proof it must push harder.

R3 – Occupation and outrage. Coercive acts → more troops to enforce them → friction between soldiers and crowds → violent incidents (the Boston Massacre) → grievance → resistance → defiance → more acts → more troops.

R4 – Propaganda amplifier. Violent incidents → circulating pamphlets and engravings → grievance → resistance → more incidents. Bloodshed becomes durable political capital because propaganda is modelled as a stock that outlives the event.

R5 – Identity and union. Grievance and shared print culture → American identity → committees of correspondence and Congress → coordinated resistance → more coercion → more shared grievance. Coercion aimed at Massachusetts created the very continental solidarity it was meant to prevent.

R6 – The cost of coercion. More troops → higher garrison spending → higher debt → heavier taxes → more grievance → more defiance → more coercion → more troops. Enforcement pays for itself only in resentment.

R7 – The arms race. Troops → perceived military threat (amplified by the alarm networks) → militia mobilization → armed clashes → open hostilities → British reinforcements → still more threat. This is the loop that fires at Lexington and Concord.

R8 – Loyalty collapse. Grievance → erosion of allegiance → willingness to commit open defiance and to shoot at the King's troops → coercion and clashes → more grievance. Loyalty gates both defiance and armed clashes, so its decay unlocks the violent parts of the system.

Balancing loops (why it could have gone otherwise, and why they failed)

B1 – Debt repayment. Revenue actually collected retires debt and relieves the tax pressure. R1 overwhelms it because compliance collapses.

B2 – Boycott, merchant lobby, repeal. Resistance → non importation → British exporters lobby → repeal → grievance eases and some loyalty returns. This loop genuinely worked in 1766 and 1770; it is the system's main safety valve, and Parliament shut it off after 1773 by choosing punishment over concession.

B3 – Deterrence. Troops are supposed to suppress protest. The suppression curve is deliberately weak and saturating: the garrison intimidated a little and provoked a great deal, so B3 is dominated by R3.

B4 – Reconciliation. Fighting can wind down only in proportion to surviving loyalty. Once R8 has drained that stock, the brake disappears and hostilities are self sustaining.

Formulation notes

  • Aggregations such as resistance, defiance, boycott intensity and perceived threat are auxiliaries, not stocks; only genuine accumulations (debt, grievance, laws in force, troops, propaganda, identity, coordination, militia, loyalty, hostilities) are stocks.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock. Troop deployment is a single bidirectional adjustment flow so withdrawals are possible.
  • All numeric parameters are named variables; the only bare numbers inside equations are structural complements such as one minus loyalty.
  • The three graphical functions (compliance, mobilization, deterrence) all pass through the point (1, 1) so that normal conditions produce normal behaviour.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Index of the imperial debt left by the French and Indian War (1754-63). It is the initial driver of the whole story: Britain needed colonial revenue to service it.

variables.name: War And Garrison Spending
variables.documentation: Annual imperial military and administrative outlay. Grows with the size of the garrison stationed in America, so coercion is self-financing only in the wrong direction.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Debt retired using revenue actually collected from the colonies.

variables.name: Baseline Imperial Spending
variables.documentation: Fixed imperial costs independent of the American garrison.

variables.name: Cost Per Troop
variables.documentation: Cost of maintaining one unit of troops in North America.
variables.units: debt index per Year per troop unit

variables.name: Tax Effort Per Unit Debt
variables.documentation: How strongly Parliament converts fiscal pressure into new colonial taxes such as the Stamp Act and Townshend duties.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The level of taxation Parliament attempts to impose without colonial representation. Proportional to the debt pressure it is trying to relieve.

variables.name: Tax Revenue From Colonies
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected. Equals what is levied times normal compliance, degraded by smuggling, non importation and refusal to pay.

variables.name: Normal Compliance Fraction
variables.documentation: Share of levied taxes collected under quiet, pre 1765 conditions.

variables.name: Compliance Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of organized resistance on tax collection. At normal resistance the multiplier is 1; heavy resistance drives collection toward zero.

variables.name: Reference Resistance Activity
variables.documentation: Normal reference level of colonial resistance used to normalize the compliance lookup.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: Accumulated anti British sentiment. It is a stock because outrage persists in memory, pamphlets and sermons long after the provoking act.

variables.name: Grievance Accumulation
variables.equation: Weight_Of_Taxation * Colonial_Tax_Burden + Weight_Of_Coercion * Coercive_Legislation + Weight_Of_Propaganda * Revolutionary_Propaganda + Weight_Of_Violence * (Violent_Incidents + Armed_Clashes)
variables.documentation: New grievance created each year by taxes without representation, coercive laws, circulating propaganda and bloodshed.

variables.name: Grievance Easing
variables.documentation: Fading of grievance over time, accelerated when Britain repeals offending measures as it did with the Stamp Act in 1766.

variables.name: Weight Of Taxation
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of tax burden imposed without representation.

variables.name: Weight Of Coercion
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of coercive legislation in force.
variables.units: grievance per law index per Year

variables.name: Weight Of Propaganda
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of circulating patriot propaganda.
variables.units: grievance per propaganda index per Year

variables.name: Weight Of Violence
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per violent incident or armed clash, such as the Boston Massacre of 1770.

variables.name: Grievance Memory Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which an unaddressed grievance fades if nothing new happens.

variables.name: Conciliation Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How much faster grievance fades when Britain repeals coercive measures.

variables.name: Coercive Legislation
variables.documentation: Stock of punitive statutes in force: Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Quartering, and above all the Intolerable Acts that closed Boston harbour.

variables.name: Enactment Of Coercive Acts
variables.documentation: Parliament's punitive legislative response to colonial defiance such as the Boston Tea Party.

variables.name: Repeal Of Coercive Acts
variables.documentation: Withdrawal of measures when British merchants hurt by boycotts lobby Parliament, as with the 1766 Stamp Act repeal.

variables.name: Punitive Response Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly Parliament answers defiance with new coercion rather than negotiation.

variables.name: Repeal Responsiveness
variables.documentation: How readily Parliament yields to commercial lobbying.

variables.name: British Merchant Pressure
variables.documentation: Lobbying by British exporters losing the American market to non importation agreements.

variables.name: Merchant Political Influence
variables.documentation: Weight of commercial interests inside Parliament.

variables.name: Colonial Boycott Intensity
variables.documentation: Share of resistance expressed as non importation and non consumption of British goods.

variables.name: Boycott Fraction Of Resistance
variables.documentation: Fraction of resistance energy channelled into economic rather than confrontational action.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance Activity
variables.documentation: Overall level of protest, petitioning, boycotting and crowd action. Grievance supplies the motive, intercolonial organization the means, and troops provide some suppression.

variables.name: Mobilization Effect Of Coordination
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how committees of correspondence and the Continental Congress turn scattered anger into coordinated action. Normal coordination gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Reference Coordination
variables.documentation: Normal reference level of intercolonial organization.

variables.name: Deterrence Effect Of Troops
variables.documentation: Intended suppressive effect of redcoats on open protest. It is deliberately weak and saturating: garrisons intimidated a little but provoked much more.

variables.name: Reference Troop Level
variables.documentation: Normal peacetime garrison used to normalize the deterrence lookup.

variables.name: Acts Of Defiance
variables.documentation: Open, illegal challenges to imperial authority such as the Boston Tea Party. Only resisters who have stopped feeling loyal will destroy property or defy Parliament outright.

variables.name: Loyalty To Crown
variables.documentation: Fraction of colonial allegiance still attached to King and Parliament. It starts near total in 1763 and erodes as grievance accumulates.

variables.name: Loyalty Erosion
variables.documentation: Loss of allegiance caused by sustained grievance.

variables.name: Loyalty Restoration
variables.documentation: Partial return of allegiance when Britain repeals offending measures.

variables.name: Erosion Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Rate at which grievance dissolves allegiance.

variables.name: Restoration Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Rate at which repeals win back allegiance.

variables.name: British Troops In Colonies
variables.documentation: Redcoats stationed in America, quartered in Boston and elsewhere to enforce the acts.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Net reinforcement or withdrawal of the garrison as London adjusts toward the force it thinks enforcement requires. Bidirectional, so it can be negative when troops are pulled back.

variables.name: Desired British Troops
variables.documentation: Force level London believes is needed to enforce the acts in force and to meet open fighting.

variables.name: Baseline Garrison
variables.documentation: Peacetime garrison retained after 1763.

variables.name: Troops Per Coercive Act
variables.documentation: Soldiers required to enforce each unit of coercive legislation.

variables.name: Troops Per Hostility
variables.documentation: Reinforcements sent per unit of open fighting.

variables.name: Troop Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time to move troops across the Atlantic and redistribute them.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Street confrontations between soldiers and crowds. The Boston Massacre is the archetype: it requires both a garrison and an angry, mobilized populace.

variables.name: Friction Coefficient
variables.documentation: Chance that a troop crowd contact turns violent.
variables.units: incidents per Year per troop unit per resistance index

variables.name: Revolutionary Propaganda
variables.documentation: Circulating pamphlets, engravings and newspaper accounts, such as Revere's print of the Massacre, that keep outrage alive.

variables.name: Propaganda Production
variables.documentation: Creation of patriot publicity material from each bloody incident.

variables.name: Propaganda Fading
variables.documentation: Loss of salience of older stories as attention moves on.

variables.name: Propaganda Yield
variables.documentation: Publicity generated per violent incident.

variables.name: Propaganda Attention Span
variables.documentation: Average time a story keeps its emotional force.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The sense of being American rather than British. It accumulates from shared grievance and shared stories and, once formed, does not easily disappear.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Growth of a common American self image from jointly suffered injuries and jointly read pamphlets.

variables.name: Identity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which shared experience becomes shared identity.
variables.units: identity index per grievance index per Year

variables.name: Intercolonial Coordination
variables.documentation: Institutional capacity for joint action: Stamp Act Congress, Sons of Liberty, committees of correspondence, Continental Congress.

variables.name: Coordination Building
variables.documentation: Creation of joint institutions, driven both by a common identity and by the shared threat of coercive laws such as the Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: Coordination Decay
variables.documentation: Lapse of committees and networks when nothing sustains them.

variables.name: Identity Effect On Coordination
variables.documentation: Contribution of shared identity to building joint institutions.
variables.units: coordination index per identity index per Year

variables.name: Threat Effect On Coordination
variables.documentation: Contribution of a common external threat to building joint institutions.
variables.units: coordination index per law index per Year

variables.name: Coordination Lifetime
variables.documentation: Average life of an unmaintained committee or network.

variables.name: Perceived Military Threat
variables.documentation: How menacing the garrison looks to the colonists, amplified by networks that broadcast alarms about troop movements.

variables.name: Threat Per Troop
variables.documentation: Alarm generated by each unit of stationed troops.

variables.name: Colonial Militia Strength
variables.documentation: Armed and drilled minutemen with stockpiled powder, the force that met the regulars at Lexington and Concord.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Recruitment, drilling and arming in response to the perceived British military threat.

variables.name: Militia Demobilization
variables.documentation: Men returning to farms and stores when alarm subsides.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization Rate
variables.documentation: Speed of turning perceived threat into armed companies.
variables.units: militia unit per threat index per Year

variables.name: Militia Service Time
variables.documentation: Average time a militiaman stays mobilized absent new alarms.

variables.name: Armed Clashes
variables.documentation: Exchanges of fire between militia and regulars. They need armed colonists, deployed regulars and enough lost allegiance for men to shoot at the King's troops.

variables.name: Clash Probability Per Contact
variables.documentation: Chance a militia and regular encounter becomes a firefight, as at Lexington in April 1775.
variables.units: clashes per Year per militia unit per troop unit

variables.name: Open Hostilities
variables.documentation: The state of declared war between Britain and the colonies. This is the outcome the model is built to explain.

variables.name: Escalation To Hostilities
variables.documentation: Each firefight commits both sides further to war.

variables.name: Hostility Deescalation
variables.documentation: Winding down of fighting, possible only to the extent allegiance to the Crown survives. Once loyalty collapses, this brake disappears.

variables.name: Reconciliation Time
variables.documentation: Time needed to stand down from fighting when the will to reconcile exists.
