testParams.name: include a minimum number of feedback loops for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says about road rage

Road rage is not caused by "bad drivers". It is produced by a set of interlocking feedback loops linking traffic, physiology, psychology and culture. I built eight accumulations — Traffic Volume, Road Capacity, Accident Blockages, Driver Stress, Sleep Debt, the Aggressive Driving Norm, Enforcement and Awareness, and Recent Road Rage Incidents — and connected them through frustration, impatience and perceived provocation. A slow growth in travel demand is the only external push; everything else is generated internally.

Reinforcing loops (the engines of escalation)

R1 – Retaliation spiral. Incidents raise perceived provocations, which raise frustration, which raises aggressive driving, which produces more incidents. Anger is contagious in real time.

R2 – Learned behaviour. Aggression that is repeatedly observed becomes the accepted norm, and a more permissive norm converts the same frustration into more overt aggression. This is the slowest and most dangerous loop, because a norm built over years does not fade quickly even if congestion improves.

R3 – Crash–congestion trap. Aggressive and distracted driving causes crashes; crashes block lanes; blocked lanes cut effective capacity; congestion and delay rise; frustration rises; aggression rises again. Aggression literally manufactures the traffic jams that feed it.

R4 – Stress spiral. Delay creates impatience, impatience accumulates as stress, and stressed drivers become frustrated by events they would otherwise shrug off — feeding aggression, crashes and more delay.

R5 – Fatigue spiral. Stress and long commutes eat into sleep; sleep debt lowers tolerance for delay; lower tolerance means more impatience and more stress, which costs more sleep. Fatigue is a hidden amplifier of everything else.

R6 – Crowding and provocation. Congestion multiplies the number of close encounters between drivers, so the same rate of aggression yields more felt provocations, more anger and more crashes, which worsen congestion.

Balancing loops (the brakes, and why they are weak)

B1 – Enforcement response. Rising incidents create public concern, which builds policing and awareness, which deters aggression. But this loop is slow — a six-month build-up plus a three-month memory — so it always arrives late and lapses as soon as attention moves on.

B2 – Road building. Congestion triggers capacity expansion, which relieves congestion. This is a classic fixes that fail: new capacity lowers delay, which revives suppressed trips (B3), so traffic grows back and congestion returns, this time with more vehicles exposed to conflict.

B3 – Trip avoidance. Long journeys suppress discretionary driving, which is the only fast-acting relief valve in the system — and it is the one that induced demand cancels out.

B4/B5 – Stress and sleep recovery. Stress dissipates and sleep debt is repaid, but only if conditions ease; if delay stays high, both stocks settle at a permanently elevated plateau.

B6 – Norm erosion, B7 – incident fading, B8 – blockage clearance, B9 – road wear-out are the remaining self-limiting drains that keep each stock finite.

Formulation choices and corrections made

  • Total incidents modelled as a stock of recent incidents, not a running total. A cumulative counter would never come back down; a decaying pool correctly represents what drivers actually witness and what policymakers react to.
  • Congestion, frustration, impatience and aggression are auxiliaries, not stocks — they are algebraic combinations computed each instant, not accumulations.
  • No conditional logic and no bare constants inside equations. Every behavioural non-linearity is a named graphical relationship (delay from congestion, tolerance from fatigue, frustration from stress, anger from provocation, deterrence from enforcement, norm licensing, investment appetite, trip suppression), and each passes through the point (1,1) so that normal input gives normal output.
  • The learned-behaviour loop was deliberately given a saturating response. A linear norm loop would have a gain of exactly one and would run away without limit, which is not credible; the saturating curve keeps the loop amplifying but bounded.
  • Every stock is initialised in dynamic equilibrium, so any change in behaviour you see is genuinely caused by the feedback structure responding to growing travel demand, not by an arbitrary starting imbalance.
  • Flows that can only run one way (crashes, clearance, sleep loss, norm reinforcement, enforcement investment, incident occurrence) are constrained to be non-negative; the traffic adjustment flow is left bidirectional because traffic can genuinely shrink.

The forecast

With demand growing only 0.2% a month, congestion creeps up faster than road building can respond. Delay rises non-linearly near saturation, impatience and stress plateau higher, sleep debt deepens, and aggression rises. The crash loop then removes capacity just when it is scarcest. Enforcement eventually pushes back, but the aggressive-driving norm has by then ratcheted upward and decays only over years. The result is a system that drifts to a permanently higher level of road rage — the leverage lies not in punishing individual drivers but in breaking the congestion–delay–stress chain and in refusing to let aggressive driving become normal.

variables.name: Initial Trip Demand
variables.documentation: Reference level of driving demand at the start of the simulation, expressed in thousands of trips per month. Used as the normalizing reference for the whole model.

variables.name: Demand Growth Fraction
variables.documentation: Fractional monthly growth in underlying travel demand from population and economic growth. This is the external driver that pushes the system out of equilibrium and lets us see how road rage evolves into the future.

variables.name: Baseline Trip Demand
variables.documentation: Underlying desire to travel, growing steadily over time. It is the exogenous pressure on the road system.

variables.name: Trip Demand Effect of Delay
variables.documentation: When journeys take longer, some discretionary trips are cancelled, retimed or shifted to other modes. Normalized so that normal delay (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Desired Trip Volume
variables.documentation: The volume of driving people actually want to do once they take account of how bad the traffic is.

variables.name: Trip Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time it takes drivers to change their travel habits in response to travel conditions.

variables.name: Traffic Volume Adjustment
variables.documentation: Gradual movement of actual traffic toward desired traffic. It is bidirectional because traffic can grow or shrink.
variables.units: thousand trips per month per month

variables.name: Traffic Volume
variables.documentation: The amount of driving actually taking place on the network. It is a stock because habits, routes and vehicle ownership change only gradually.

variables.name: Weather Severity
variables.documentation: Index of adverse weather (rain, snow, fog) with 1 being normal conditions. Bad weather cuts usable road capacity, raises crash risk and adds directly to driver stress.

variables.name: Road Lifetime
variables.documentation: Average service life of road infrastructure before it wears out and must be replaced.

variables.name: Investment Response to Congestion
variables.documentation: Political and budgetary willingness to build new road capacity, driven by how congested the network is. Saturates because money, land and construction capacity are limited. Normal congestion (1) gives normal replacement investment (1).

variables.name: Capacity Expansion
variables.documentation: Building and widening of roads. At normal congestion it exactly replaces worn-out capacity; heavy congestion accelerates it.
variables.units: thousand trips per month per month

variables.name: Capacity Degradation
variables.documentation: Wear-out and obsolescence of existing road infrastructure.
variables.units: thousand trips per month per month

variables.name: Road Capacity
variables.documentation: The design throughput of the road network, including the quality of road design and intersections. A stock because infrastructure accumulates slowly through construction and decays through wear.

variables.name: Normal Accident Fraction
variables.documentation: Crashes and breakdowns per unit of traffic under normal driving, weather and attention conditions.

variables.name: Distracted Driving Prevalence
variables.documentation: Index of phone use, texting and eating while driving, with 1 as the current norm. Distraction multiplies crash risk and creates the erratic behaviour that provokes other drivers.

variables.name: Accident Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which crashes and incidents create physical blockages of the road. Aggression, distraction and bad weather all multiply the underlying exposure from traffic volume.

variables.name: Blockage Clearance Time
variables.documentation: Average time a crash site, repair or resulting disruption keeps degrading effective capacity.

variables.name: Blockage Clearance
variables.documentation: Removal of crash sites and restoration of full road capacity.

variables.name: Accident Blockages
variables.documentation: Crashes, breakdowns and works currently obstructing the network. A stock because blockages persist until cleared.

variables.name: Normal Blockage Level
variables.documentation: The blockage level that would exist under baseline traffic and normal driving. Used to express blockages as a relative index.

variables.name: Relative Blockages
variables.documentation: Blockages compared with the normal level, so that 1 means business as usual.

variables.name: Blockage Capacity Effect
variables.documentation: How much crash blockages reduce the usable share of road capacity. Normal blockages (1) give the normal multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Effective Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Capacity actually available to drivers after blockages and weather take their toll.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Ratio of traffic to usable capacity. A value of 1 is the normal loading of the network; above 1 means stop-and-go conditions.

variables.name: Travel Delay
variables.documentation: Journey time relative to normal. Delay rises sharply and non-linearly once the network approaches saturation, which is why small increases in traffic can cause large jumps in frustration.

variables.name: Sleep Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant over which sleep debt builds up or is paid back.

variables.name: Sleep Load
variables.documentation: Pressure on sleep from stress and from long commutes that eat into rest time.

variables.name: Sleep Loss
variables.documentation: Accumulation of fatigue from stress and long journeys.

variables.name: Sleep Recovery
variables.documentation: Recovery of rest, which drains sleep debt back toward zero.

variables.name: Sleep Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated fatigue in the driving population, indexed so 1 is normal. Fatigue impairs judgement and shortens tempers.

variables.name: Fatigue Effect on Tolerance
variables.documentation: Tired drivers tolerate less delay before becoming impatient. Normal fatigue (1) gives normal tolerance (1).

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Delay experienced relative to the delay drivers are willing to accept. Rises with congestion and falls with tolerance.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant over which driver stress builds and dissipates.

variables.name: Stress Load
variables.documentation: The stress being imposed on drivers by being late and by difficult driving conditions.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Build-up of stress and anxiety from driving conditions.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Natural decay of stress when conditions ease. This is the self-correcting side of the stress stock.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress and anxiety carried by the driving population, indexed at 1 for normal. It is a stock because stress persists between journeys.

variables.name: Stress Effect on Frustration
variables.documentation: Stressed drivers become frustrated far more easily by the same on-road events. Normal stress (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Incident Memory Time
variables.documentation: How long a road rage incident stays salient in drivers' experience and in public awareness.

variables.name: Normal Incident Fraction
variables.documentation: Road rage incidents per unit of traffic when aggression is at its normal level.

variables.name: Incident Occurrence
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents happen. It scales with exposure (how much driving there is) and with how aggressively people are driving.

variables.name: Incident Fading
variables.documentation: Incidents fading out of drivers' recent experience and public attention.

variables.name: Recent Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The pool of road rage incidents that are recent enough to be experienced, witnessed or reported. Making this a stock captures the fact that today's aggression shapes tomorrow's perceived provocation and tomorrow's policy response.

variables.name: Normal Incident Level
variables.documentation: The pool of recent incidents that would exist under baseline traffic and normal aggression. Used as the reference for the relative index.

variables.name: Relative Incident Level
variables.documentation: Road rage incidents relative to the historical normal. This is the key output of the model.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often a driver feels cut off, tailgated or honked at. It rises both with the amount of aggression circulating on the roads and with how densely packed drivers are, since congestion multiplies the number of interactions.

variables.name: Provocation Effect
variables.documentation: How much being provoked raises frustration, with saturation because there is a ceiling to how angry the average driver gets. Normal provocation (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: The felt sense of being blocked and angered while driving. It combines impatience with delay, provocation by other drivers, and the background stress the driver brings into the car.

variables.name: Impulsive Personality Prevalence
variables.documentation: Share of drivers with impulsive, hostile or competitive traits, indexed at 1 for the current population. It converts frustration into action more readily.

variables.name: Norm Effect on Aggression
variables.documentation: How much the prevailing social norm licenses aggressive behaviour. It saturates so that social learning amplifies but does not run away without limit. Normal norm (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier on aggressive behaviour from policing, cameras, penalties and public awareness campaigns. More enforcement means a lower multiplier. Normal enforcement (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Intensity
variables.documentation: How aggressively the average driver is behaving right now, relative to normal. Frustration is the trigger, personality and social norms are the amplifiers, and enforcement is the brake.

variables.name: Norm Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: How long it takes observed behaviour on the road to become an accepted social norm, and how long an old norm takes to fade.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Learned behaviour: watching others drive aggressively normalizes it and builds it into the shared norm.

variables.name: Norm Erosion
variables.documentation: Fading of the aggressive norm as drivers turn over and old behaviour is forgotten.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially accepted level of aggression behind the wheel. A stock because norms are slow-moving cultural accumulations built from repeated observation of others.

variables.name: Enforcement Response Time
variables.documentation: Delay between public concern about road rage and enforcement and awareness capacity actually being in place, and the rate at which it lapses when concern fades.

variables.name: Enforcement Investment
variables.documentation: Society responds to visible road rage by funding policing, cameras and awareness campaigns.

variables.name: Enforcement Decay
variables.documentation: Attention wanes, budgets are cut and campaigns are forgotten.

variables.name: Enforcement and Awareness
variables.documentation: Accumulated policing, penalties and public education aimed at aggressive driving. A stock because capability and public awareness build and erode gradually.

testParams.name: include a maximum number of feedback loops for American Revolution
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the Revolution built itself

The model treats the Revolution not as a list of causes but as an escalation system with one balancing loop that tried to solve Britain's problem and three reinforcing loops that turned the attempted solution into a war.

Stocks (things that accumulated): British War Debt, Colonial Grievance, Colonial Unity, Troops in Colonies, and Armed Hostilities. Everything else is a rate or an algebraic consequence.

Loop 1 (Balancing): Debt repayment — the fix that failed

The French and Indian War left a huge debt, plus ongoing costs of defending America. Debt raises Fiscal Pressure, which raises the Tax Burden on Colonies (Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act), whose revenue pays the debt down. Viewed from London this is a sensible goal-seeking loop. But it has a side effect: because Colonial Representation in Parliament is zero, the Representation Deficit converts every shilling of tax into Perceived Tax Injustice rather than mere expense. This is the classic fixes that fail structure — the cure for the debt generated the grievance.

Loop 2 (Reinforcing): Defiance and repression spiral

Colonial Grievance drives Colonial Resistance (boycotts, Stamp Act riots, the Boston Tea Party). Resistance provokes British Coercion (the Intolerable Acts closing Boston's port), which generates still more grievance. Each turn of this loop makes the next turn sharper; no concession is offered because Parliament's response strength is set by its claim to sovereignty.

Loop 3 (Reinforcing): Coercion forged an American identity

Coercion aimed at one colony taught all thirteen that they shared a fate, so it feeds Colonial Unity — committees of correspondence, Sons of Liberty, the Continental Congress. Because resistance is the product of grievance and unity, growing unity multiplies the effectiveness of anger, provoking more coercion and more unity. This is why punishing Boston produced a continental movement instead of an isolated surrender.

Loop 4 (Reinforcing): Occupation, bloodshed, and propaganda

Enforcing coercion required soldiers, so Troops in Colonies rises toward the level London desires. Troops among defiant civilians produce Violent Incidents — the Boston Massacre of 1770. A graphical Propaganda Amplification relationship (normalized so that ordinary incident levels give a multiplier of one, rising steeply as killings mount) captures how printers and engravers magnified five deaths into continental outrage, which feeds both grievance and unity, which draws in more troops.

The outcome

Armed Hostilities accumulates only when armed resistance and armed enforcement coexist: the flow is the product of resistance and coercion, which is why nothing happens for years and then Lexington and Concord happen very quickly. Grievance never resets to zero, so the repeal of the Stamp Act and the Townshend duties only slowed the loops rather than reversing them.

Modeling notes

  • Grievance, unity and troops are stocks because they accumulate history; resistance, coercion and tax burden are auxiliaries because they are computed instantaneously from those stocks.
  • Troop Deployment is the only bidirectional flow (withdrawals are possible); births-like one-way processes such as grievance formation, coercion-driven unity building and the outbreak of fighting are constrained to be non-negative.
  • All empirical magnitudes (debt size, garrison size, response strength, propaganda effect) are named constants rather than numbers buried in equations, so each assumption can be challenged separately.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: The accumulated imperial debt left by the French and Indian War (1754-63) plus ongoing costs of defending North America. This debt is the origin of the whole story: it is what pushed Parliament to tax the colonies.

variables.name: Initial War Debt
variables.documentation: Approximate size of the British national debt at the close of the French and Indian War, the starting condition of the model.

variables.name: Annual Imperial Defense Cost
variables.documentation: Recurring cost of garrisoning and administering the North American empire, which keeps adding to the debt.

variables.name: Imperial Defense Spending
variables.documentation: Ongoing spending that adds to the debt stock.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Revenue raised from the colonies (Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act) applied against the debt. This is the corrective action Parliament took.

variables.name: Reference War Debt
variables.documentation: Benchmark debt level used to express fiscal pressure as a dimensionless index.

variables.name: Fiscal Pressure
variables.documentation: How urgently the Treasury feels it must raise revenue, expressed relative to the postwar benchmark debt.

variables.name: Reference Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The revenue Parliament sought from the colonies under normal fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Tax Burden on Colonies
variables.documentation: Taxes and duties actually levied on the colonies. It rises with fiscal pressure, which is why new taxes kept appearing after 1763.

variables.name: Colonial Representation in Parliament
variables.documentation: Fraction of colonial consent embodied in Parliament. It is zero, which is the whole meaning of 'no taxation without representation'.

variables.name: Representation Deficit
variables.documentation: The legitimacy gap: taxes imposed without colonial consent. This multiplier converts an ordinary tax into a constitutional grievance.

variables.name: Grievance Sensitivity to Taxation
variables.documentation: How much resentment each unit of unconsented taxation generates per year.

variables.name: Perceived Tax Injustice
variables.documentation: Resentment generated by taxation, which only bites because the colonists had no voice in Parliament.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: The accumulated store of colonial resentment against British rule. Grievance is a stock because it builds up over a decade of episodes and only slowly fades.

variables.name: Grievance Formation
variables.documentation: New resentment created each year by taxes, coercive laws such as the Intolerable Acts, and bloodshed such as the Boston Massacre.

variables.name: Grievance Fading Time
variables.documentation: Average time for anger to cool when nothing new happens (as during the calm after the Townshend repeal).

variables.name: Grievance Fading
variables.documentation: Gradual cooling of resentment over time.

variables.name: Colonial Unity
variables.documentation: The shared American identity and inter-colonial organization (Sons of Liberty, committees of correspondence, Continental Congress). It accumulates as colonies discover a common cause.

variables.name: Unity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: How quickly shared outrage is converted into durable inter-colonial organization and identity.

variables.name: Unity Building
variables.documentation: Coercive acts aimed at one colony (closing the port of Boston) and shared atrocities taught all thirteen colonies to see themselves as one people.

variables.name: Unity Decay Time
variables.documentation: Time over which inter-colonial solidarity would dissolve back into local loyalties without reinforcement.

variables.name: Unity Erosion
variables.documentation: Slow decay of shared identity in the absence of new common causes.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Active defiance: boycotts, Stamp Act riots, the Boston Tea Party, militia drilling. It requires both anger and the organization to act on it, so it is the product of grievance and unity.

variables.name: Coercion Response Strength
variables.documentation: Parliament's determination to answer defiance with punishment rather than concession, reflecting its insistence on sovereignty.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: Punitive legislation and enforcement, above all the Intolerable Acts that closed Boston's port after the Tea Party.

variables.name: Normal Garrison
variables.documentation: Peacetime level of regular troops stationed in North America, used as the baseline for troop presence.

variables.name: Desired Troops
variables.documentation: The garrison London believes it needs to enforce its laws; it grows with each coercive measure (troops quartered in Boston, Gage's army).

variables.name: Deployment Time
variables.documentation: Time required to ship and station reinforcements across the Atlantic.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Net adjustment of the garrison toward the desired level; it can be negative when troops are withdrawn, so it is bidirectional.

variables.name: Troops in Colonies
variables.documentation: Redcoats actually present in the colonies. Their daily friction with townspeople is what turned political dispute into bloodshed.

variables.name: Incident Frequency
variables.documentation: Baseline rate of violent confrontations when a normal garrison meets normal levels of defiance.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Clashes between soldiers and civilians, such as the Boston Massacre of 1770. They require both soldiers on the streets and crowds willing to defy them.

variables.name: Propaganda Amplification
variables.documentation: How strongly patriot printers and engravers magnified bloodshed into political meaning. At normal incident levels the multiplier is one; as killings mount, each one is amplified far more, as with Revere's engraving of the Massacre.

variables.name: Outrage per Incident
variables.documentation: Resentment generated by a single violent confrontation before propaganda amplification.

variables.name: Outrage from Violence
variables.documentation: Anger produced by bloodshed once it has been publicized throughout the colonies.

variables.name: Escalation Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which simultaneous defiance and repression convert into actual armed engagement.

variables.name: Outbreak of Fighting
variables.documentation: The step from political defiance to shooting, which happens only when armed resistance and armed enforcement meet, as at Lexington and Concord in 1775.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Accumulated open warfare between colonists and Crown forces: the outcome variable of the model.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains road rage

Road rage is represented as an accumulation of recent incidents that drivers commit, witness and remember. Incidents are generated by a per-driver propensity that is amplified by four kinds of pressure taken from your background material: driver stress (psychological), the prevailing norm of aggressive driving (learned behavior), impairment (fatigue, sleep loss, distraction) and personality composition — and damped by enforcement and awareness. Congestion, road design and weather enter through the stress channel.

Four stocks carry the dynamics because each of these things builds and unwinds slowly rather than instantly: incidents, driver stress, the aggressive-driving norm, and enforcement capacity. Congestion is also a stock since queues form and clear over time.

The four feedback loops

R1 — Retaliation spiral (reinforcing). Incidents → perceived provocations (being cut off, tailgated, honked at) → anger and stress → more incidents. This is the fast loop that turns one rude manoeuvre into a chain of retaliations.

R2 — Normalization of aggression (reinforcing, slow). Incidents → drivers observe and imitate aggression → the aggressive-driving norm strengthens → more incidents, and also more everyday provocation feeding R1. Because the norm decays slowly, this loop is what makes a temporary surge become the new baseline — a classic eroding-goals pattern, since the reference level against which society judges the problem also anchors what counts as "normal".

R3 — Congestion trap (reinforcing). Incidents → crashes, blockages and rubbernecking → more congestion and delay → frustration and impatience → more incidents. Poor road design and bad weather make this loop stronger by pushing congestion up for the same demand.

B1 — Enforcement and awareness (balancing, delayed). Incidents → public and political pressure → enforcement/education capacity → deterrence → fewer incidents. This is the only correcting loop, and it has a long response delay, so it acts late and tends to be withdrawn once the problem quiets down — producing overshoot and recurrence rather than a stable fix.

What this implies for the future

The system starts in balance. Any sustained push — rising traffic demand, worse weather, more phone use, or a stress shock in society — is first absorbed by stress, then locked in by the normalization loop, and amplified by the congestion trap, while the enforcement loop responds only after months. So road rage tends to ratchet upward in steps and to resist quick correction. The highest-leverage interventions are the ones that weaken the reinforcing loops rather than chase the symptom: reducing congestion through road design and demand management (R3), cutting impairment and distraction, and de-normalizing aggression with continuous rather than episodic enforcement and public campaigns (weakening R2 and preventing B1 from being switched off).

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The prevalence of recent aggressive-driving/road rage incidents circulating in the driving population. Modeled as a stock because incidents accumulate and stay salient (witnessed, retold, reported) for a while before fading. Initialized at the reference level so the system starts in balance.

variables.name: Incident Onset
variables.equation: Driving_Population * Base_Incident_Propensity * Stress_Effect_On_Incidents * Aggressive_Driving_Norm * Deterrence_Effect * Driver_Impairment * Aggressive_Personality_Prevalence
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents occur. It is the exposed driving population times a base propensity, amplified or damped by driver stress, the prevailing norm of aggressive driving, deterrence from enforcement, impairment (fatigue and distraction) and the share of impulsive/hostile personalities. Uniflow because incidents cannot occur at a negative rate.

variables.name: Incident Resolution
variables.documentation: Rate at which incidents are resolved and fade from immediate experience and memory. A simple first-order decay of the incident stock over its persistence time.

variables.name: Incident Persistence Time
variables.documentation: Average time an incident remains salient (being witnessed, discussed, blocking traffic, or provoking retaliation) before it fades.

variables.name: Driving Population
variables.documentation: Number of active drivers exposed to traffic conditions; the population at risk of committing a road rage act.

variables.name: Base Incident Propensity
variables.documentation: Baseline monthly chance that a driver commits an aggressive act under normal stress, normal norms and normal enforcement.

variables.name: Aggressive Personality Prevalence
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of the share of drivers with impulsive, hostile or competitive personality traits. Held exogenous because personality composition changes only over generations, but it scales the whole incident rate.

variables.name: Driver Impairment
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of fatigue, sleep loss and distracted driving (phones, texting, eating). Impairment degrades judgment and increases both the chance of provoking others and of reacting aggressively.

variables.name: Relative Incident Level
variables.documentation: Incident prevalence expressed relative to the historically normal level, so all downstream effects can be written as dimensionless multipliers around 1.

variables.name: Reference Incident Level
variables.documentation: The incident prevalence society treats as normal; used to normalize perception, enforcement pressure and social learning.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Index of how often a typical driver feels cut off, tailgated or honked at. It rises both with the number of incidents on the road and with how aggressively driving is normally done.

variables.name: Provocation Stress Effect
variables.documentation: How much perceived provocation raises anger and stress. Normalized so that normal provocation (1) yields a normal stress multiplier (1), with saturating growth as provocation becomes frequent.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress, anger and impatience carried by the average driver. Modeled as a stock because psychological arousal builds up and unwinds gradually rather than instantly tracking conditions.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment
variables.documentation: Net gradual movement of driver stress toward the pressure created by current driving conditions. Bidirectional (not uniflow) because stress can relieve as well as build.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time for driver stress to adapt to prevailing conditions; the psychological build-up and recovery time.

variables.name: Stress Pressure
variables.documentation: The level of stress that current conditions would eventually produce: everyday life stress amplified by congestion frustration, provocation from other drivers, and adverse weather.

variables.name: Baseline Stress
variables.documentation: Background stress and anxiety drivers bring from outside the traffic system (work, money, time pressure). Normal = 1.

variables.name: Weather Severity Index
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of adverse weather such as heavy rain or snow, which both slows traffic and makes driving more demanding and stressful.

variables.name: Congestion Frustration Effect
variables.documentation: How stop-and-go conditions and delay translate into frustration and impatience. Passes through (1,1) so normal congestion gives normal stress, and rises steeply once traffic exceeds normal.

variables.name: Stress Effect On Incidents
variables.documentation: Multiplier on incident onset from driver stress and anger. Normalized at (1,1) with a convex shape, reflecting that highly stressed drivers are disproportionately likely to lash out.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Index of congestion, delay and stop-and-go conditions on the network (normal = 1). Treated as a stock because queues build and dissipate over time rather than instantly.

variables.name: Congestion Adjustment
variables.documentation: Net build-up or clearing of congestion toward the level implied by demand, road design, weather and incident blockages. Bidirectional because queues both form and clear.

variables.name: Congestion Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time for congestion to build up or clear toward the level implied by current conditions.

variables.name: Target Congestion
variables.documentation: The congestion level current conditions imply: travel demand relative to road capacity, worsened by incident blockages and bad weather, improved by good road design (wide lanes, clear intersections).

variables.name: Baseline Congestion Pressure
variables.documentation: Underlying travel demand relative to road capacity, normal = 1. Rising vehicle numbers or trip-making would raise this.

variables.name: Road Design Quality
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of road design adequacy: lane width, merge geometry, intersection clarity. Better design absorbs the same demand with less congestion.

variables.name: Blockage Effect From Incidents
variables.documentation: How aggressive driving, near misses and crashes add lane blockages and rubbernecking, worsening congestion. Passes through (1,1) so normal incident levels imply normal congestion.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of how socially normalized aggressive driving has become. Modeled as a stock because learned behavior accumulates through repeated observation and decays only slowly when aggression becomes rare.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Strengthening of the aggressive-driving norm through witnessing and imitating aggressive behavior. Proportional to how common incidents currently are.

variables.name: Norm Erosion
variables.documentation: Gradual fading of the aggressive-driving norm as drivers turn over and aggression is not reinforced.

variables.name: Norm Adoption Rate
variables.documentation: Strength of social learning: how fast observed aggression is absorbed into accepted driving practice.

variables.name: Norm Fading Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive-driving norm decays absent reinforcement. Set equal to the adoption rate so normal incident levels sustain a normal norm.

variables.name: Enforcement Capacity
variables.documentation: Index (normal = 1) of enforcement, education and public-awareness capacity aimed at aggressive driving. A stock because policing and campaign capacity is built and dismantled slowly.

variables.name: Enforcement Adjustment
variables.documentation: Net build-up or draw-down of enforcement capacity toward what the perceived severity of the problem justifies. Bidirectional because capacity is also withdrawn when the problem seems solved.

variables.name: Enforcement Response Delay
variables.documentation: Time for political attention, budgets and patrols to respond to a change in the road rage problem. The long delay is why the corrective loop tends to act late.

variables.name: Desired Enforcement
variables.documentation: Enforcement effort society wants, driven by how bad road rage appears relative to the accepted norm.

variables.name: Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier on incident onset from enforcement and awareness. Declining and passing through (1,1): normal enforcement gives normal incidents, more enforcement suppresses them with diminishing returns.

testParams.name: include a maximum number of feedback loops and a maximum number of variables for American Revolution
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The story as feedback, not a list of causes

The listed causes (French and Indian War debt, the Stamp Act, the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, the Intolerable Acts, colonial identity) are not independent causes — they are successive turns of the same escalating spiral. The model captures that with five variables and four reinforcing loops.

Stocks (things that accumulate and remember):

  • Colonial Grievance — resentment built up by taxation without representation and by bloodshed. Its initial value stands for the post-1763 situation where Britain, deep in war debt, demanded the colonies pay for their own defense.
  • American Colonial Identity — the slowly accumulating sense of being one American people.

Auxiliaries (present-moment conditions): Colonial Resistance is the product of grievance and identity — anger alone yields riots, but anger plus shared identity yields organized boycotts and congresses. British Coercion is a saturating response to resistance: London answered every challenge to sovereignty more harshly (troops in Boston, the port closed), but its reach across the Atlantic had limits.

Flow: Escalation of Conflict is the incident rate — the geometric mean of coercion and resistance, so a confrontation requires both a defiant colonial act and a forceful British answer. If either side had stood down, no new outrage would have been manufactured. It feeds both stocks.

The four reinforcing loops (all vicious escalation loops):

  1. Grievance → Resistance → Coercion → Escalation → Grievance. The classic repression spiral: taxes provoke protest, protest brings troops, troops kill five men in Boston, the Massacre becomes propaganda that deepens anger.
  2. Grievance → Resistance → Escalation → Grievance. Colonial provocations (destroying the tea) themselves generate the confrontations that harden opinion.
  3. Identity → Resistance → Coercion → Escalation → Identity. Punishing Boston with the Intolerable Acts taught all thirteen colonies that any of them could be next, forging union.
  4. Identity → Resistance → Escalation → Identity. Coordinated defiance created shared experience, which created more capacity for coordinated defiance.

Because every loop is reinforcing and none of the balancing mechanisms (repeal, representation, negotiated debt settlement) is present in the structure, the system has no way to settle. Britain's coercion saturates while colonial resistance keeps compounding — which is why the escalation ends at Lexington and Concord rather than at a compromise. The policy implication is that hostilities were not caused by any single act but by the absence of a balancing loop: colonial representation in Parliament, or genuine repeal, would have drained the grievance stock and broken the spiral.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Spiral Behind Revolutionary Hostilities

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: The accumulated stock of colonial anger at British rule: war-debt taxes such as the Stamp Act and Townshend duties levied without colonial representation, the Boston Massacre, and the Intolerable Acts. It is a stock because grievance is remembered and accumulates over time; it only changes through escalating incidents. Its initial value represents the resentment already present at the end of the French and Indian War, when Britain began demanding that the colonies pay for their own defense.

variables.name: American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulated sense of being American rather than British, including inter-colonial solidarity expressed through committees of correspondence, the Continental Congress, and shared support for besieged Boston. It is a stock because identity is built up slowly by shared experience of conflict and does not decay quickly.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: The current level of organized colonial defiance: petitions, non-importation boycotts, tarring of tax collectors, the Boston Tea Party, and finally militia mustering. It is the product of grievance and identity because anger only becomes effective collective action when colonists see themselves as one people with a common cause.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: Britain's coercive response to defiance: stationing troops in Boston, new revenue acts, closing the port of Boston, altering the Massachusetts charter, and finally sending regulars to seize colonial arms. Modeled as a graphical function of resistance that rises steeply at first and then saturates, because Parliament felt compelled to reassert sovereignty against every challenge but had limited means to project force across the Atlantic. Normal resistance (1) produces normal coercion (1).

variables.name: Escalation of Conflict
variables.documentation: The rate at which each confrontation between colonial defiance and British coercion adds new grievance and new shared identity: the Stamp Act riots, the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts that answered it, and Lexington and Concord. It is the geometric mean of coercion and resistance because an incident requires both a defiant colonial act and a forceful British answer; if either side stands down, no new outrage is created.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model keeps a single accumulation, Road Rage Incidents, an index of how much aggressive driving is circulating in society (1 = today's normal). It is filled by an Escalation Rate and drained by a Calming Rate. Two auxiliaries carry the causal story: Traffic Congestion (situational and environmental pressure: road design, demand, weather, plus disruption caused by rage itself) and Driver Stress (the psychological channel: impatience, hostility, fatigue, and learned aggressive norms).

Simple sums such as stress and congestion are auxiliaries, not stocks, because they are computed algebraically each moment rather than accumulated. Both are normalized so that normal inputs give a value of 1, and at that point escalation exactly balances calming — the system sits in equilibrium unless something pushes it.

The four feedback loops

R1 – Provocation and imitation (reinforcing). Incidents → Driver Stress → Escalation Rate → Incidents. Every act of aggression is a provocation to someone else and a lesson to onlookers that this is how you drive. Retaliation and learned behavior make rage self-propagating.

R2 – Rage makes the jam that makes the rage (reinforcing). Incidents → Traffic Congestion → Driver Stress → Escalation Rate → Incidents. Aggressive driving causes crashes, hard braking and blocked lanes; the resulting delay raises impatience, which produces more aggression. This is the vicious-cycle engine behind long-run growth in incidents.

B1 – Cooling off and deterrence (balancing). Incidents → Calming Rate → Incidents. Tempers subside, trips end, enforcement and social disapproval bite. This drain is proportional to the stock and is what normally holds road rage at a stable level.

B2 – The gridlock brake (balancing). Incidents → Traffic Congestion → Escalation Rate (negatively) → Incidents. Total gridlock leaves no room to speed, weave or tailgate, so extreme congestion mechanically suppresses some aggressive acts even while it raises anger.

What this implies for the future

As long as the cooling-off loop B1 and the gridlock brake B2 outweigh the two reinforcing loops, incidents return to normal after any shock. But the reinforcing loops strengthen with anything that makes stress more responsive — chronic fatigue, distraction, tighter schedules, or a culture that normalizes aggression. The structure is an escalation / vicious cycle archetype: past a tipping point, rage-induced congestion and imitation outrun cooling off, and incidents grow steadily rather than settling. Leverage lies in weakening the reinforcing links (calming baseline stress, better road design so congestion is not attributed to other drivers, reducing exposure to modeled aggression) rather than only strengthening enforcement, which merely speeds the drain while the source keeps refilling.

variables.name: Escalation Rate

variables.name: Traffic Congestion

variables.name: Driver Stress

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and at least 8 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains the outbreak of war

The story is built as an escalation structure: an external shock (the French and Indian War) loads a debt stock, and the attempts to service that debt set off several mutually reinforcing loops that the few balancing loops in the system could not hold.

Stocks (things that accumulate memory and capability): British War Debt, Colonial Grievance, Colonial Identity, Coercive Acts in Force, British Troops in Colonies, Militia Readiness, and Armed Hostilities. Everything else is a rate or an algebraic auxiliary. Note that aggregates such as Perceived Colonial Defiance and Colonial Resistance Activity are auxiliaries, not stocks, because they are computed sums/products rather than accumulations.

Reinforcing loops (the escalation engine)

  1. Tax–resistance–revenue trap (R1): Debt → tax demands → grievance (magnified because the colonies had no representation) → resistance (boycotts, smuggling, intimidating stamp officers) → collapsing compliance → less revenue → debt stays high → still heavier demands. Britain's attempt to solve the problem made the problem worse — the classic "fixes that fail."
  2. Coercion spiral (R2): Resistance → perceived defiance in London → new punitive laws (Stamp Act, Coercive/Intolerable Acts, closing Boston's port) → fresh grievance → more resistance. Escalation between two adversaries.
  3. Occupation and bloodshed (R3): Perceived defiance → troops sent to Boston → soldiers and crowds in the same streets → violent incidents such as the Boston Massacre → propaganda and outrage → more resistance → more troops.
  4. Identity loop (R4): Resisting together built committees of correspondence, non-importation networks and congresses, i.e., an American identity; a stronger identity converted the same grievance into far more effective continental resistance. This is the growth loop that turned local riots into a revolution.
  5. Militarization / arms race (R5): Resistance → militia arming and powder stores → this arming itself reads as defiance → more regulars sent → armed militia and regulars in contact → open fighting at Lexington and Concord → new grievance and further mobilization. Once this loop closed, hostilities were self-sustaining.
  6. Cost of empire (R6): Troops in America → enforcement costs → larger debt → still heavier taxes → more grievance. Coercion financed itself by deepening the grievance it was meant to suppress.

Balancing loops (why it took twelve years, and why they failed)

  1. Merchant lobby / repeal loop (B1): Boycotts hurt British exporters → lobbying → repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties → sudden grievance relief. This loop repeatedly cooled the crisis, but it only removes acts, not the accumulated grievance stock or the identity and militia stocks, so each cycle left the colonies more organized than before.
  2. Debt repayment loop (B2): Revenue collected retires debt and reduces the need to tax — but this loop is disabled by the very resistance the taxes create, so it never gains strength.
  3. Decay loops: grievance fading, garrison rotation and militia demobilization provide the only other restraint; their time constants are far too slow relative to the escalation loops.

Why hostilities broke out

War requires two armed parties in contact. Hostilities in this model can only start when the militia stock and the troop stock are both large, which happens only after grievance, identity and coercion have each accumulated for a decade. The Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts are the point where the balancing repeal loop is abandoned in favour of coercion, letting the reinforcing loops run unchecked into Lexington and Concord.

Formulation notes

  • No conditional statements are used anywhere; escalation emerges from stock accumulation and two normalized nonlinear relationships (tax compliance versus resistance, and resistance effectiveness versus identity), both passing through (1,1).
  • All numeric parameters are named variables (e.g., Representation Deficit, Friction Coefficient, Confrontation Propensity) rather than constants buried in equations.
  • All one-directional processes (grievance formation, enactment, repeal, deployment, withdrawal, mobilization, outbreak, borrowing, repayment) are marked as one-way flows so they cannot run backwards; no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated Crown debt, driven up first by the French and Indian War (1754-1763) and then by the cost of garrisoning and policing America. This debt is the root pressure that made Parliament tax the colonies.

variables.name: Debt Accumulation
variables.documentation: New borrowing each year: wartime military spending plus the recurring cost of keeping troops and customs enforcement in the colonies.

variables.name: War Spending
variables.documentation: Time-shaped military expenditure for the French and Indian War, rising to a peak around 1760 and ending in 1763. It is the exogenous trigger of the whole story.

variables.name: Enforcement Cost
variables.documentation: Annual cost of maintaining the standing garrison in America. Coercion is expensive, so it feeds back into the debt that motivated taxation in the first place.

variables.name: Cost per Troop
variables.documentation: Average annual cost of maintaining one thousand troops in North America.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Debt actually retired, equal to the tax revenue Britain manages to collect from the colonies. Because collection depends on colonial compliance, resistance directly blocks debt relief.

variables.name: Taxation Effort
variables.documentation: Fraction of outstanding debt that Parliament attempts to raise each year from the colonies through measures like the Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend duties and Tea Act.

variables.name: Tax Burden
variables.documentation: Amount of tax Parliament demands from the colonies each year. The larger the debt, the heavier the demand.

variables.name: Normal Resistance Level
variables.documentation: Reference level of ordinary colonial political friction, used to normalize resistance before it enters the compliance relationship.

variables.name: Relative Resistance
variables.documentation: Colonial resistance expressed as a multiple of normal political friction; the input to the tax compliance function.

variables.name: Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Multiplier on tax collection. At normal resistance (input 1) collection is normal (output 1); as boycotts, smuggling, tarring of collectors and non-importation agreements spread, collection collapses toward zero.

variables.name: Tax Revenue Collected
variables.documentation: Revenue Britain actually receives. Demanding more while compliance falls is the core frustration that pushed Parliament toward coercion.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial anger over taxation without representation, coercive legislation, military occupation and bloodshed. It is a memory stock, not an instantaneous reaction, which is why repeals never fully erased the resentment.

variables.name: Grievance Formation
variables.equation: Tax_Burden * Representation_Deficit + Coercive_Acts_in_Force * Coercion_Grievance_Weight + (Violent_Incident_Rate + Armed_Hostilities) * Violence_Grievance_Weight
variables.documentation: New grievance created each year by taxes levied without colonial representation, by coercive laws such as the Intolerable Acts, and by violence such as the Boston Massacre and open fighting.

variables.name: Representation Deficit
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of tax demanded, reflecting that the colonies had no members in Parliament. Without this constitutional objection the same taxes would have produced far less anger.

variables.name: Coercion Grievance Weight
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per year by each coercive act in force, such as closing Boston harbour or quartering troops.

variables.name: Violence Grievance Weight
variables.documentation: Grievance generated by each violent incident or unit of open fighting. Bloodshed was amplified by pamphlets and engravings, making it a powerful propaganda input.

variables.name: Grievance Relief
variables.documentation: Grievance that dissipates, either by slow forgetting or suddenly when Parliament backs down, as with the repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties.

variables.name: Grievance Fade Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which unaddressed grievance fades from public memory.

variables.name: Repeal Relief Strength
variables.documentation: Grievance removed per act repealed, representing the calming effect of British concessions.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Accumulated sense of a shared American people, built by committees of correspondence, boycott networks, congresses and joint suffering. It converts local complaints into coordinated continental action.

variables.name: Baseline Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Pre-1763 level of shared colonial self-consciousness, used as the initial value and as the normalization reference.

variables.name: Identity Strengthening
variables.documentation: Acting together in resistance builds intercolonial trust, shared symbols and institutions, so identity grows out of the struggle itself.

variables.name: Solidarity Effect
variables.documentation: Identity built per unit of joint resistance activity per year.

variables.name: Identity Fading
variables.documentation: Slow erosion of common identity when there is no shared cause, reflecting the colonies' habitual provincial rivalries.

variables.name: Identity Fade Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which shared identity weakens in the absence of reinforcing action.

variables.name: Relative Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Identity relative to its pre-war baseline, used as the normalized input to the resistance effectiveness function.

variables.name: Identity Effect on Resistance
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how a stronger American identity turns the same grievance into far more organized resistance. At baseline identity (input 1) the multiplier is 1.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance Activity
variables.documentation: Intensity of colonial protest: petitions, mobs, non-importation, smuggling, destruction of tea. It is grievance amplified by organizational identity.

variables.name: Coercive Acts in Force
variables.documentation: Number of punitive British measures currently in force, from the Stamp Act through the Coercive or Intolerable Acts that closed Boston's port.

variables.name: Act Enactment
variables.documentation: Rate at which Parliament passes new punitive legislation, driven by its perception that colonial defiance must be met with firmness to preserve sovereignty.

variables.name: Coercion Propensity
variables.documentation: Parliament's willingness to answer each unit of perceived defiance with new coercive law.

variables.name: Act Repeal
variables.documentation: Rate of repeal, which historically happened when British merchants hurt by boycotts lobbied Parliament, as with the Stamp Act in 1766.

variables.name: Repeal Responsiveness
variables.documentation: How quickly Parliament yields to commercial lobbying pressure.

variables.name: British Merchant Pressure
variables.documentation: Lobbying pressure from British merchants and manufacturers whose exports collapse under colonial non-importation agreements.

variables.name: Trade Disruption Effect
variables.documentation: Commercial damage in Britain generated per unit of colonial resistance, chiefly through boycotts.

variables.name: British Troops in Colonies
variables.documentation: Redcoats stationed in America, quartered in cities such as Boston after 1768. Their presence both enforces British authority and creates daily friction with civilians.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Reinforcements sent to overawe the colonies, increasing with perceived defiance and colonial arming.

variables.name: Deployment Propensity
variables.documentation: Troops dispatched per unit of perceived colonial defiance per year.

variables.name: Troop Withdrawal
variables.documentation: Routine reduction and redeployment of the garrison, for example the removal of regiments from Boston after the Massacre.

variables.name: Garrison Rotation Time
variables.documentation: Average time a deployment remains in place before being withdrawn or rotated home.

variables.name: Friction Coefficient
variables.documentation: Likelihood of a violent street clash per unit of troop presence and resistance activity, the mechanism behind the Boston Massacre.

variables.name: Violent Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Rate of bloody confrontations between soldiers and crowds. Troops and angry crowds in the same streets make incidents like the 1770 Massacre nearly inevitable.

variables.name: Militia Readiness
variables.documentation: Armed and drilled colonial militia, minutemen, and stockpiled powder and shot. This is the capability that turned protest into the possibility of war.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Rate of arming, training and stockpiling by colonial committees of safety as resistance intensifies.

variables.name: Mobilization Propensity
variables.documentation: Militia capability created per unit of resistance activity per year.

variables.name: Militia Demobilization
variables.documentation: Militia losing readiness when the crisis cools, as men return to farms and drilling lapses.

variables.name: Militia Decay Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which militia readiness erodes without renewed alarm.

variables.name: Perceived Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: How rebellious the colonies look to London, combining open protest with visible arming. It is the trigger for both new coercive laws and new troops.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Accumulated open fighting, beginning with Lexington and Concord in April 1775. Once blood is shed at scale it feeds grievance and forecloses reconciliation.

variables.name: Hostility Outbreak
variables.documentation: Rate at which armed militia and British regulars actually collide, as when troops marched to seize colonial powder stores. War requires both sides armed and in contact.

variables.name: Confrontation Propensity
variables.documentation: Chance per year that armed militia and regulars in contact produce open fighting.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says about road rage

Road rage is treated not as an individual character flaw but as the output of a traffic system that keeps feeding back on itself. Six accumulations carry the story forward in time: traffic demand, road capacity, driver stress, the aggressive driving norm (learned behaviour), enforcement intensity, and the running total of incidents. Everything else is a rate or a multiplier attached to them.

Reinforcing loops that escalate incidents

R1 – Congestion breeds anger breeds congestion (crash spiral). Congestion raises stress pressure, stress raises aggression, aggression and distraction raise the crash rate, crashes block lanes, blocked lanes cut effective capacity, and congestion worsens. A classic vicious circle in which the anger the road produces comes back to clog the road.

R2 – Provocation and retaliation. The more normalised aggressive driving becomes, the more often each driver is cut off, tailgated or honked at. Perceived provocation both loads stress and directly triggers retaliation, which produces more incidents, which further normalises aggression.

R3 – Social learning. Every witnessed incident teaches onlookers that this is how people drive here. The norm stock rises, incidents rise, and the norm rises again. This loop is slow but very hard to reverse because the norm only fades over years.

R4 – Stress, sleep loss and fatigue. Chronic stress costs sleep; fatigue impairs judgement and self control, which raises both incidents and distraction; distraction raises crashes and congestion, which raises stress again.

R5 – Induced demand (a fixes that fail structure). Congestion triggers road building. New capacity temporarily relieves congestion, but free flowing roads attract new trips, demand grows back, and congestion returns – now with more vehicles and more potential conflicts than before. The engineering fix relieves the symptom and quietly strengthens the problem.

Balancing loops that hold it in check

B1 – Capacity relief. Congestion drives construction which lifts effective capacity and lowers congestion, at least in the short run.

B2 – Trip avoidance. Once congestion passes the point of tolerance, drivers retime, reroute or abandon trips, which relieves demand. This is the market's own brake on gridlock.

B3 – Enforcement and awareness. Rising incidents eventually change public perception (smoothed with a perception delay), which funds policing and campaigns, which deter aggression and reduce incidents. Because attention decays, enforcement erodes as soon as the problem looks solved – producing the familiar cycle of crackdown and relapse.

B4 – Stress recovery and B5 – Norm fading are the natural decay loops: tension unwinds with rest and learned habits fade without reinforcement. They are what any intervention has to work with.

Formulation choices worth noting

  • Cumulative incidents is an accumulation with a genuine flow, while totals such as effective capacity, congestion and stress pressure are algebraic auxiliaries rather than stocks.
  • Public perception uses a smoothing function, not a delay, because opinion averages recent experience.
  • All behavioural non‑linearities (stress to aggression, fatigue to aggression, provocation to retaliation, enforcement to deterrence, weather and distraction to crashes) are graphical functions normalised to pass through (1,1), so normal conditions produce normal behaviour and the curves express deviations in both directions.
  • Every numerical assumption – weights, sensitivities, time constants, weather and design quality – is an explicitly named variable so it can be argued about and tested.

Implication for the future

Because the reinforcing loops (learning, retaliation, crash‑congestion, fatigue, induced demand) act on slow stocks while the balancing loops act with delays, the expected trajectory is a gradual upward drift in incidents punctuated by enforcement crackdowns that fade. Building more road alone will not help; leverage lies in the stress and norm stocks – reducing time pressure and exposure, improving road design so the network delivers its capacity, clearing crashes fast, and sustaining rather than pulsing enforcement and social messaging.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Structure Driving Societal Road Rage
