variables.name: Travel Demand
variables.documentation: The number of vehicles trying to use the road network at peak times. It accumulates as trips are added (induced demand) and falls as drivers avoid or reschedule trips.

variables.name: Initial Travel Demand
variables.documentation: Starting level of peak travel demand on the network.

variables.name: Demand Growth
variables.documentation: New trips attracted to the road network. When roads feel free flowing (low congestion index) more people choose to drive - the classic induced demand response to added capacity.

variables.name: Demand Suppression
variables.documentation: Trips abandoned, retimed or shifted to other modes when driving becomes too congested. Only operates once demand exceeds effective capacity.

variables.name: Demand Growth Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly free flowing conditions attract additional driving each month.

variables.name: Trip Avoidance Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly congestion pushes drivers to give up or reschedule trips each month.

variables.name: Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Physical throughput of the road network, built up over time by construction and widening projects.

variables.name: Initial Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Starting physical throughput of the road network.

variables.name: Capacity Expansion
variables.documentation: Road building triggered by visible congestion. Political pressure to widen roads rises only when demand exceeds capacity.

variables.name: Capacity Investment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Fraction of existing capacity added per month per unit of congestion pressure.

variables.name: Road Design Quality
variables.documentation: How well lanes, merges and intersections are designed. Below one means poor geometry wastes part of the built capacity and creates friction points that frustrate drivers.

variables.name: Weather Severity Index
variables.documentation: Index of adverse weather (rain, snow, fog) with one representing normal conditions.

variables.name: Weather Capacity Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how bad weather slows traffic and reduces usable road capacity. Normal weather returns a multiplier of one.

variables.name: Effective Road Capacity
variables.documentation: The throughput actually available to drivers after design flaws, weather and crash blockages are taken into account.

variables.name: Congestion Index
variables.documentation: Ratio of demand to usable capacity. Values above one mean queueing, delay and stop and go conditions.

variables.name: Baseline Crash Fraction
variables.documentation: Crashes per hour generated by each unit of peak traffic under normal driving conditions.
variables.units: crashes per hour per vehicle per hour

variables.name: Crash Rate
variables.documentation: Collisions occurring per hour. Rises with traffic volume, with how normal aggressive driving has become, with distraction and with bad weather.

variables.name: Effect of Weather on Crashes
variables.documentation: Multiplier capturing how slippery, low visibility conditions raise crash risk. Normal weather gives one.

variables.name: Effect of Distraction on Crashes
variables.documentation: Multiplier translating phone use, texting and eating behind the wheel into extra crash risk. Normal distraction gives one.

variables.name: Blockage Per Crash
variables.documentation: Share of capacity lost per crash per hour while lanes are blocked and cleared.

variables.name: Max Blockage Fraction
variables.documentation: Upper bound on how much of the network can be blocked by incidents at once.

variables.name: Crash Blockage Fraction
variables.documentation: Portion of road capacity lost to crash scenes and rubbernecking, capped at a physical maximum.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Average accumulated stress and arousal carried by drivers in the population, indexed so that one is the normal level. It is a stock because tension builds up and takes time to dissipate.

variables.name: Stress Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which current driving conditions load stress onto drivers.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Natural unwinding of accumulated stress through rest and calm driving conditions.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Average time for driver stress to adjust toward the pressure imposed by conditions.

variables.name: Stress Pressure
variables.equation: Congestion_Stress_Weight * Congestion_Index + Provocation_Stress_Weight * Perceived_Provocation_Rate + Weather_Stress_Weight * Weather_Severity_Index + Baseline_Life_Stress
variables.documentation: The total stress load conditions place on drivers: delays, being cut off or tailgated, difficult weather, and stress carried in from the rest of life.

variables.name: Congestion Stress Weight
variables.documentation: Contribution of delay and stop and go traffic to driver stress.

variables.name: Provocation Stress Weight
variables.documentation: Contribution of perceived provocations by other drivers to driver stress.

variables.name: Weather Stress Weight
variables.documentation: Contribution of difficult weather to driver stress.

variables.name: Baseline Life Stress

variables.name: Perceived Provocation Rate

variables.name: Baseline Fatigue

variables.name: Fatigue Level

variables.name: Effect of Stress on Fatigue

variables.name: Baseline Distraction Level

variables.name: Distracted Driving Level

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement

variables.name: Norm Memory Time

variables.name: Enforcement Decay

variables.name: Enforcement Response Strength

variables.name: Enforcement Decay Time

variables.name: Public Perception Delay

variables.name: Perceived Incident Level
variables.documentation: Smoothed public view of how bad road rage has become. A smoothing function is used because perception averages recent experience rather than merely lagging it.

variables.name: Enforcement Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier by which visible enforcement and awareness suppress aggressive acts. Normal enforcement gives one, more enforcement gives less than one.

variables.name: Baseline Incident Fraction
variables.documentation: Road rage incidents generated each month per unit of peak traffic under fully normal psychological conditions.
variables.units: incidents per month per vehicle per hour

variables.name: Road Rage Incident Rate
variables.equation: Travel_Demand * Baseline_Incident_Fraction * Effect_of_Stress_on_Aggression * Aggressive_Driving_Norm * Effect_of_Fatigue_on_Aggression * Effect_of_Provocation_on_Retaliation * Enforcement_Deterrence_Effect
variables.documentation: Number of aggressive driving incidents occurring per month. It scales with exposure (traffic) and is multiplied up or down by stress, learned norms, fatigue, provocation and deterrence.

variables.name: Cumulative Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Running total of road rage incidents, used to track the societal burden over time.

variables.name: Reference Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Historically normal monthly incident rate against which current experience is judged.

variables.name: Relative Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Current incidents compared with the historic norm. This is what drivers witness and what the public reacts to.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and at least 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the Revolution emerged from feedback, not single events

The model treats the Revolution as the output of four interacting loops rather than a list of causes.

Core stocks (accumulations): War Debt (from the French and Indian War), Colonial Resentment, British Troop Presence, Colonial Unity, and Armed Hostilities. Resentment and unity are stocks because grievances and institutions persisted in memory and organization long after the provoking event; simple sums and indicators were kept as auxiliaries, not stocks.

B1 – Fiscal balancing loop (the trigger)

War debt raises Tax Burden (Stamp Act, Townshend duties), tax revenue repays debt, which lowers the pressure to tax. This is the goal-seeking loop that started the whole story: without the 1754–63 war debt there is no revenue drive.

R1 – Provocation and defiance escalation (reinforcing)

Tax Burden and each punitive act feed Grievance Accumulation → Colonial Resentment → Acts of Colonial Defiance (boycotts, the Boston Tea Party) → British Coercive Measures (the Intolerable Acts, closing Boston's port) → still more grievance. This is a classic escalation archetype: each side responds to the other's last move, so mild resistance in 1765 becomes revolution by 1775.

R2 – Military occupation loop (reinforcing)

Coercion requires enforcement, so troops are quartered in colonial towns. Soldiers plus defiant crowds produce Violent Confrontations — the Boston Massacre of 1770 — which generate propaganda and more resentment, more defiance, and hence more coercion and more troops. Repression intended to restore order manufactured the very disorder it was meant to suppress (a "fixes that fail" dynamic).

R3 – Shared threat builds American identity (reinforcing)

A saturating relationship converts coercion into Unity Building: punishing Massachusetts persuaded the other colonies their liberties were jointly at risk, producing committees of correspondence and the Continental Congresses. Unity then multiplies defiance, drawing further coercion. Identity is thus an effect of British policy that becomes a cause of resistance.

Why hostilities broke out

Outbreak of Fighting requires both a violent trigger and enough organizational capacity to sustain resistance — violent confrontations times colonial unity. Isolated riots (1765) did not become war; the same friction after a decade of accumulated resentment and continental organization did, at Lexington and Concord. The balancing fiscal loop was far too slow and weak to relieve pressure before the three reinforcing loops dominated.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Loops Turned Taxation Into Revolution

variables.name: Confrontation Friction

variables.name: Violent Confrontations

variables.name: Unity Erosion

variables.name: Colonial Unity

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and at least 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains future road rage

Road rage is treated as a rate produced by three slow-moving accumulations — the stock of driver stress, the stock of congestion, and the stock of the learned aggressive driving norm — pushed back on by a fourth stock, enforcement and awareness. Because incidents feed back into all four accumulations, the future path of road rage is driven by loop dominance rather than by any single cause.

Reinforcing loop R1 — Learned behaviour (norm escalation)

Incidents → norm reinforcement → Aggressive Driving Norm → perceived provocations → frustration → more incidents. This is the classic escalation / success-to-the-successful pattern applied to social norms: watching others drive aggressively legitimizes doing so. It is the slowest loop (a year-scale norm adjustment time), so it sets the long-run drift.

Reinforcing loop R2 — Incident-congestion spiral

Incidents → lane blockages and crashes → Traffic Congestion → frustration → more incidents. Aggression physically degrades the road system that then produces more aggression.

Reinforcing loop R3 — Stress spiral

Congestion and provocations → stress pressure → Driver Stress Level → incidents → more congestion and provocations. Fatigue, distraction and bad weather enter here as external loads that pre-charge this loop; they don't create the spiral but they set how hot it runs.

Balancing loop B1 — Delayed societal response

Incidents → public concern → Enforcement and Awareness → deterrence → fewer incidents. This is the only loop pulling the system back, and it acts with a multi-month delay and erodes when attention shifts. That delay is why road rage tends to overshoot: the response arrives after the norm and stress stocks have already been charged, and then decays before the norm has unwound.

What this implies for the future

At normal settings all four stocks sit in equilibrium and incidents stay at the reference level. A sustained push — rising traffic demand, worse road design, a stretch of bad weather, or more phone use and sleep loss — charges stress and congestion quickly, which the reinforcing loops amplify into an elevated incident level. The enforcement loop eventually bends the curve down, but because the aggressive-norm stock unwinds slowly, incidents settle at a permanently higher plateau than before the shock unless deterrence is sustained rather than pulsed. Leverage therefore lies in the slow stocks: reducing congestion pressure at the source and keeping enforcement and civility education continuous, so the learned-behaviour loop is starved rather than repeatedly fed.

Formulation choices

  • Total pressures (stress pressure, congestion pressure) are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are algebraic combinations.
  • Only genuine accumulations — stress, congestion, norms, enforcement — are stocks, each with a paired inflow and outflow so every feedback loop passes through an accumulation rather than forming an instantaneous algebraic loop.
  • All arbitrary magnitudes are named variables (adjustment times, impatience, weather, fatigue), and the three nonlinear relationships (blockage, public concern, deterrence) are graphical functions normalized to pass through the point (1,1).

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The rate of aggressive driving episodes in society, expressed as an index where 1 equals the historically normal level. It rises with accumulated driver stress, with momentary frustration on the road, and falls when enforcement and public awareness deter aggression.

variables.name: Driver Frustration
variables.documentation: The immediate sense of being blocked or wronged while driving. It is the average of provocations experienced and congestion endured, amplified by how impatient drivers are (schedule pressure, low tolerance for delay).

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often a typical driver feels cut off, tailgated or honked at. It grows both with how aggressive driving norms have become and with how densely packed traffic is, since congestion multiplies opportunities for contact between drivers.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The accumulated social norm of aggressive driving: what drivers have learned by watching others behave on the road. It is a stock because norms build up slowly through repeated observation and fade only slowly when aggression becomes rare.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which observed aggressive episodes teach and normalize aggression for other drivers.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive driving norm fades through forgetting, driver turnover and civility campaigns.

variables.name: Norm Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which social driving norms are learned and unlearned. Norms are the slowest-moving part of this system.

variables.name: Driver Stress Level
variables.documentation: The accumulated stress, anxiety and fatigue carried by the driving population. It is a stock because stress builds up over repeated bad commutes and dissipates only gradually through rest and recovery.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which daily driving conditions add to the pool of driver stress.

variables.name: Stress Relief
variables.documentation: Rate at which rest, sleep and calm periods drain accumulated stress.

variables.name: Stress Pressure
variables.documentation: The combined load of stressors acting on drivers: congestion, provocations by others, fatigue and distraction, and difficult weather. Averaging the four keeps the index comparable to the normal value of one.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time for driver stress to adjust to prevailing conditions; stress responds much faster than social norms.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: The prevailing level of traffic density, delay and stop-and-go conditions. Treated as a stock because queues and blockages accumulate and take time to dissipate after they form.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which travel demand, poor road design, weather and incident blockages create queues.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which queues dissipate once the blocking pressure eases.

variables.name: Congestion Pressure
variables.documentation: The forces creating congestion: how much traffic wants to move, how badly the road network is designed, how much weather degrades flow, and how much road rage related incidents block lanes.

variables.name: Congestion Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time for congestion levels to adjust to underlying pressures.

variables.name: Incident Blockage Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how collisions, confrontations and erratic manoeuvres caused by road rage physically block lanes and worsen congestion. Normal incident levels give a multiplier of one.

variables.name: Enforcement and Awareness
variables.documentation: Accumulated policing presence, penalties, driver education and public awareness aimed at aggressive driving. A stock because capability and public attention build and erode over time.

variables.name: Enforcement Investment

variables.name: Enforcement Erosion
variables.documentation: Rate at which enforcement effort and public attention fade as other priorities take over.

variables.name: Perceived Public Concern

variables.name: Enforcement Adjustment Time

variables.name: Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier on incidents from enforcement and awareness. Normal enforcement yields one; stronger enforcement suppresses incidents with diminishing returns, absent enforcement inflates them.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The story as feedback

The Revolution is modeled not as a list of causes but as an escalation system that ran away between 1763 and 1775. Four accumulations carry the history: British Debt (the legacy of the French and Indian War), Colonial Grievance, Colonial Unity, and British Coercion, with Armed Confrontation as the outcome.

Reinforcing loops (the engines of revolution)

R1 – Revenue frustration: Debt → Tax Burden → Grievance → Defiance → less Tax Revenue → debt stays high → still heavier taxes. Smuggling and boycotts meant the Stamp and Townshend duties never paid for themselves, so Parliament kept trying again.

R2 – Identity amplifier: Grievance → Unity → Grievance Formation. Committees of correspondence and propaganda (the engraving of the Boston Massacre) turned a local injury into a continental one, so shared identity made every new tax feel worse.

R3 – Provocation spiral (classic escalation archetype): Defiance → Coercion Escalation → Coercion → Grievance → Defiance. The Tea Party begets the Intolerable Acts, which beget the Continental Congress.

R4 – Coercion pays for itself in debt: Coercion → Enforcement Spending → Debt → Tax Burden → Grievance → Defiance → Coercion. Garrisoning America cost the very money the taxes were meant to raise — a self-defeating trap.

R5 – Punishment unifies: Coercion → Unity Building → Unity → Defiance → Coercion. Closing Boston's port persuaded Virginia and the rest that their liberties were next.

R6 – Arms race to war: Defiance + Coercion → Militia Mobilization → Armed Confrontation → more Coercion. Attempts to seize colonial powder produced Lexington and Concord, which produced full military response.

Balancing loops (why it might have cooled, and why it didn't)

B1 – Debt repayment: collected revenue reduces debt and hence the tax demanded. This loop was disabled by defiance.

B2 – Forgetting: grievance naturally fades (as after the Stamp Act repeal), but ongoing coercion — troops quartered in Boston, the closed port — suppresses that decay, which is why the 1774 crisis never cooled.

B3 – Saturating solidarity: unity can only grow until the colonies are fully united; once the Continental Congress existed, further coercion added no more unity, only more anger and arms.

Modeling notes

Total accumulations of resentment, identity, and force are stocks; the tax load, actual collections, and defiance are algebraic consequences of those stocks. Defiance is deliberately the product of grievance and unity: anger without organization produced riots, organization without anger produced nothing — only together did they produce a revolution. The model is normalized (indices around 1) so the structure, not calibrated numbers, carries the explanation.

variables.name: British Debt
variables.documentation: Normalized index of the Crown's imperial debt, starting at 1 to represent the large debt left by the French and Indian War (1754-63). It grows with the cost of garrisoning and policing America and falls only as colonial revenue is actually collected.

variables.name: Enforcement Spending
variables.documentation: Cost of troops, customs officers, warships and the occupation of Boston. The more coercion Britain applies, the more it must spend, which adds back to the debt it was trying to pay off.

variables.name: Tax Revenue
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected from the colonies. It is the intended tax burden degraded by defiance: smuggling, non-importation boycotts, intimidation of stamp distributors and destruction of tea all cut collections below what Parliament legislated.

variables.name: Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The tax load Parliament attempts to place on the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act). It is set by how much debt must be recovered over the intended recovery period.

variables.name: Debt Recovery Time
variables.documentation: The period over which the ministry wants the colonies to help retire the war debt. A shorter time means more aggressive taxation per year.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial anger at 'taxation without representation', standing armies, the Boston Massacre and the Intolerable Acts. It is a stock because resentment accumulates in memory, pamphlets and public ritual rather than resetting each year.

variables.name: Grievance Formation
variables.documentation: New grievance created each year by taxes and by coercive acts. Unity multiplies the effect because committees of correspondence and propaganda (for example Revere's engraving of the Boston Massacre) spread a local injury to every colony.

variables.name: Grievance Decay
variables.documentation: Cooling of tempers over time, as happened after the repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties. Ongoing coercion (troops in Boston, the closed port) suppresses this forgetting, keeping grievance alive.

variables.name: Colonial Unity
variables.documentation: Shared American identity and inter-colonial organization: the Stamp Act Congress, committees of correspondence, the Continental Congress. Scaled 0 to 1 where 1 is full continental solidarity.

variables.name: Unity Building
variables.documentation: Rate at which grievance and especially collective punishment (closing Boston's port) convert separate colonies into a single political community. The remaining-room term keeps unity from exceeding complete solidarity.

variables.name: Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: Active resistance: smuggling, boycotts, tarring customs men, the Boston Tea Party. It requires both anger and the organization to act on it, so it is the product of grievance and unity.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: Accumulated apparatus of force and punishment: Quartering Acts, troops in Boston, vice-admiralty courts, the Coercive or Intolerable Acts, and the port closure. Once established these measures persist.

variables.name: Coercion Escalation
variables.documentation: Britain hardens its stance in response to acts of defiance, to the shortfall between taxes legislated and taxes collected, and to armed clashes. This is the classic 'assert authority' response of an empire whose sovereignty is being tested.

variables.name: Armed Confrontation
variables.documentation: Accumulated armed capacity and open fighting: minutemen, seized powder, Lexington and Concord, Bunker Hill. This is the outcome variable representing hostilities breaking out.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Rate at which defiant, unified colonists arm and drill. It requires both the will to resist and the visible military threat of occupation and attempts to seize colonial arms.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says

Road rage is treated not as an individual failing but as the output of three accumulations that feed each other: Traffic Congestion, Driver Frustration (the pool of accumulated anger) and the Aggressive Driving Norm (learned, socially normalised aggression). Incidents are the product of anger available and the willingness to express it.

Reinforcing loops (the escalation engines)

  1. Retaliation spiral (R1) – aggressive norm → more drivers cut off and tailgated → provocations → frustration → incidents → witnessing normalises aggression → stronger norm. This is the classic escalation archetype: each side's aggression is justified by the other's.
  2. Rage causes jams (R2) – incidents → crashes, brake checks and roadside confrontations block lanes → congestion → stress → frustration → more incidents.
  3. Congestion provocation loop (R3) – congestion also multiplies close vehicle interactions → more perceived provocations → more anger → more incidents → more blockages → more congestion.

Balancing loops (the brakes)

  1. Enforcement response (B1) – rising incidents eventually trigger policing, penalties and campaigns, which erode the aggressive norm and pull incidents down. It is deliberately non‑linear: society barely reacts until road rage becomes visibly serious, so the correction arrives late.
  2. Cooling off (B2) – frustration naturally decays with rest and leaving traffic.
  3. Queue clearing (B3) – congestion drains as vehicles get through.
  4. Trip deferral (B4) – when roads jam, people cancel or retime optional trips, relieving pressure. A shifting the burden risk lives here: relieving congestion by adding capacity would restore trip making instead of curing anger.
  5. Norm forgetting (B5) – the norm decays if it is not continuously reinforced by fresh incidents.

Behaviour over time

From a normal starting point the reinforcing loops dominate first: congestion, anger and incidents all climb together because rage feeds jams and jams feed rage. Growth is eventually halted by the enforcement loop and by drivers avoiding the network, and the system settles at a higher plateau of congestion and incidents than it started from. The leverage points are therefore not the incidents themselves but the loops that manufacture them: reducing baseline stress and fatigue, designing roads that produce fewer forced conflicts, and de‑normalising aggression early (before enforcement is forced to act) all weaken the reinforcing loops at their source.

Formulation notes

  • Congestion, frustration and the aggressive norm are stocks (they accumulate); total incident rate, provocations, stress and enforcement are auxiliaries, since they are algebraic results, not accumulations.
  • Non‑linear responses (stress from congestion, trip deferral, enforcement escalation) are expressed as graphical functions normalised through the point (1,1) rather than as hard‑coded constants.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback engines driving societal road rage escalation

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: An index of how congested the road network is (1 = normal congestion). It accumulates from traffic entering the network and drains as vehicles clear. Congestion is treated as a stock because delays build up and dissipate over time rather than instantaneously.

variables.name: Congestion Formation
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion builds, driven by the volume of trips people choose to make plus the extra obstruction caused by road rage related crashes, stops and confrontations.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which queues dissipate as the network drains. The more congestion there is, the more clears per unit time, giving the road system its natural self correcting behaviour.

variables.name: Discretionary Trip Making
variables.documentation: Willingness of drivers to make optional trips or to travel at peak times. When roads are jammed people defer, reroute or retime trips, which relieves pressure. Normalised so that normal congestion (1) yields normal trip making (1).

variables.name: Incident Blockages
variables.documentation: Extra obstruction of the road created by aggressive driving: collisions, sudden braking, brake checking and roadside confrontations. Only a portion of incidents actually block traffic, hence the halving.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: The general arousal, impatience and time pressure drivers feel, driven mainly by stop and go conditions and delay. Saturating because stress eventually plateaus. Normal congestion (1) gives normal stress (1).

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Rate at which drivers feel cut off, tailgated, blocked or honked at. It rises with the prevalence of aggressive driving norms and with congestion, since dense traffic creates far more close interactions between vehicles.

variables.name: Driver Frustration
variables.documentation: The pool of accumulated anger and frustration carried by the driving population. Modelled as a stock because anger builds up over a trip or a period of days and then cools off, rather than resetting instantly.

variables.name: Frustration Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which anger accumulates. Stress (fatigue, time pressure, congestion) sets the fuse and perceived provocations light it, so the two multiply.

variables.name: Frustration Relief
variables.documentation: Rate at which anger cools once drivers leave traffic, rest or calm down. Proportional to the frustration held, giving natural decay.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The rate of aggressive driving events in society. Frustration supplies the emotional charge and the prevailing aggressive norm determines how readily that charge is expressed as aggression rather than suppressed.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: How socially normal and acceptable aggressive driving has become. It is a stock of learned behaviour: every witnessed incident teaches drivers that aggression is normal, while enforcement and social disapproval erode it.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which observing aggressive driving normalises it for onlookers. Only a fraction of witnesses adopt the behaviour, hence the halving.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive norm is unlearned through policing, penalties, campaigns and social disapproval. Proportional to the norm present and to how hard society is pushing back.

variables.name: Enforcement Pressure
variables.documentation: Society's corrective response: policing, cameras, penalties and public campaigns. It responds slowly at low incident levels but escalates sharply once road rage becomes visibly serious. Normalised so normal incidents (1) give normal enforcement (1).

testParams.name: include requested variables for American Revolution
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include the variables "Taxation", "Anti British Sentiment" and "Colonial Identity".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains the outbreak of hostilities

The model treats the Revolution not as a list of causes but as a set of interacting feedback loops that overwhelmed the loops that should have stabilized the empire.

The intended balancing loop ("fixes that fail"). The French and Indian War inflates British War Debt, which raises Fiscal Pressure, which drives New Tax Enactment into the Taxation stock (Sugar, Stamp, Townshend, Tea). Collections were supposed to pay the debt down and relieve the pressure. This is the policy's own balancing loop.

Why the fix backfired. Because Colonial Representation in Parliament is essentially zero, taxation converts into Taxation Grievance rather than mere expense. Grievance fills the Anti British Sentiment stock, which combined with Intercolonial Coordination yields Colonial Resistance — boycotts, smuggling and the Tea Party. Resistance collapses the Compliance Multiplier, so Tax Revenue falls even as taxes rise. The debt is not repaid, fiscal pressure persists, and Parliament legislates still more taxes: a reinforcing loop where the fix deepens the problem.

The escalation archetype. Resistance provokes Coercion Escalation (customs enforcement, troops, the Intolerable Acts closing Boston's port), and coercion directly feeds Sentiment Escalation. Coercion plus crowds produces Violent Incidents — the Boston Massacre — which the Propaganda Effect magnifies far beyond five deaths, adding again to anti-British sentiment. Each side's defensive move is the other side's provocation.

The identity loop. Acting together generates Identity Formation, so Colonial Identity accumulates from the shared experience of resistance. Stronger identity improves coordination, which makes resistance more effective, which builds identity further — a slow reinforcing loop that converted thirteen provinces into one political actor capable of a Continental Congress.

Where hostilities come from. When petitions and boycotts stop working, resistance flows into Militia Mobilization. Armed Hostilities requires the product of armed colonists and British force in contact — precisely the collision at Lexington and Concord in 1775 — and fighting then feeds back into further coercion, locking in war.

Modeling choices. Taxation, sentiment, identity, coercion and militia strength are stocks because they accumulate and persist; grievance, resistance, revenue, incidents and hostilities are algebraic auxiliaries, not accumulations. Wartime spending is a time-based input since the war's timing is historical. All rate parameters and reference levels are named variables rather than embedded numbers, and one-directional processes (enactment, repeal, escalation, mobilization) are constrained against negative flows.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated British public debt, driven up sharply by the French and Indian War (1754-63). This debt is the fiscal trigger that made London look to the colonies for revenue.

variables.name: Wartime Spending
variables.documentation: Exogenous military expenditure over time: heavy during the French and Indian War, dropping to a small garrison cost afterwards. Modeled as a time-based graphical function because the war's timing is historical input, not a model outcome.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Debt retired using revenue actually collected from the colonies. This closes the intended balancing loop: tax the colonies, pay down the debt, relieve fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Initial War Debt
variables.documentation: Pre-war level of British debt used as the starting condition.

variables.name: Reference Debt
variables.documentation: Normal or tolerable debt level used to scale debt into a dimensionless fiscal pressure index.

variables.name: Fiscal Pressure
variables.documentation: How urgently Parliament feels it must raise revenue, expressed relative to a tolerable debt level.

variables.name: Taxation
variables.documentation: The accumulated burden of taxes and duties in force on the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act). It is a stock because it changes only as acts are enacted or repealed.

variables.name: Initial Taxation
variables.documentation: The light pre-1763 level of imperial taxation in the colonies.

variables.name: New Tax Enactment
variables.documentation: Rate at which Parliament passes new revenue measures, driven by fiscal pressure from war debt.

variables.name: Tax Enactment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly Parliament responds to fiscal pressure by legislating new colonial taxes.

variables.name: Tax Repeal
variables.documentation: Withdrawal of taxes in the face of colonial protest and boycott, as with the Stamp Act repeal of 1766 and most Townshend duties in 1770. This is the balancing loop that repeatedly cooled the crisis without resolving it.

variables.name: Repeal Responsiveness
variables.documentation: Willingness of Parliament to back down on taxes when resistance is high.

variables.name: Colonial Representation in Parliament
variables.documentation: The near-zero degree to which colonists had a voice in the body taxing them. Its absence is what converted taxes into a constitutional grievance: no taxation without representation.

variables.name: Taxation Grievance
variables.documentation: The felt injustice of taxation. Identical taxes create far more grievance when the taxed have no representation, so grievance is taxation weighted by the lack of representation.

variables.name: Normal Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Fraction of nominal taxes actually collected under ordinary conditions, given smuggling and weak enforcement.

variables.name: Compliance Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of resistance (boycotts, non-importation, smuggling, tarring of collectors) on how much tax is actually paid. Normalized so that normal resistance yields normal compliance.

variables.name: Tax Revenue
variables.documentation: Revenue actually reaching the Treasury. Because resistance collapses compliance, higher taxes yielded less and less money, defeating the policy's own purpose.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial resentment and distrust of British authority. It is a stock because grievances accumulate in memory and only fade slowly, so each new provocation builds on the residue of the last.

variables.name: Initial Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Low baseline resentment in 1754, when most colonists considered themselves loyal Britons.

variables.name: Sentiment Escalation
variables.documentation: Rate at which resentment builds, fed by unjust taxation, coercive measures such as troops and the Intolerable Acts, and the propaganda use of bloodshed like the Boston Massacre.

variables.name: Sentiment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How quickly public opinion converts grievances into hostility toward Britain.

variables.name: Sentiment Moderation
variables.documentation: Natural cooling of anger over time when provocations stop, as during the quiet years 1770-1773.

variables.name: Moderation Fraction
variables.documentation: Rate at which grievances are forgotten in the absence of new provocation.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Accumulated sense of a shared American, rather than provincial British, identity. It is a stock because it is built up slowly through shared experience of resistance, committees of correspondence and congresses.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak intercolonial identity in 1754, when the colonies could barely cooperate at the Albany Congress.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Joint acts of resistance, boycotts and congresses forge a common identity. Acting together as Americans is what made them Americans.

variables.name: Identity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: How strongly shared resistance experience builds common identity.

variables.name: Identity Erosion
variables.documentation: Slow decay of common identity through loyalist attachment to the Crown and intercolonial rivalry.

variables.name: Identity Erosion Fraction
variables.documentation: Weak rate at which shared identity fades once formed.

variables.name: Reference Identity
variables.documentation: Benchmark level of identity used to normalize the effect of identity on coordination.

variables.name: Relative Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Colonial identity expressed relative to a normal benchmark so it can drive a nonlinear coordination effect.

variables.name: Intercolonial Coordination
variables.documentation: Ability of the colonies to act as one through committees of correspondence, Sons of Liberty networks and the Continental Congress. Normal identity yields normal coordination; strong identity multiplies the effectiveness of protest.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Active defiance: petitions, boycotts, mob action, the Boston Tea Party. Resentment only becomes effective resistance when colonists are organized enough to act together.

variables.name: Reference Resistance
variables.documentation: Benchmark resistance level used for normalization.

variables.name: Relative Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Resistance expressed relative to normal, used to drive tax compliance and the chance of repeal.

variables.name: British Coercive Measures
variables.documentation: Accumulated apparatus of force and punishment: customs enforcement, troops quartered in Boston, and the Intolerable Acts closing the port and revoking self government. A stock because each measure stays in place until repealed.

variables.name: Initial British Coercive Measures
variables.documentation: Minimal imperial coercion in the era of salutary neglect.

variables.name: Coercion Escalation
variables.documentation: London answers defiance with more force: troops after the 1768 riots, the Intolerable Acts after the Tea Party, and military expeditions once fighting begins.

variables.name: Coercion Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly British authorities respond to colonial defiance with coercion rather than concession.

variables.name: Coercion Relaxation
variables.documentation: Slow withdrawal of troops and lifting of punitive measures, such as pulling regiments out of Boston after the Massacre.

variables.name: Relaxation Fraction
variables.documentation: Slow rate at which coercive measures are relaxed once imposed.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Bloodshed produced when armed enforcement meets crowds of protesters, as in the Boston Massacre of 1770. Violence requires both troops present and people in the streets.

variables.name: Confrontation Frequency
variables.documentation: Likelihood that a given level of troops and protest produces a violent clash.

variables.name: Propaganda Effect
variables.documentation: Amplification of bloodshed by pamphlets, engravings and the press, which turned five deaths in Boston into an empire-wide grievance.

variables.name: Propaganda Multiplier
variables.documentation: How much publicity magnifies the emotional impact of violent incidents.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Armed, organized colonial manpower: minutemen, stockpiled powder and provincial congresses' military preparations. Accumulating this stock is what turned protest into the possibility of war.

variables.name: Initial Militia Strength
variables.documentation: No anti-British military organization exists at the start.

variables.name: Mobilization
variables.documentation: Rate at which resistance is organized into armed readiness once petitions and boycotts appear insufficient.

variables.name: Mobilization Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How readily political resistance translates into military preparation.

variables.name: Demobilization
variables.documentation: Decay of military readiness when the crisis subsides.

variables.name: Demobilization Fraction
variables.documentation: Slow rate at which armed readiness dissipates.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Open fighting, as at Lexington and Concord. It requires both an armed populace and a British force attempting to enforce authority, which is exactly the collision of April 1775.

variables.name: Clash Propensity

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include the variables "Traffic Congestion", "Driver Stress" and "Accidents".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says about how road rage arises

Road rage is treated not as an event but as the output of several interlocking feedback loops. Four accumulations carry the system's memory: Traffic Congestion (queues), Driver Stress (accumulated arousal that does not reset between trips), Accidents (crashes physically occupying lanes), and an Aggressive Driving Norm (what drivers have learned is acceptable). A fifth, Road Rage Incidents, is the pool of active confrontations.

The reinforcing engines (why incidents can escalate over time)

  1. Stress spiral (R1): Congestion raises the stress load faster than proportionally → accumulated Driver Stress lowers the anger threshold → more incidents → aggressive manoeuvring and rubbernecking cut road throughput → more congestion.
  2. Retaliation loop (R2): Incidents are experienced by others as being cut off, tailgated or honked at. Perceived Provocations feed both stress and direct retaliation, so aggression breeds aggression. Note this loop is multiplied by congestion: crowding creates the encounters that make provocation possible.
  3. Crash loop (R3): Aggression raises Accidents; crashes block lanes, deepening congestion, which feeds back into stress and impatience. Distraction, fatigue and weather load this loop from outside.
  4. Learned-behaviour loop (R4, slow): Observed aggression accumulates into a social norm over months. This is the slowest and most dangerous loop — it ratchets the baseline upward, so even after a congestion wave passes, incident rates settle higher than before.

The balancing responses (why it does not explode)

  • Enforcement (B1): Visible road rage eventually mobilises policing and campaigns, which deter escalation — but only after a policy delay, so it always arrives late.
  • Cool-down (B2) and clearance (B3): Stress decays with rest and queues discharge; these are the stabilisers that ordinary conditions rely on.
  • Build more roads (B4) — a fixes-that-fail structure: Congestion triggers capacity investment, but ampler roads induce extra driving, returning the load ratio toward where it started. Capacity expansion therefore buys temporary relief rather than a permanent cure for road rage.

Formulation choices

  • Congestion, stress, crashes and norms are stocks because each persists after its cause is gone; road rage prevalence is a stock of active episodes so that it can be observed and learned from by others.
  • Aggregates such as Total Stress Load, Perceived Provocations and Traffic Demand Ratio are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are instantaneous calculations.
  • All soft effects are expressed as normalised graphical functions passing through (1, 1), so "normal" conditions reproduce the historical baseline and every scenario is a clearly interpretable deviation.
  • No arbitrary numbers sit inside equations; delays, reference levels and risk rates are named constants that can be tested.

Implication for the future

With driving demand growing slightly faster than capacity, the load ratio drifts upward. Because the stress, retaliation and crash loops are all nonlinear, road rage does not rise linearly with congestion — it stays flat for a long while and then accelerates once congestion passes the knee of the stress curve. The norm stock then locks the higher level in. Leverage lies less in enforcement (delayed, and it only trims the symptom) than in cutting the load ratio, shortening crash clearance, reducing schedule pressure, fatigue and distraction, and interrupting the normalisation of aggressive driving.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Loops Driving Road Rage Escalation

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: An index of how congested the road network is (1 = normal). It accumulates as demand and accident blockages build queues, and drains as traffic clears. Congestion is the central situational trigger that raises stress and impatience.

variables.name: Congestion Formation
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion builds up, driven by how much traffic demand exceeds effective road capacity and worsened by lanes blocked by crashes.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which queues dissipate. Aggressive manoeuvres, hard braking and rubbernecking lower throughput, so more road rage slows clearing.

variables.name: Congestion Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Characteristic time for congestion to build or dissipate toward the level implied by demand and capacity.

variables.name: Traffic Demand Ratio
variables.documentation: How heavily the network is loaded: vehicle trips relative to the capacity actually available. A value of 1 is the normal balanced condition.

variables.name: Effective Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Usable capacity of the network after accounting for design quality (narrow lanes, confusing intersections) and weather.

variables.name: Road Capacity
variables.documentation: Physical capacity of the road network, expanded slowly through investment when congestion becomes politically visible.

variables.name: Capacity Expansion
variables.documentation: Rate of road building. Investment accelerates when congestion is high, a classic balancing response that is later offset by induced demand.
variables.units: thousand vehicles per month per month

variables.name: Capacity Expansion Fraction
variables.documentation: Normal fractional rate at which road capacity is expanded each month.

variables.name: Congestion Investment Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of congestion on the willingness to invest in new capacity. Normal congestion (1) gives normal investment (1).

variables.name: Vehicle Demand
variables.documentation: Volume of driving demanded by society. It grows with population and economic activity and is further induced when roads feel uncongested.

variables.name: Demand Growth
variables.documentation: Growth in driving. Underlying growth is amplified when new capacity makes driving attractive (induced demand) and suppressed when roads are already jammed.
variables.units: thousand vehicles per month per month

variables.name: Baseline Demand Growth Rate
variables.documentation: Underlying monthly fractional growth of driving demand from population and economic activity.

variables.name: Capacity Adequacy
variables.documentation: How ample the road system feels relative to the driving people want to do.

variables.name: Induced Demand Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of perceived road adequacy on demand growth. Ample roads (adequacy above 1) induce extra driving; jammed roads suppress it.

variables.name: Road Design Quality
variables.documentation: Quality of geometric design (lane widths, intersection clarity, merges). Poor design lowers the capacity actually delivered.

variables.name: Weather Severity
variables.documentation: Severity of driving conditions such as rain, snow or fog, expressed relative to a normal month.

variables.name: Weather Capacity Multiplier
variables.documentation: Bad weather forces slower speeds and larger headways, cutting effective capacity. Normal weather (1) leaves capacity unchanged (1).

variables.name: Weather Accident Multiplier
variables.documentation: Adverse weather raises crash risk per vehicle. Normal weather (1) gives normal risk (1).

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: The accumulated arousal, tension and irritability carried by the driving population. Stress builds under congestion, provocation and fatigue and decays with rest and calm driving.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions add to the stress pool.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Natural decay of accumulated stress once drivers leave the road and rest.

variables.name: Stress Recovery Time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated driver stress to dissipate.

variables.name: Total Stress Load
variables.documentation: The combined stress-producing pressure of the driving environment: delay, provocation by others, and fatigue.

variables.name: Baseline Stress Load
variables.documentation: Normal background stress of driving under ordinary conditions.

variables.name: Congestion Stress Multiplier
variables.documentation: Stop-and-go conditions and delay raise stress more than proportionally. Normal congestion (1) gives normal stress load (1).

variables.name: Provocation Stress Multiplier
variables.documentation: Being cut off, tailgated or honked at raises the stress load. Normal provocation exposure (1) gives normal stress (1).

variables.name: Fatigue Level
variables.documentation: Prevalence of sleep deprivation and tiredness among drivers relative to normal.

variables.name: Fatigue Stress Multiplier
variables.documentation: Tired drivers experience the same conditions as more stressful and have less emotional control. Normal fatigue (1) gives normal stress (1).

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often a typical driver feels wronged by another driver. It rises with the prevalence of aggressive behaviour and with congestion, because crowding creates far more close encounters.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: The gap between the trip time drivers expect and what traffic delivers, amplified by how tightly scheduled they are.

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: How time-pressed drivers are (running late, tight appointments), relative to normal.

variables.name: Impatience Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of impatience on the chance a driver escalates. Normal impatience (1) gives normal escalation (1).

variables.name: Stress Aggression Multiplier
variables.documentation: Stressed and anxious drivers have a much lower threshold for anger. Normal stress (1) gives normal aggression propensity (1).

variables.name: Provocation Trigger Multiplier
variables.documentation: Direct retaliation effect: each perceived provocation is itself an opportunity for a new incident. Normal provocation (1) gives normal onset (1).

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The pool of active aggressive-driving episodes on the network at any time. It fills as new confrontations start and empties as they cool off.

variables.name: Incident Onset
variables.equation: Vehicle_Demand * Road_Rage_Propensity * Stress_Aggression_Multiplier * Impatience_Multiplier * Provocation_Trigger_Multiplier * Norm_Multiplier * Enforcement_Deterrence_Multiplier
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage episodes begin. It combines exposure (how much driving happens), dispositional propensity, stress, impatience, provocation, social norms and deterrence.

variables.name: Incident Deescalation
variables.documentation: Rate at which active confrontations end as drivers separate and calm down.

variables.name: Incident Duration
variables.documentation: Average time an aggressive episode remains active and visible to other road users.

variables.name: Road Rage Propensity
variables.documentation: Baseline dispositional tendency of the driving population toward hostile, impulsive or competitive behaviour, per unit of driving exposure.
variables.units: incidents per thousand vehicles per month

variables.name: Relative Road Rage
variables.documentation: Prevalence of aggressive driving compared with the historically normal level. Used so all effects are normalised around 1.

variables.name: Reference Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Historically normal number of active road rage episodes, used as the yardstick for judging prevalence.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially learned acceptability of aggressive driving. It accumulates slowly from what drivers repeatedly observe on the road and fades slowly when aggression becomes rare.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which observing aggressive driving normalises it for the observer.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the tolerance of aggressive driving fades in the absence of fresh examples.

variables.name: Norm Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for social learning: how long it takes shared driving culture to adjust to what people see.

variables.name: Norm Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of the prevailing culture on individual willingness to escalate. A normal norm (1) gives normal escalation (1).

variables.name: Enforcement Intensity
variables.documentation: Level of policing, camera coverage and public campaigns targeting aggressive driving. It adjusts with a delay toward what the visible problem seems to warrant.

variables.name: Enforcement Adjustment
variables.documentation: Bidirectional change in enforcement effort as authorities respond to, or relax after, a wave of incidents.

variables.name: Indicated Enforcement
variables.documentation: Enforcement level society believes is warranted given how visible road rage has become. Normal prevalence (1) calls for normal enforcement (1).

variables.name: Enforcement Response Time
variables.documentation: Delay between a rise in aggressive driving and the arrival of extra enforcement and campaigns.

variables.name: Enforcement Deterrence Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of enforcement on incident onset. Normal enforcement (1) leaves onset unchanged (1); more enforcement suppresses escalation.

variables.name: Accidents
variables.documentation: Crashes currently on the network occupying lanes. Modelled as a stock because a crash keeps blocking traffic until it is cleared, which is how it feeds back into congestion.

variables.name: Accident Occurrence
variables.documentation: Rate of new crashes, rising with exposure, aggressive driving, distraction and bad weather.

variables.name: Accident Clearance
variables.documentation: Rate at which crash scenes are cleared and lanes reopened.

variables.name: Accident Clearance Time
variables.documentation: Average time a crash keeps blocking road space.

variables.name: Accident Risk per Vehicle
variables.documentation: Baseline crash risk per unit of driving under normal behaviour, attention and weather.
variables.units: accidents per thousand vehicles per month

variables.name: Relative Accidents
variables.documentation: Crash burden compared with the normal level, used to normalise the blockage effect around 1.

variables.name: Reference Accident Level
variables.documentation: Normal number of crashes occupying the network, used as the comparison yardstick.

variables.name: Accident Blockage Multiplier
variables.documentation: Extra congestion generated by lanes blocked with crashes. Normal crash levels (1) give normal congestion formation (1).

variables.name: Aggression Accident Multiplier
variables.documentation: Tailgating, weaving and speeding during aggressive episodes raise crash risk. Normal prevalence (1) gives normal risk (1).

variables.name: Distracted Driving Prevalence
variables.documentation: How widespread phone use, texting and eating while driving are, relative to normal.

variables.name: Distraction Accident Multiplier
variables.documentation: Distraction raises crash risk and produces the erratic behaviour that provokes others. Normal distraction (1) gives normal risk (1).

variables.name: Aggression Throughput Penalty
variables.documentation: Aggressive lane changes, hard braking and rubbernecking destabilise flow and slow queue clearing. Normal prevalence (1) leaves clearing normal (1).

errorExplanations.name: total_incubation
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Infection' flow as input, not the 'Exposed population' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and corrected

1. Total incubation — three separate errors in one equation (the source of the unit warning). Original: DELAY3(Exposed_population/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week, Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week)

  • Wrong time constant: the drain of the exposed stock was divided by the asymptomatic infectious period, a parameter that belongs to a completely different stage of the disease. The latent stage must be governed by the average COVID incubation time.
  • Wrong unit conversion: the stock was divided by days and then divided again by days per week, giving People·Weeks/Days², exactly the dimensional error the unit checker flagged. A day-based parameter must be divided by days per week (giving weeks), and the stock divided by that.
  • Double delay on a stock drain: the expression already drained the exposed stock (a first-order delay) and then wrapped a third-order DELAY3 around it. Delaying a stock's own outflow relative to its content lets the outflow keep running after the stock is empty, which can drive the exposed population negative and stretches the latent period far beyond three days.

Fixed to Exposed_population/(Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week) — a clean first-order (exponential) drain of the exposed stock over the incubation time expressed in weeks. Units are now Person/Week, the exposed stock can never go negative, and the mean latent period is exactly three days.

2. Spurious causal link removed. Because the asymptomatic period no longer (and never should have) appeared in the incubation equation, the causal link Average period of asymptomatic infections → Total incubation was deleted. That parameter now influences only the asymptomatic recovery delay, where it belongs.

3. Missing one-way flow restrictions. None of the flows carried a uniflow setting, so numerical overshoot could produce negative births, deaths, infections or recoveries. All physical, one-directional flows (Infection, Incubation, Asymptomatic incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery, Recovery without symptoms, Dying of COVID, Losing immunity, Influx from abroad) are now marked as one-directional so they can never run backwards.

Formulations checked and deliberately left unchanged

  • The other DELAY3 formulations are valid pipeline (third-order material) delays, not errors. In each case the delayed quantity is exactly the sum of that stock's inflows (Developing symptoms delays Incubation + Influx; Recovery without symptoms delays Asymptomatic incubation; Total exiting symptomatic infectious delays Developing symptoms; Losing immunity delays Recovery + Recovery without symptoms). Material is conserved and each stock simply holds the people still in transit, so it never goes negative. To respect the existing modelling style these were kept as pipeline delays rather than converted to first-order drains.
  • Aggregations are correctly auxiliaries. Total population and Infectious population are algebraic sums and are correctly typed as auxiliaries, not stocks. Cumulative COVID deaths is correctly a stock because it is a genuine accumulation of the death flow. Deaths are correctly excluded from the living total used in the contact-mixing term.
  • Total exiting symptomatic infectious is correctly an auxiliary: the actual outflows of the symptomatic stock are Recovery and Dying of COVID, which split it by the case fatality rate — the standard, correct way to split a single exit rate.
  • No misuse of delays for averaging was present (no DELAY1/DELAY3 used where a SMOOTH would be required); all delays represent genuine material transit.
  • Graphical functions for imported cases and social distancing are driven by time, so the normalisation-through-(1,1) rule does not apply to them.
  • Time step of 1/128 week remains appropriate: it is well below one third of the shortest delay stage (the three-day presymptomatic pipeline).
