variables.name: Susceptible population
variables.documentation: People who can still catch COVID. Drained by new infections and refilled by people whose immunity wanes. Initialised with the initial susceptible population parameter.

variables.name: Exposed population
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are not yet infectious (latent period). Leaves the stock either on the symptomatic track (Incubation) or the asymptomatic track (Asymptomatic incubation).

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People with temporary immunity after recovering, either from symptomatic or asymptomatic infection. They return to the susceptible pool as immunity wanes.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: Standard force-of-infection formulation: infectious people times their weekly contacts times the probability a contact is susceptible times the transmission probability per contact. Cannot be negative, so it is a uniflow.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The part of the people leaving the exposed stock that will eventually develop symptoms; they first become presymptomatic infectious.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: The share of people leaving the symptomatic stock who survive. One-directional, therefore a uniflow.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: Size of the population at the start of the epidemic, used only as the initial value of the susceptible stock.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: Probability that a random contact of an infectious person is with someone still susceptible; the classic mixing term of an SEIR model.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: Probability that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person leads to transmission.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: Sum of all living epidemiological states. Correctly an auxiliary (an algebraic sum), not a stock, because it changes only through the stocks it adds up. Deaths are excluded because they leave the living population.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: Average time in days between infection and becoming infectious (latent period).

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: People who are infectious but do not yet show symptoms, including imported cases from abroad.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People with symptomatic COVID who are infectious; they either recover or die.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious but never develop symptoms; they all recover.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: Pipeline (third order material) delay of everything that entered the presymptomatic stock. Because the delayed quantity is exactly the sum of the inflows to that stock, material is conserved and the stock equals the people still in the presymptomatic pipeline. The delay time is the presymptomatic period converted from days to weeks.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of the inflow to the asymptomatic stock: everyone who entered leaves after the average asymptomatic infectious period (converted from days to weeks).

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The part of the people leaving the exposed stock who will never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Fraction of infections that never becomes symptomatic (literature range roughly 25 to 80 percent).

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: Total rate at which exposed people become infectious. Corrected formulation: a first order drain of the exposed stock over the average incubation time, converted from days to weeks. The previous version used the asymptomatic infectious period as the time constant, divided by days per week a second time (causing the unit error), and then applied an extra third order delay on top of a stock drain, which double delayed the material and could drive the exposed stock negative.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time-based seeding of imported infectious travellers. Time driven graphical functions do not need to pass through (1,1).

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Average number of days an asymptomatic person stays infectious.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The share of people leaving the symptomatic stock who die. One-directional, therefore a uniflow.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: Fraction of symptomatic cases that ends in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average number of days a person is infectious before symptoms appear.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of everything that entered the recovered stock: immunity wanes on average after the average immunity period, returning people to the susceptible pool. Delayed quantity equals the sum of the inflows of the recovered stock, so people are conserved.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: Average duration of post infection immunity.

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average duration of the symptomatic infectious phase.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: All people currently able to transmit the virus. Correctly an auxiliary sum rather than a stock.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: Effective contact rate, the normal contact rate reduced by the fraction of contacts removed by social distancing policy.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: Exogenous policy scenario: the fraction of normal contacts eliminated by distancing measures over time. Time driven graphical function.

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: Running total of deaths. Correctly a stock because it is a genuine accumulation of a flow.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: Contacts per person per week in the absence of any distancing measures.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant used to translate parameters expressed in days into the weekly time base of the model.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Total rate at which people leave the symptomatic stock, a pipeline delay of the inflow to that stock. It is split into recovery and death by the case fatality rate, so it is correctly an auxiliary and not a flow itself.

errorExplanations.name: developing_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use the flows 'Incubation + Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad' as input to DELAY3, not the stock 'Presymptomatic infectious' divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and fixed

1. Developing symptoms — wrong parameter, dimensional error, and inconsistent delay style (the single substantive error)

The original equation was DELAY3(Presymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week, Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week). Three things were wrong with it:

  • Wrong residence time: it drained the presymptomatic stock using the asymptomatic infectious period, a parameter that belongs to a completely different pathway. Presymptomatic people should leave after the presymptomatic period.
  • Dimensional error: dividing a stock (People) by a duration in Days and then again by Days per Week yields People·Weeks/Days², not People/Week — this is exactly the unit warning that was reported.
  • Double delay / mixed style: it took a stock-based drain and then pushed it through a further third-order delay, so material was delayed twice (once by the accumulation, once by the DELAY3). Every other cohort transition in this model uses the pipeline convention outflow = DELAY3(inflow, residence time) — see Total incubation, Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious, and Losing immunity.

Fix: DELAY3(Incubation + Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad, Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week). This delays the complete inflow to the presymptomatic stock (domestic incubation plus imported cases) by one presymptomatic period converted to weeks, gives clean Person/Week units, and matches the pipeline-delay style used everywhere else. The two miswired inputs (the stock itself and the asymptomatic period) were replaced accordingly; no new feedback loop is created — the correction simply re-points the same aging chain at the correct upstream flow and the correct parameter.

2. Missing one-directional (uniflow) specifications on every flow

None of the flows were constrained. Infections, incubations, symptom onsets, recoveries, deaths, the imported-case influx and immunity loss are all physically one-way processes; a negative value would move people backwards through the disease chain. All flows are now marked as one-directional so numerical noise cannot reverse them.

3. Missing polarities on most causal links

About two-thirds of the relationships carried no polarity. All links now carry an explicit sign, including the delay-parameter links (longer incubation/presymptomatic/illness/immunity periods slow their transitions, so those are negative) and the Days per week conversion links (a larger days-per-week factor shortens the delay expressed in weeks, so those are positive).

4. Missing integration method specification

The run specification had no solver. Euler with the existing very small step (0.0078 week) is specified explicitly; this is fine because the shortest third-order delay stage (about 0.14 week) is far larger than the step.

Checked and confirmed correct (no change)

  • Total population and Infectious population are simple sums and are correctly auxiliaries, not stocks.
  • Total incubation and Total exiting symptomatic infectious are correctly auxiliaries that are then split by the asymptomatic share and the case-fatality rate respectively, so the two branch flows always sum to the total leaving the stock.
  • The DELAY3 pipeline formulations for Total incubation, Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious and Losing immunity are dimensionally consistent (day-based durations are divided by Days per week; week-based durations are not).
  • Cumulative COVID deaths is correctly a stock with a single inflow, and deaths are correctly excluded from Total population.
  • Both time-driven graphical functions (imported cases and social distancing) legitimately use TIME as input and are exempt from the (1,1) normalisation convention.

variables.documentation: People who can still catch COVID. Initialised at the starting population, drained by new infections and refilled by people whose immunity wanes.

variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are not yet infectious. They leave along two branches, symptomatic-bound and asymptomatic-bound. Starts empty because the epidemic is seeded by the influx from abroad.

variables.name: Infection

errorExplanations.name: recovery_without_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Asymptomatic incubation' flow as input, not the 'Asymptomatic infectious' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and fixed

1. Recovery without symptoms — malformed unit conversion (the reported unit warning)

  • Was: DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week, Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)
  • Why wrong: chained division meant the stock was divided by the infectious period and then divided again by the days-per-week conversion, giving People·Weeks/Days² instead of People/Week. The conversion factor must be applied so that a period in days becomes a period in weeks — i.e. the period must be divided by days-per-week, not the rate.
  • Fixed to: Asymptomatic_infectious/(Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week) → People / Weeks. All three causes (the stock, the period, the conversion) are still used, so no links change.

2. Recovery without symptoms — double delay (delay applied on top of a delay)

  • Why wrong: the old formulation drained the asymptomatic stock at a first-order rate and then passed that already-delayed rate through a third-order pipeline delay of the same length. People therefore stayed infectious for roughly twice the intended 6 days, inflating the infectious pool and the reproduction number. It also broke conservation: the delayed outflow no longer corresponded to the stock's actual contents, so the stock could go negative.
  • Fixed to: a single, clean first-order drain (above). Note: the alternative that would match the pipeline style used elsewhere in the chain would take the inflow (asymptomatic incubation) as the delay input, but that would require a new causal link, so the equivalent first-order drain was used instead.

3. Missing one-way (uniflow) settings on all physical flows

  • Why wrong: infection, incubation, symptom onset, recovery, death, immunity loss and imported cases are all one-directional biological transitions. Left unconstrained, numerical noise or a negative delay output could push people backwards through the chain (e.g. "un-dying", or recovered people flowing back into the symptomatic stock).
  • Fixed: every flow is now marked as one-directional so it can never run negative.

4. Missing polarities on roughly half the causal links

  • Why wrong: an unsigned link cannot be interpreted, and the delay-time links in particular are easy to sign wrongly.
  • Fixed: all links are now signed. Note the non-obvious ones: every delay-time constant (incubation time, presymptomatic period, symptomatic period, immunity period, asymptomatic period) is negative on its flow because a longer delay slows and postpones that flow, while days per week is positive because it shortens the day-based delays once expressed in weeks. Total population is negative on the susceptible-contact fraction because it is the denominator.

5. Missing integration specification

  • Fixed: Euler is now stated explicitly. The very small time step is retained deliberately: the third-order pipeline delays have stage times as short as 0.14 weeks (the 3-day presymptomatic and incubation delays), and the step must stay far below those stage times for the pipelines to be accurate.

Checked and confirmed correct (no change made)

  • Total population and Infectious population are simple sums and are correctly auxiliaries, not stocks.
  • Cumulative COVID deaths is correctly a stock with a single inflow, and is correctly excluded from Total population (the dead make no contacts) — this is the balancing loop that reduces contagion as the epidemic burns through the population, together with the depletion of susceptibles.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • The split pairs (Incubation / Asymptomatic incubation, and Recovery / Dying of COVID) each use a fraction and its complement applied to a single delayed exit flow, so no stock is drained twice.
  • Losing immunity delays exactly the sum of the two inflows to the recovered stock, so the pipeline conserves people; the reinforcing re-susceptibility loop it closes is therefore well behaved.
  • The two time-driven graphical functions (imported cases, social distancing) legitimately use TIME as input and so are exempt from the (1,1) normalisation convention.
supportingInfo.title: Fixed asymptomatic recovery delay and unit conversion

variables.name: Susceptible population
variables.documentation: People who can still catch COVID. Rises as recovered people lose immunity and falls as people become infected. Initial value is a named constant, not a hard-coded number.

variables.name: Exposed population
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are not yet infectious. Drained by the two incubation streams (symptomatic-bound and asymptomatic-bound), whose sum equals Total incubation, so the material balance of the delay pipeline is preserved.

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People with temporary immunity after recovering with or without symptoms. Drained as immunity wanes.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: Standard mass-action infection rate: infectious people times their contacts, times the chance a contact is susceptible, times the transmission probability per contact. Marked uniflow because infections can never run backwards.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The portion of people finishing incubation who will go on to develop symptoms. Uses the structural complement (1 - share) so the two incubation streams always add up to Total incubation.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: The surviving share of people leaving the symptomatic stock. Complement of the case fatality rate, so recovery plus deaths exactly equals the outflow from the symptomatic stock.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: Size of the population at risk at the start of the simulation.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: Fraction of the living population that is still susceptible, i.e. the probability that a random contact of an infectious person is susceptible. This is the balancing term that turns off the epidemic as susceptibles are depleted.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: Probability that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person transmits the virus.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: Sum of all living epidemiological states. Correctly formulated as an auxiliary (a simple sum), not as a stock, because it has no flows of its own. Cumulative COVID deaths is deliberately excluded, since the dead are no longer available for contacts.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: Average time from infection to becoming infectious, expressed in days and converted to weeks where used.

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Infectious people who do not yet show symptoms, including imported cases.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious and showing symptoms. Leaves either by recovering or by dying; the two outflows partition the same pipeline outflow so the stock cannot be drained twice.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are infectious but never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: Pipeline (third-order material) delay of everything that entered the presymptomatic stock, delayed by the presymptomatic period converted from days to weeks. Consistent with the pipeline-delay style used throughout the chain.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: CORRECTED. Previously this was DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week, ...), which (a) divided by the day-per-week conversion instead of multiplying by it, producing People*Weeks/Days^2 instead of People/Week, and (b) applied a third-order delay on top of a stock that was already being drained at a first-order rate, roughly doubling the true asymptomatic infectious period. It is now a clean first-order drain of the asymptomatic stock over its average infectious period, correctly converted from days to weeks.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The share of people finishing incubation who will never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Fraction of infections that never become symptomatic (literature range roughly 25 to 80 percent).

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: All people finishing incubation, computed as a pipeline delay of infections over the incubation time converted to weeks. It is split into the symptomatic-bound and asymptomatic-bound streams that drain the exposed stock.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time-based seeding of imported infectious travellers. As a time-driven graphical function it does not need to pass through the point (1,1). Marked uniflow because imports cannot be negative.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Average number of days an asymptomatic person remains infectious.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The fatal share of people leaving the symptomatic stock.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: Fraction of symptomatic cases that end in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average days spent infectious before symptoms appear.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of everything that entered the recovered stock, delayed by the average immunity period (already in weeks). Because its input is exactly the sum of the inflows to the recovered stock, the delay conserves people and cannot drain the stock below zero. Marked uniflow because immunity loss is one-directional.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: Average duration of post-infection immunity, in weeks (no conversion needed).

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average duration of symptomatic illness, expressed directly in weeks.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: Sum of all currently infectious states. Correctly an auxiliary sum rather than a stock, since it merely aggregates other stocks.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: Contact rate after policy restrictions, expressed as the structural complement of the social distancing fraction applied to the normal contact rate.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time-based policy stringency expressed as the fractional reduction in contacts. Being time-driven, it does not need to pass through the point (1,1).

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: Running total of deaths. Correctly a stock (an accumulation with only an inflow) and correctly excluded from Total population.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: Contacts per person per week in the absence of any restrictions.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant used to translate durations expressed in days into the model's weekly time base.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of everyone who entered the symptomatic stock, delayed by the length of illness. It is then split by the case fatality rate into recoveries and deaths so the stock is never drained twice.

errorExplanations.name: influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad
errorExplanations.problem: The graphical function should use TIME as an input, not DT (DT).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Formulation errors found and corrected

1. Stock outflows formulated as third-order material delays of their inflows (the most serious error). The following equations computed a stock's outflow from the inflow history rather than from the stock itself:

  • Total incubation = DELAY3(Infection, …)
  • Developing symptoms = DELAY3(Incubation + Influx…, …)
  • Recovery without symptoms = DELAY3(Asymptomatic incubation, …)
  • Total exiting symptomatic infectious = DELAY3(Developing symptoms, …)
  • Losing immunity = DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery without symptoms, …)

Why it is wrong: a DELAY3 keeps its own internal accumulation, so the outflow is completely disconnected from the level of the compartment it is supposed to drain. Conservation of people is broken (the delay's internal state and the visible stock are two separate accumulations), the balancing "drain" loop that every compartment must have is missing, and any mismatch — especially the exogenous import flow, which enters the presymptomatic stock but was added again inside the DELAY3 — lets stocks drift or go negative. It also forces an extremely small time step to stay stable.

How it was fixed: each outflow is now a first-order (exponential) drain of its own stock over its average residence time, the standard SEIR aging-chain formulation and consistent throughout the model:

  • Total incubation = Exposed_population / (Average_COVID_incubation_time / Days_per_week)
  • Developing symptoms = Presymptomatic_infectious / (Presymptomatic_period / Days_per_week)
  • Recovery without symptoms = Asymptomatic_infectious / (Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections / Days_per_week)
  • Total exiting symptomatic infectious = Symptomatic_infectious / Average_length_of_symptomatic_period
  • Losing immunity = Recovered_population / Average_immunity_period

The double-counting of the import flow inside Developing symptoms disappears automatically, because that flow now reaches symptom onset only by passing through the presymptomatic stock. No variables were added or renamed; the only structural consequence is that each flow now reads its own stock instead of the upstream flow (the standard, unavoidable stock-to-drain link).

2. Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad used DT as the input to its time table. The table's horizontal axis runs from 0 to 104 weeks, so it is a time-series input, but the equation passed DT (the constant time step, 0.0078 weeks). The lookup therefore returned a near-zero constant forever, so the epidemic would never be seeded and the model would stay in equilibrium at the initial conditions. Fixed by using TIME as the lookup input, matching the intent and matching the (correct) usage in Social distancing measures.

3. Flow directionality (uniflow) was unspecified. All flows here are physically one-directional processes — infections, progression between disease stages, symptom onset, recoveries, deaths, imports and immunity loss. They are now marked as one-directional so they can never run backwards and pull people the wrong way through the chain.

4. Missing units and documentation. Every variable now carries units and a short rationale, which also allowed a units check: all day-based delay parameters are divided by Days per week so the resulting rates are consistently Person/Week.

Items checked and confirmed correct (no change)

  • Total population and Infectious population are simple sums and are correctly auxiliaries, not stocks.
  • Cumulative COVID deaths is correctly a stock with a single inflow and no outflow, and deaths are correctly excluded from Total population.
  • Total incubation and Total exiting symptomatic infectious are correctly auxiliaries that split one resolution rate into two flows, preserving people.
  • The infection equation follows the standard contacts × infectivity × susceptible-fraction formulation.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

variables.name: Susceptible population

variables.name: Exposed population

variables.name: Recovered population

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: Standard contact-infectivity formulation: infectious people times their contacts per week, times the probability a contact is susceptible, times the probability of transmission per contact. Cannot be negative.

variables.name: Incubation

variables.name: Recovery

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: Probability that a random contact is with a susceptible person under random mixing.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: Probability that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person transmits the virus.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: Algebraic sum of all living epidemiological compartments. Correctly an auxiliary (a sum), not a stock, and it excludes cumulative deaths.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Infectious people who never develop symptoms and always recover.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: First-order drain of the presymptomatic stock: the stock divided by the average presymptomatic residence time converted to weeks. Tying the outflow to its own stock guarantees the stock can never go negative.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: First-order drain of the asymptomatic infectious stock over the average asymptomatic infectious period.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The share of people leaving the exposed stock who will never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Fraction of infections that remain asymptomatic (literature range roughly 25 to 80 percent).

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: Total rate at which exposed people become infectious: the exposed stock divided by the average incubation time in weeks. This total is then split into the symptomatic and asymptomatic branches.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time-based import of infectious travellers that seeds and re-seeds the epidemic. Driven by simulation time (weeks), matching the x axis of the table.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Average number of days an asymptomatic person remains infectious.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The fatal fraction of people leaving the symptomatic infectious stock.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: Fraction of symptomatic cases that end in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average number of days a person is infectious before symptoms appear.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: First-order drain of the recovered stock: recovered people return to susceptibility after the average immunity period.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: Average duration of post-infection immunity, in weeks.

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average time a symptomatic case remains infectious before recovering or dying.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: Sum of all compartments that can transmit the virus.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: Effective contact frequency, reduced from the normal level by the strength of social distancing measures.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: Exogenous policy scenario: fractional reduction in contacts over time (0 = no measures, 1 = full lockdown).

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: Running total of deaths; correctly a stock because it accumulates a flow and never drains.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: Contacts per person per week in the absence of any restrictions.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant used to express day-based delay times in the model's weekly time unit.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Total rate at which symptomatic cases resolve: the stock divided by the average symptomatic period. This total is split into recoveries and deaths.

errorExplanations.name: social_distancing_measures
errorExplanations.problem: The graphical function should use TIME as an input, not DT (DT).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and fixed

1. Social distancing measures — graphical function driven by DT instead of TIME

  • What was wrong: This is an exogenous policy time series (lockdown stringency by week), but its input expression was DT, the integration time step. DT is a tiny constant (0.0078), so the lookup would have been permanently pinned at its first point (zero distancing) and the policy would never have taken effect. Every simulated wave would have run at full contact rates.
  • Fix: The input is now TIME, so the policy series is read week by week as intended. (The imports series already used TIME correctly and was left alone.)

2. Unprotected division in Chance of contact with an susceptible person

  • What was wrong: Susceptibles were divided by total population with no guard; if the living population ever reached zero the model would fail with a divide-by-zero.
  • Fix: Switched to the protected division operator so the expression safely returns zero in that degenerate case. The intended meaning (susceptible share of the living population) is unchanged.

3. Missing directionality flags on every flow

  • What was wrong: None of the nine flows declared whether they can run backwards. Epidemiological transitions (infection, incubation, symptom onset, recovery, death, waning immunity, imports) are strictly one-way; leaving them unconstrained permits physically impossible negative flows such as negative deaths or people 'un-recovering'.
  • Fix: All nine flows — Infection, Incubation, Asymptomatic incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery, Recovery without symptoms, Dying of COVID, Losing immunity, and Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad — are now marked one-directional.

4. Missing link polarities

  • What was wrong: Roughly forty of the causal links carried no polarity, so the loop structure could not be read. In particular the two central loops were unlabelled: the contagion reinforcing loop (infectious people → infections → more infectious people) and the susceptible-depletion balancing loop (infections → fewer susceptibles → lower contact probability → fewer infections).
  • Fix: Polarity assigned to every link. Delay-time parameters (incubation time, presymptomatic period, asymptomatic period, illness duration, immunity period) are all negative, since lengthening a pipeline delay postpones and lowers the current exit rate; the Days per week conversion is positive because it shortens those delays when expressed in weeks.

5. Simulation horizon too short to exercise the reinfection loop

  • What was wrong: The run stopped at week 60 while the average immunity period is 52 weeks and both exogenous time series carry data out to week 104. The waning-immunity balancing/reinforcing structure (recovered people returning to susceptibility) barely appeared before the run ended.
  • Fix: Stop time extended to 104 weeks and the integration method made explicit (Euler with the existing small step, which is comfortably below one quarter of the shortest delay stage — the presymptomatic pipeline stage of about 0.14 week — so the third-order delays integrate accurately).

Formulations checked and deliberately left unchanged

  • Pipeline (third-order) delay style is internally consistent. Every delayed outflow delays exactly the sum of its stock's own inflows with a constant delay time: Total incubation delays Infection; Developing symptoms delays incubation plus imports; Recovery without symptoms delays asymptomatic onset; Total exiting symptomatic infectious delays symptom onset; Losing immunity delays both recovery flows. Because delay times are constant, material is conserved and no compartment can be driven negative, so these were kept rather than converted to first-order drains.
  • Splits conserve people. Symptomatic and asymptomatic branches sum to the total incubation flow, and recoveries plus deaths sum to the total symptomatic exits — no leakage or duplication.
  • Total population and Infectious population are correctly auxiliaries, not stocks — they are algebraic sums, not accumulations, so they must not be integrated.
  • Cumulative COVID deaths is correctly a stock with a single inflow and no outflow, and is correctly excluded from the living population used in the contact-probability calculation.
  • Unit conversions are dimensionally sound: clinical periods in days are divided by Days per week before being used as weekly delay times, and the infection equation resolves to people per week.

variables.name: Susceptible population
variables.documentation: People who can still catch COVID. It is drained by new infections and refilled by people whose immunity wanes after recovery.

variables.name: Exposed population
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are not yet infectious (latent). Emptied through the incubation pipeline, split between those who will become symptomatic and those who stay asymptomatic.

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People who are temporarily immune after recovering, either from a symptomatic or an asymptomatic infection. They return to the susceptible pool when immunity wanes.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: Standard infection formulation: infectious people times their contacts per week, times the probability a contact is with a susceptible person, times the transmission probability per contact. Marked uniflow because people cannot become 'un-infected' through this flow.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The share of people finishing incubation who go on to become presymptomatic and later symptomatic. One-directional transition.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: The surviving share of people leaving the symptomatic stage. One-directional transition from illness to immunity.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: Size of the population at the start of the epidemic, all assumed susceptible.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: Fraction of the living population that is still susceptible, i.e. the probability that any given contact is with a susceptible person. Protected division is used so the model cannot divide by zero if the population ever reaches zero.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: Probability that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person transmits the virus.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: Sum of all living compartments. Correctly an auxiliary (an algebraic sum), not a stock, and correctly excludes cumulative deaths since dead people do not participate in contacts.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: Average latent period between infection and becoming infectious, expressed in days.

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Infectious people who have not yet developed symptoms, including imported cases from abroad.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People currently ill with symptoms. They leave either by recovering or by dying.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Infected people who never develop symptoms but can still transmit the virus.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: Pipeline (third order) delay of everything that entered the presymptomatic stock, delayed by the presymptomatic period converted from days to weeks. Because it delays exactly the stock's inflows with a constant delay time, the material is conserved and the stock cannot go negative.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of the asymptomatic inflow by the average asymptomatic infectious period, converted from days to weeks. One-directional transition to immunity.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The share of people finishing incubation who never develop symptoms.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Fraction of infections that remain asymptomatic; estimates range between 25% and 80%.

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: Everyone finishing the latent period, computed as a pipeline delay of new infections by the incubation time in weeks. It is then split into the symptomatic and asymptomatic tracks, so the two outflows of the exposed stock together conserve exactly what flowed in.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time-based seeding of the epidemic through travellers arriving while infectious. Because it is a time series it is driven by TIME and is always non-negative.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: How long an asymptomatic person stays infectious, in days.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: The fatal share of people leaving the symptomatic stage. Deaths are irreversible, hence one-directional.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: Fraction of symptomatic cases that end in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: Time between becoming infectious and showing symptoms, in days.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: Pipeline delay of everything that entered the recovered stock by the average immunity period, returning people to susceptibility. It delays exactly the two inflows of the recovered stock with a constant delay time, so material is conserved.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: How long protection after recovery lasts, in weeks.

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average duration of symptomatic illness before recovery or death, in weeks.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: All people currently able to transmit the virus. An algebraic sum, therefore an auxiliary rather than a stock.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: Effective contact rate: the normal contact rate reduced by the fraction of contacts removed by social distancing policies.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: Exogenous policy stringency expressed as the fraction of normal contacts eliminated. It is a historical time series, so the graphical function is driven by simulated TIME.

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: Running total of deaths. Correctly a stock with a single inflow and no outflow, and deliberately excluded from the living population.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: Contacts an average person has per week in the absence of any restrictions.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant used to translate clinical periods given in days into the model's weekly time base.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Everyone leaving the symptomatic stock, a pipeline delay of its single inflow by the average length of illness. It is then split into recoveries and deaths so the two outflows together conserve the inflow.

errorExplanations.name: total_population
errorExplanations.problem: Total population should be an auxiliary/converter variable that sums the population stocks, not a stock.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and corrections

1. Total population was formulated as a stock (worst error).

  • What was wrong: A total is an accounting identity, not an accumulation. It was declared a stock with initial value 0 and a single inflow whose equation was the sum of the six population stocks. That means every week the model poured an amount equal to the entire population into the total, so Total population grew without bound (it integrated a level). It also started at zero, which makes Chance of contact with an susceptible person divide by zero at time zero.
  • Fix: Total population is now an auxiliary equal to the sum of the six living stocks (susceptible, exposed, presymptomatic, symptomatic, asymptomatic, recovered). It is now always correct by construction, it starts at 17 million, and it correctly falls as people die.

2. Total population net flow was a level disguised as a rate (the reported unit warning).

  • What was wrong: Its equation summed six stocks measured in People, but it was declared a rate in People/Week — the unit inconsistency the checker flagged. It existed only to keep the erroneous stock formulation alive.
  • Fix: The rate was removed and its causal inputs now point directly at Total population. No causal structure or feedback loop was lost: the susceptible → susceptible-share → infection loop still runs through Total population exactly as before, only now dimensionally correct.

3. Unsafe division in Chance of contact with an susceptible person.

  • What was wrong: A plain division by Total population, which was zero at the start of the run.
  • Fix: Safe division is used, and with the corrected total the denominator can no longer be zero.

4. No flow direction (uniflow) was specified anywhere.

  • What was wrong: Every flow was left bidirectional, so numerical transients in the third-order delays could in principle push people backwards through a pipe (negative births of infections, negative deaths, people un-recovering).
  • Fix: All flows — infection, incubation, asymptomatic incubation, developing symptoms, recovery, recovery without symptoms, dying of COVID, losing immunity and the imported-case influx — are marked one-directional. These are all irreversible epidemiological transitions.

5. Documentation and readability.

  • Every variable now carries documentation and units, and the initial population is written as 17000000 instead of scientific notation.

Formulations checked and deliberately left unchanged

  • Delay style is consistent and correct. The model uses third-order material (pipeline) delays throughout the disease progression chain: infection → becoming infectious → symptom onset → recovery/death → loss of immunity. Each delayed flow delays exactly the total inflow of the stock it drains, so material is conserved and no stock can go negative. I kept this pipeline style rather than converting to first-order exponential draining, because mixing the two styles inside one chain would change the epidemic timing and would be inconsistent with the rest of the structure. All delay times are correctly converted from days to weeks with Days per week; Average immunity period and Average length of symptomatic period are already in weeks and correctly are not converted.
  • No delay function is being misused as an average. The delays here represent genuine physical residence times, not smoothing, so no SMOOTH replacement was needed.
  • Infectious population, Total incubation and Total exiting symptomatic infectious are correctly auxiliaries (a sum and two rates), not stocks.
  • Cumulative COVID deaths is a legitimate accumulation; Dying of COVID correctly drains the symptomatic stock while filling it, and no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • The two time-driven graphical functions (imported cases and policy stringency) are exogenous drivers of time, so the (1,1) normalisation rule does not apply to them.

variables.name: Susceptible population
variables.documentation: People who can still catch COVID. It is drained by new infections and refilled as previously recovered people lose immunity. Initialised at the size of the population at the start of the epidemic.

variables.name: Exposed population
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are not yet infectious (latent period). They leave either on the symptomatic track (Incubation) or the asymptomatic track (Asymptomatic incubation).

variables.name: Recovered population
variables.documentation: People with temporary immunity after recovering from a symptomatic or asymptomatic infection. They return to the susceptible pool when immunity wanes.

variables.name: Infection
variables.documentation: New infections per week: infectious people times the contacts they make, times the probability a contact is with a susceptible person, times the probability that such a contact transmits the virus. Uniflow because people cannot become 'un-infected' through this pipe.

variables.name: Incubation
variables.documentation: The part of the people finishing the latent period who will eventually develop symptoms; they move into the presymptomatic infectious stock.

variables.name: Recovery
variables.documentation: Symptomatic patients who survive their illness and gain temporary immunity. It is the complement of the case fatality share of everyone leaving the symptomatic stock.

variables.name: Initial Susceptible population
variables.documentation: Population of the modelled country at the start of the epidemic. Written as a plain number instead of scientific notation for readability.

variables.name: Chance of contact with an susceptible person
variables.documentation: Probability that a random contact of an infectious person is with someone who can still be infected. Safe division is used so the model cannot divide by zero if the living population were ever zero.

variables.name: Infection rate per contact
variables.documentation: Probability that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person actually transmits the virus.

variables.name: Total population
variables.documentation: The living population: the algebraic sum of all six epidemiological stocks. A total is an accounting identity, not an accumulation, so it is an auxiliary rather than a stock.

variables.name: Average COVID incubation time
variables.documentation: Average time between being infected and becoming infectious (latent period), expressed in days.

variables.name: Presymptomatic infectious
inflows: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Infectious people who do not yet show symptoms, fed by domestic incubation and by imported cases.

variables.name: Symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: People who are ill with symptoms and infectious. They leave the stock either by recovering or by dying.

variables.name: Asymptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Infectious people who never develop symptoms; they only leave the stock by recovering.

variables.name: Developing symptoms
variables.documentation: Everyone who entered the presymptomatic stock develops symptoms after the presymptomatic period. A third order material delay of the complete inflow (domestic plus imported) keeps this pipeline consistent with the rest of the model, which uses material (pipeline) delays throughout. The delay time is converted from days to weeks with Days per week.

variables.name: Recovery without symptoms
variables.documentation: Asymptomatic people clear the infection after the average asymptomatic infectious period; modelled as a third order material delay of the inflow to that stock, in weeks.

variables.name: Asymptomatic incubation
variables.documentation: The share of people finishing the latent period who will never develop symptoms; they move into the asymptomatic infectious stock.

variables.name: Share of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Fraction of infections that never produce symptoms. Reported estimates range between 25 and 80 percent.

variables.name: Total incubation
variables.documentation: Total rate at which exposed people become infectious: the infection rate delayed by the latent period. It is an auxiliary rate that is then split into the symptomatic and asymptomatic tracks.

variables.name: Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad
variables.documentation: Exogenous, time based seeding of imported infectious travellers. This is a time driven graphical function, so it does not need to pass through the point (1,1). Uniflow because imported cases can only add people.

variables.name: Average period of asymptomatic infections
variables.documentation: Average number of days an asymptomatic person stays infectious.

variables.name: Dying of COVID
variables.documentation: Deaths per week: the fatal share of everyone leaving the symptomatic infectious stock. This flow drains the symptomatic stock and fills the cumulative death stock.

variables.name: Case fatality rate of COVID patients
variables.documentation: Fraction of symptomatic cases that end in death.

variables.name: Presymptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average number of days a person is infectious before symptoms appear.

variables.name: Losing immunity
variables.documentation: Recovered people return to the susceptible pool after the average immunity period, modelled as a third order material delay of everyone entering the recovered stock. This closes the reinfection loop.

variables.name: Average immunity period
variables.documentation: Average duration of post infection immunity, already expressed in weeks so no day to week conversion is required.

variables.name: Average length of symptomatic period
variables.documentation: Average duration of symptomatic illness, expressed directly in weeks.

variables.name: Infectious population
variables.documentation: All people currently able to transmit the virus. A simple sum, therefore an auxiliary and not a stock.

variables.name: Contacts per person per week
variables.documentation: Effective contact frequency: the normal contact rate reduced by the strength of social distancing policy.

variables.name: Social distancing measures
variables.documentation: Exogenous policy stringency over time, expressed as the fractional reduction in contacts. Time driven graphical function, so the (1,1) normalisation does not apply.

variables.name: Cumulative COVID deaths
variables.documentation: Running total of deaths. A genuine accumulation with a single inflow and no outflow.

variables.name: Normal number of contacts per week
variables.documentation: Contacts a person makes per week in the absence of any distancing policy.

variables.name: Days per week
variables.documentation: Unit conversion constant used to translate delay times expressed in days into the model time unit of weeks.

variables.name: Total exiting symptomatic infectious
variables.documentation: Rate at which people finish their symptomatic illness, obtained as a third order material delay of the inflow of new symptomatic cases. It is then split into recoveries and deaths.

errorExplanations.name: infectious_population
errorExplanations.problem: Infectious population should be an auxiliary/converter variable that sums the three infectious stocks, not a stock.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors found and fixed

1. Infectious population — an aggregation wrongly formulated as a stock (critical)

  • What was wrong: It was a stock whose only inflow was Infectious population net flow, which itself equals the sum of the three infectious stocks. This meant the model was integrating a headcount: every time step it added the entire current infectious population again, so the "infectious population" grew without bound (it is really the time-integral of person-weeks, not people) and it could never decline because the stock had no outflow. Since this variable drives the Infection equation, the contagion loop was permanently reinforcing and the epidemic could never turn over — a purely artefactual runaway reinforcing loop.
  • Why it is an error: A simple sum of other stocks is an algebraic aggregation and must be an auxiliary. Stocks are reserved for genuine accumulations that change only through their own flows; the people concerned are already accumulated in Presymptomatic infectious, Symptomatic infectious and Asymptomatic infectious, so accumulating them again double counts them.
  • How it was fixed: Infectious population is now an auxiliary that reports the current number of infectious people, taken directly from Infectious population net flow. No inflow or outflow remains, so the spurious accumulation and the artificial runaway loop are gone.

2. Infectious population net flow — wrong variable type and inconsistent units (the flagged unit warning)

  • What was wrong: It was typed as a flow with units of Person/Week, but its equation adds three stocks measured in People. The unit checker correctly reported "units Person/Week but the equation suggests Person". It is not a rate of change at all; nothing in its equation is a flow.
  • How it was fixed: It is now an auxiliary with units of Person, holding the sum of the presymptomatic, symptomatic and asymptomatic stocks. This resolves the unit warning and makes the variable a straightforward headcount that feeds the infection formulation.

3. Missing directionality settings on the flows

  • What was wrong: None of the flows declared whether they may go negative. Physically, infections, incubations, symptom onsets, recoveries, deaths, imported cases and immunity loss are strictly one-way processes; leaving them unconstrained allows negative rates (e.g. "negative deaths" pushing people back into the symptomatic stock) if a delay or a graphical function ever produced a negative value.
  • How it was fixed: Every flow (Infection, Incubation, Asymptomatic incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery, Recovery without symptoms, Dying of COVID, Losing immunity, Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad) is now marked as one-directional, so it is clipped at zero rather than reversing.

4. Missing integration method / solver specification

  • The run specification did not state a solver. Because the model relies heavily on delay functions, it is now explicitly set to Euler with the existing small time step, which is the appropriate and stable choice for delay-based structures. Start time, stop time, time step and time units are unchanged.

Formulations that were checked and deliberately left alone

  • Delay style. The chain Total incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious and Losing immunity all use third-order material (pipeline) delays of the corresponding inflow. This is internally consistent and, because each delay time is constant, the material entering each stage is exactly conserved and eventually leaves, so no stock can go negative. Converting some of these to first-order (exponential) drains would have mixed two incompatible styles, so the pipeline style was preserved throughout. Note that the delay functions here are used to represent transit time through a disease stage, not to compute moving averages — a delay is the correct tool for the former, whereas smoothing would be required for the latter.
  • Total population is correctly an auxiliary sum rather than a stock, and correctly excludes Cumulative COVID deaths, which is correctly a stock accumulating a genuine flow.
  • Day-to-week conversions are handled by the explicit Days per week conversion factor everywhere a duration is specified in days, and Average immunity period and Average length of symptomatic period are already in weeks, so they are used without conversion. Units on all equations now balance.
  • Time-driven graphical functions (Social distancing measures and Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad) are exogenous scenario inputs; time-based lookups are not required to pass through the normalising point, so their shapes were left unchanged.

No variables, names, relationships or feedback loops were added.

testParams.name: Exponential Growth Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates exponential growth behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential growth behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential growth occurs when the rate of increase is proportional to the current value. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where larger values grow faster. Examples include compound interest, viral spread, and unconstrained population growth. A classic example would be compound interest or unconstrained population growth where the rate of growth is proportional to the current value.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

The model is the minimal canonical structure for exponential growth — a single reinforcing (positive) feedback loop, the same archetype behind compound interest, viral spread, and unconstrained population growth.

  • output (stock): the accumulation whose behavior is of interest. Modeled as a stock because it accumulates over time and can change only through its flow. Its equation is only the initial value (no INTEG), as required.
  • growth (flow): the single inflow into output, equal to output * growth_rate. This proportionality is exactly what makes the behavior exponential rather than linear — the rate of increase is proportional to the current value, so larger values grow faster. Marked as a one-directional flow since growth here can never be negative.
  • growth_rate (auxiliary constant): the fractional rate of increase per period, abstracted out into its own named variable rather than hard-coded inside the flow equation.
  • initial_output (auxiliary constant): the seed value of the stock, also abstracted into a named variable. A non-zero seed is required, otherwise the reinforcing loop has nothing to compound.

The feedback loop

output → growth → output is a reinforcing loop: more output produces more growth, which produces still more output. With no balancing loop, no carrying capacity, and no outflow, nothing constrains the loop, so output follows a pure exponential curve, doubling in a fixed amount of time (roughly every 7 periods at the chosen rate).

Simulation settings

A 50-year horizon with a time step of 0.25 and Euler integration gives a smooth, clearly visible exponential rise of roughly two orders of magnitude, which is more than enough to make the characteristic accelerating shape unmistakable.
supportingInfo.title: Reinforcing Loop Driving Exponential Output Growth

testParams.name: Exponential Decay Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates exponential decay behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential decay behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential decay occurs when the rate of decrease is proportional to the current value. This creates a negative feedback loop where the value decreases rapidly at first, then more slowly as it approaches zero. Examples include radioactive decay, drug elimination from the body, and temperature cooling. The output should show rapid decrease that slows over time, asymptotically approaching zero.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

  • output (stock): the single accumulation whose behavior is of interest. Its initial value is set by a named constant rather than a hard-coded number.
  • decay rate (outflow, uniflow): defined as output * decay_fraction. This is the essential first-order, proportional-drain formulation. Because the outflow is proportional to the stock it drains, the loop output → decay rate → output is a balancing (negative) feedback loop — the archetype behind all goal-seeking/decay behavior, here with a goal of zero.
  • decay fraction (auxiliary constant): the fractional loss per time unit; its reciprocal is the decay time constant. Abstracting it into its own variable keeps the equation readable and lets the user experiment with the decay speed.
  • initial output (auxiliary constant): the starting level, isolated so the scale of the curve can be changed independently of its shape.

Why this produces the required behavior

With a constant fractional loss, the absolute loss is large while the stock is large and shrinks as the stock shrinks. The result is a rapid initial drop that slows continuously, asymptotically approaching zero without ever crossing it — exactly the radioactive-decay / drug-elimination / Newtonian-cooling pattern.

Formulation checks applied

  • No conditional logic and no hard-coded values inside equations; all parameters are named variables.
  • The stock's equation is its initial value only (no INTEG), and the flow appears solely as an outflow — never as both an inflow and an outflow.
  • The decay flow is marked uniflow so the process can only deplete, never spontaneously refill, the stock.
  • No delay or averaging functions were needed, so no DELAY-for-averaging error is present.
  • A small time step (0.125) with Euler integration is used so the discrete solution stays close to the true smooth exponential.
supportingInfo.title: First order proportional drain yields exponential decay

testParams.name: Logistic Growth Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic growth (S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic growth (S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic growth combines reinforcing and balancing feedback. Initially, growth is exponential due to reinforcing feedback. As the system approaches its carrying capacity, balancing feedback becomes dominant, slowing growth until the system stabilizes at the maximum sustainable level. Examples include population growth with limited resources, market adoption of new products, and epidemic spread with limited susceptible population. The output should start with exponential growth but gradually slow and level off as it approaches a carrying capacity or maximum limit.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

Stock: output — the accumulation that displays the S-curve. It changes only through its single inflow, satisfying the stock-flow rule. Its equation is just its initial value (initial_output), not an integral expression.

Flow: net_growth — the classic logistic rate: intrinsic_growth_rate * output * remaining_capacity_fraction. No conditional logic and no hard-coded constants appear inside it.

Auxiliaries: remaining_capacity_fraction, carrying_capacity, intrinsic_growth_rate, initial_output. All arbitrary numeric values were abstracted into named constants; the only bare number inside a formula is the structural complement 1 - x.

Two feedback loops produce the S-curve

  1. Reinforcing loop (growth engine): output → net_growth → output (+). More output generates more growth, which generates more output. This dominates early and yields exponential take-off from a small seed.
  2. Balancing loop (limit to growth): output → remaining_capacity_fraction (−) → net_growth (+) → output. As the stock fills the available capacity, the unused fraction shrinks toward zero and throttles the inflow.

This is the Limits to Growth archetype: dominance shifts from the reinforcing loop to the balancing loop at roughly half of carrying capacity (the inflection point), after which growth decelerates and the stock asymptotes at the ceiling.

Formulation checks applied

  • remaining_capacity_fraction is an auxiliary (an algebraic ratio), not a stock — sums and ratios must never be modeled as accumulations.
  • No DELAY functions were used; none were needed since no averaging or smoothing is involved.
  • net_growth is left bidirectional so the system self-corrects gracefully if the stock is ever initialized above capacity.
  • A 50-year horizon with a small time step lets the full exponential, inflection, and saturation phases appear clearly.
supportingInfo.title: Logistic S-Curve via Reinforcing and Balancing Loops

variables.documentation: The accumulating quantity of interest (e.g., population, adopters, infected individuals). It is a stock because it accumulates over time only through its net growth flow, and it is the variable that displays the S-shaped logistic trajectory.

variables.name: net_growth
variables.documentation: The rate at which output increases each time period. It is the product of a fractional growth rate, the current size of output (the reinforcing loop: more output means more growth), and the remaining capacity fraction (the balancing loop: as output nears the carrying capacity, growth is throttled toward zero). testParams.name: Logistic Decay Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic decay follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) decline and is the mirror image of logistic growth. The output starts high and declines only slowly at first while it is near its initial level. The decline then accelerates, reaching its maximum rate around the midpoint between the starting value and the floor, before slowing again as balancing feedback becomes dominant near the floor, until the system stabilizes at a lower equilibrium. Because the decline is slow at both the top and the bottom and fastest in the middle, the curve has an inflection point (it is NOT exponential decay, which declines fastest at the very start). A natural structure is an outflow proportional to both the distance still remaining above the floor and the distance already fallen from the initial value (for example, rate proportional to (initial - output) * (output - floor)), which is near zero at both ends and largest in between. Examples include the decline phase of a product life cycle and the abandonment of a technology following an inverse S-curve. The output should start high and nearly flat, decline most steeply through the middle, and then level off as it approaches a minimum sustainable level or floor.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

Behavior target: an inverse S-curve in output — high and nearly flat at first, steepest in the middle, then flattening onto a floor.

Core structure (mirror-image logistic):

  • output is a stock with a single outflow, decline rate. All change in output happens through this flow, as required.
  • decline rate is proportional to the product of two gaps:
    • remaining above floor = output − minimum sustainable level (the balancing loop: as output nears the floor, this shrinks toward zero and the decline stalls, creating the lower plateau).
    • distance already fallen = reference ceiling − output (the reinforcing loop: erosion feeds on itself, so decline accelerates out of the initial plateau).
  • Because the product of these two gaps is near zero at both ends and maximal near the midpoint, the flow peaks in the middle — producing the inflection point that distinguishes logistic decay from exponential decay (which would be fastest at time zero).

Why a reference ceiling above the start: if the ceiling equaled the initial value, the "distance already fallen" would be exactly zero at time zero and the system would sit frozen forever. A small named initiation gap seeds the reinforcing loop, giving a slow but non-zero initial decline — matching the described "starts high and declines only slowly at first."

Formulation hygiene:

  • No arbitrary numbers are buried in equations. The floor, starting level, seeding gap, and transition speed are each separate, clearly named constants; the flow equation divides only by the structural decline range to normalize.
  • The two gaps are broken out as explicit auxiliaries so each causal link has an unambiguous polarity (output raises one gap and lowers the other).
  • No conditional logic, no delay-based averaging, and the single flow appears only as an outflow — never as both an inflow and outflow of the same stock.
  • The flow is marked one-directional, so the output can never be pushed back up by a negative decline.

Resulting trajectory: output starts at 100, drains slowly (about 1.35 units/month), accelerates to a maximum near 3.75 units/month around 60, then decelerates and settles at the minimum sustainable level of 10 well within the 100-month horizon.
supportingInfo.title: Logistic Decay via Dual Gap Outflow

testParams.name: Standing Oscillation Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates sustained oscillation behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits sustained oscillation behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Standing oscillations occur in systems with delays and feedback loops that create periodic behavior. The system oscillates around an equilibrium point with relatively constant amplitude. Examples include predator-prey models (Lotka-Volterra), inventory management with ordering delays, economic business cycles, and many engineering control systems. The oscillation is sustained rather than dampening out. The output should oscillate periodically with relatively constant amplitude over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure chosen: a classic predator–prey (Lotka–Volterra) system, the canonical structure for sustained (undamped) oscillation.

  • Two stocks with delay: prey population and predator population. Predators can only grow by first eating prey, so their response is delayed relative to prey abundance. That phase lag is what turns the coupled loops into an oscillator rather than a simple approach to equilibrium.
  • One reinforcing loop: prey → prey births → prey. Left alone prey grow exponentially.
  • Two balancing loops: predation limits prey, and predator deaths limit predators. The interaction of the reinforcing prey loop with the delayed balancing predation loop produces the cycle.
  • Why amplitude stays constant: no density-dependent (carrying-capacity) damping term was added. Without such damping the system is conservative and cycles indefinitely around its equilibrium (prey* = 60, predator* = 50). The initial prey value of 80 displaces the system from equilibrium so the cycle is visible immediately.
  • output is an auxiliary that simply reports the prey population — it is an algebraic reporting variable, not a stock, since it accumulates nothing of its own.
  • Formulation checks applied: every constant (birth rate, predation coefficient, conversion efficiency, death rate) is a named variable rather than a number buried in an equation; all flows are one-directional and marked as such; no conditional logic is used; stocks carry only initial values.
  • Numerics: RK4 integration with a small time step is used because Euler adds artificial energy to a conservative oscillator, which would make the amplitude grow rather than stay constant.
supportingInfo.title: Predator prey structure producing sustained oscillation

testParams.name: Simple Pendulum
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A simple pendulum consists of a mass suspended from a fixed point by a massless string. For small angles, the motion approximates simple harmonic motion. Newton's second law for rotational motion states: τ = I*α, where τ is torque, I is moment of inertia, and α is angular acceleration. For a simple pendulum: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ), where g is gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²), L is length, and θ is angle. For small angles, sin(θ) ≈ θ, giving α ≈ -(g/L)*θ. The angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, and angular acceleration α = dω/dt. Energy is conserved: E = (1/2)*I*ω² + mgh, where potential energy depends on height h = L*(1-cos(θ)).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The pendulum is a classic second-order oscillator, so it is built as a chain of two stocks linked by a balancing feedback loop:

  • angle (stock) accumulates change_in_angle, whose equation is simply the angular velocity — this is the definition ω = dθ/dt.
  • angular_velocity (stock) accumulates angular_acceleration, which is the flow form of α = dω/dt.
  • angular_acceleration implements Newton's second law for rotation, α = −(g/L)·sin(θ). Because it depends negatively on the angle, it closes a balancing loop (angle → acceleration → velocity → angle) that, with the delay inherent in two stocks in series, produces sustained oscillation rather than simple decay.

Both flows are bidirectional (not uniflows) because the pendulum genuinely swings in both directions; forcing them non-negative would break the physics.

Constants abstracted

No physical numbers appear inside equations. Gravity (9.8 m/s²), length (1 m), bob mass (1 kg), the small initial displacement (0.1 rad ≈ 5.7°, where sin θ ≈ θ holds to within 0.2%), and the at-rest initial velocity are each named variables, so any of them can be varied without editing formulas.

Energy check

Rotational kinetic energy (I·ω²/2 with I = m·L²), height L·(1 − cos θ), potential energy m·g·h, and their sum are included as auxiliaries. In a frictionless pendulum total_energy must stay flat — this is the diagnostic that the numerical integration is faithful to Newton's laws.

Simulation settings

Euler integration systematically pumps energy into an oscillator, so RK4 is used with a small time step (0.03125 s, roughly 1/64 of the ~2.0 s natural period) over 20 seconds, which conserves energy to a very high accuracy and keeps the amplitude constant across all ten swings.
supportingInfo.title: Two Stock Newtonian Pendulum With Energy Check
