variables.name: Installed Base
variables.documentation: The number of customers currently served by the company. It accumulates customers won by the sales force and is drained by customers lost. It is the driver of the order rate, so it is the central accumulation in the growth engine.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled orders waiting to be shipped. It rises when orders arrive faster than capacity can fill them and falls as orders are filled. Backlog relative to capacity determines the delivery delay customers experience.

variables.name: Sales Force
variables.documentation: Number of salespeople employed. It accumulates net hiring, which is funded out of revenue. A larger sales force wins customers faster, closing the reinforcing growth loop.

variables.name: Capacity Under Construction
variables.documentation: Capacity that has been ordered and paid for but is not yet operational. This stock creates the construction delay: investment decisions today only add usable capacity months later, which is a key source of overshoot and oscillation.

variables.name: Production Capacity
variables.documentation: Operational production capacity, i.e. the maximum rate at which orders can be filled. It grows only as construction completes and shrinks through depreciation, so it cannot respond instantly to demand.

variables.name: Customer Acquisition Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new customers are won. Equals the number of salespeople times the number of customers each can win per month. Acquisition can never be negative, so it is a one-directional flow.

variables.name: Customer Loss Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing customers are lost, modeled as a constant fractional loss of the installed base determined by the average time a customer stays. Losses can never be negative.

variables.name: Order Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which customers place new orders. Each customer orders at a normal rate, scaled up or down by how attractive the company is given its current delivery delay. This is the entry point of the balancing delivery-delay loop.

variables.name: Order Fulfillment Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which orders are shipped. It is limited either by available production capacity or, when the backlog is small, by the minimum time needed to process an order. Shipments cannot be negative.

variables.name: Sales Force Net Hiring Rate
variables.documentation: Net change in the sales force as the company closes the gap between the sales force it can afford and the one it has. It is bidirectional because the company hires when revenue grows and lets salespeople go when the budget shrinks.

variables.name: Capacity Ordering Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new capacity is ordered and put into construction. The company orders what it needs to close its capacity gap, but never more than its capacity budget can pay for. Orders cannot be negative, so a surplus of capacity simply means no new orders.

variables.name: Capacity Completion Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which capacity under construction becomes operational, spread over the average construction delay. This delay means capacity always lags the demand that justified it.

variables.name: Capacity Depreciation Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing capacity wears out and is retired, modeled as a constant fraction of capacity set by its average lifetime. Retirement is one-directional.

variables.name: Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The average time a customer waits for an order, calculated as the backlog divided by the capacity available to work it off (Little's Law). Safe division prevents a divide-by-zero if capacity ever reaches zero.

variables.name: Relative Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: Delivery delay expressed as a ratio to the delay customers consider normal. A value of one means service is as expected; larger values mean service is worse than expected. Used as the dimensionless input to the attractiveness function.

variables.name: Effect Of Delivery Delay On Attractiveness
variables.documentation: A multiplier capturing how attractive the company is to buyers given its service. It equals one when delivery delay is normal, rises modestly when service is better than normal, and falls sharply as delays lengthen. It reduces both ordering by existing customers and the productivity of salespeople, which is how the capacity shortage feeds back to restrain growth.

variables.name: Sales Productivity
variables.documentation: Customers won per salesperson per month. It equals normal productivity scaled by company attractiveness, so long delivery delays make each salesperson less effective and slow customer acquisition.

variables.name: Revenue
variables.documentation: Money earned per month from orders actually filled, equal to shipments times price. Revenue is the single funding source for both sales force and capacity investment, so unfilled demand generates no cash to fix the shortage.

variables.name: Sales Budget
variables.documentation: The portion of revenue allocated to funding the sales force each month.

variables.name: Desired Sales Force
variables.documentation: The number of salespeople the company can afford, equal to the sales budget divided by the cost of one salesperson. It is the goal that net hiring moves toward.

variables.name: Capacity Budget
variables.documentation: The portion of revenue allocated each month to investment in new production capacity.

variables.name: Affordable Capacity Order Rate
variables.documentation: How much new capacity per month the capacity budget can actually buy, given the capital cost of a unit of capacity. This is the financial ceiling on capacity expansion and a main reason capacity cannot keep up with fast demand growth.

variables.name: Desired Production Capacity
variables.documentation: The capacity management believes it needs, set as current incoming orders times a desired coverage margin so that some slack exists to keep delivery delay near normal.

variables.name: Capacity Gap
variables.documentation: The shortfall between desired capacity and the capacity already operating plus that already on order. Counting the supply line prevents over-ordering, but the long construction delay still allows large gaps to persist.

variables.name: Indicated Capacity Order Rate
variables.documentation: The rate of capacity ordering that would close the capacity gap over the intended adjustment time, before checking whether the money is available.

variables.name: Normal Order Rate Per Customer
variables.documentation: Units ordered per customer per month when delivery service is normal. Sets the scale of demand generated by the installed base.

variables.name: Average Customer Lifetime
variables.documentation: Average time a customer remains in the installed base before being lost. Its inverse is the fractional customer loss rate.

variables.name: Normal Sales Productivity
variables.documentation: Customers a salesperson wins per month when delivery service is normal. Benchmark for the effect of attractiveness on selling effectiveness.

variables.name: Normal Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers regard as acceptable. Used as the reference point for judging service quality.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: The shortest time in which an order can be picked, packed and shipped. It prevents the backlog from being emptied instantaneously when capacity is ample.

variables.name: Unit Price
variables.documentation: Revenue earned per unit shipped. Converts physical shipments into the cash that funds investment.

variables.name: Fraction Of Revenue To Sales
variables.documentation: Share of revenue devoted to the sales force. A policy parameter governing the strength of the reinforcing sales growth loop.

variables.name: Cost Per Salesperson
variables.documentation: Fully loaded monthly cost of employing one salesperson. Converts the sales budget into an affordable headcount.

variables.name: Sales Force Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Average time needed to recruit or release salespeople so that actual headcount reaches the affordable level.

variables.name: Fraction Of Revenue To Capacity
variables.documentation: Share of revenue devoted to capacity expansion. A policy parameter that determines how fast the supply side can grow.

variables.name: Capital Cost Per Unit Capacity
variables.documentation: Capital required to add one unit per month of production capacity. Together with the capacity budget it sets the affordable expansion rate.

variables.name: Capacity Coverage Target
variables.documentation: Desired ratio of capacity to current orders. Values above one give service slack; a low target keeps the firm chronically short of capacity.

variables.name: Capacity Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: The time over which management intends to close a capacity gap through ordering decisions.

variables.name: Capacity Construction Delay
variables.documentation: Average time between ordering capacity and its coming online. This long delay is the principal cause of overshoot and oscillation in sales.

variables.name: Average Capacity Lifetime
variables.documentation: Average service life of production capacity before retirement; its inverse is the fractional depreciation rate.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of population growth. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

  • Population is the single stock, initialized at 1000 individuals. It changes only through its two flows.
  • births is an inflow computed as Population * fractional_birth_rate. It is marked one-directional since births cannot be negative.
  • deaths is an outflow computed as Population * fractional_death_rate, also one-directional.
  • fractional birth rate (0.03/year) and fractional death rate (0.015/year) are separate named constants rather than numbers buried inside the flow equations, so they can be inspected and varied.

Feedback

The model contains the classic pair of loops: a reinforcing loop (more population → more births → more population) driving exponential growth, and a balancing loop (more population → more deaths → less population). Because the fractional birth rate exceeds the fractional death rate, the reinforcing loop dominates and the population grows exponentially at a net 1.5% per year, roughly quadrupling over the 100-year horizon.

Simulation settings

Start year 0, stop year 100, time step 0.25 years, Euler integration — matching the specified horizon and time unit.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

  • balance is the single stock, initialized numerically through initial balance (5000 dollars). It changes only through its flows, as required.
  • deposits and interest is the single inflow, formed by adding interest earned and deposits. It is marked one-directional since it can only add money.
  • withdrawals is the single outflow, driven by withdrawal rate (1200 dollars per year), also one-directional.
  • interest earned is an auxiliary calculated as balance times annual interest rate. Keeping the rate as its own named variable avoids embedding an arbitrary constant inside an equation.

Dynamics

The balance-to-interest-to-inflow-to-balance path forms a reinforcing loop (compound growth): the bigger the balance, the more interest it earns, which grows the balance further. Because net non-interest cash flow is positive (2400 in versus 1200 out), the balance rises steadily and the reinforcing interest loop accelerates that rise, producing accelerating exponential-plus-linear growth over the 30-year horizon.

Formulation checks

  • Interest earned is an auxiliary (an algebraic calculation), not a stock — sums and products of other quantities must never be modeled as accumulations.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the balance.
  • No conditionals or hard-coded numeric constants appear inside equations; all parameters are named variables.

Simulation specs

Years 0 to 30, time step 0.25 years, Euler integration.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic SIR structure with three stocks: susceptible people, infected people, and recovered people. Susceptible people become infected and flow into the infected stock; infected people recover and flow into the recovered stock. The infection rate equals the contact rate times the infectivity times the number of infected people times the fraction of the total population that is still susceptible (susceptible divided by total population). The recovery rate equals the infected population divided by the average duration of illness. Use a total population of 10000, with 9990 initially susceptible, 10 initially infected, and 0 recovered. Use a contact rate of 6 contacts per person per day, an infectivity of 0.05, and an average duration of illness of 5 days. Simulate from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, using days as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic SIR chain of three stocks connected by two flows:

  • Susceptible Population (9990) → Infection Rate → Infected Population (10) → Recovery Rate → Recovered Population (0). Total population is a fixed 10000.

Equations

  • Infection Rate = contact rate × infectivity × infected × (susceptible / total population). Each infected person makes contacts each day; only the susceptible share of those contacts can result in transmission, and each such contact infects with probability equal to the infectivity. All parameters are separate named variables rather than numbers buried in the equation.
  • Recovery Rate = infected / average duration of illness, a standard first-order draining of the infected stock.
  • Both flows are one-directional (uniflow) because people cannot "un-infect" or "un-recover" through these pipes.

Feedback behavior

Two loops drive the epidemic curve. A reinforcing loop — more infected people produce more infections, which produce still more infected people — causes the initial exponential takeoff. A balancing loop operates through depletion of the susceptible pool: every infection reduces the susceptible fraction, which slows further infection. Recovery adds a second balancing drain on the infected stock. Together these produce the familiar rise, peak, and decline of an outbreak in a closed population.

With these parameters the reproduction number is contact rate × infectivity × duration = 1.5, so the disease spreads and eventually burns out as susceptibles run low. Simulation runs from day 0 to day 100 with a 0.5-day time step in days.
supportingInfo.title: Classic SIR Outbreak Model in Fixed Population

Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds a single stock of inventory, in units. Inventory rises through a production/delivery inflow and falls through a shipment outflow. Shipments equal customer demand, which is a constant 100 units per week. The store wants to keep inventory at a desired level equal to a target coverage of expected sales: desired inventory equals demand multiplied by a desired coverage of 4 weeks. The production rate equals demand plus a correction that closes the gap between desired inventory and current inventory over an inventory adjustment time of 8 weeks (that is, production equals demand plus (desired inventory minus inventory) divided by the adjustment time). Start with an initial inventory of 200 units, which is below the desired level, so the correction loop is active. Simulate from week 0 to week 52 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

One stock, two flows. Inventory starts at 200 units, is increased by production and decreased by shipments. No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow.

Demand side. customer_demand is a constant 100 units/week and directly sets shipments, so the store always meets demand.

Goal-seeking (balancing) loop. This is the classic stock-adjustment archetype:

  • desired inventory = demand × desired coverage (100 × 4 = 400 units)
  • inventory gap = desired inventory − Inventory
  • inventory correction = gap ÷ inventory adjustment time (8 weeks)
  • production = demand + correction

The loop is balancing: as inventory rises, the gap shrinks, the correction shrinks, and production falls back toward demand. Starting 200 units below target, inventory approaches 400 units along an exponential (first-order) path with a time constant of 8 weeks — roughly 99% of the gap closed by week 40, well inside the 52-week horizon.

Formulation choices

  • All numeric parameters (demand, coverage, adjustment time) are separate named constants rather than being buried inside equations, so the equations read as plain relationships.
  • desired inventory and inventory gap are auxiliaries, not stocks — they are algebraic calculations, not accumulations.
  • Both flows are marked one-directional since production and shipments cannot physically run backwards; with these parameters neither ever goes negative anyway.
  • No delays or smoothing are used, matching the description of an instantaneous correction policy.

Simulation settings

Weeks 0 to 52, time step 0.25, Euler integration — a step of 0.25 is far smaller than the 8-week adjustment time, so the solution is numerically accurate.
supportingInfo.title: Goal Seeking Inventory Stock Adjustment Model

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of predator-prey dynamics. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic Lotka-Volterra structure with two stocks: a prey population and a predator population. The prey population grows through prey births and shrinks through prey deaths caused by predation. Prey births equal a prey birth rate coefficient times the prey population. Prey deaths equal a predation coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. The predator population grows through predator births and shrinks through predator deaths. Predator births equal a predator efficiency coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. Predator deaths equal a predator death rate coefficient times the predator population. Use an initial prey population of 100 and an initial predator population of 20. Use a prey birth rate coefficient of 0.5, a predation coefficient of 0.02, a predator efficiency coefficient of 0.01, and a predator death rate coefficient of 0.4 (all per appropriate time unit). Because this system oscillates, use a small time step for numerical stability: simulate from time 0 to time 50 with a time step of 0.03125, using months as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system built from two accumulations and four rates.

Stocks

  • prey population starts at 100 animals; it gains from prey births and loses from prey deaths.
  • predator population starts at 20 animals; it gains from predator births and loses from predator deaths.

Flows

  • prey births = prey birth rate coefficient × prey population — a reinforcing loop driving exponential prey growth when predators are scarce.
  • prey deaths = predation coefficient × prey population × predator population — a mass-action encounter term; this is the balancing loop that curbs prey growth.
  • predator births = predator efficiency coefficient × prey population × predator population — food captured is converted into new predators, coupling predator growth to prey abundance.
  • predator deaths = predator death rate coefficient × predator population — a balancing loop that shrinks the predator stock when prey become scarce.

All four flows are one-directional (uniflow), so births and deaths can never run backwards.

Constants were abstracted into named auxiliaries rather than buried in the flow equations: prey birth rate coefficient (0.5/month), predation coefficient (0.02), predator efficiency coefficient (0.01), and predator death rate coefficient (0.4/month).

Why it oscillates

The two balancing loops are coupled through a delay: predators only build up after prey are abundant, and they only decline after prey have already crashed. This delayed negative feedback produces the familiar out-of-phase cycles, with the predator peak lagging the prey peak.

Simulation settings

Run from month 0 to month 50 with a time step of 0.03125 months. A fourth-order integration method is used together with the small step so the oscillation amplitude does not artificially grow from numerical error.
supportingInfo.title: Lotka Volterra Predator Prey Oscillation Model

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of software project rework. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Model a fixed-scope software project with three stocks, all measured in tasks: work to be done, undiscovered rework, and work truly done. The team completes tasks at a work rate that flows out of work to be done. The work rate equals the number of developers times their productivity. A fraction of completed work is done correctly and flows into work truly done; the remaining fraction contains defects and flows into undiscovered rework instead. Undiscovered rework is not visible immediately: it is detected and flows back into work to be done at a rework discovery rate equal to the undiscovered rework stock divided by an average discovery delay. Use an initial work to be done of 500 tasks, an initial undiscovered rework of 0 tasks, and an initial work truly done of 0 tasks. Use 10 developers, a productivity of 0.4 tasks per developer per week, a fraction correct of 0.85 (so 0.15 of completed work becomes undiscovered rework), and an average discovery delay of 4 weeks. To avoid completed work continuing to be generated once the backlog is empty, the work rate should not exceed the amount of work remaining to be done. Simulate from week 0 to week 200 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

  • Three stocks in tasks: Work to be Done (500), Undiscovered Rework (0), Work Truly Done (0). All initial values are numeric, and each changes only through its flows.
  • Execution flow: Work Rate drains Work to be Done. It equals MIN(Potential Work Rate, Work to be Done/DT), so the team never completes more work than actually remains — this prevents phantom completed work and negative backlog once the queue empties. Potential Work Rate = Developers × Productivity (10 × 0.4 = 4 tasks/week), keeping the arbitrary values in named constants rather than buried in the equation.
  • Quality split: Work Completion Rate = Work Rate × Fraction Correct feeds Work Truly Done; Rework Generation Rate = Work Rate × Fraction Incorrect feeds Undiscovered Rework. Fraction Incorrect is written as the structural complement 1 - Fraction Correct so the two shares always sum to one.
  • Hidden rework loop: Rework Discovery Rate = Undiscovered Rework / Average Discovery Delay is a standard first-order drain (not a delay function used as an average), and it returns discovered defects to Work to be Done.

Why the project runs late

The model contains a reinforcing rework cycle: executing work creates hidden defects, which after a 4-week detection delay reappear as new backlog, which must be executed again and itself generates further defects. With 15% defect creation, the effective work required is roughly the original scope divided by the fraction correct (about 588 tasks rather than 500), so a project that looks like a 125-week job at 4 tasks/week stretches well beyond that. The delay also means the visible backlog falls smoothly and encourages an optimistic "almost done" reading, while Work Truly Done lags and Undiscovered Rework holds a hidden inventory that must still be worked off — the classic "90% syndrome" tail.

Formulation checks applied

  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • All one-directional flows (execution, correct completion, defect creation, defect discovery) are marked as non-negative.
  • No conditional logic or hidden numeric constants inside equations; only the structural complement, a boundary-limiting MIN, and the time step appear.
  • Simulation runs from week 0 to 200 with a 0.25-week step in weeks, using Euler integration.
supportingInfo.title: Software project rework cycle stock flow model

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this non-modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please recreate the system with two modules.

            Use the following module names exactly:
            hare, lynx

            Component naming instructions:
            - Specifically rename "Hares" to "hare.hares", "area" to "hare.area", and "Lynx" to "lynx.lynx".
            - Otherwise, name components within each module by removing the animal prefix, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'hares killed per lynx' should be renamed to 'hare.killed_per_lynx', 
              and 'lynx births' should be renamed to 'lynx.births'.
            - Preserve the names of components that are not placed in modules.
            - When ghosting, preserve the original name of the ghosted component, including the module name if appropriate.
              For example, to create a ghost of "lynx.births" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx births".
              To create a ghost of "lynx.lynx" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx",
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly, adding as few additional variables as possible
            and only when strictly necessary.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Restructured into two modules

The predator-prey system is now split into a hare module and a lynx module, each containing its own population stock, birth and death flows, and the parameters that drive them.

hare module: hares (stock), births, deaths, birth fraction, area, density, and killed per lynx (the prey-density graphical function).

lynx module: lynx (stock), births, deaths, birth fraction, and death fraction (the starvation graphical function driven by prey density).

Closing the two feedback loops across modules

The system's two coupling links cross module boundaries, so each is carried by a cross-level ghost — the only variables added:

  • hare.lynx ghosts the lynx population into the hare module so predation losses can be computed. This closes the balancing predation loop: more lynx → more hare deaths → fewer hares.
  • lynx.hare density ghosts hare density into the lynx module so the mortality fraction can respond to food supply. This closes the second balancing loop: fewer hares → lower density → higher lynx mortality → fewer lynx → fewer hare deaths.

Together with the two reinforcing growth loops (each population compounding through its own births), these interlocking balancing loops produce the classic predator-prey oscillation.

Other notes

All equations inside each module reference only local names or the local ghosts, never the other module's variables directly. Both birth and death flows are one-directional (they can never run backwards). Initial values, parameter values, graphical function points, and simulation settings are unchanged from the original model.

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please recreate the system with no modules, while preserving key causal relationships.

            Component naming instructions:
            - Name components by removing the module name, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'Hares.hare density' should be renamed to 'hare_density'.
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly.
            You are allowed to remove variables and modify relationships that are no longer appropriate in a non-modular context.
            Do not add any components that do not have a modular equivalent in my source model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Flattening the modular predator-prey system

  • Removed the module wrappers and renamed each element by simply dropping its module prefix (for example, the hare density variable in the Hares module is now just hare_density).
  • Deleted the two cross-level ghost variables (the lynx population inside the Hares module and the hare density inside the Lynx module). In a single-level model there are no boundaries to cross, so the predation and starvation equations now reference the original stock and density variables directly. No causal information is lost — the same influences remain, they are simply drawn as direct links.
  • All original structure is preserved: both populations remain stocks driven by a birth inflow and a death outflow; the two nonlinear graphical relationships (hares killed per lynx as a function of prey density, and lynx mortality as a declining function of prey density) are unchanged, including the initialization of the lynx stock below equilibrium.

Feedback loops now explicitly closed

With the ghosts removed, the causal links make all four loops visible in one diagram:

  1. Hare growth (reinforcing): hares → births → hares.
  2. Lynx growth (reinforcing): lynx → births → lynx.
  3. Predation (balancing): hares → hare density → kills per lynx → hare deaths → hares. Prey abundance increases its own losses.
  4. Predator-prey coupling (balancing, the oscillation engine): hares → hare density → lynx death fraction → lynx deaths → lynx → hare deaths → hares. Abundant prey sustains predators, whose growth then depletes the prey, which starves the predators — the classic limits to growth with a delayed resource archetype that produces the characteristic lagged oscillation.

No new concepts were introduced; the added links are exactly those the ghost variables previously carried across module walls.
supportingInfo.title: Flattened predator-prey model with closed loops

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            Please recreate the system with no modules, while preserving key causal relationships.

            Component naming instructions:
            - Name components by removing the module name, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'Population.target housing per person' should be renamed to 'target housing per person'.
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly.
            You are allowed to remove variables and modify relationships that are no longer appropriate in a non-modular context.
            Do not add any components that do not have a modular equivalent in my source model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Flattening the model

All three modules were merged into a single flat structure. Every variable keeps its original name with the module prefix stripped (for example Population.target housing per person becomes target housing per person). The four cross-level ghost variables (Population.Housing Stock, Population.total jobs, Housing.Population, Commerce.Population) were deleted because in a flat model the equations can reference the single real Population, Housing Stock and total jobs directly. All stock/flow structure, graphical functions, parameter values and causal links from the modular version are preserved exactly.

Closing open feedback loops

The original model had growth engines with no physical limit: population attracts construction and business formation, which in turn attract more population, but nothing ever stopped that expansion except the relative-ratio balancing loops among the three sectors themselves. Two limits-to-growth structures were added, using only mechanisms already implied by the city context.

1. Land constraint (balancing loop on both development sectors). land area, land per housing unit and land per business structure combine into land occupied, then land fraction occupied, available land fraction and a land availability multiplier that now multiplies both construction and business starts. This closes two balancing loops: building more housing (or more businesses) consumes the land that makes further building possible, so development self-limits as the city fills in. The multiplier is normalized so that fully vacant land gives the normal development rate.

2. Congestion feedback (balancing loop on migration). population density (people per acre of the same land area) is compared with normal population density to give relative population density, which drives attractiveness from congestion. This multiplier now joins housing and job attractiveness in the migration equation, so growth in population raises crowding, which lowers attractiveness and shuts off in-migration. This closes the loop that previously ran only one way — population affected housing and job availability, but the accumulated crowding it created never fed back on the desirability of the city itself.

Together these turn the model from an essentially open-ended growth machine into a classic limits-to-growth city: reinforcing population–jobs–housing growth eventually runs into the fixed land base and rising congestion.
supportingInfo.title: Flattened urban model with land and congestion limits

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please add a third module called 'cougars', representing cougars.
            
            As an apex predator, cougars are not hunted by any animal, and hunt lynxes to survive. 
            Cougars do not have any direct interactions with hares.

            Use the following component names in each module where appropriate:
            [animals], 
            [animal] births, [animal] deaths, 
            [animals] killed per [animal], [animal] density,
            [animal] birth fraction, [animal] death fraction
            - Note: [animal] is either "hare", "lynx", or "cougar"
            - Note: [animals] is either "hares", "lynx", or "cougars" (note the plural of "lynx" is "lynx")
            
            When ghosting, preserve the same variable name as in the source module. For instance, a ghost of "Hares.Hares"
            should be named "Lynx.Hares" in the "Lynx" module.

            You may add any necessary components, using appropriate names (as listed above) whenever possible.
            Do not modify or remove any existing causal relationships between lynxes and hares.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

New Cougars module (apex predator)

  • Cougars.Cougars — stock of cougars (initially 50), with cougar births as its only inflow and cougar deaths as its only outflow. Because cougars are apex predators, nothing hunts them, so their outflow contains no predation term.
  • Cougars.cougar births = Cougars × cougar birth fraction — the same reinforcing (compounding) birth loop used for hares and lynx.
  • Cougars.cougar deaths = Cougars × cougar death fraction, where the death fraction is a declining graphical function of lynx density. This is the balancing loop that regulates the apex predator: scarce prey → higher starvation → fewer cougars.
  • Cougars.lynx density — cross-level ghost of Lynx.lynx density.

Additions inside the Lynx module (to close the predation loop)

  • Lynx.lynx density = Lynx / area — the prey-availability signal cougars respond to, mirroring hare density in the Hares module.
  • Lynx.area — cross-level ghost of Hares.area, since all species share one habitat.
  • Lynx.lynx killed per cougar — a saturating graphical function of lynx density (zero kills at zero density), mirroring hares killed per lynx.
  • Lynx.Cougars — cross-level ghost of Cougars.Cougars.
  • Lynx.lynx deaths now adds a predation term, Cougars × lynx killed per cougar, on top of the existing starvation term Lynx × lynx death fraction. No existing hare–lynx relationship, equation term, or variable name was changed or removed.

Feedback loops now closed

  1. Cougar–lynx balancing loop: more cougars → more lynx killed → fewer lynx → lower lynx density → higher cougar death fraction → fewer cougars.
  2. Cougar reinforcing growth loop: more cougars → more cougar births → more cougars.
  3. Cross-trophic coupling: cougar predation reduces lynx, which relieves predation pressure on hares, raising hare density, which lowers lynx starvation — linking the new predator into the existing hare–lynx oscillator without altering it.

No interaction between cougars and hares was created, as specified.
supportingInfo.title: Cougar apex predator module closes predation loops

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            However, I no longer need to simulate commerce dynamics. Please remove the 'Commerce' module from my model.

            Please do not add any variables or modify any processes or relationships unrelated to commerce.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Removed the Commerce module entirely. All of its contents were deleted: the Business Structures stock, business starts and business closures flows, base start fraction, closure fraction, target labor per business, relative labor availability, start multiplier, jobs per structure, total jobs, and the ghost of Population used inside Commerce.

Cleaned up the dangling references that Commerce left behind in the Population module. Because total jobs no longer exists anywhere in the model, the following Population variables were also removed, since they had no remaining source of information and would otherwise break the simulation:

  • the cross-level ghost of total jobs
  • relative job availability
  • target jobs per person
  • attractiveness from jobs

Adjusted one equation. Net migration previously averaged housing attractiveness and job attractiveness. It now depends only on housing attractiveness, so migration is still driven by the city's ability to house people, but no longer references the deleted employment structure.

What remains intact. The two surviving reinforcing/balancing structures are untouched: population grows through births and net migration and declines through deaths; housing construction responds to crowding (persons per house), which in turn relieves crowding. The classic balancing loop between population pressure and housing supply — and the attractiveness loop where more housing draws more migrants, which reduces available housing per person — still closes properly. The cross-level ghosts linking the Population and Housing modules (housing stock into Population, population into Housing) are preserved so both loops remain connected.

No new variables, processes, or relationships unrelated to commerce were introduced.
supportingInfo.title: Commerce Module Removed, Housing Population Loops Preserved

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            rookies, associates, partners, promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate,
            rookie_promotions, associate_promotions, rookie_hires,
            rookie_departures, associate_departures, partner_departures

            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The career hierarchy is modeled as an aging chain: three stocks (rookies → associates → partners) connected by promotion flows, with each stock also drained by its own departure flow.

  • rookies is filled by rookie_hires (a constant policy inflow equal to hire_rate) and drained by rookie_promotions and rookie_departures.
  • associates is filled by rookie_promotions and drained by associate_promotions and associate_departures.
  • partners is filled by associate_promotions and drained only by partner_departures, since there is no rank above partner.

Key causal mechanisms

  • Every promotion and departure flow is a fixed fraction of the stock it drains (promotion_rate, departure_rate), which is the strict-percentage policy described. Each of these fractional outflows forms a balancing loop with its own stock: the bigger the level, the more people leave it, which pulls the level back down.
  • Because of these balancing loops, each level settles to an equilibrium set by its inflow divided by its total fractional outflow. Rookies stabilize at hires ÷ (promotion + departure) percentage; associates and partners then stabilize in turn, one link further down the chain and with a time lag.
  • Hiring is the only exogenous inflow, so the entire hierarchy's ultimate size is anchored by hire_rate, while the shape of the pyramid is set by the ratio of promotion to departure percentages.

Formulation choices

  • All rates are broken out as named constants rather than embedded numbers, so policy experiments (faster promotion, higher attrition, more hiring) can be run directly.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since people cannot be "un-promoted" or "un-hired" through these pipes.
  • total employees is an auxiliary sum, not a stock, because it is a simple algebraic aggregation of the three levels rather than an independent accumulation.
supportingInfo.title: Three Level Promotion Chain With Attrition

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            fox_reproductionRate, fox_count, fox_reproduction,
            chicken_reproductionRate, chicken_count, chicken_reproduction, chicken_predation
            
            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is a simple, non-modular predator–prey structure with two accumulations:

  • chicken_count (prey stock): grows by chicken_reproduction (a fixed fraction of the current flock — a reinforcing growth loop) and is drained by chicken_predation.
  • fox_count (predator stock): grows by fox_reproduction (a fixed, smaller fraction of the current fox population — a second reinforcing loop).

Key causal mechanism

Predation couples the two populations: total chickens eaten equals the number of foxes times the appetite of a single fox. The per-fox appetite is held in its own named parameter (chickens_eaten_per_fox = 1 chicken/fox/day) rather than being buried as a hard-coded number inside an equation.

Because the fox population grows exponentially while consumption per fox is constant, predation eventually grows faster than chicken births, so the initially dominant chicken population is drawn down and can collapse — the classic "success to the limits" dynamic in which the prey's own reinforcing growth is overtaken by an exponentially growing drain. Note that, as described in the background, foxes have no death or starvation flow, so their growth is unchecked; this is intentional fidelity to the description and is the main reason the system does not settle into a sustained oscillation.

Modeling choices

  • Both birth flows and the predation flow are one-directional (they can never be negative).
  • Initial conditions put chickens (1000) far above foxes (10), and the chicken fractional growth rate (10%/day) exceeds the fox rate (2%/day), matching the described setup.
  • No modules and no arrays were introduced, per the request.
supportingInfo.title: Fox and chicken predator prey model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Please create a model with two modules, 'foxes' and 'chickens'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            reproduction rate, count, reproduction, predation

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two modules were created, chickens and foxes, each built around a population stock named count.

  • chickens.count is an accumulation with one inflow (reproduction) and one outflow (predation).
  • foxes.count is an accumulation with one inflow (reproduction).

Causal mechanisms

  1. Reinforcing growth loops. In each module, reproduction = count * reproduction rate. This compounding loop is the engine of exponential growth for both species. The fox fractional rate is set lower than the chicken rate, as described.
  2. Predation coupling. Foxes feed on chickens: predation = foxes count * chickens eaten per fox, with the per-fox appetite abstracted into its own named constant (one chicken per fox per day). This is the balancing pressure that drains the chicken stock and is the only cross-module linkage.

Modularity

Because predation is calculated inside the chickens module but depends on the fox population, a cross-level ghost named chickens.foxes count was created, pointing at foxes.count. The chickens module's predation equation references only the ghost, preserving module encapsulation.

Behavior

The model exhibits the classic predator preying on a faster-growing prey pattern: both populations grow exponentially, with predation losses proportional to predator numbers. Because chickens compound faster than foxes, chickens stay ahead unless fox numbers become large relative to the chicken flock, at which point predation becomes the dominant drain. predation and both reproduction flows are marked one-directional so they can never run backwards.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain city, a population depends on a nonrenewable resource.
            The population reproduces and dies off at steady rates proportional to the total population.
            The resource starts with a large initial quantity, but cannot be refilled.
            Over time, the resource diminishes at a rate proportional to the population.
            Define the "resource density" as the ratio of resource quantity to the population.
            If the resource density drops below a fixed threshold, then members of the population migrate away at
            a rate proportional to the total population and the difference between the resource density 
            and the minimum threshold.

            Please create a model with two modules, 'population' and 'resource'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, births, death rate, deaths, usage rate, usage, density, density threshold, migrations

            All "rate" variables should be constant percentages.
            Please compute the resource density inside the 'resource' module, not the 'population' module.
            (The resource density threshold should be in the 'population' module, however.)
            Do not create any intermediate variables when calculating population migrations.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two modules, as requested: population and resource, with no extra modules.

Population module holds a stock count with an inflow births (= count × birth rate) and two outflows: deaths (= count × death rate) and migrations. Birth and death rates are constant fractions, giving the classic reinforcing growth loop (more people → more births → more people) balanced by a proportional death loop.

Resource module holds the nonrenewable stock count with a single outflow usage (= usage rate × population). There is no inflow, so the stock can only decline. density (resource per person) is computed here, as specified.

Key causal mechanism

The interesting behavior comes from the coupling between the modules:

  • Population drives resource consumption (resource.population count ghost → usage), depleting a finite stock.
  • Falling resource and rising population both push density down (a depletion-driven balancing loop).
  • Once density falls below density threshold, migrations = count × (threshold − density) drains people out. This flow is one-directional, so no in-migration occurs while density is above the threshold — the migration loop only engages after the resource becomes scarce.

This produces the characteristic overshoot-and-decline pattern of a population living off a nonrenewable resource: exponential growth while resource is plentiful, then a sharp turnaround as density crosses the threshold and out-migration dominates.

Modeling conventions applied

  • Cross-module references use ghosts named with the source module prefix separated by a space: population.resource density (ghost of resource.density) and resource.population count (ghost of population.count). All equations inside a module reference the local ghost, never the foreign variable directly.
  • Migration is computed in a single expression with no intermediate variables.
  • Division for density uses the safe-division operator to avoid a divide-by-zero if population reaches zero.
  • A small time step is used because the migration response is fast relative to birth and death dynamics.
supportingInfo.title: Population depleting nonrenewable resource drives migration

            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Create a model with three modules named 'rookies', 'associates', and 'partners'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:        
            count, 
            promotions, departures, hires,
            promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate
            
            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is a classic aging chain (co-flow of people through career stages), built as three modules that mirror the three-role hierarchy.

  • rookies: count is a stock filled by hires (a constant onboarding policy, hire_rate) and drained by two outflows: promotions (a strict percentage, promotion_rate, of the current pool) and departures (a stable attrition percentage, departure_rate).
  • associates: count is a stock whose hires inflow is exactly the rookie promotion flow, brought in through the ghost rookies promotions. It is drained by its own promotions to partner and its own departures.
  • partners: count is a stock whose hires inflow is the associate promotion flow, brought in through the ghost associates promotions. Because partner is the top of the hierarchy there is no promotion outflow — only departures.

Key causal mechanisms

Each level is a first-order draining process: the larger the pool, the larger the outflow, because both promotions and departures are fixed fractions of the current headcount. That is a balancing loop at every level, so each stock converges to an equilibrium where inflow equals the sum of fractional outflows.

Because the only exogenous driver is the constant hire rate, the whole system settles at a steady state determined by the ratios of the rates:

  • rookies settle at hire rate divided by (promotion rate + departure rate)
  • associates settle at rookie promotions divided by (their promotion rate + departure rate)
  • partners settle at associate promotions divided by their departure rate

This makes the leverage points explicit: the shape of the pyramid is set by the relative promotion and attrition percentages, while its overall size is set by the hiring constant. Each downstream level responds to upstream changes with a delay, since the promotion flow must first accumulate.

Modeling choices

All flows are one-directional (people cannot un-hire or un-promote), so they are marked as uniflows. Rates are held as separate named constants rather than embedded in equations, so each policy lever can be adjusted independently.

testParams.prompt:
Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three modules — lions, foxes, and chickens — each hold a population count stock driven by a births inflow and a deaths outflow. Both are simple fractional formulations (count * birth rate, count * death rate), giving each species a reinforcing growth loop and a balancing mortality loop.

Predation chain

  • chickens.predation rate is an additional outflow from the chicken stock, computed as chicken count × a per-fox predation fraction × the fox population (brought in via the ghost chickens.foxes count).
  • foxes.predation rate is an additional outflow from the fox stock, computed the same way using the lion population (ghost foxes.lions count).
  • Lions, having no predator, have no predation flow.

This creates a top-down trophic cascade: lion abundance suppresses foxes, and fox abundance suppresses chickens, so a rise in lions indirectly relieves pressure on chickens.

Modeling choices

  • Every arbitrary coefficient is a named variable (predation fraction per lion, predation fraction per fox) rather than a number embedded in an equation.
  • Cross-module references use ghost variables named with the source module prefix separated by a space, and all local equations reference the ghost rather than the original.
  • All flows are one-directional (uniflow), since births, deaths, and kills cannot be negative.
  • Initial values and rates are set so the three populations start near balance, making the dynamic consequences of any parameter change easy to see.
supportingInfo.title: Three level trophic cascade population model

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure identified

Only one object appears in the background information — the frimbulator — so a single module Frimbulators was created.

  • Frimbulators.count — a stock (accumulation) holding the inventory, initialized at 20 units. Its value is set only by its flow, per stock-and-flow rules.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

  • Created a single module Frimbulators for the object described, with the quantity held in Frimbulators.count.
  • Frimbulators.count is a stock initialized at 100 frimbulators, since it is an accumulation that can only change through its flows.
  • Frimbulators.growth is an inflow equal to the stock times growth fraction (0.05 per week). Because the inflow depends on the stock itself, this forms a reinforcing loop (exponential growth).
  • Frimbulators.decline is an outflow equal to a named constant decline amount (5 frimbulators per week). It does not depend on the stock, so it is a simple constant drain, not a balancing loop.

Modeling choices

  • All numeric values (5% and 5 units) were abstracted into clearly named constants rather than embedded in equations.
  • Both flows are marked one-directional since neither growth nor removal can meaningfully be negative.
  • No ghost variables were required because there is only one component and no cross-module references.

Behavior

With 100 units, growth begins at 5/week and exactly offsets the 5/week decline, so the system starts at an unstable equilibrium; any upward perturbation makes growth dominate and the inventory compounds upward.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, the baseline inventory shows one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two modules were created, one per object, each holding its quantity in a variable named count:

  • whatajigs: count starts at 100, grows through an inflow equal to 5% of itself, and drains through an outflow equal to 300% of the current balack count.
  • balacks: count starts at 200, is replenished by an inflow equal to 5% of the current whatajig count, and drains through an outflow equal to 3% of itself.

Causal links captured

  • Reinforcing loop inside whatajigs: the stock feeds its own growth flow (self-reinforcing 5% growth).
  • Balancing loop inside balacks: the stock feeds its own decline flow (3% loss), which stabilizes it.
  • Cross-module balancing loop: more whatajigs → more balacks (replenishment) → far greater whatajig depletion (300% per balack) → fewer whatajigs. This is the dominant negative feedback and produces oscillatory/predator-prey-like behavior, so RK4 integration with a small time step is used.

Modeling choices

  • All percentages were abstracted into named rate variables (growth fraction, depletion per balack, replenishment fraction, decline fraction) rather than embedded numbers in equations.
  • Cross-module dependencies use ghost variables (whatajigs.balacks count and balacks.whatajigs count) following the requested naming convention, and each module's equations reference only its own local ghost.
  • All flows are one-directional (growth, depletion, replenishment, decline) so they cannot reverse direction.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, we have on hand fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory gains from exactly ten new marticatenes. Simultaneously, each month the stock has outgoing 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory benefits from 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock loses a constant eight refluppers.  Meanwhile, we have on hand one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory gains from exactly eight new exemintes. Simultaneously, each month the stock suffers depletion of 10% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three separate inventories are represented, each in its own module with its quantity stored in a variable named count:

  • marticatenes: starts at 50, gains a constant 10 per month, and loses a fixed fraction (20%) of whatever is on hand. The proportional outflow creates a balancing loop that drives the stock toward an equilibrium of 50.
  • refluppers: starts at 75, gains 20% of the current marticatenes count each month, and loses a constant 8 per month. Because its inflow depends on another module's stock, a cross-level ghost (refluppers.marticatenes count) carries the marticatenes quantity into this module; all local equations reference the ghost rather than the source.
  • exemintes: starts at 120, gains a constant 8 per month, and loses 10% of the current amount, again a balancing loop with equilibrium at 80.

Modeling choices

  • Every numeric parameter (arrival quantities, loss quantity, and the percentage rates) is abstracted into its own clearly named variable, so no arbitrary constants appear inside equations.
  • All flows are one-directional (uniflow), since receipts and depletions cannot run backwards.
  • Only the refluppers inflow is coupled across modules; the marticatenes and exemintes inventories are independent, and nothing feeds back from refluppers into marticatenes, so the coupling is one-way.
supportingInfo.title: Three Coupled Inventory Modules With Ghost Link

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we start the period with one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock decreases by a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we start the period with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock is reduced through 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory receives new additions of exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock experiences losses of 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three separate accumulations were identified, each given its own module with the quantity stored in count.

Pablanksills – starts at 110. A reinforcing inflow (growth) is proportional to the current count via a 6% quarterly growth rate, while a fixed outflow (attrition) removes 18 units per quarter. The proportional inflow versus fixed outflow creates a reinforcing structure once the stock is above the break-even level.

Posistorathers – starts at 70. A constant inflow of 25 units per quarter is offset by a balancing outflow of 35% of the current count, so the stock settles toward an equilibrium near 71 units.

Crypterals – starts at 95. Two inflows: a fixed 18 units per quarter, plus a transfer equal to 35% of the current posistorather count. A balancing outflow removes 22% of the current stock.

Coupling

The posistorather outflow feeds the crypteral stock, so a cross-level ghost of the posistorather count (Crypterals.Posistorathers count) was created inside the crypterals module and drives the transfer inflow — the only inter-module causal link.

Formulation notes

  • All percentages and fixed quantities were abstracted into explicitly named rate/constant variables rather than embedded numbers in equations.
  • All flows are one-directional (uniflow) since none of the described processes can reverse.
  • No variable is both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
supportingInfo.title: Three coupled quarterly inventory stocks modularized

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we start the period with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory grows through incoming exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock loses 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four modules were created, one per object, each holding a stock named count plus its flows and rate parameters:

  • Proptimatires — starts at 40; a constant inflow of 5 per week and a proportional outflow of 25% of the stock. The proportional drain is a balancing loop that pushes the stock toward an equilibrium of 20.
  • Houtals — starts at 60; a constant inflow of 7 per week and a proportional outflow of 8% of the stock (another balancing loop, equilibrium 87.5).
  • Ocs — starts at 25; inflow driven by 15% of the proptimatires count, and a constant outflow of 3 per week.
  • Priaries — starts at 80; inflow driven by 10% of the proptimatires count, and outflow driven by 5% of the houtals count.

Cross-module coupling (ghosts)

All inter-module drivers are represented with cross-level ghosts so each module's equations refer only to local names:

  • Ocs.proptimatires count → ghost of Proptimatires.count
  • Priaries.proptimatires count → ghost of Proptimatires.count
  • Priaries.houtals count → ghost of Houtals.count

Note the coupling is strictly one-way (proptimatires and houtals drive ocs and priaries), so there are no cross-module feedback loops — only the two internal balancing loops.

Modeling choices

  • Every numeric rate or fraction was abstracted into its own named parameter variable (e.g. oc replenishment fraction, houtal loss fraction) rather than embedded in flow equations.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since they represent physical additions and removals that cannot run backwards.
  • Time base is weeks, with a small time step so the proportional drains integrate accurately.
supportingInfo.title: Four Coupled Inventories Modeled As Modules

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gains from exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory increases due to 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four modules were created, one per object, each holding its quantity in a variable named count:

  • Outrances: starts at 150; gains a constant 20 per hour; loses two separate proportional outflows (40% and 10% of the current stock). These were kept as two distinct flows because the description states them as two separate depletion processes. Together they form a balancing (goal-seeking) loop that drives the stock toward equilibrium.
  • Illigents: starts at 30; gains 40% of the current outrance count each hour (driven by a ghost of the outrance stock); loses a constant 5 per hour. There is no self-referencing loop here, so the stock is driven entirely by the outrance level.
  • Yelbs: starts at 65; gains 10% of the current outrance count (ghost of outrances); loses 12% of the currently available trazes (ghost of trazes). Both drivers are external, so yelbs are a pure accumulation of two other subsystems.
  • Trazes: starts at 85; gains a constant 15 per hour; loses 18% of its own stock per hour — a classic balancing loop.

Conventions applied

  • Every percentage and constant rate was abstracted into a clearly named variable (e.g., primary depletion fraction, arrival rate) rather than being buried in an equation.
  • All cross-module dependencies are carried by ghost variables named with the source's full path, period replaced by a space: Illigents.outrances count, Yelbs.outrances count, Yelbs.trazes count. Local equations reference only the ghosts.
  • All flows are one-directional (uniflows), since each represents an arrival or a departure that cannot run in reverse.

Causal chain

Outrances drive both illigents and yelbs; trazes independently drain yelbs. Nothing feeds back into outrances or trazes, so those two are the exogenous drivers of the system.
supportingInfo.title: Modular stock flow model of four interlinked inventories

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Each of the five described objects becomes its own module containing a stock named count, one addition flow, one removal flow, and named rate parameters so no bare numbers sit inside equations.

  • whatajigs: starts at 100; grows by a fraction of itself (a reinforcing compounding loop) and drains by a fixed three units per year — a constant drain against exponential growth.
  • balacks: starts at 200; fed by a fraction of the whatajigs count, drained by a fraction of itself (a balancing loop).
  • whoziewhats: starts at 200; fed by a fraction of the balacks count, drained by a fraction of itself.
  • funkados: starts at 12; fed by a fraction of the whoziewhats count, drained by a fraction of the maxabizers count.
  • maxabizers: starts at 88; fed by a fraction of the funkados count, drained by a fraction of the whoziewhats count.

Cross-module coupling

Every reference to a quantity owned by another module is made through a ghost that carries the requested naming style (for example, balacks.whatajigs count), and all local equations use those ghosts rather than reaching directly into another module. This keeps each module self-contained while preserving the causal chain.

Notable loops

The chain runs whatajigs → balacks → whoziewhats → funkados → maxabizers, and then closes back on itself: maxabizers drain funkados while funkados feed maxabizers, forming a balancing loop between the last two components. Whoziewhats additionally drain maxabizers, creating a second cross-coupling that dampens the downstream end of the chain.

All drain and add flows are one-directional, so none can reverse and become a spurious inflow.
supportingInfo.title: Modular Five Stock Causal Chain Model
