variables.name: volume
variables.documentation: The stock represents the gas volume (m^3). It starts at baseline_volume and accumulates the net effect of volume_change_rate over time. Because the driving flow is a pure sine wave (amplitude*SIN(angular_frequency*TIME)) whose time-integral is (amplitude/angular_frequency)*(1-cos(angular_frequency*TIME)), and (1-cos(x)) is always in [0,2], the integral term is always non-negative. Therefore volume = baseline_volume + a non-negative term, guaranteeing volume never falls below the strictly positive baseline_volume - this is a structural (not clamped) guarantee of positivity.

variables.name: volume_change_rate
variables.documentation: This flow represents an oscillating exogenous driver (e.g. piston motion) that alternately expands (positive) and compresses (negative) the gas volume. Since PySD does not support the XMILE SINWAVE built-in, the oscillation is built explicitly with the plain SIN() trig function applied to angular_frequency*TIME, using named amplitude and angular_frequency parameters rather than hardcoded numeric constants. Because it is a pure sine starting at zero, its integral is always non-negative, which is the structural mechanism that keeps volume above baseline_volume at all times.

variables.name: angular_frequency
variables.documentation: Converts the named oscillation_period parameter into the angular frequency used inside the SIN() function, via the standard trig-to-period identity omega = 2*pi/period. The 2*pi factor is a structural mathematical constant required by this identity, not an arbitrary empirical constant, so it is written inline.

variables.name: baseline_volume
variables.documentation: The reference/starting volume of the gas chamber before any oscillatory expansion or compression is applied. Serves as the initial condition for the volume stock and, being strictly positive, as the structural floor that keeps volume strictly positive for all time given the non-negative integral of the sine driver.

variables.name: volume_oscillation_amplitude
variables.documentation: Named parameter controlling the magnitude of the oscillating volume_change_rate driver, expressed in m^3/hr. Kept as its own named variable so no arbitrary amplitude constant is embedded directly inside the flow equation.

variables.name: oscillation_period
variables.documentation: Named parameter controlling the period (in hours) of one full expansion/compression cycle of the piston. Feeds into angular_frequency, which then drives the SIN() based oscillation of volume_change_rate.

variables.name: temperature
variables.documentation: Gas temperature, held constant throughout the simulation to represent the isothermal assumption of the process (T constant). Used directly in the ideal gas law to compute pressure each instant.

variables.name: moles
variables.documentation: The fixed amount of gas substance (moles) present in the closed system, a constant input to the ideal gas law PV=nRT.

variables.name: gas_constant
variables.documentation: The universal gas constant R used in the ideal gas law PV=nRT. Defined as its own named parameter rather than embedded as a literal inside the pressure equation.

variables.name: pressure
variables.documentation: Pressure is computed algebraically each instant from the ideal gas law, P = nRT/V, using the safe division operator (//) to guard against divide-by-zero even though volume is structurally guaranteed to stay strictly positive. Because temperature, moles and gas_constant are held constant and positive while volume oscillates but never reaches zero, pressure remains strictly positive and moves inversely with volume, which is the core relationship this model is built to illustrate.

testParams.name: Isobaric Gas Process
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of an isobaric process where gas pressure remains constant while temperature changes. The model must include variables named 'pressure' (pressure in Pascals), 'volume' (volume in cubic meters), and 'temperature' (absolute temperature in Kelvin). The model should obey the ideal gas law (PV = nRT).

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a gas system model that accurately represents an isobaric process where gas pressure remains constant while temperature changes and follows the ideal gas law.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For an ideal gas at constant pressure, V/T = nR/P = constant (Charles's Law). If temperature increases, volume must increase proportionally to maintain the ideal gas law PV = nRT. If temperature decreases, volume decreases. The relationship is V = (nR/P)*T. Pressure remains constant while volume and temperature vary together. Temperature must be measured in absolute scale (Kelvin) and cannot be negative.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Empty model — proceeding to build the isobaric gas system from scratch.

Dynamic hypothesis: Temperature is the driver (heated by an external source), pressure is held constant by definition of the isobaric process, and volume is the dependent variable that adjusts to satisfy the ideal gas law at every instant (Charles's Law: V/T = nR/P = constant).

Now let's inspect what was actually built.

Model structure matches requirements exactly — all required names present, no hard-coded literals inside formulas, temperature stock is structurally protected from going negative (positive initial value + uniflow-only positive inflow). No errors/warnings surfaced in the returned model. Proceeding to structural inspection and a validation run.

Structural check:

  • temperature (stock, K, init 300) ← heating_rate (uniflow, K/day) = heating_constant (5 K/day) — monotonic rise, never negative. Good.
  • pressure (constant, 101325 Pa) — no inflows/equations depending on time, truly held fixed. Good.
  • moles_of_gas, universal_gas_constant — named constants, not embedded literals. Good.
  • volume = (moles_of_gas * universal_gas_constant * temperature) / pressure — correct algebraic form of PV=nRT solved for V, matches Charles's Law V/T = nR/P. Good.

No unit warnings were reported by the engine on get_current_model, so I'll treat units as consistent (moles×J/(mol·K)×K / Pa = J/Pa = m^3, which is dimensionally correct as an aside — but per the rule I'm only reporting what the engine surfaces, and it surfaced nothing).

Now running the simulation to verify behavior (temperature rises linearly, volume rises proportionally, pressure stays flat):

Model built and validated. Here's the summary.

Model structure (Stock Flow Diagram, 7 variables, all documented and unitized):

Variable Type Equation Units
temperature stock init 300, inflow: heating_rate K
heating_rate flow (uniflow) heating_constant K/day
heating_constant constant 5 K/day
pressure constant 101325 Pa
moles_of_gas constant 1 mol
universal_gas_constant constant 8.314 J/(mol·K)
volume auxiliary (moles_of_gas × universal_gas_constant × temperature) / pressure m^3

Simulation horizon: 50 days, dt=0.25.

Structural critique:

  • pressure has no inflows and no time-dependent equation — it is a true constant, correctly enforcing the isobaric assumption. No structure exists anywhere that could perturb it.
  • temperature is a stock fed only by a uniflow (heating_rate), which is itself set to a positive constant (heating_constant, 5 K/day) rather than a bare literal. Because the inflow can't go negative and the initial value (300 K) is positive, temperature is structurally guaranteed to stay positive for all time — this satisfies the absolute-scale requirement without needing a MIN/MAX clamp.
  • volume is correctly modeled as an algebraic auxiliary (not a stock) because it has no memory — it's fully determined by the instantaneous state of temperature, pressure, moles, and R, exactly matching PV=nRT solved for V.
  • universal_gas_constant (R) is a named variable rather than embedded in the volume equation, satisfying the no-hard-coded-constants rule.
  • No unit warnings were returned by the engine when I inspected the model, and no errors are present.

Behavioral critique (from the run):

  • pressure is flat at 101325 Pa across all 50 days — confirmed isobaric.
  • temperature rises linearly from 300 K to 550 K, never dips — matches the intended monotonic heating scenario and never goes negative.
  • volume rises from ~0.02462 m^3 to ~0.04513 m^3, tracking temperature proportionally.
  • Checking Charles's Law directly: V/T = 0.02462/300 = 8.205e-5 at t=0, and 0.04513/550 = 8.205e-5 at t=50 — the ratio is constant to machine precision, confirming V/T = nR/P holds throughout the run, as required.

The model has earned structural and behavioral credibility: it enforces constant pressure by construction, keeps temperature physically valid without artificial clamping, and reproduces Charles's Law exactly.

Since I haven't called the feedback-loop analysis tool in this turn, I'm not making any claims about feedback structure — this model is a straight causal chain (heating → temperature → volume) with pressure held exogenously fixed, so there isn't feedback loop behavior to characterize here.

What would you like to do next — adjust parameters (e.g., a different heating rate, a cooling scenario, a different gas or initial temperature), visualize temperature vs. volume, or extend the model (e.g., add a scenario where pressure itself is allowed to vary for comparison)?

supportingInfo.explanation:
No assembly-finding tools are registered in this session, so I'll formulate the isochoric gas structure directly from ideal-gas first principles.

Proceeding to build the model now.

Now let's inspect what was actually built.

The generated model correctly implements the ideal gas law (P/T = nR/V held exactly constant at 8.314 throughout the run), volume stays fixed, and required variable names/units match exactly. However, inspecting the simulated data revealed a structural flaw: the temperature driver was defined with a graphical function meant to produce a heating-then-cooling schedule, but the simulation engine did not apply that lookup table — temperature_change_rate output identical to raw TIME, producing an unbounded monotonic rise (300 K to 1543 K) rather than the intended heat-then-cool behavior. I'm rebuilding the driver as a simple, deterministic parameter-based formulation to eliminate this engine ambiguity entirely.

Now let's verify the rebuilt structure, check for errors/warnings, and confirm behavior by running it.

No errors or warnings reported by the engine (get_current_model returned no errors, warnings, or unitWarnings fields). Structure is now clean: heating_rate (constant) → temperature_change_rate → temperature (stock) → pressure (algebraic, via ideal gas law), with volume fixed. Let's run and verify behavior.

Model Built: Isochoric Ideal Gas Process (SFD)

Actions taken:

  1. Generated a quantitative SFD from first principles (no assembly-search tool was registered in this session, so I formulated the ideal-gas structure directly).
  2. Retrieved the actual built model via get_current_model/read_model_section rather than assuming the generator did what I asked.
  3. Ran the model and inspected the raw variable data — this caught a real defect: the first build drove temperature_change_rate with a graphical function of TIME meant to heat-then-cool, but the simulation engine passed raw TIME straight through unmodified, producing an unbounded, undocumented monotonic temperature rise. I regenerated the model with a deterministic algebraic driver instead of a TIME-based lookup, then re-verified the new output.

Structure actually present in the model (confirmed via read_model_section, not assumed):

Variable Type Equation Units
initial_temperature parameter 300 Kelvin
temperature stock starts at initial_temperature, inflow = temperature_change_rate Kelvin
heating_rate parameter 2 Kelvin/time
temperature_change_rate flow heating_rate Kelvin/time
volume parameter (true constant) 1 cubic meters
moles_of_gas (n) parameter 1 moles
universal_gas_constant (R) parameter 8.314 Joules/(mole·Kelvin)
pressure algebraic variable moles_of_gas * universal_gas_constant * temperature / volume Pascals

This satisfies the required exact names (pressure, volume, temperature) and units, with n and R as their own named parameters rather than hard-coded constants inside the pressure equation — the only numeric literals in the model are the parameter values themselves (300, 2, 1, 1, 8.314), not embedded magic numbers inside formulas.

Validation performed:

  • get_current_model reports no errors, warnings, or unit warnings.
  • Simulated 0–50 seconds: volume stays exactly 1 m³ throughout (true isochoric condition — never touched by any flow).
  • temperature rises linearly 300 K → 400 K (deterministic, no lookup-table ambiguity).
  • pressure rises 2494.2 Pa → 3325.6 Pa, and P/T = 8.314 (= nR/V) exactly at every timestep — Gay-Lussac's Law holds structurally, not just numerically at one point.
  • Extreme-condition check: no stock goes negative in this scenario. One caveat worth flagging structurally: temperature_change_rate is not uniflow (it can be negative for cooling scenarios), and the temperature stock currently has no floor — if a user later drives heating_rate negative for long enough, temperature could cross into physically-impossible territory (below 0 K absolute). This isn't a defect in the current heating-only reference run, but it's a latent gap if the model is extended to bidirectional heating/cooling scenarios.

Next steps — let me know which you'd like:

  • Add a structural safeguard so temperature cannot fall below absolute zero if you plan to model cooling scenarios
  • Visualize temperature and pressure together to see the proportional (Gay-Lussac) relationship
  • Run feedback-loop analysis (note: this model is exogenously driven — heating_rate → temperature → pressure — so I'd expect no closed feedback loops, but I won't characterize that until get_feedback_information is actually called)
  • Extend to a variable-volume (isothermal/adiabatic) comparison, or make heating_rate itself a controllable step/ramp input

supportingInfo.explanation:
No assembly/template tools are registered in this session, so I'll formulate the classic births/deaths population structure directly.

Model Built: Population Growth and Decline

Structure (1 stock, 2 flows, 2 parameters):

Variable Type Equation Units Documentation
Population Stock initial value 1000 people Total number of individuals; accumulates via Births (inflow) and Deaths (outflow)
Births Flow (inflow to Population) Population * fractional_birth_rate people/year New individuals added per unit time, scaling with current population size
Deaths Flow (outflow from Population) Population * fractional_death_rate people/year Individuals removed per unit time, scaling with current population size
fractional_birth_rate Variable 0.02 1/year Constant fraction of population born per unit time; controls speed of growth
fractional_death_rate Variable 0.01 1/year Constant fraction of population dying per unit time; controls speed of decline

Simulation specs: 0–50 years, dt = 0.25, Euler integration.

Validation performed:

  • get_current_model returned no errors and no unit warnings.
  • Structural check: both flows are proportional to Population itself (first-order formulation), so Population is self-limiting on the downside — it can approach but never cross zero, even under Deaths alone. No MIN/MAX clamps needed.
  • No hard-coded arbitrary constants embedded in equations — the only numbers are the two named rate parameters and the stock's initial value, all of which are explicit, documented parameters rather than buried constants.

Structure and behavior check out. The model is complete, validated, and behaviorally credible at baseline. Here's the summary:

Model Built: Retail Inventory Management (SFD)

Stock

  • Inventory (units) — product units physically held by the store; rises via Delivery Rate, falls via Sales.

Flows

  • Delivery Rate (units/Days) — inflow; DELAY3(Order Rate, Order Fulfillment Delay), a third-order material delay representing the distributed lag between ordering and physical restocking.
  • Sales (units/Days) — outflow; MIN(Customer Demand, Inventory / Minimum Order Processing Time). This is the first-order control that throttles sales down as Inventory approaches zero, so the stock structurally cannot go negative.

Auxiliaries / Parameters

  • Customer Demand (units/Days) — exogenous driver of desired purchases (held at a constant 100 units/day baseline).
  • Expected Sales (units/Days) — SMTH1(Customer Demand, Time to Average Demand), the store's smoothed demand forecast.
  • Desired Inventory (units) — Expected Sales * Desired Inventory Coverage, the target stock level.
  • Desired Inventory Coverage (Days) — policy parameter for how many days of expected sales to hold as buffer (=10).
  • Inventory Gap (units) — Desired Inventory − Inventory, shortfall/surplus vs. target.
  • Adjustment for Inventory (units/Days) — Inventory Gap / Inventory Adjustment Time, corrective ordering term.
  • Inventory Adjustment Time (Days) — how fast the store closes the gap (=5).
  • Order Rate (units/Days) — MAX(0, Expected Sales + Adjustment for Inventory), total ordering, floored at zero.
  • Order Fulfillment Delay (Days) — average lead time from order to delivery (=4).
  • Minimum Order Processing Time (Days) — floor on how fast inventory can be sold down (=1).
  • Time to Average Demand (Days) — smoothing constant for the demand forecast (=3).

Every variable carries documentation and units; get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings.

Validation performed:

  • Structural check: Sales is capped by available Inventory (first-order outflow control) rather than a MIN/MAX clamp on the stock itself — this is the "correct" way to prevent negative inventory per SD practice.
  • Simulation run (baseline, constant Customer Demand = 100 units/day): Inventory settles at exactly 1000 units — its steady-state target (Desired Inventory Coverage × Customer Demand = 10 × 100) — with Order Rate = Delivery Rate = Sales = 100 units/day throughout. This confirms the equilibrium logic and conservation (inflow = outflow at steady state) are correct, and no extreme-condition failures (negative inventory, runaway orders) occurred.

Since demand was held constant for this baseline check, the system sits at equilibrium and shows no fluctuation yet — that's expected, not a flaw. To actually see the "fluctuation" behavior the problem statement is about, a logical next step would be to perturb Customer Demand (e.g., a step or random variation) and observe how Inventory, Order Rate, and Delivery Rate respond and oscillate around the target as the ordering delay and adjustment policy interact.

variables.documentation: The stock of product units physically held by the store. It rises with deliveries from restocking/production and falls as units are sold to customers. Initialized at the steady-state target level (desired coverage times current demand) so the model starts near equilibrium.

variables.name: Delivery Rate
variables.documentation: Units arriving into inventory from restocking or production. Modeled as a third-order material delay of the Order Rate over the Order Fulfillment Delay, capturing the realistic distributed lag between placing an order and receiving goods. Cannot be negative since deliveries are a one-directional physical process.

variables.name: Sales
variables.documentation: Units sold to customers per day. Limited to the lesser of Customer Demand and the maximum rate at which existing Inventory can be depleted (Inventory divided by the Minimum Order Processing Time), which prevents Inventory from ever going negative even when demand exceeds available stock.

variables.name: Customer Demand
variables.documentation: Exogenous input representing the rate at which customers wish to purchase the product, independent of whether inventory is available to satisfy it. Held at a constant baseline level for this analysis; could be changed to a step input to test store responsiveness.

variables.name: Expected Sales
variables.documentation: A smoothed forecast of Customer Demand used by the store for planning purposes, calculated as a first-order exponential smooth of Customer Demand over the Time to Average Demand. Smoothing prevents the store from overreacting to short-term noise in demand.

variables.name: Desired Inventory
variables.documentation: The target level of inventory the store aims to hold, calculated as expected sales multiplied by the desired number of days of coverage. This represents the store's inventory policy goal.

variables.name: Desired Inventory Coverage
variables.documentation: A constant policy parameter specifying how many days' worth of expected sales the store wants to keep on hand as a buffer against demand variability and delivery delays.

variables.name: Inventory Gap
variables.documentation: The shortfall or surplus between the desired inventory target and the actual current inventory. A positive gap indicates the store is understocked relative to its target and should order more; a negative gap indicates overstocking.

variables.name: Adjustment for Inventory
variables.documentation: The rate at which the store adjusts its ordering to close the Inventory Gap over the Inventory Adjustment Time. This is added to Expected Sales to determine total ordering needs, implementing a standard stock-adjustment control policy.

variables.name: Inventory Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: A constant parameter representing how quickly (in days) the store attempts to close any gap between desired and actual inventory through its ordering decisions. Shorter times mean more aggressive correction.

variables.name: Order Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which the store places orders for new units, combining the need to replace expected sales with an adjustment to correct any inventory gap. Constrained to be non-negative since orders cannot be placed in negative quantities.

variables.name: Order Fulfillment Delay
variables.documentation: A constant parameter representing the average time between when the store places an order and when the corresponding units are delivered and added to inventory. Used as the delay time in the third-order material delay governing Delivery Rate.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: A constant parameter representing the minimum time required to sell down existing inventory, acting as a first-order control that caps the maximum possible Sales rate at Inventory divided by this time, ensuring Inventory cannot be depleted faster than physically reasonable and cannot go negative.

variables.name: Time to Average Demand
variables.documentation: A constant smoothing time parameter that determines how quickly Expected Sales adjusts to changes in Customer Demand. Longer times produce smoother but slower-responding forecasts.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In a classic epidemic model a population is divided into people who are susceptible, people who are currently infected, and people who have recovered. Susceptible people become infected through contact with infected people, at a rate that depends on the contact rate and the infectivity of the disease. The model has been built and validated. Here's a summary of what was actually constructed and confirmed in the model.

Structure — three stocks in series:

  • Susceptible_People (stock, units: people) — people who have not yet been infected and are capable of contracting the disease. Starts at 9,990. Depletes via the Infection_Rate outflow.
  • Infected_People (stock, units: people) — people currently infected and capable of transmitting the disease. Starts at 10 (the index cases). Gains via Infection_Rate (inflow), loses via Recovery_Rate (outflow).
  • Recovered_People (stock, units: people) — people who were infected and have since recovered, no longer contributing to transmission. Starts at 0. Gains via Recovery_Rate (inflow), no outflow.

Flows:

  • Infection_Rate (flow, people/day) = Contact_Rate × Infectivity × Susceptible_People × Infected_People / Total_Population. Moves people from Susceptible_People to Infected_People. Uniflow (non-negative), since infection cannot run backward.
  • Recovery_Rate (flow, people/day) = Infected_People / Average_Duration_of_Illness. Moves people from Infected_People to Recovered_People. Uniflow (non-negative), since recovery cannot run backward.

Auxiliary variables (all documented, all with units):

  • Contact_Rate (contacts/person/day, = 6) — average number of contacts a person has per day; a social-mixing parameter.
  • Infectivity (dimensionless, = 0.03) — probability a contact between a susceptible and infected person transmits the disease.
  • Average_Duration_of_Illness (days, = 7) — average time a person remains infectious before recovering.
  • Total_Population (people) — algebraic sum of the three stocks, used only to normalize contact probability (not itself a stock, since it isn't accumulated by its own flows).

Validation performed:

  1. Fixed a naming-consistency error the generator introduced (flow/stock/relationship references didn't exactly match variable names) by aligning all names, equation references, inflows/outflows, and relationship endpoints to a single consistent identifier per variable. get_current_model now reports zero errors and zero warnings.
  2. Ran the simulation (365 days, dt = 1, Euler integration). Inspected the actual time-series data for all three stocks and Total_Population:
    • Susceptible_People declines monotonically from 9,990 toward ~6,133 and never goes negative.
    • Infected_People rises from 10 to a peak of about 240 people around day 119–127, then declines back toward zero — the classic single-hump epidemic curve.
    • Recovered_People rises monotonically to about 3,867 and never exceeds the population.
    • Total_Population holds constant at 10,000 throughout (to floating-point precision) — conservation of population is satisfied, confirming the three stocks aren't leaking or creating people.

Structurally and behaviorally this model reproduces the reference mode expected of a classic epidemic outbreak: exponential-like initial growth in infections, a peak, and decay as the susceptible pool is depleted, with population mass conserved throughout.

variables.documentation: The average number of contacts a person has with other people per unit of time (per day). This parameter reflects the social mixing behavior of the population and is a key driver of how quickly the disease can spread through contact between susceptible and infected individuals.

variables.name: Infectivity
variables.documentation: The probability that a contact between a susceptible person and an infected person results in transmission of the disease. This is a biological/epidemiological property of the disease itself, representing how easily it spreads per contact.

variables.name: Average_Duration_of_Illness
variables.documentation: The average number of days an infected person remains infectious before recovering. This parameter determines how quickly people move out of the Infected_People stock and into the Recovered_People stock, and is a key determinant of the overall duration and intensity of the outbreak.

variables.name: Total_Population
variables.documentation: The total number of people in the population, calculated as the sum of the three stocks: Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered. This is used to normalize the probability that any given contact a susceptible person has will be with an infected person, since contacts are assumed to be random across the whole population. This is a simple algebraic sum, not an accumulation via its own flows, so it is modeled as a variable rather than a stock.

variables.name: Infection_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible people become infected, moving from the Susceptible_People stock into the Infected_People stock. It depends on the Contact_Rate (how many contacts each person has), the Infectivity (probability of transmission per contact), the number of Susceptible_People and Infected_People (since a contact must be between a susceptible and an infected person to cause transmission), and is normalized by the Total_Population to represent the probability that a random contact is with an infected person. This flow is one-directional and can never be negative, since infections only move people forward from susceptible to infected.

variables.name: Recovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which infected people recover and move from the Infected_People stock into the Recovered_People stock. It is calculated as the number of Infected_People divided by the Average_Duration_of_Illness, reflecting the standard first-order outflow assumption that a constant fraction of infected people recover each time period. This flow is one-directional and can never be negative, since recovery only moves people forward from infected to recovered.

testParams.name: Software Project Rework variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A software project has a fixed scope of work. Tasks begin in a backlog of work still to be done and move to a pool of completed work as the team finishes them at a work rate. The work rate depends on the number of developers and their productivity. Not all completed work is actually correct: a fraction contains defects and becomes undiscovered rework instead of being truly finished. Undiscovered rework is not visible to the team until it is found during testing, after a discovery delay, at which point it flows back into the backlog of work to be done. As the deadline approaches with work remaining, schedule pressure rises. Higher schedule pressure pushes developers to work faster, raising the work rate, but it also raises the fraction of work done incorrectly (haste makes waste), which generates still more undiscovered rework and further delays the project. Sustained overtime also erodes productivity as developers fatigue.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let me pull the actual built model and validate it structurally, per the mandatory workflow.

Simulation succeeded. Let me verify the model structure again and check stock behavior for negativity/plausibility.

The Backlog stock goes negative late in the run (physically impossible — you can't complete more tasks than remain), which also sends Schedule Pressure negative and corrupts the dynamics. I need to add first-order availability control on the work completion flow before this model earns credibility.

Now let's re-validate: check the model, run it, and inspect key stocks.

Simulation succeeded. Let's check the stocks for negativity and reasonable behavior.

Software Project Rework Model — Built and Validated

Structure (4 stocks, 8 flows, 19 auxiliaries/constants):

Stocks

Stock Units Role
Backlog tasks Work still to be done; starts at Total Scope, drained by completion, replenished when rework is discovered
Undiscovered Rework tasks Defective work that has been "completed" but not yet found to be wrong
Completed Work tasks Truly finished, correct work — the real measure of progress
Developer Fatigue dimensionless (0–1 index) Accumulated tiredness from sustained overtime

Flows

  • Correct Work Rate, Defective Work Rate (Backlog → Completed Work / Undiscovered Rework, split by Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly)
  • Rework Discovery Rate (Undiscovered Rework → back to Backlog, first-order delay on Discovery Delay)
  • Fatigue Accumulation Rate / Fatigue Recovery Rate (drive Developer Fatigue up/down)

Key auxiliaries: Total Scope, Developers, Nominal Productivity, Desired Work Completion Rate, Work Completion Rate, Developer Productivity, Productivity Multiplier from Schedule Pressure, Productivity Multiplier from Fatigue, Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly, Deadline, Time Remaining Until Deadline, Required Work Rate, Normal Work Rate, Schedule Pressure, Overtime Fraction, Discovery Delay, Fatigue Accumulation/Recovery Time, Simulation Time Step.

Every variable carries units and a documentation string.

Validation performed

  1. Two build-time errors caught and fixed: an invalid TIME() call (this engine uses the bare TIME builtin) and an invalid bare DT reference (replaced with an explicit named constant, Simulation Time Step = 0.25 days, matching the model's dt spec).
  2. Structural defect found and fixed: Backlog is a physical task count and initially went negative near the end of the run, because Work Completion Rate was purely capacity-driven (Developers × Productivity) with no check on how much backlog actually remained. Fixed by splitting it into Desired Work Completion Rate (capacity-driven) and an availability-limited Work Completion Rate = MIN(Desired Work Completion Rate, Backlog / Simulation Time Step) — a first-order control that lets the completion rate taper naturally as the backlog is exhausted, rather than clamping the stock after the fact.
  3. Re-run confirmed: Backlog, Undiscovered Rework, Completed Work, and Developer Fatigue all stay non-negative through day 250. Conservation holds — Backlog + Undiscovered Rework + Completed Work ≈ Total Scope (1000 tasks) at every point checked.
  4. No unit warnings were reported by the engine on the current model.

Structural and behavioral critique

Structurally, the model now closes 14 distinct feedback loops around Backlog, Schedule Pressure, Developer Fatigue, and the rework-discovery delay — including loops where schedule pressure raises productivity but simultaneously raises the incorrect-work fraction, and a longer loop where undiscovered rework returns to the backlog and re-elevates schedule pressure. This gives the model the two causal mechanisms specified in the problem statement (haste-makes-waste, and fatigue eroding productivity under sustained overtime), each closing through Backlog rather than being a dead-end effect.

Behaviorally, in the base run (Total Scope = 1000 tasks, 5 developers, Deadline = 200 days): Backlog empties out around day ~204, a few days past the deadline — a modest overrun consistent with the reference mode of "late even though the team works hard." Schedule Pressure stays near 1 for most of the run, then spikes sharply (peaking near 9.7) in the final stretch as backlog lingers close to the deadline, which is exactly when Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly saturates near its 0.55 ceiling and Developer Fatigue peaks near 0.62 — showing the haste-makes-waste and fatigue-erosion mechanisms both engaging hardest right when the project is most overdue, then relaxing once the backlog is finally cleared.

One point worth flagging for your own judgment: Developers and Nominal Productivity are currently held constant — the model does not yet represent hiring more staff under pressure (which the classic "adding people to a late project" dynamic would require) or attrition from burnout. That's a deliberate scope choice matching what you described, but worth naming explicitly.

What would you like to do next?

Options include: adjusting the graphical functions (e.g., how sharply the defect fraction rises with schedule pressure) or constants (deadline, discovery delay, team size) and re-running; a deeper feedback-loop discussion of why the project runs late; a sensitivity analysis on Deadline or Discovery Delay; or a visualization of Backlog, Schedule Pressure, and Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly over time.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: The pool of tasks still to be done. Starts at the full project scope and shrinks as work is completed (correctly or defectively) and grows again when previously completed defective work is discovered and returned for rework.

variables.name: Undiscovered_Rework
variables.documentation: Work that was marked completed but actually contains defects that have not yet been found. It accumulates from defective work and drains as defects are discovered during testing and sent back to the backlog.

variables.name: Completed_Work
variables.documentation: Truly finished, correct work that will never need to be revisited. This is the real measure of project progress toward completion.

variables.name: Developer_Fatigue
variables.documentation: An index (0 to about 1) representing accumulated developer tiredness from sustained overtime. Rises with overtime work and dissipates over time, and erodes productivity when high.

variables.name: Correct_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which work is completed correctly and moves from the backlog into truly completed work. It is the portion of gross work completion that is not defective.

variables.name: Defective_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which work is completed but contains hidden defects, moving from the backlog into undiscovered rework. This is the portion of gross work completion that is done incorrectly due to haste.

variables.name: Rework_Discovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which defects hidden in undiscovered rework are found during testing and returned to the backlog to be redone. Modeled as a first-order delay process based on the average discovery delay.

variables.name: Fatigue_Accumulation_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which developer fatigue builds up as a result of working overtime in response to schedule pressure.

variables.name: Fatigue_Recovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which accumulated fatigue naturally dissipates over time as developers rest and recover.

variables.name: Total_Scope
variables.documentation: The fixed total amount of work defined for the project. Used to set the initial size of the backlog.

variables.name: Developers
variables.documentation: The constant number of developers assigned to the project team.

variables.name: Nominal_Productivity
variables.documentation: The baseline number of tasks a single developer can complete per day under normal conditions, absent schedule pressure or fatigue effects.

variables.name: Desired_Work_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: The capacity-driven gross rate at which the team could complete work based on headcount and productivity alone, ignoring whether enough backlog exists to work on.

variables.name: Simulation_Time_Step
variables.documentation: The simulation integration time step (matches the model's dt specification), used to compute the maximum amount of backlog that can physically be worked through in one step.

variables.name: Work_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: The actual gross rate at which work is completed, limited by the availability of remaining backlog so the team cannot complete more tasks in a time step than currently remain in the backlog. This first-order availability control prevents Backlog from going negative.

variables.name: Developer_Productivity
variables.documentation: The actual productivity per developer per day, adjusted from the nominal baseline by the effects of schedule pressure (working faster) and fatigue (working slower when tired).

variables.name: Productivity_Multiplier_from_Schedule_Pressure
variables.documentation: A graphical function representing how developers speed up as schedule pressure rises. Equals 1 at normal pressure (Schedule Pressure=1) and rises above 1 as pressure increases, with diminishing returns at high pressure since there is a physical limit to how fast people can work.

variables.name: Productivity_Multiplier_from_Fatigue
variables.documentation: A graphical function representing how accumulated fatigue erodes productivity. Equals 1 at zero fatigue and declines toward a floor as fatigue approaches its maximum, reflecting tired developers working less effectively.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly
variables.documentation: A graphical function capturing the haste-makes-waste effect: as schedule pressure rises, developers cut corners and the fraction of completed work that is actually defective increases, generating more undiscovered rework.

variables.name: Discovery_Delay
variables.documentation: The average number of days it takes for a defect to be found during testing after it was introduced into undiscovered rework.

variables.name: Deadline
variables.documentation: The scheduled day on which the project is supposed to be finished.

variables.name: Minimum_Time_Remaining
variables.documentation: A small positive floor placed on time remaining until the deadline so that the required work rate calculation never divides by zero or a negative number as the deadline passes.

variables.name: Time_Remaining_Until_Deadline
variables.documentation: The number of days left until the project deadline, floored at a small positive minimum to keep downstream division calculations safe as the deadline is reached or passed.

variables.name: Required_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate of work completion that would be needed, starting now, to finish all remaining backlog exactly by the deadline. Safe division is used since time remaining could otherwise approach zero.

variables.name: Normal_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The team's capacity to complete work at the nominal, unpressured pace, used as a benchmark for measuring schedule pressure.

variables.name: Schedule_Pressure
variables.documentation: A dimensionless index of how much faster than normal the team must work to hit the deadline. A value of 1 means the required pace equals the normal pace; values above 1 indicate the team is behind schedule. Safe division protects against a zero normal work rate.

variables.name: Overtime_Fraction
variables.documentation: A graphical function representing how much developers work beyond normal hours in response to rising schedule pressure. Stays near zero at normal pressure and grows as pressure builds, which in turn drives fatigue accumulation.

variables.name: Fatigue_Accumulation_Time
variables.documentation: The time constant governing how quickly sustained overtime translates into accumulated fatigue.

variables.name: Fatigue_Recovery_Time
variables.documentation: The time constant governing how quickly accumulated fatigue dissipates once overtime pressure eases.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of fishery boom and bust. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A fish population grows through births and shrinks through natural deaths and through harvesting by a fishing fleet. The population regenerates fastest at intermediate levels and its net regeneration falls toward zero as it approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat or is driven near depletion. The harvest rate rises with both the number of fishing ships and the density of fish, since the catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant. Revenue from the harvest, less the operating cost of running the ships, determines the profit per ship. Profit drives investment in new ships, though new capacity is added only after a construction and financing delay; when profit turns negative, ships are scrapped or leave the fishery. More ships raise the harvest, which depletes the fish population, which lowers the catch per ship and eventually profit — a balancing process — but the investment delays cause the fleet to overshoot the sustainable level, producing cycles of boom and collapse.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure and units check out — no errors or unit warnings were reported. Now let's simulate and inspect key stocks for structural validity (no negative fish/ships, plausible cycles).

Model built and validated. Here's the summary:

Model Structure

Stocks (3):

  • Fish Population [fish] — inflow: Net Regeneration; outflow: Harvest Rate. Initialized at 800,000 (below Carrying Capacity of Habitat).
  • Ships Under Construction [ships] — inflow: Ship Order Rate; outflow: Ship Completion Rate. Represents the construction/financing pipeline. Initialized at 0.
  • Fishing Fleet [ships] — inflow: Ship Completion Rate; outflow: Ship Scrapping Rate. Initialized at 10 (small relative to a fully-exploiting fleet).

Flows (5):

  • Net Regeneration = Regeneration Rate Constant × Fish Population × (1 − Fish Population / Carrying Capacity of Habitat) — logistic growth, fastest at intermediate density, zero at carrying capacity or depletion.
  • Harvest Rate = Catchability Coefficient × Fishing Fleet × Fish Population — rises with both fleet size and fish density.
  • Ship Order Rate = Fishing Fleet × Investment Fraction.
  • Ship Completion Rate = Ships Under Construction / Construction and Financing Delay.
  • Ship Scrapping Rate = Fishing Fleet × Scrapping Fraction.

Auxiliaries (13): Carrying Capacity of Habitat, Regeneration Rate Constant, Catchability Coefficient, Catch per Ship (= Harvest Rate // Fishing Fleet, safe division), Price per Fish, Revenue per Ship, Operating Cost per Ship, Profit per Ship, Reference Profit per Ship, Relative Profitability (normalized profit), Investment Fraction (graphical function, near-zero at Relative Profitability ≤ 0, saturating as it rises), Scrapping Fraction (graphical function, rising steeply as Relative Profitability goes negative), Construction and Financing Delay.

Every variable carries documentation and units; mcp__builtin__get_current_model reported no errors and no unit warnings.

Structural Critique

  • The delay is isolated cleanly in the Ships Under Construction stock, so the overshoot mechanism (order → build → operate, versus immediate scrapping) is transparent rather than buried in a black-box DELAY function.
  • Investment and Scrapping are asymmetric graphical functions (as specified), not mirror images — investment saturates, scrapping accelerates — which is a reasonable structural choice but worth flagging as an assumption you may want to revisit.
  • No hard-coded constants inside equations; all parameters are named variables.

Behavioral Critique (from the test run, 0–100 years)

  • Fish Population never goes negative (bottoms near 376,800 fish, well above zero) and Fishing Fleet/Ships Under Construction stay non-negative throughout — no structural violations.
  • Fleet grows from 10 to a peak of 63.5 ships (t=20-22) while Profit per Ship is still positive, then Profit per Ship crosses negative around t≈17 as Harvest Rate outpaces Fish Population's regenerative capacity — this is the classic delayed-response overshoot the background describes.
  • After the overshoot, Fishing Fleet contracts (scrapping dominates), Fish Population partially recovers, and the system settles into a damped oscillation converging toward an equilibrium near Fish Population ≈ 396,000 and Fishing Fleet ≈ 60 ships by t=100 — consistent with a balancing loop with delay producing boom-and-bust rather than sustained divergence.
  • I have not yet run get_feedback_information, so I'm not making any claims here about loop dominance or naming specific loops — only describing the stock/flow trajectories themselves.

The model has earned initial credibility on both structural and behavioral grounds. What would you like to do next — inspect the feedback loop structure (Loops That Matter) to see what's driving this cycle, test extreme/sensitivity scenarios (e.g., shorter construction delay, higher price per fish), or visualize the run?

variables.name: Ships_Under_Construction
variables.documentation: ships that have been ordered/financed by the fleet but are not yet operational; represents the construction and financing delay pipeline.

variables.name: Fishing_Fleet
variables.documentation: the number of operational fishing ships actively harvesting fish; initialized small relative to the fleet size that would fully exploit the fish population.

variables.name: Net_Regeneration
variables.documentation: net births minus natural deaths; logistic regeneration that is fastest at intermediate population levels and falls to zero as population approaches Carrying Capacity of Habitat or approaches zero (depletion).

variables.name: Harvest_Rate
variables.documentation: fish removed by the fishing fleet; rises with both number of ships and fish density, since catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant.

variables.name: Ship_Order_Rate
variables.documentation: rate at which new ships are ordered/financed, driven by fleet profitability.

variables.name: Ship_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: rate ships become operational after the construction and financing delay.

variables.name: Ship_Scrapping_Rate
variables.documentation: rate ships are scrapped or leave the fishery when profit per ship is negative.

variables.name: Carrying_Capacity_of_Habitat
variables.documentation: maximum sustainable fish population supported by the habitat.

variables.name: Regeneration_Rate_Constant
variables.documentation: intrinsic regeneration rate coefficient of the fish population at low density.

variables.name: Catchability_Coefficient
variables.documentation: technology/efficiency coefficient converting fleet size and fish density into harvested fish.

variables.name: Catch_per_Ship
variables.documentation: average catch per ship per year; declines as fish population is depleted, using safe division to avoid divide-by-zero when the fleet is empty.

variables.name: Price_per_Fish
variables.documentation: market price received per fish landed.

variables.name: Revenue_per_Ship
variables.documentation: revenue earned per ship per year from landed catch.

variables.name: Operating_Cost_per_Ship
variables.documentation: fixed operating cost of running one ship for one year (fuel, crew, maintenance).

variables.name: Profit_per_Ship
variables.documentation: net profit earned per ship per year; the key driver of investment and scrapping decisions.

variables.name: Reference_Profit_per_Ship
variables.documentation: reference/normal profit per ship used to nondimensionalize profitability for graphical investment/scrapping functions.

variables.name: Relative_Profitability
variables.documentation: profitability of ship operation normalized to the reference profit; drives both investment and scrapping decisions.

variables.name: Investment_Fraction
variables.documentation: fraction of the existing fleet ordered as new ships per year, increasing with profitability; near zero or zero when Relative Profitability is at or below zero, increasing and saturating for positive Relative Profitability.

variables.name: Scrapping_Fraction
variables.documentation: fraction of the existing fleet scrapped/leaving per year, increasing as profit turns negative; near zero when Relative Profitability is at or above zero.

variables.name: Construction_and_Financing_Delay
variables.documentation: time required to finance and build new ships before they become operational; this delay causes fleet investment to overshoot the sustainable level, producing boom-and-bust cycles.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of market growth and capacity. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A company's installed base of customers grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. Customers place orders, and orders that cannot be filled immediately accumulate in a backlog. Production capacity limits how quickly the backlog can be filled, so the delivery delay experienced by customers is the backlog divided by the available capacity. A longer delivery delay reduces the company's attractiveness, which lowers the order rate and slows customer acquisition — a balancing loop that constrains growth. Revenue from filled orders funds investment in both the sales force and additional production capacity, but new capacity comes online only after a construction delay. A larger sales force wins customers faster, creating a reinforcing growth loop, while the capacity and delivery-delay dynamics push back against that growth and can cause sales to overshoot and oscillate.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let's inspect what was actually built.

Let's verify the fix and re-run.

Good, the fix is in place. Now re-run and check behavior.

Model Built: Market Growth and Capacity

I built the SFD, validated it against the engine (get_current_model / read_model_section), ran it, and inspected the resulting time series before reporting. One structural defect surfaced during validation and was corrected — details below.

Stocks (5)

Stock Units In / Out
Installed Base of Customers customers in: Customer Acquisition Rate — out: Customer Loss Rate
Backlog orders in: Order Rate — out: Order Fulfillment Rate
Sales Force salespeople in: Sales Force Investment Rate — no outflow (no attrition specified in the problem)
Capacity Under Construction orders/week in: Capacity Investment Rate — out: Capacity Completion Rate
Production Capacity orders/week in: Capacity Completion Rate — no outflow (no depreciation specified)

Flows and key converters

  • Customer Acquisition Rate = Sales Force × Sales Productivity × Company Attractiveness — customers won per week.
  • Customer Loss Rate = Installed Base of Customers // Average Customer Lifetime — customer churn.
  • Order Rate = Installed Base of Customers × Average Order Rate per Customer × Company Attractiveness — orders placed per week.
  • Delivery Delay = Backlog // Production Capacity — the delay customers actually experience; feeds Company Attractiveness only.
  • Company Attractiveness = graphical function of (Delivery Delay / Reference Delivery Delay), dimensionless, =1 at the reference delay, rising above 1 when delivery is faster and falling below 1 when it's slower. Drives both Order Rate and Customer Acquisition Rate down when delivery is slow.
  • Order Fulfillment Rate = MIN(Production Capacity, Backlog // Minimum Order Fulfillment Time) — see correction below.
  • Revenue = Order Fulfillment Rate × Price per Order — funds both investment streams.
  • Sales Force Investment Rate = (Revenue × Fraction of Revenue Invested in Sales Force) // Cost per Salesperson.
  • Capacity Investment Rate = (Revenue × Fraction of Revenue Invested in Capacity) // Cost per Unit of Capacity.
  • Capacity Completion Rate = Capacity Under Construction // Construction Delay — the delay between funding capacity and it becoming usable.

Ten fixed parameters (Sales Productivity, Average Customer Lifetime, Average Order Rate per Customer, Reference Delivery Delay, Price per Order, the two investment fractions, the two unit costs, Construction Delay) plus one added structural parameter (below) round out the model. Every variable carries plain-language documentation of its meaning and causal role.

Structural correction made during validation

My first pass defined Order Fulfillment Rate as Backlog // Delivery Delay with Delivery Delay = Backlog // Production Capacity. Algebraically these two equations cancel out to Order Fulfillment Rate = Production Capacity regardless of Backlog's sign — so once Backlog approached zero, the model kept shipping at full capacity and drove Backlog deeply negative (confirmed in a test run: Backlog fell to roughly -324,000 by week 200, which is physically meaningless for a count of unfilled orders).

I fixed this by introducing Minimum Order Fulfillment Time (≈1 week) as a first-order control: Order Fulfillment Rate = MIN(Production Capacity, Backlog // Minimum Order Fulfillment Time). This throttles shipments toward zero as Backlog empties, so Backlog is structurally prevented from going negative, while Delivery Delay keeps its original definition and role of driving Company Attractiveness. I documented this variable explicitly as a non-negativity safeguard, not part of the original causal narrative.

Behavioral check (post-fix, 200-week run, dt=0.25)

  • Backlog stayed non-negative throughout (roughly 500 → 190 → climbing to ~7,290 orders by week 200) — no physically impossible values.
  • Installed Base of Customers, Sales Force, Production Capacity, and Capacity Under Construction all grow monotonically and smoothly in this baseline parameterization — no runaway blow-up or divide-by-zero artifacts.
  • Company Attractiveness settles around 1.43, comfortably inside its defined graphical-function range (0.2 to 1.5) rather than pinned at the boundary — the balancing check is exerting real leverage rather than saturating.
  • No unit warnings were reported by the engine for this model.

One credibility caveat worth flagging: at this baseline parameter set the model shows sustained growth rather than a visible overshoot-and-oscillation cycle — whether the delivery-delay and construction-delay mechanisms actually produce oscillation is a matter of parameter magnitudes (construction delay length, investment fractions, reference delay) relative to the reinforcing growth rate, not a structural limitation of the model. This is a natural next test.

Suggested next steps: run Loops That Matter analysis to see which feedback mechanisms dominate at different times, or explore parameter changes (e.g., a longer Construction Delay or lower Reference Delivery Delay) to see whether the model produces the overshoot-and-oscillation pattern you're investigating. Let me know which you'd like to pursue.

variables.name: Installed_Base_of_Customers
variables.documentation: The stock of customers currently served by the company. Grows as the sales force wins new customers (Customer Acquisition Rate) and shrinks as existing customers are lost (Customer Loss Rate). This is the core measure of market growth and the target of the reinforcing sales-driven growth loop.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled customer orders waiting to be processed. Accumulates when orders arrive (Order Rate) faster than they can be fulfilled (Order Fulfillment Rate). Backlog is a physical count of unfilled orders and can never be negative; the corrected Order Fulfillment Rate formulation structurally prevents this stock from going below zero.

variables.name: Sales_Force
variables.documentation: Number of salespeople employed by the company. Grows through investment funded by revenue; no attrition is modeled. A larger sales force drives faster customer acquisition, forming the reinforcing growth loop that pushes against the capacity-constrained balancing loop.

variables.name: Capacity_Under_Construction
variables.documentation: Production capacity that has been funded but is not yet operational, pending completion of construction. This stock represents the pipeline of capacity investment and is the source of the construction delay that causes capacity to lag demand.

variables.name: Production_Capacity
variables.documentation: Operational capacity available to fulfill orders. Grows only as construction projects complete; no depreciation is modeled. This stock caps how quickly backlog can be worked down and is the ceiling in the corrected Order Fulfillment Rate formulation.

variables.name: Customer_Acquisition_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new customers are won, driven by the size of the sales force, their productivity, and how attractive the company currently is (which depends on delivery delay). This is the engine of the reinforcing growth loop. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Customer_Loss_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing customers leave the installed base, proportional to the base size and inversely related to how long customers typically stay. Safe division (//) guards against division by zero. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Order_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which customers place new orders, scaled by the installed base, typical ordering frequency per customer, and company attractiveness (which falls when delivery delay is long, discouraging orders). Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Delivery_Delay
variables.documentation: The delay customers experience between placing an order and receiving it, calculated as backlog divided by available production capacity (safe division). In this corrected model, Delivery Delay is used ONLY as the input driving Company Attractiveness (perceived customer experience); it is no longer used inside the Order Fulfillment Rate equation, since that self-referential formulation previously caused fulfillment to always equal Production Capacity regardless of Backlog sign, allowing Backlog to go negative.

variables.name: Order_Fulfillment_Rate
variables.documentation: CORRECTED formulation. Rate at which backlogged orders are fulfilled. This is a first-order control: the company ships at full Production Capacity whenever Backlog is large enough to support that rate (Backlog / Minimum Order Fulfillment Time exceeds Production Capacity), but as Backlog shrinks toward zero the shipment rate is throttled down proportionally to the backlog on hand, so Backlog can never be driven below zero. This replaces the prior algebraically self-canceling formulation (Backlog / Delivery Delay, where Delivery Delay = Backlog / Production Capacity), which collapsed to always equal Production Capacity and allowed Backlog to become deeply negative near zero. Revenue generated by this flow funds future growth.

variables.name: Company_Attractiveness
variables.documentation: A decreasing function of the ratio of actual delivery delay to a reference delivery delay. Equals 1 when delay equals the reference (normal conditions), rises above 1 when delivery is faster than reference, and falls below 1 when delivery is slower. This represents how customers and the market perceive the company, and it drives the balancing loop that constrains growth when backlog builds up. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Revenue
variables.documentation: Income generated from filled orders, calculated as the fulfillment rate multiplied by the price charged per order. This revenue is the source of funding for both sales force expansion and capacity investment. Unchanged in form, but now driven by the corrected Order Fulfillment Rate.

variables.name: Sales_Force_Investment_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new salespeople are added, funded by the portion of revenue allocated to sales investment divided by the cost of hiring each salesperson. Safe division guards against a zero cost value. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Capacity_Investment_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new production capacity is funded and enters construction, based on the portion of revenue allocated to capacity investment divided by the cost per unit of capacity. Safe division guards against a zero cost value. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Capacity_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which capacity under construction becomes operational, determined by the amount under construction divided by the typical construction delay. This delay is the key mechanism causing capacity to lag demand and drive overshoot and oscillation. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Sales_Productivity
variables.documentation: Number of new customers a single salesperson can win per week under normal conditions. A fixed parameter reflecting sales effectiveness. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Average_Customer_Lifetime
variables.documentation: Average length of time a customer remains part of the installed base before being lost. A fixed parameter governing customer churn. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Average_Order_Rate_per_Customer
variables.documentation: Typical number of orders placed by a single customer per week under normal attractiveness conditions. A fixed parameter reflecting customer ordering behavior. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Reference_Delivery_Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers consider normal or acceptable. Used as the benchmark against which actual delivery delay is compared to determine company attractiveness. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Price_per_Order
variables.documentation: The price charged to customers per order fulfilled. A fixed parameter used to convert fulfillment activity into revenue. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Revenue_Invested_in_Sales_Force
variables.documentation: The share of revenue that management allocates to expanding the sales force. A fixed policy parameter. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Revenue_Invested_in_Capacity
variables.documentation: The share of revenue that management allocates to expanding production capacity. A fixed policy parameter. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Cost_per_Salesperson
variables.documentation: The cost required to add one new salesperson to the sales force. A fixed parameter used to convert investment dollars into new hires. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Cost_per_Unit_of_Capacity
variables.documentation: The cost required to fund one unit of new production capacity (one order per week of throughput). A fixed parameter used to convert investment dollars into capacity under construction. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Construction_Delay
variables.documentation: The typical time required to bring newly funded capacity online. This delay is the critical bottleneck that causes production capacity to lag behind rapidly growing demand, driving overshoot and oscillation in the system. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: Minimum_Order_Fulfillment_Time
variables.documentation: NEW variable added solely as a structural non-negativity safeguard on the Backlog stock, not as part of the original causal narrative. It represents the fastest conceivable time to ship an order still sitting in backlog (about 1 week) and acts as the proportionality constant in the first-order control law Order Fulfillment Rate = MIN(Production Capacity, Backlog / Minimum Order Fulfillment Time). As Backlog approaches zero, this term throttles the fulfillment rate down toward zero, preventing the physically impossible outcome of Backlog going negative that occurred in the previous, algebraically self-canceling formulation.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built, validated, and simulated successfully. Summary:

Structure

  • Stock: Population (individuals), initial value 1000
  • Inflow: Births = Population * Fractional_Birth_Rate (individuals/year)
  • Outflow: Deaths = Population * Fractional_Death_Rate (individuals/year)
  • Auxiliaries: Fractional_Birth_Rate = 0.03 (1/year), Fractional_Death_Rate = 0.015 (1/year), both constants
  • Sim specs: start 0, stop 100, dt 0.25, time units years, Euler integration

No errors or warnings were reported by the engine (get_current_model returned no unitWarnings, no error/warning fields).

Simulation results (eval-run-1) Population grows smoothly from 1000 at year 0 to about 4469 at year 100, consistent with the net fractional growth rate of 0.03 − 0.015 = 0.015/year producing exponential growth (doubling roughly every ~46 years). Births rise from 30 to ~134/year; Deaths rise from 15 to ~67/year, tracking the growing stock proportionally — consistent with the multiplicative formulation. Population never goes negative and both flows stay non-negative throughout (uniflow enforced), which is physically correct for this simple model.

What I did not do: I have not called get_feedback_information this turn, so I'm not describing any loop structure or dominance — only the stock/flow composition and simulated behavior above.

What would you like to do next — inspect feedback-loop structure (reinforcing/balancing dynamics via Seldon/LTM), visualize the Population/Births/Deaths trajectory, or modify parameters (e.g., time-varying rates, carrying capacity)?

relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Population leads to an increase in Births, and a decrease in Population leads to a decrease in Births, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The fractional birth rate determines what proportion of the population is added as new births each year.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the Fractional Birth Rate leads to an increase in Births (more births per existing individual), so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: A larger population produces a proportionally larger number of deaths since deaths are calculated as a fraction of the total population.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Population leads to an increase in Deaths, and a decrease in Population leads to a decrease in Deaths, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The fractional death rate determines what proportion of the population is lost to death each year.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the Fractional Death Rate leads to an increase in Deaths (more deaths per existing individual), so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: Births directly add new individuals into the Population stock, increasing its accumulated value over time.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Births leads to an increase in Population (faster accumulation), so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: Deaths directly remove individuals from the Population stock, decreasing its accumulated value over time.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Deaths leads to a decrease in Population (faster depletion), so the relationship is negative.

variables.name: Population
variables.documentation: The stock of individuals in the population. It starts at an initial value of 1000 individuals and changes over time solely due to Births (inflow) and Deaths (outflow).

variables.name: Births
variables.documentation: The number of new individuals added to the population each year. Calculated as the current Population multiplied by the Fractional Birth Rate. Marked as uniflow since births cannot logically be negative.

variables.name: Deaths
variables.documentation: The number of individuals removed from the population each year due to death. Calculated as the current Population multiplied by the Fractional Death Rate. Marked as uniflow since deaths cannot logically be negative.

variables.name: Fractional_Birth_Rate
variables.documentation: A constant fractional rate representing the proportion of the population that gives birth each year, set to 0.03 (3%) per year as specified.

variables.name: Fractional_Death_Rate
variables.documentation: A constant fractional rate representing the proportion of the population that dies each year, set to 0.015 (1.5%) per year as specified.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure and specs match the request exactly — no errors, no warnings to check yet. Let me confirm via a full model check and then run it.

The model built, validated, and ran cleanly. Here's the summary:

Model structure

  • Stock — Balance (dollars): initial value 5000. Inflows: Interest_Earned, Deposits. Outflow: Withdrawals.
  • Flow — Interest_Earned (dollars/year): Balance * Annual_Interest_Rate, uniflow.
  • Flow — Deposits (dollars/year): constant 2400, uniflow.
  • Flow — Withdrawals (dollars/year): constant 1200, uniflow.
  • Auxiliary — Annual_Interest_Rate (1/year): constant 0.03.

Simulation specs: start = 0, stop = 30, dt = 0.25, time units = years — exactly as specified.

Validation

  • get_current_model / read_model_section show no errors or warnings; every stock has a numeric initial value, every flow/auxiliary has a defined equation, no arbitrary hard-coded constants are embedded in relational equations (all rates and amounts are their own named variables).
  • Structural check: Balance's only outflow (Withdrawals) is a constant rather than a stock-dependent fractional outflow. Given deposits (2400/yr) exceed withdrawals (1200/yr) plus the balance only grows via positive interest, Balance never approaches zero over the 30-year horizon under these parameters, so the lack of first-order control on the outflow is not a structural defect here — it only becomes an issue if withdrawals were increased well beyond deposits+interest, which is outside the scope given.
  • Ran the model (run "eval-run-1") and inspected Balance, Interest_Earned, Deposits, Withdrawals numerically: Balance rises smoothly and monotonically from 5000 to ≈70,311 dollars by year 30, Interest_Earned grows from 150 to ≈2109 dollars/year tracking the growing balance, Deposits and Withdrawals hold constant at 2400 and 1200 respectively. No negative values, no discontinuities — behavior is consistent with compounding growth net of a fixed deposit/withdrawal spread.

Since I have not yet called the feedback-loop analysis tool, I'm not describing any loop structure — only what's in the stock/flow diagram above.

What would you like to do next — inspect feedback loop dominance (reinforcing growth from compounding vs. the net constant flows), run a sensitivity analysis on the interest rate or deposit/withdrawal levels, or visualize Balance over time?
