variables.equation: normal_stress_accumulation_rate * (Traffic_Congestion / normal_congestion_reference) ^ congestion_stress_exponent * (Weather_Conditions / reference_Weather_Conditions) ^ weather_stress_exponent * (Perceived_Provocations / reference_Perceived_Provocations) ^ provocation_stress_exponent
variables.documentation: Rate at which stress builds up, raised by heavy traffic and stop-and-go conditions, adverse weather that makes driving more challenging, and by provocations suffered from other drivers. Each driver is a normalized, dimensionless ratio.

variables.name: stress relief
variables.documentation: First-order recovery from stress over the stress recovery time; the balancing drain that bounds the stress stock.

variables.name: Learned Behavior
variables.documentation: Socially learned normalization of aggressive driving: the more aggression drivers observe, the more normal it seems. Measured as a normalization index initialized at its reference value.

variables.name: aggressive driving normalization
variables.documentation: Rate at which observing aggressive driving normalizes it. Exposure is measured by active road rage incidents relative to their reference level.

variables.name: unlearning of aggressive norms
variables.documentation: First-order decay of learned aggressive norms over the norm unlearning time; social memory erodes when aggression is no longer observed.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Vehicles queued or delayed on the network. This is a stylized aggregate stock at the annual time scale: entries accumulate and are cleared first-order so congestion can never become negative. Initialized at the normal congestion reference.

variables.name: vehicle entry rate
variables.documentation: Vehicles entering the congested network per year: the driving population times trips per driver, reduced when trips are deferred because the road is already jammed (congestion deterrence).

variables.name: congestion clearance rate
variables.documentation: First-order clearance of queued vehicles. Because it is proportional to the stock, Traffic Congestion can never go negative. Longer clearance times mean slower clearance and more congestion.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Accumulated sleep debt (fatigue) in the driving population. Fatigue impairs judgement and makes drivers more susceptible to anger. Initialized at reference for near equilibrium.

variables.name: sleep deficit accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which sleep debt builds up; stress and anxiety cost drivers sleep, so the rate rises with the normalized stress level.

variables.name: sleep recovery
variables.documentation: First-order recovery of sleep debt over the sleep recovery time; balancing drain that bounds fatigue.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Feeling blocked by other drivers. Rises with traffic congestion relative to the normal congestion reference and with the stock of perceived provocations. Equals its reference value (1) at reference conditions.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Low tolerance for delay among drivers running late. Rises with average trip delay relative to the delay drivers will tolerate (reference delay times the delay tolerance parameter).

variables.name: average trip delay
variables.documentation: Aggregate delay per trip, computed as queued vehicles divided by the network clearance capacity (Little's law form). More congestion for a given capacity means longer delays.

variables.name: congestion deterrence effect
variables.documentation: Balancing loop B1: when delays exceed the reference delay, some trips are deferred or abandoned, reducing vehicle entries. Equals 1 at reference delay.

variables.name: average clearance time
variables.equation: normal_average_clearance_time * (Road_Design / reference_Road_Design) ^ road_design_clearance_exponent * (Weather_Conditions / reference_Weather_Conditions) ^ weather_clearance_exponent * (collisions_from_distracted_driving_and_road_rage / normal_collision_rate) ^ collision_clearance_exponent
variables.documentation: Average time a vehicle spends in congested conditions. Lengthened by poor road design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections), adverse weather, and collisions caused by distracted driving and road rage. Equals the normal clearance time at reference conditions.

variables.name: collisions from distracted driving and road rage
variables.documentation: Collisions per year produced by phone use, texting or eating while driving and by aggressive driving episodes. Collisions block lanes and lengthen clearance time, closing the congestion reinforcing loop R3.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Normalized index of using a phone, texting or eating while driving. Exogenous, starting at its reference value and worsening mildly over the 20-year horizon. It raises collision risk and generates provocations.

variables.name: Road Design
variables.documentation: Normalized index of poor road design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections). Exogenous parameter that degrades clearance capacity; it deteriorates mildly over time, providing the external push that lets the reinforcing loops take over.

variables.name: Weather Conditions
variables.documentation: Normalized index of adverse weather (heavy rain or snow) as a graphical function of TIME. Starts at the reference value and drifts mildly worse with fluctuations; it both degrades clearance and raises stress.

variables.name: Personality Traits
variables.documentation: Normalized prevalence of impulsive, hostile or competitive personalities in the driving population. Exogenous parameter held at its reference level in the base run.

variables.name: aggressive driving propensity
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplicative composite of all psychological, situational and environmental drivers of aggression. Because every factor is normalized to 1 at its reference value, the propensity equals 1 in reference conditions and multiplies the normal incident occurrence rate.

variables.name: effect of Frustration on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of feeling blocked by other drivers on aggressive driving; equals 1 at reference frustration.

variables.name: effect of Impatience on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of impatience (running late, low delay tolerance) on aggressive driving; equals 1 at reference impatience.

variables.name: effect of Stress and Anxiety on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of stress and anxiety on irritability and aggressive reactions; equals 1 at reference stress.

variables.name: effect of Learned Behavior on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of socially normalized aggression on the likelihood that a driver engages in road rage; equals 1 at reference norms.

variables.name: effect of Lack of Sleep on judgement impairment
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of fatigue on impaired judgement, which makes drivers more susceptible to anger; equals 1 at reference sleep debt.

variables.name: effect of Personality Traits on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of the prevalence of impulsive, hostile, competitive personalities on aggressive driving; equals 1 at reference prevalence.

variables.name: effect of Distracted Driving on aggression
variables.documentation: Nonlinear normalized effect of distracted driving on aggressive behaviour, capturing the anger provoked by erratic distracted drivers; equals 1 at reference distraction.

variables.name: driving population
variables.documentation: Number of drivers using the network. Held constant so that the dynamics come from feedback, not from population growth.

variables.name: trips per driver
variables.documentation: Average number of congestion-exposed trips each driver makes per year at reference conditions.

variables.name: clearance capacity
variables.documentation: Throughput capacity of the network used to convert the congestion stock into an average trip delay. Set equal to the reference vehicle entry rate.

variables.name: reference trip delay
variables.documentation: Delay per trip experienced at reference congestion. Used to normalize impatience and the congestion deterrence effect so both equal 1 at reference.

variables.name: reference Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Reference (initial, near-equilibrium) level of active road rage episodes, used to normalize all incident-driven effects.

variables.name: average road rage episode duration
variables.documentation: Average time an aggressive-driving episode stays active/recent before de-escalating. Sets the first-order drain of the incident stock.

variables.name: normal incident occurrence rate
variables.documentation: Occurrence rate of new episodes when the aggressive driving propensity equals 1. Derived from the reference stock and episode duration so the incident stock is exactly in equilibrium at time zero.

variables.name: reference Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Reference (initial) level of perceived provocations, used to normalize provocation-driven effects.

variables.name: provocation memory time
variables.documentation: Average time a driver keeps feeling provoked; sets the first-order fading of the provocation stock.

variables.name: normal provocation rate
variables.documentation: Provocation perception rate at reference incidents and reference distraction; derived to place the provocation stock in equilibrium at time zero.

variables.name: incident provocation exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of perceived provocations to the number of drivers currently raging (retaliation loop R1 gain).

variables.name: distraction provocation exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of perceived provocations to distracted driving.

variables.name: reference Stress and Anxiety
variables.documentation: Reference (initial) stress level of the driving population, used to normalize stress effects.

variables.name: stress recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time over which accumulated stress is relieved; sets the first-order stress drain.

variables.name: normal stress accumulation rate
variables.documentation: Stress build-up rate at reference congestion, weather and provocations; derived to place the stress stock in equilibrium at time zero.

variables.name: congestion stress exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of stress build-up to heavy traffic and stop-and-go conditions.

variables.name: weather stress exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of stress build-up to adverse weather conditions.

variables.name: provocation stress exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of stress build-up to perceived provocations (stress spiral R4 gain).

variables.name: reference Learned Behavior
variables.documentation: Reference (initial) level of the aggressive-driving normalization index.

variables.name: norm unlearning time
variables.documentation: Average time over which socially learned aggressive norms are forgotten; long because social norms are slow to change.

variables.name: normal normalization rate
variables.documentation: Normalization rate at reference exposure to road rage; derived to place the learned-behaviour stock in equilibrium at time zero.

variables.name: incident normalization exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of norm formation to observed road rage incidents (learned-behaviour loop R2 gain).

variables.name: reference Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Reference (initial) sleep debt of the driving population, used to normalize fatigue effects.

variables.name: sleep recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time over which accumulated sleep debt is repaid; sets the first-order fatigue drain.

variables.name: normal sleep deficit rate
variables.documentation: Sleep debt build-up rate at reference stress; derived to place the fatigue stock in equilibrium at time zero.

variables.name: stress sleep exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of sleep debt accumulation to stress and anxiety (fatigue spiral R5 gain).

variables.name: normal congestion reference
variables.documentation: Normal (initial, equilibrium) number of vehicles queued or delayed, equal to the reference entry rate times the normal clearance time. Used to normalize all congestion effects.

variables.name: normal average clearance time
variables.documentation: Average clearance time at reference road design, weather and collisions. Chosen at the annual aggregate scale so the first-order congestion drain is numerically stable with the model time step.

variables.name: road design clearance exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of clearance time to poor road design such as narrow lanes and confusing intersections.

variables.name: weather clearance exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of clearance time to adverse weather conditions.

variables.name: collision clearance exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of clearance time to collisions blocking the network (congestion loop R3 gain).

variables.name: normal collision rate
variables.documentation: Collisions per year at reference distraction and reference road rage; used both as the base rate and as the normalizing constant for the collision effect on clearance.

variables.name: distraction collision exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of collisions to distracted driving (phone use, texting, eating).

variables.name: incident collision exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of collisions to active road rage episodes.

variables.name: congestion deterrence exponent
variables.documentation: Strength of trip deferral when delays rise; the gain of balancing loop B1.

variables.name: reference Road Design
variables.documentation: Reference value of the poor-road-design index, at which clearance time is normal.

variables.name: road design deterioration rate
variables.documentation: Mild yearly worsening of the road design deficiency index, representing roads becoming increasingly inadequate for demand. This is one of the two exogenous pushes that let the reinforcing loops take over.

variables.name: reference Weather Conditions
variables.documentation: Reference value of the adverse weather index, at which clearance time and stress build-up are normal.

variables.name: reference Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Reference value of the distracted driving index, at which its effects equal 1.

variables.name: distracted driving growth rate
variables.documentation: Mild yearly growth of distracted driving, representing increasing phone use behind the wheel; the second exogenous push over the 20-year horizon.

variables.name: reference Frustration
variables.documentation: Reference level of frustration, at which the frustration effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: congestion frustration exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of frustration to traffic congestion relative to normal.

variables.name: provocation frustration exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of frustration to perceived provocations (feeling blocked or cut off by other drivers).

variables.name: reference Impatience
variables.documentation: Reference level of impatience, at which the impatience effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: delay tolerance
variables.documentation: Dimensionless parameter for how much delay drivers will tolerate before becoming impatient; lower tolerance means impatience rises sooner.

variables.name: delay impatience exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of impatience to trip delay relative to the tolerated delay.

variables.name: reference Personality Traits
variables.documentation: Reference prevalence of impulsive, hostile and competitive personalities, at which their effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: frustration aggression exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of aggressive driving propensity to frustration.

variables.name: impatience aggression exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of aggressive driving propensity to impatience.

variables.name: stress aggression exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of aggressive driving propensity to stress and anxiety.

variables.name: learned behavior aggression exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of aggressive driving propensity to the social normalization of aggressive driving.

variables.name: sleep judgement exponent
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of judgement impairment, and therefore aggression, to accumulated sleep debt.

variables.name: personality traits aggression exponent

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a compact 5-variable stock-flow model of the escalation dynamic described in your background material, then run it and analyze the feedback structure.

Model built, run, and analyzed. Here is the answer.

The model (exactly 5 variables)

Variable Type Units Equation / Init
Colonial Identity stock dmnl init 1 (1763 baseline)
Intensification of Anti British Sentiment inflow to Colonial Identity dmnl/Year Colonial Identity × British Taxation and Intolerable Acts
British Taxation and Intolerable Acts stock 1/Year init 0
British Coercion Provoked by Colonial Defiance inflow to that stock 1/Year/Year Colonial Identity × French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand
French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand constant 1/Year/Year 0.03

Simulated 1763–1776, Euler, dt 0.125. The engine reported no errors and no unit warnings. Both flows are uniflows, so neither stock can go negative — correct, since enacted laws and accumulated grievance do not un-happen.

The feedback structure

The feedback analysis on run eval-run-1 returned exactly two loops, both reinforcing:

L1 (reinforcing, 4 links) — the escalation spiral: British Coercion Provoked by Colonial Defiance (+) → British Taxation and Intolerable Acts (+) → Intensification of Anti British Sentiment (+) → Colonial Identity (+) → back to British Coercion Provoked by Colonial Defiance.

L2 (reinforcing, 2 links) — self-amplifying identity: Colonial Identity (+) → Intensification of Anti British Sentiment (+) → Colonial Identity.

No LTM dominance scores were returned for this run, only loop structure and polarity, so I cannot give you percentage contributions over time.

The feedback-based explanation

The French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand is the only thing in this structure that is not part of a loop. It is the exogenous push: Britain wants the colonies to pay for their own defence. That push does not by itself cause a revolution — it causes the first turn of L1.

L1 is the grievance-repression spiral. Britain legislates (Stamp Act, then the Intolerable Acts closing the port of Boston), which raises the accumulated stock of British Taxation and Intolerable Acts. Because the colonists had no representatives in Parliament, each new act registers not as policy but as injury, so it intensifies anti-British sentiment and builds Colonial Identity. A stronger American identity produces more defiance — the Boston Tea Party being the pivotal instance — and defiance provokes more coercion. The loop closes. Note what makes it a loop rather than a chain: the Intolerable Acts were a response to the Tea Party, which was a response to taxation. Britain and the colonists were each reacting to the other's last move.

L2 is the propaganda loop, and it is why the Boston Massacre mattered out of all proportion to five deaths. Sentiment intensifies in proportion to existing identity, not just to the size of the grievance. An event only becomes a shared American injury once there is enough American identity to interpret, print and circulate it as one. The stronger the identity, the more efficiently each new grievance is converted into more identity.

The two loops multiply. L1 must fill the taxation stock before L2 has anything to work with, which is why the first years look quiet: Colonial Identity rises only from 1.00 to 1.08 between 1763 and 1765, and to 2.33 by 1770. Then both loops are loaded and the curve bends hard: 8.1 by 1773, 17.1 by 1774, 46.6 by 1775, 472 by 1776. Hostilities break out not because any single act was intolerable, but because by 1774 the loop gain had compounded to the point where each British act produced more defiance than the act was meant to suppress.

Extreme condition check: set the French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand to zero and the coercion inflow becomes zero, so the taxation stock stays at zero, so intensification stays at zero, and Colonial Identity remains at 1 forever. No war debt, no revolution — in this structure the loops are real but they need a push to start turning.

Critique — where this model is weak

I ran the structure past Seldon, and two objections are serious enough that you should not take the trajectory at face value:

  1. There is no balancing loop anywhere. The taxation stock has no outflow, so grievance can only ratchet up and the model says revolution was inevitable from 1763. History does not support that: Britain repealed the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties, and the model cannot reproduce those lulls. The single highest-value sixth variable would be a colonial boycott creating economic pressure on Britain, feeding a repeal outflow from the taxation stock. That one addition buys a balancing loop, the reversibility of the conflict before 1774, and it makes the post-Intolerable-Acts escalation meaningful as the moment Britain stopped conceding.

  2. The superexponential blow-up is a formulation artifact. Two mutually multiplicative accumulations with no saturation give finite-time blow-up as a matter of arithmetic. Colonial Identity at 472 times its 1763 value has no historical referent. The credible reference mode is punctuated and bounded — rise, partial relief, sharp re-escalation after 1774 — not a singularity.

  3. Nothing in the model dates 1775. There is no threshold and no hostilities variable; the timing is set entirely by the 0.03 and the initial conditions. This model explains why escalation was self-reinforcing, not why then.

Within your 5-variable ceiling, this is the honest maximum: the escalation is right, the inevitability is an artifact of the missing balancing loop.

Want me to relax the ceiling to 6 and add the boycott-and-repeal balancing loop, or plot the current run against the feedback structure?

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a compact SFD that captures the causal core of road rage from the background you provided, within the 5-variable limit.

I built and simulated a 5-variable stock-and-flow model, ran it, and retrieved the loop analysis. Here is what is actually there.

The model (exactly 5 variables)

Variable Type Equation Units
Normalized Aggressive Driving stock init 0.15 dimensionless
Normalization from Observing Aggressive Driving inflow Road Rage Incidents * (1 - Normalized Aggressive Driving) 1/Months
Road Rage Incidents auxiliary Perceived Provocations * Normalized Aggressive Driving 1/Months
Perceived Provocations auxiliary Normalized Aggressive Driving * Traffic Congestion 1/Months
Traffic Congestion constant 0.5 1/Months

The single accumulation is Normalized Aggressive Driving — the fraction of drivers for whom aggressive driving has become learned, normal behavior. Because you capped the model at five variables, stress, personality traits, impatience, lack of sleep, distracted driving, road design and weather could not be given their own variables; road design and weather are folded into Traffic Congestion, and the psychological triggers are folded into the conversion of Perceived Provocations into Road Rage Incidents. Units are consistent and the engine reported no unit warnings.

Feedback structure (from the loop analysis of run eval-run-1)

The analysis returned three loops:

  • L3, reinforcing — the road rage contagion loop. Normalized Aggressive Driving increases Perceived Provocations (more drivers cutting others off, tailgating, honking), which increases Road Rage Incidents, which increases Normalization from Observing Aggressive Driving, which raises the stock further. This is the learned-behavior mechanism: observing aggression normalizes it.
  • L2, reinforcing — the direct escalation loop. Normalized Aggressive Driving raises Road Rage Incidents directly (a driver who treats aggression as normal retaliates rather than absorbing a provocation), which feeds normalization, which raises the stock.
  • L1, balancing — susceptible-pool exhaustion. As the stock rises, the pool of drivers who have not yet normalized aggressive driving shrinks, so the normalization flow slows.

Because Normalized Aggressive Driving enters the chain twice, incidents scale roughly with the square of the stock: the reinforcing gain grows faster than linearly.

What the simulation actually did

I inspected the numerical output. Normalized Aggressive Driving rises S-shaped from 0.15 to essentially 1.0 by about month 22. Road Rage Incidents rise from 0.011 per month to a plateau of 0.5 per month — a ceiling set entirely by Traffic Congestion. Nothing goes negative and the stock stays inside 0 to 1.

Seldon's dominance reading of that trajectory: the reinforcing pair L2 and L3 dominate months 0 to about 14 (the normalization flow itself is rising, from 0.0096 to 0.073 per month — an accelerating flow is the signature of reinforcing dominance). The flow peaks near month 16 at a stock of about 0.71; that inflection is the handover point where the shrinking-pool drag of L1 exactly cancels the reinforcing gain. From month 18 onward L1 dominates and the system goal-seeks toward saturation.

The answer to your question

Road rage in this model is not caused by any single trigger. Congestion, provocations and short tempers are the fuel, but the engine is a reinforcing contagion loop: aggression produces provocations, provocations produce incidents, and incidents are observed and learned, which produces more aggression. That is why road rage grows slowly at first and then takes off — the loop gain rises with the stock.

Left alone, this structure predicts road rage incidents keep climbing until they hit a ceiling set by how much traffic congestion there is. The future is not a return to civility; it is a plateau at a high level.

Critique — where this model should not be trusted

The most important structural flaw is that the stock has no outflow. Nothing de-normalizes aggressive driving: no enforcement, no deterrence, no social disapproval, no driver turnover. So the model is guaranteed to reach total normalization from any positive start, and its only brake, L1, is pool exhaustion rather than a policy-relevant mechanism. The forecast of inevitable saturation is partly an artifact of that missing flow, not a hard-won result. Also, Traffic Congestion being constant means the model cannot yet speak to remote work, road-design improvement or weather variation, even though it alone fixes the equilibrium incident rate.

The highest-leverage interventions the structure points to, in order: add visible consequences so that observing aggression teaches deterrence rather than acceptance (this weakens the incidents-to-normalization link that both reinforcing loops run through); reduce congestion, which lowers the incident ceiling and slows takeoff but does not by itself prevent normalization; and act early, since the gain grows with the square of the stock.

Recommended next steps: relax the 5-variable cap by one to add a de-normalization outflow, which turns inevitable escalation into a genuine tug-of-war with a tipping threshold; and make Traffic Congestion time-varying to test congestion-reduction policy. If you want to see the dynamics, a time-series plot of Normalized Aggressive Driving and Road Rage Incidents with dominant-loop bands overlaid, or a causal loop diagram of the three loops, would both be informative — say the word and I will produce either.

variables.name: Normalized Aggressive Driving
variables.documentation: The fraction of drivers in society for whom aggressive driving has become normalized learned behavior. Observing aggressive driving behavior from others normalizes it and increases the likelihood of engaging in road rage. Ranges from 0 (nobody treats aggressive driving as normal) to 1 (universally normalized).

variables.name: Normalization from Observing Aggressive Driving
variables.documentation: Rate at which aggressive driving becomes normalized learned behavior as drivers observe road rage incidents. The (1 - Normalized Aggressive Driving) term represents the shrinking pool of drivers who have not yet normalized aggressive driving.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Rate of road rage incidents, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration. Perceived provocations turn into actual incidents in proportion to how normalized aggressive driving has become in the driving population.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Rate at which drivers perceive being provoked - being cut off, tailgated, or honked at. More normalized aggressive driving means more provoking behavior on the road, and traffic congestion increases the exposure of drivers to each other.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Severity of heavy traffic, delays and stop-and-go conditions, including the contribution of poor road design and adverse weather conditions. Congestion increases stress, impatience and frustration, and determines how many provocative encounters each driver experiences per month.

testParams.name: include a minimum number of feedback loops for American Revolution
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of the escalation dynamics. Let me start by loading the model tools and checking current state.

Model is empty. I'll build the escalation model from scratch, using the background's own terms as variable names.

All 11 stocks present. Let me inspect the flows and auxiliaries.

Structure is good and no stock goes negative, but hostilities never actually break out within the horizon (0.001 clashes by 1776) — the outbreak condition can't be reached because the garrison decays instead of building. Let me fix that structurally.

Outbreak now shows the right shape (flat, then sharp takeoff) but lands about a year late. One reference-level adjustment:

Behavior now matches the reference mode: grievance builds 1765-1770, sharp escalation after the Tea Party, hostilities breaking out in 1775. No stock goes negative. Now the feedback analysis.

50 feedback loops identified. Let me get the LTM dominance narrative and an expert critique.

The causal loop diagram renderer is returning a server-side error (temperature may only be set to 1 when thinking is enabled) on both attempts, so I'll give you the structure in text. Everything below comes from the simulated model and the Loops That Matter dominance analysis of run eval-run-3.

What was built

A quantitative SFD, 1754-1780, quarterly, with eleven stocks: French and Indian War Debt, Colonial Taxation Burden, Anti British Sentiment, American Colonial Identity, Colonial Defiance, Intolerable Acts, British Troops in the Colonies, Boston Massacre Propaganda, Colonial Militia Mobilization, British Perception of Colonial Rebelliousness, and Hostilities. The four events in your background enter as dated, named components rather than as assumptions about the outcome: the Stamp Act of 1765 tax imposition, the Boston Massacre 1770 event, the Boston Tea Party defiance pulse of 1773, and a post Boston Tea Party coercion switch that turns Parliament punitive. The engine reports no unit warnings and no errors; every stock outflow is first-order, and no stock goes negative.

Simulated behavior: sentiment 0.10 → 0.52 by 1764, 1.28 by 1770, 1.63 by 1773, 2.14 by late 1775. Tax compliance falls 0.73 → 0.26 by 1773, then collapses to 0.13 after the Tea Party. Troops climb 2,000 → 7,100; militia 500 → 3,800. Hostilities are effectively zero until 1774, cross threshold in 1775, and explode in 1776.

The feedback explanation

The model finds 50 loops. Eleven carry the story.

R1 Taxation Without Representation Grievance. American Colonial Identity → Taxation without Representatives in Parliament → Anti British Sentiment → American Colonial Identity. This is the ideological core: the same duty becomes more intolerable the more distinctly American the payer feels. Identity does not merely accompany the grievance, it manufactures it.

R5 Noncompliance Sustaining the Tax Demand. Sentiment → Colonial Defiance → lower tax compliance fraction → less revenue → French and Indian War Debt stays high → pressure for colonial repayment → new taxes → more grievance. Resistance to paying taxes guaranteed more taxes, not fewer. This is why the fiscal and political problems could not be solved separately.

B3 Debt Service Through Colonial Taxes. Debt → taxation → revenue → debt down. The loop that started everything, and the only one doing what London intended. It drives the tax burden from zero to about 159,000 by 1764 — loading the gun the political loops later fire.

B1 Repeal as Appeasement. High sentiment → tax repeal → lower burden → less perceived illegitimacy → lower sentiment. This loop works: the Colonial Taxation Burden peaks in 1765 and falls every year afterward. And it fails anyway, because by 1766 sentiment is no longer under the control of the tax loops.

R2 Coercion and Outrage and R3 Coercion Forging Identity. Defiance → Intolerable Acts → sentiment, and → identity. Punishment read as insult rather than deterrent. Between 1765 and 1770 sentiment more than doubles and identity rises 0.30 → 0.66 while the tax burden is falling. This is the pivot of the whole run: the dispute stops being about money and becomes self-sustaining on coercion and resistance alone.

R4 Confrontation and Propaganda. Defiance → friction between troops and colonists → Boston Massacre incidents → Boston Massacre Propaganda → sentiment → defiance. The 1770 event injects one incident and the propaganda stock jumps from 574 to 4,490 pamphlets. Note the structure: five deaths mattered not as casualties but as a stock of memory with a six-year half-life feeding grievance continuously.

R6 Mutual Arming and Occupation Incidents. Sentiment → Colonial Militia Mobilization → British Perception of Colonial Rebelliousness → British Troops in the Colonies → friction → propaganda → sentiment. Occupation is structurally self-defeating here: every regiment sent to reassure London enlarges the surface on which friction occurs.

R7 Coercion Charged to the Colonies. Defiance → Intolerable Acts → cost of enforcing the Intolerable Acts and garrisoning troops → French and Indian War Debt → new taxes → grievance. The fiscal trap: the expense of governing an angry population is met by making the population angrier.

B2 Port of Boston Closure Discipline, B4 Deployment Quieting Observed Defiance, and plain defiance suppression are the empire's control loops. They are not weak — they are why Colonial Defiance actually falls from 2.48 in 1774 to 1.99 by 1776. Boston is subdued in the narrow sense. But they act on the wrong variable. Identity rises 1.01 → 1.57 and militia 1,301 → 3,820 over exactly the same window.

Why hostilities broke out

The outbreak flow requires the multiplicative coincidence of armed colonists, armed regulars, and grievance. Any one alone produces nothing. The dominance handoff is what assembles all three: the fiscal loops (B3) built the tax burden, the legitimacy loops (R1, R5) converted it into grievance, the coercion loops (R2, R3, R7) made grievance self-sustaining after repeal removed the original cause, the propaganda loop (R4) radicalized it, and the arming loop (R6) finally put muskets on both sides of the same street.

The deepest finding is this: every instrument the empire had for restoring order — troops, coercive statutes, closing the Port of Boston, and even repeal — was wired into a loop feeding the identity and grievance it was meant to suppress. By 1775 the tax burden was still falling while the colonies armed.

Critique and open questions for you

Structural weaknesses worth your judgment. The model has no loyalist stock, so there is no organized internal opposition to defiance; the colonies act as one actor. The post Boston Tea Party coercion switch is exogenous — it imposes the hardening of British policy rather than deriving it, which is a real boundary limitation given that this hardening is doing heavy lifting in 1774. And there is no cross-Atlantic negotiation channel other than repeal.

Some questions I cannot settle for you:

  • If B1 (repeal) genuinely relieved the tax grievance, what does it say about the Revolution's causes that it changed nothing after 1766?
  • The model makes coercion the strongest identity-forming force in the system. Does that match your reading of the period, or is identity better modeled as forming independently of British action?
  • Was there any parameterization of the balancing loops under which Britain could have kept the colonies — or does the loop structure itself make the outcome inevitable once the debt exists?

Useful next steps: sensitivity analysis on conciliation_repeal_gain and post_Boston_Tea_Party_coercion_multiplier to test whether restraint could have averted 1775, or a run with the Boston Massacre and Boston Tea Party pulses switched off to see how much the discrete events actually contributed versus the underlying loops. Say the word and I will run either, or produce the dominance and time-series plots.

variables.documentation: Accumulated British national debt attributed to defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-1763), plus the later cost of garrisoning troops and enforcing coercive legislation. This debt is the fiscal motive behind every attempt to tax the colonies.

variables.name: French and Indian War spending
variables.documentation: War expenditure that accrues to the debt only while the French and Indian War is being fought.

variables.name: French and Indian War switch
variables.documentation: Named on/off switch that equals one between the start and end year of the French and Indian War and zero otherwise.

variables.documentation: Year the French and Indian War begins.

variables.name: French and Indian War end year
variables.documentation: Year the French and Indian War ends.

variables.name: annual French and Indian War spending rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which the war added to the British debt while it was being fought.

variables.name: cost of enforcing the Intolerable Acts and garrisoning troops
variables.documentation: The fiscal trap: coercion is expensive. Enforcing the Intolerable Acts and keeping regiments in America adds to the very debt the colonies are being taxed to repay.

variables.name: enforcement cost per act
variables.documentation: Annual administrative and naval cost of enforcing each coercive act.

variables.name: garrison cost per troop
variables.documentation: Annual cost of maintaining one soldier in the American colonies.

variables.name: debt repayment from colonial tax revenue
variables.documentation: First-order retirement of the debt, accelerated in proportion to how much colonial tax revenue is actually collected relative to a reference level. Being first order in the stock, it can never drive the debt negative.

variables.name: debt repayment time
variables.documentation: Time constant for retiring the war debt at reference revenue.

variables.name: reference colonial tax revenue
variables.documentation: Normal colonial tax revenue used to normalise the effect of revenue on debt repayment.

variables.name: Colonial Taxation Burden

variables.name: new tax impositions

variables.name: base tax repeal time

variables.name: British pressure for colonial repayment of the French and Indian War

variables.name: colonial tax revenue collected

variables.documentation: Reports crossing the Atlantic raise British perception toward what is actually happening.

variables.documentation: First-order forgetting of old reports, which together with the inflow makes perception a delayed image of reality.

variables.documentation: Time for news and dispatches to change ministerial opinion.

variables.documentation: What London hears about: open defiance and colonists arming themselves.

variables.name: Hostilities
variables.documentation: Cumulative armed clashes between colonists and regulars, the outbreak of the Revolutionary War.

variables.name: outbreak of hostilities
variables.documentation: Armed clashes occur only when armed colonists, armed regulars and burning grievance all coincide.

variables.name: hostilities gain
variables.documentation: Clashes per year when the readiness index is at its normal reference value.

variables.name: hostilities readiness index
variables.documentation: Multiplicative coincidence of armed colonists, armed troops and grievance. Because it is a product, all three must be present for war to break out.

variables.name: hostilities threshold effect
variables.documentation: Strongly nonlinear threshold: almost nothing happens below the reference coincidence, and clashes multiply rapidly above it. Normalised so that an index of one gives an effect of one.

variables.name: baseline garrison establishment
variables.documentation: The peacetime establishment of regular troops Britain intended to keep in America after the French and Indian War. Replacement at this level continues regardless of perceived rebelliousness, so the garrison does not simply decay away.

variables.name: baseline militia establishment
variables.documentation: The customary provincial militia establishment kept up in the colonies irrespective of political grievance, replaced as men rotate out.

testParams.name: include a minimum number of feedback loops for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD from your background information. Let me start by loading the model tools.

Tools loaded. Let me check the current model state first.

Empty model. Building the quantitative SFD now, using your background factors as named variables.

Model generated. Now validating what was actually built.

Structure looks clean — 9 stocks, all with first-order outflows, no hard-coded constants inline. Checking specs and running.

One structural defect found: deterrence_effect reads 1.3 at t=0 when enforcement is at its normal value of 1 — the engine interpolates the graphical function's x-points as evenly spaced, so the non-uniform x spacing broke the intended pass-through-(1,1) calibration. B1 never actually deters. Fixing with uniformly spaced points.

Names use spaces on disk. Applying the fix correctly.

No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine. Re-running.

Behavior is now correct (deterrence starts at 1.0), but the transient completes in ~7 months on a 120-month horizon — too fast to show the slow social dynamic. The slow normalization loop (18-month norm stock) is under-weighted. Strengthening it so the long-run trend is norm-driven.

Behavior is now credible: escalation to a peak at month 12, overshoot, and settlement at ~38% above the starting level, with the norm stock and enforcement peaking later than incidents — the delayed-response signature. All nine stocks stay strictly positive. Now retrieving the feedback loop analysis.

All 23 loops confirmed, including every loop I specified. Running LTM narrative and a Seldon structural critique.

Seldon flags a numerical concern worth testing: DT=0.25 against 1-month time constants. Let me verify the overshoot is structural, not numerical.

DT test passes: peak 1600.1 vs 1603.6 (0.2% difference), identical timing and final values. The overshoot is structural, not numerical. Keeping the finer DT. Let me render the feedback structure behind this behavior.

The diagram renderer is returning a server-side API configuration error (temperature may only be set to 1 when thinking is enabled) on both attempts — that is a fault in the tool's own request, not in the loop specification, so I can't render the visual. The written analysis follows.

How Road Rage Happens: A Feedback Explanation

What was built

A quantitative stock-and-flow model, simulated over 120 months. Every trigger you listed became a named accumulation rather than a static risk factor, because each one builds up and drains at its own speed — and it is that difference in speeds that produces the dynamics.

Nine stocks: Road Rage Incidents, Stress and Anxiety, Frustration, Traffic Congestion, Perceived Provocations, Impatience, Learned Behavior, Lack of Sleep, Distracted Driving. Three exogenous conditions: Personality Traits, Road Design, Weather Conditions.

The incident rate is a base rate scaled by the driving population, multiplied by dimensionless effects from each trigger — so no single factor causes road rage; they compound. The engine reported no unit warnings.

Validation performed. I found and fixed one real defect: the deterrence graphical function was interpolated on evenly spaced x-values, so deterrence read 1.3 instead of 1.0 at normal enforcement — the deterrence loop was silently amplifying rather than restraining. I also confirmed the overshoot is structural, not numerical: halving DT twice moved the peak by 0.2 percent (1603.6 to 1600.1) with identical timing and identical final values.

The behavior

Incidents rise from 1000 to a peak of 1604 at month 12, fall to a trough of 1362 at month 44, then drift up to a plateau of 1380 — permanently about 38 percent above where they started. Learned Behavior peaks later, at month 19.5, and never returns to baseline. Enforcement peaks later still, at month 24.5. Distracted Driving falls throughout.

The lags between those peaks are the whole story.

The feedback structure

The analysis identified 23 loops. Here are the ones that drive the behavior.

Reinforcing — the escalation engine

  • R1 Frustration-Congestion Spiral. Incidents block lanes, congestion rises, drivers feel blocked, Frustration builds, more incidents. Aggression physically recreates the conditions that produce aggression.
  • R2 Retaliation Spiral. An incident is experienced by someone else as being cut off or honked at. Perceived Provocations accumulate, retaliation follows, and that retaliation is itself the next driver's provocation. This is the shortest reinforcing path in the model and therefore the fastest to gain strength.
  • R3 Aggression Normalization Spiral. Every incident is also a demonstration. Observers come to treat aggression as ordinary, Learned Behavior rises, and the incident rate rises with it. This is the slow loop — an 18-month norm stock against 1-to-3-month emotional stocks.
  • R4 Aggressive Weaving Gridlock. Congestion breeds Impatience; impatient drivers tailgate, weave and block merges; that degrades traffic flow directly, with no confrontation required, which breeds more impatience.
  • R5 Stress-Irritability Spiral. Aggressive roads raise Stress and Anxiety across the whole population, stressed drivers are more irritable, irritable drivers escalate faster.
  • R6 Fatigue Spiral. Stress erodes sleep, Lack of Sleep impairs judgment and impulse control, incidents rise, stress rises again. This is how a physiological trigger and a psychological one sustain each other.
  • R7 Distraction Spiral. Stop-and-go congestion is exactly the condition in which drivers reach for a phone. Distracted Driving produces drifting and missed signals that others read as provocation, incidents follow, congestion worsens.

Balancing — what stops it

  • B1 Delayed Deterrence. Visible aggression eventually calls forth enforcement and social disapproval, which suppresses escalation in the moment. Critically, this loop runs through a 12-month perception delay while the reinforcing loops run through 1-to-3-month stocks. The overshoot exists precisely because society reacts on a slower clock than drivers do.
  • B2 Trip Avoidance. As congestion worsens, some drivers delay, reroute or cancel. This quietly caps the strength of every congestion-driven trigger.
  • B3 Sanctioned Norm Reversal. Sanction strips aggressive driving of its social licence, accelerating denormalization. This is the direct counterweight to R3.
  • B4 Incident Resolution. Disputes end and drivers separate at a rate proportional to how many incidents are active. As the stock grows, this drain grows with it — it is what ultimately halts the escalation.

Alongside these, each stock's own drain (grudge forgetting, stress recovery, frustration venting, impatience relief, sleep catch-up, congestion clearing, norm fading) provides local balancing that keeps every accumulation finite.

Why the trajectory has that shape

Months 0 to 12 — escalation. The fast reinforcing loops dominate. R2, R5, R7, R1 and R4 all route through the same shared quantities, so their effects compound: provocations climb from 40 to 49, stress from 30 to 35, congestion from 50 to 56. R3 is building too, but through a slow stock, so it contributes late.

Months 12 to 24.5 — the turn. As the incident stock grows, B4 grows proportionally and eventually exceeds the escalating pressure. Simultaneously enforcement finally arrives, and B1, B3 and the distraction-enforcement loops engage. What all these have in common: the visibility of aggression calls forth the very responses that remove its causes.

Months 24.5 to 44 — overshoot downward. With enforcement past its peak, the drains dominate. Grudges are forgotten, stress recovers, fatigue is repaid, congestion clears. Incidents undershoot to 1362 because the emotional conditions drained faster than the incident level could re-establish.

Months 44 to 120 — the new plateau. Incidents drift back to 1380 and hold. The decisive feature: the trigger left standing is cultural, not emotional. Stress, frustration and impatience have returned close to baseline. Learned Behavior has not — it settles at 20.3 against an initial 18, so R3 keeps supplying a baseline propensity to escalate that the other loops no longer do.

What this implies about the future

The surge is self-limiting; the residue is not. Escalation is fast because retaliation, stress and time pressure amplify one another — but it is also self-defeating, because it triggers resolution, deterrence and disapproval that bring the wave down.

What does not come back down is what was learned. Aggressive driving gets normalized during the surge and erodes only slowly afterward. Society is left with a permanently higher floor even after every emotional and traffic trigger has subsided.

The leverage implication is sharp: interventions aimed at emotional and traffic triggers shorten the surge; only interventions aimed at norms lower the plateau that follows. And because B1 operates through a 12-month delay, faster societal response is itself a lever — much of the overshoot is a delay artifact, not an inevitability.

Where this model should be doubted

I ran a structural critique and it surfaced genuine weaknesses you should weigh:

  • Correlated multipliers double-count. Frustration, Impatience and Distraction are all driven by the same congestion signal, yet are multiplied as though independent. One congestion shock gets amplified three times.
  • Effects are linear and unsaturated. Only deterrence saturates. At extremes, nine compounding multipliers behave superlinearly, and driving congestion to zero cuts incidents by only about 20 to 25 percent — implausibly insensitive.
  • No capacity ceiling. Set Personality Traits very high and the reinforcing set can overwhelm the bounded deterrence loop and run away, which is physically impossible.
  • The permanently elevated norm is a genuine equilibrium, not hysteresis. It is the unique steady state implied by a raised incident level, and I verified it analytically. True cultural lock-in would need a tipping point or cohort transmission, which this model does not have. Do not read this result as proof of irreversible cultural change.
  • Missing boundary: no crashes or casualties (and so no outrage-driven enforcement loop), no endogenous exposure (mode shift, licence revocation, avoiding driving out of fear), no enforcement capacity or habituation to penalties, no induced demand from road building, no media amplification.

The most valuable next moves, in order: add a saturating capacity ceiling on incidents so extreme-conditions tests behave, then bring crashes and casualties inside the boundary — that missing loop is the one most likely to change the policy conclusion. I can also run a sensitivity analysis on the enforcement perception delay, since the overshoot magnitude appears to hinge on it.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Accumulated pool of active aggressive-driving (road rage) incidents in the driving population. It rises with new incidents and falls as incidents are resolved/defused.

variables.name: road rage incident rate
variables.equation: base_road_rage_incident_rate * effect_of_Frustration * effect_of_Perceived_Provocations * effect_of_Learned_Behavior * effect_of_Impatience * irritability * impaired_judgment * effect_of_Distracted_Driving * effect_of_Personality_Traits * deterrence_effect
variables.documentation: New road rage incidents per month. Formed as a normalized driver-population base rate multiplied by dimensionless effect multipliers for frustration, perceived provocations, learned behavior, impatience, irritability (stress), impaired judgment (sleep debt), distracted driving, personality predisposition, and deterrence.

variables.name: road rage incident resolution rate
variables.documentation: First-order draining of active incidents: incidents cool down, are resolved or dropped after an average duration. Guarantees the stock cannot go negative.

variables.name: base road rage incident rate
variables.documentation: Population-scaled reference incident generation rate that would occur if every driver, situational and environmental multiplier were at its normal (=1) value.

variables.name: Driving Population
variables.documentation: Exogenous constant number of active drivers exposed to road conditions.

variables.name: base incidents per driver
variables.documentation: Normal propensity of a single driver to start a road rage incident per month under reference conditions. Set slightly above the resolution capacity so that reinforcing loops are initially dominant.

variables.name: average road rage incident duration
variables.documentation: Average time an aggressive-driving incident stays active (anger episode, dispute, aftermath) before being resolved.

variables.name: initial road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Strictly positive initial level of active road rage incidents.

variables.name: reference road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Normal (reference) level of road rage incidents used to normalize the stock to a dimensionless index.

variables.name: normalized road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of incidents relative to the normal level; equals 1 at normal conditions.

variables.name: Stress and Anxiety
variables.documentation: Accumulated psychological stress and anxiety carried by the driving population. High stress makes drivers irritable and prone to aggression.

variables.name: stress accumulation rate
variables.documentation: Monthly build-up of stress from everyday life and driving, amplified when road rage incidents are above normal (stress spiral R5/R6).

variables.name: stress recovery rate
variables.documentation: First-order recovery from stress through rest and coping; keeps the stress stock non-negative.

variables.name: normal stress accumulation rate
variables.documentation: Reference monthly stress accumulation, calibrated so the stress stock is in equilibrium at its reference value under normal conditions.

variables.name: stress recovery time

variables.name: irritability sensitivity

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

No unit warnings or errors were reported. Behavior is non-negative and monotonic, but the reference-mode timing is off — the massacre and tea-party indices fire far too late. Let me tune the gains offline before editing.

Reference-mode fit needs two calibration constants adjusted. The only model-mutation tool available in this session is update_model, whose documented workflow is edit-the-session-file-then-push, so I'll use that path for these two constants.

Engine runs slower than my offline replication; tightening two calibration constants once more.

Reference-mode fit is now good. Retrieving the feedback-loop analysis before interpreting any of this causally.

21 loops detected. Getting the LTM dominance narrative before I distill to four.

I built and calibrated a quantitative stock-and-flow model of the escalation from 1754 to 1776, ran it, and applied Loops That Matter dominance analysis. Here is what the model says.

The four loops

The engine detected 21 loops in the structure. The LTM analysis of the run identifies four as the ones that actually drive the behavior, and they take over from one another in sequence.

B1 — Debt-Driven Taxation (balancing). British War Debt from the French and Indian War raises the Stamp Act Tax Rate, which raises Taxation on the Colonies, whose revenue flows back as Debt Repayment from Colonial Taxation and draws the debt down. This is the disturbance, not the escalation. It solves Britain's fiscal problem while handing the colonial side of the system its input: taxes levied on people whose Representation in Parliament is zero.

R1 — Taxation and Coercion Cycle (reinforcing). Anti British Sentiment produces Colonial Acts of Defiance; defiance is read in London as British Perception of Colonial Disorder; disorder justifies a British Coercive Response of firmer taxes and enforcement; that raises Taxation on the Colonies, which becomes Taxation without Representation, which feeds Anti British Sentiment. This is the loop that converts a one-time fiscal shock into a self-sustaining political process.

R2 — Occupation and Propaganda (reinforcing). The same coercive response also deploys British Troops Stationed in the Colonies. A garrison living among a defiant population generates Violent Incidents, which produce the Boston Massacre, which produces Colonial Propaganda, which feeds Anti British Sentiment. The propaganda stock is the crucial element: it stores the meaning of one episode of bloodshed and releases it into sentiment for years afterward.

R3 — Port Closure and Colonial Union (reinforcing). Defiance crossing a threshold produces the Boston Tea Party; the Tea Party produces the Intolerable Acts; the Intolerable Acts produce the Closure of the Port of Boston; the closure raises Intercolonial Coordination, which raises Anti British Sentiment and further defiance. This is the strongest amplifier in the run.

How they hand off

The escalation is a relay, not one mechanism:

  • 1754 to 1763. B1 governs. Debt climbs to about 126 by 1763 and then falls steadily for the rest of the run. Anti British Sentiment actually dips slightly to 0.161 around 1757 to 1758 before turning up — the erosion of old grievance exceeds the trickle of new. Accumulated Pressure Toward Armed Conflict rises almost linearly to 1.9.
  • 1765 to 1770. R1 dominates and the curve turns from linear drift to compounding growth. Anti British Sentiment goes 0.41 to 0.77, defiance 0.26 to 0.54. The telling detail: Taxation on the Colonies climbs to 0.90 while the war debt that justified it is falling. Taxation is no longer fiscally driven — it is being driven by the political loop. Troops build to roughly 2,800, loading the gun for the next phase.
  • 1770 to 1773. R2 dominates. The Boston Massacre index rises steeply and saturates; Colonial Propaganda accumulates from near zero to 2.7. Sentiment keeps accelerating even though Taxation on the Colonies is essentially flat near 0.95. Escalation has detached from tax rates entirely.
  • 1773 to 1776. R3 dominates and the run steepens sharply. The Boston Tea Party index crosses one in late 1773, the Intolerable Acts accumulate through 1774, and Intercolonial Coordination — which had crept from 0.13 to 0.88 over nineteen years — multiplies to 2.68 in the final two and a half. Accumulated Pressure adds more between 1773 and 1776 than in the previous nineteen years combined.

The answer to your question

Hostilities broke out because every British instrument for restoring order was an input to a loop that produced more disorder. Taxes levied to retire a war debt landed on colonists with no Representation in Parliament, so revenue collection generated grievance (R1). Troops sent to enforce those taxes generated the Boston Massacre, and the massacre was worth more to the colonists as Colonial Propaganda than the crowd was worth to Britain as a suppressed crowd (R2). Punishment aimed at one harbor after the Boston Tea Party — the Closure of the Port of Boston — was read by twelve other colonies as a precedent, and converted a local sanction into continental organization (R3).

The model does contain the intended deterrent, as Suppression Effect of the Intolerable Acts on Defiance. It is real but weak, and it is swamped: the same Intolerable Acts stock that damps defiance a little through suppression raises it far more through grievance and coordination. The backfire is a simulated outcome here, not a built-in assumption.

American Colonial Identity is what makes this irreversible. It is a slow stock, built by shared grievance and eroding over a generational time constant, and it rises from 0.20 to 2.00 across the run. Because it underwrites Intercolonial Coordination, the colonies retained the capacity to act jointly long after any particular tax was repealed. Britain could repeal a statute; it could not repeal the identity.

Model critique

Structurally sound: no errors, no unit warnings, every stock outflow is first-order so nothing goes negative, and the four historical episodes are endogenous consequences rather than dated inputs. Calibration is decent — the Boston Massacre index crosses one in late 1770, the Boston Tea Party index in late 1773, the Intolerable Acts accumulate through 1774, and pressure is steepest in 1775 to 1776.

Three honest limitations. The Boston Massacre index saturates at its curve ceiling from 1772 onward, so after that point the model represents continuous confrontation rather than a discrete event. The model has no strong balancing loop capable of arresting the escalation — no conciliation faction, no repeal politics beyond first-order tax lapse, so once R3 engages the outcome is foreordained; a Britain that backed down is not in the model boundary. And Representation in Parliament is a constant at zero rather than a policy lever, which forecloses the most interesting counterfactual.

Useful next steps: I can draw the causal loop diagram of these four loops, plot Accumulated Pressure Toward Armed Conflict with the dominant-loop periods shaded, or test the counterfactual of giving the colonies nonzero Representation in Parliament in 1765 to see whether R1 can be broken before R2 and R3 engage.
