variables.name: British War Debt from the French and Indian War
variables.documentation: Accumulated British debt from defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-63). It starts at zero in 1754, grows while the war is fought, and is slowly paid down out of colonial tax revenue. It is the exogenous trigger of the taxation spiral R1.

variables.name: War Spending on Colonial Defense
variables.documentation: Annual borrowing to pay for the French and Indian War. The STEP function switches spending off when the war ends - the only genuinely exogenous shock in the model.

variables.name: Annual War Spending on Colonial Defense
variables.documentation: Named constant for the yearly cost of the war effort in North America, borrowed by the Crown.

variables.name: Year the French and Indian War Ended
variables.documentation: The date the war ended (1763), after which Britain looked to the colonies to repay the debt. Used as the switch time in the STEP function.

variables.name: Debt Repayment from Colonial Taxation
variables.documentation: First order drain on the war debt: repayment is proportional to the debt still outstanding and to how heavily the colonies are taxed, divided by a repayment time constant. First order control guarantees the debt can never become negative.

variables.name: Debt Repayment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for paying off the war debt at reference levels of colonial taxation.

variables.name: Reference War Debt
variables.documentation: Scaling constant: the level of war debt that justifies, in British eyes, the full intended stamp duty. Used to normalise debt pressure.

variables.name: Stamp Act Tax Rate
variables.documentation: The indicated tax rate on legal documents, newspapers and playing cards (Stamp Act of 1765), generated endogenously by the size of the war debt rather than imposed by hand at a fixed date.

variables.name: Maximum Stamp Act Tax Rate
variables.documentation: The stamp duty rate index reached when the war debt equals the reference war debt.

variables.name: Taxation on the Colonies
variables.documentation: The accumulated burden of British taxes and their enforcement in the colonies. Modelled as a stock because statutes and customs machinery persist once enacted and are only gradually repealed or relaxed.

variables.name: Enactment of Taxes and Enforcement
variables.documentation: New taxes and tighter enforcement enacted by Parliament, driven both by fiscal need (the stamp duty implied by the debt) and by the wish to discipline a disorderly colony.

variables.name: Tax Enactment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for Parliament to legislate and staff up new taxation and enforcement.

variables.name: Repeal of Taxes
variables.documentation: First order relaxation and repeal of taxes (as with the repeal of the Stamp Act), proportional to the taxation currently in force, so taxation can never go negative.

variables.name: Tax Repeal Time
variables.documentation: Average time a tax measure stays on the books before being repealed or allowed to lapse.

variables.name: Reference Taxation Level
variables.documentation: Normalising constant for the taxation index, used when converting taxation into debt repayment capacity.

variables.name: Representation in Parliament
variables.documentation: Fraction of colonial interests actually represented by members of Parliament. Held at zero: the colonists had no representatives, which is precisely why taxation was felt as tyranny.

variables.name: Taxation without Representation
variables.documentation: The share of the tax burden imposed on colonists who have no voice in Parliament. This, not taxation as such, is what inflames sentiment.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Accumulated grievance and hostility toward British rule in the colonies. A stock because resentment builds up over years of taxes, bloodshed and coercive laws and fades only slowly.

variables.name: Initial Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Low background level of anti British feeling in 1754, while the colonies were still fighting alongside Britain.

variables.name: Growth of Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Grievance is generated by taxation without representation, by propaganda about bloodshed, and by the Intolerable Acts, and is amplified when the colonies are coordinating and sharing their outrage.

variables.name: Sentiment Gain from Taxation without Representation
variables.documentation: How much grievance a unit of unrepresented taxation generates per year.

variables.name: Sentiment Gain from Colonial Propaganda
variables.documentation: How much grievance a unit of circulating propaganda (engravings and pamphlets about the Boston Massacre) generates per year.

variables.name: Sentiment Gain from the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: How much grievance a unit of Intolerable Acts severity generates per year - the backfire channel of R4.

variables.name: Decay of Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: First order cooling of grievance as memories fade and grievances are settled; proportional to the sentiment stock so it can never drive it negative.

variables.name: Sentiment Decay Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which anti British feeling would fade if no new provocations occurred.

variables.name: Reference Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Normalising constant for the sentiment index.

variables.name: Colonial Acts of Defiance
variables.documentation: Rate of colonial resistance: boycotts, riots against stamp distributors, tarring, and the destruction of the tea. Driven by grievance, amplified by intercolonial coordination, and modestly damped by the coercive Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: Defiance Propensity
variables.documentation: Acts of defiance per year produced at reference grievance, reference coordination and no suppression.

variables.name: Reference Defiance Rate
variables.documentation: Normalising constant for the rate of defiance, used to form dimensionless ratios.

variables.name: Effect of Intercolonial Coordination on Defiance
variables.documentation: Nonlinear multiplier: committees of correspondence, non importation agreements and the Continental Congress make defiance far more effective and more likely. Normalised so reference coordination gives a multiplier of one.

variables.name: Effect of Intercolonial Coordination on Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Nonlinear multiplier by which shared newspapers, letters and congresses spread each grievance across all thirteen colonies. Passes through one at reference coordination.

variables.name: Suppression Effect of the Intolerable Acts on Defiance
variables.documentation: The intended deterrent effect of harsh laws: military government and a closed port do somewhat restrain open defiance. Deliberately weak so that the backfire in R4 is an outcome of the simulation rather than an assumption.

variables.name: Suppression Strength of the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Strength of the balancing deterrent channel of coercion. Small, reflecting that repression mainly enraged rather than cowed the colonists.

variables.name: British Perception of Colonial Disorder
variables.documentation: Whitehall's smoothed view of how disorderly the colonies are. A smoothing (moving average) of reported defiance is used because news crossed the Atlantic slowly and ministers judged on accumulated reports.

variables.name: British Perception Delay Time
variables.documentation: Averaging time for despatches, debate and decision in London.

variables.name: British Coercive Response
variables.documentation: The strength of Britain's disciplinary reaction: tighter taxes and enforcement plus more redcoats. Closes reinforcing loops R1 and R2.

variables.name: Coercion Strength
variables.documentation: How vigorously Britain responds to each unit of perceived colonial disorder.

variables.name: British Troops Stationed in the Colonies
variables.documentation: Redcoats quartered in the colonies to enforce taxes and coercive laws. A stock of soldiers, built by deployments and drained by rotations home.

variables.name: Troop Deployment to the Colonies
variables.documentation: Regiments sent to Boston and other ports as part of the coercive response.

variables.name: Troops Deployed per Unit Coercion
variables.documentation: Soldiers sent per year for each unit of coercive intent.

variables.name: Troop Withdrawal from the Colonies
variables.documentation: First order rotation and withdrawal of garrisons, proportional to the troops present so the garrison can never become negative.

variables.name: Troop Tour Duration
variables.documentation: Average length of a garrison posting before withdrawal.

variables.name: Reference Troop Level
variables.documentation: Normalising garrison size used to form dimensionless troop pressure. Set to the scale of the garrison actually quartered in the seaport towns, which is the level at which soldiers and crowds meet often enough for street confrontation.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Rate of street confrontations between soldiers and crowds. It takes both soldiers and defiant crowds, so the two influences multiply.

variables.name: Reference Violent Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Confrontation rate when garrison and defiance are both at reference levels.

variables.name: Boston Massacre
variables.documentation: Index of lethal confrontation of the kind that occurred in Boston in 1770, when soldiers fired on a crowd and killed five people. Modelled endogenously: once ordinary confrontations pass a threshold, shots being fired becomes very likely, hence the steep nonlinear curve.

variables.name: Threshold of Violent Incidents for a Deadly Clash
variables.documentation: Confrontation rate at which a massacre becomes the expected outcome; used to normalise the input to the massacre curve.

variables.name: Colonial Propaganda
variables.documentation: Stock of circulating pamphlets, sermons and engravings turning bloodshed into a case against British rule. A stock because printed material keeps working on opinion long after the event.

variables.name: Production of Colonial Propaganda
variables.documentation: Creation of propaganda out of each lethal incident - the massacre became the colonists' most powerful propaganda tool.

variables.name: Propaganda Generated per Deadly Clash
variables.documentation: Amount of propaganda material produced per unit of lethal incident.

variables.name: Decay of Colonial Propaganda
variables.documentation: First order loss of public attention to older propaganda, proportional to the stock so it can never go negative.

variables.name: Propaganda Attention Time
variables.documentation: Average time a piece of propaganda keeps influencing opinion.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party
variables.documentation: Index of mass destruction of property of the kind seen in Boston harbour in 1773. It emerges endogenously: only when ordinary defiance passes a threshold does resistance escalate into destroying the tea, so the curve is flat and then steep.

variables.name: Defiance Threshold for Destruction of the Tea
variables.documentation: Rate of defiance at which resistance tips over into destroying property outright; normalises the input to the tea party curve. Calibrated so the tea party index crosses one in 1773.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Severity of the harsh punitive laws the colonists called the Intolerable Acts, passed in 1774 to punish Massachusetts. A stock because statutes stay in force until relaxed.

variables.name: Enactment of the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Punitive legislation passed in direct response to the destruction of the tea.

variables.name: British Punitive Response Strength
variables.documentation: Severity of punitive law enacted per unit of destructive defiance.

variables.name: Relaxation of the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: First order relaxation of the punitive statutes, proportional to their current severity so severity can never become negative.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Relaxation Time
variables.documentation: Average time before punitive laws are softened or withdrawn - long, since Parliament refused to back down.

variables.name: Closure of the Port of Boston
variables.documentation: The most visible of the Intolerable Acts: the port of Boston shut until the colonists paid for the ruined tea. It threatened every colony's trade and so became the great spur to intercolonial cooperation.

variables.name: Port Closure Share of the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Share of the Intolerable Acts' severity represented by the closing of the port.

variables.name: American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Accumulated sense of being American rather than British. A slow moving stock: it is built by shared grievance and erodes only over a generation, which is what makes loop R3 so hard to reverse.

variables.name: Initial American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak sense of a distinct American identity in 1754.

variables.name: Formation of American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Shared grievance against Britain forges a common American self understanding.

variables.name: Identity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Identity built per year at reference levels of anti British sentiment.

variables.name: Erosion of American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Very slow first order fading of a distinct American identity, proportional to the stock so it can never go negative.

variables.name: Identity Erosion Time
variables.documentation: Generational time constant for identity to fade - deliberately long, since identity only slowly erodes.

variables.name: Reference American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Level of American identity that supports reference intercolonial coordination.

variables.name: Intercolonial Coordination
variables.documentation: Committees of correspondence, non importation associations and the Continental Congress. Grows with a shared American identity and jumps when the closure of the port of Boston shows every colony it could be next.

variables.name: Coordination Gain from the Closure of the Port of Boston
variables.documentation: Extra intercolonial coordination generated per unit of port closure - the backfire channel through which coercion unified the colonies.

variables.name: Risk of Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Output indicator of how close the colonies are to war: it needs the will to fight (grievance), the means to fight together (coordination) and an armed opponent in place (garrison).

variables.name: Weight of Anti British Sentiment in Risk
variables.documentation: Weight of grievance in the risk indicator.

variables.name: Weight of Intercolonial Coordination in Risk
variables.documentation: Weight of joint colonial organisation in the risk indicator.

variables.name: Weight of British Troops in Risk
variables.documentation: Weight of the size of the British garrison in the risk indicator.

variables.name: Accumulated Pressure Toward Armed Conflict
variables.documentation: The reservoir of unresolved conflict pressure that rises year after year until it discharges as open hostilities at Lexington and Concord. Reported as the model's main outcome.

variables.name: Pressure Buildup Toward Armed Conflict
variables.documentation: Yearly addition to conflict pressure from the prevailing risk of hostilities.

variables.name: Pressure Buildup per Unit Risk
variables.documentation: Conversion of risk into accumulated pressure per year.

variables.name: Pressure Dissipation
variables.documentation: First order release of pressure through petitions, negotiation and partial concessions; proportional to the stock, so pressure can never go negative.

variables.name: Pressure Dissipation Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for conciliation to bleed off accumulated pressure - slow relative to how fast pressure was building.

testParams.name: include a maximum number of feedback loops for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD from the background information. Let me first check the session state.

Empty model. I'll build the SFD directly from the supplied background material.

All stocks stay positive and behavior is decelerating growth — no runaway, no clamps. Now the loop analysis.

I built and simulated a quantitative SFD from your background material, then ran loop analysis on the results. Here is what it says about how road rage incidents change over time.

What the model contains

Four accumulations, everything else feeding them:

  • Recent Road Rage Incidents (incidents) — the circulating pool of aggressive driving acts other drivers are currently exposed to. Fills at the road rage incident rate, drains over a 6-month incident memory time.
  • Driver Stress and Anxiety (stress points) — fed by Traffic Congestion, Weather Driving Difficulty, Lack of Sleep and Perceived Provocations; recovers over 2 months.
  • Normalized Aggressive Driving (normalization points) — the Learned Behavior stock; observing aggression makes it seem normal. Decays over 10 months.
  • Traffic Congestion (vehicles) — clears in about half a month normally, slower when Road Design Adequacy is poor, when Weather Driving Difficulty is high, and when incidents themselves disrupt flow.

These converge on Anger and Aggression Propensity, a multiplicative index of Driver Stress and Anxiety, Frustration, Impatience, Normalized Aggressive Driving, Hostile and Competitive Personality Traits and Lack of Sleep. That index times a baseline rate gives the road rage incident rate.

Simulated behavior (run eval-run-1, 120 months)

Recent Road Rage Incidents rise from 400 to 2,077. The incident rate goes from 108 to 351 per month. Anger and Aggression Propensity roughly triples, 0.64 to 2.07. Critically, the trajectory decelerates — it is saturating growth, not an explosion. Driver Stress and Anxiety does most of its rising in the first year; Normalized Aggressive Driving is still climbing at month 120.

Four loops that explain it

The engine enumerated ten loops. Consolidated into the four stories that matter:

1. Rage breeds rage (reinforcing). An aggressive act is experienced by other drivers as Perceived Provocations — being cut off, tailgated, honked at. That raises Frustration and, over a couple of months, Driver Stress and Anxiety. Angrier, more stressed drivers commit more aggressive acts. This is the retaliation spiral and it paces the steep middle of the run.

2. Aggression becomes normal (reinforcing). Incidents feed Normalized Aggressive Driving. The more aggression people witness, the more it reads as ordinary driving, and the higher everyone's propensity. Because norms build and fade over ten months, this loop is quiet early and decisive late — it is the reason incidents keep creeping up after month 40 even though stress and congestion have flattened.

3. Rage jams the road (reinforcing). Incidents block lanes and cause near misses, lengthening Effective Clearing Time, so Traffic Congestion builds. Congestion then feeds Frustration, Impatience and stress accumulation, producing still more incidents. Poor Road Design Adequacy and adverse Weather Driving Difficulty amplify this loop by lengthening clearing time before any incident occurs.

4. Cooling off (balancing). Four self-correcting drains: queues clear, stress dissipates off the road, incidents fade from salience, aggressive norms erode with driver turnover. These are what stop the first three from running away, and their speed sets the ceiling.

Why it saturates rather than explodes

Each reinforcing loop closes through a stock that drains proportionally to its own size, while the reinforcing effects enter through fractional elasticities. The aggregate reinforcing gain sits below one, so the system approaches a finite equilibrium with substantial amplification rather than diverging. Seldon's estimate is total gain near 0.86 with roughly sevenfold steady-state amplification — note that is an analytic approximation from the equations, not an engine-computed dominance score. The practical implication stands regardless: the system is close to the threshold, so a modest worsening in any driver could tip it into genuine runaway growth.

Where the leverage is

Because everything is multiplied by that amplification factor, the useful question is not "how do we shave the incident rate once" but "how do we lower loop gain."

  • Lack of Sleep is the strongest lever in the model: it multiplies propensity directly and also feeds stress accumulation, so it enters two loops at once.
  • Road Design Adequacy is the best structural lever, because it divides Effective Clearing Time and therefore weakens the entire rage-jams-the-road loop at its narrowest point.
  • Tolerance for Delays divides Impatience outright.
  • Distracted Driving and Share of Drivers Running Late are real but weaker here — each is diluted inside a weighted index before being raised to a fractional elasticity.

Model critique

Structurally sound: all four stocks have first-order control on their outflows and none goes negative; no MIN/MAX clamps; no empirical constants buried in equations. Limitations worth naming: traffic demand is exogenous, so there is no congestion-suppresses-travel feedback; there is no enforcement, licensing or social-sanction balancing loop, because your background material does not mention one — which is precisely why the model shows growth with no policy brake; and Hostile and Competitive Personality Traits is held constant rather than modeled as a changing population composition.

Useful next steps: a sensitivity analysis over Lack of Sleep, Road Design Adequacy and Distracted Driving, or a policy run testing whether improving road design alone can break the congestion spiral. I can also plot the trajectories with dominant-loop shading if you want to see the phase handoff visually.

variables.name: Recent Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The circulating pool of aggressive driving behaviour caused by anger and frustration that other drivers are currently exposed to and remember. It accumulates new incidents and drains as incidents fade from public exposure and memory. Started well below its long run equilibrium so the base run shows growth.

variables.name: initial recent incidents
variables.documentation: Initial size of the circulating pool of road rage incidents at time zero, set below equilibrium so the reinforcing loops can be seen growing.

variables.name: road rage incident rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents occur. Equal to the baseline rate that would occur if every driver condition were normal, scaled by the overall anger and aggression propensity of the driving population.

variables.name: baseline incident rate
variables.documentation: Incidents per month that would occur when all psychological, situational and environmental conditions are at their normal reference values (propensity equal to one).

variables.name: road rage incident fading rate
variables.documentation: First order drain of the incident pool: incidents stop being salient to other drivers after an average memory time. A first order drain guarantees the stock can never become negative.

variables.name: incident memory time
variables.documentation: Average time an incident stays salient in the driving population before it stops provoking or teaching other drivers.

variables.name: Driver Stress and Anxiety
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress and anxiety carried by the driving population. High stress makes drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions.

variables.name: initial driver stress
variables.documentation: Stress level of the driving population at time zero, set below its equilibrium value.

variables.name: stress accumulation rate
variables.equation: baseline_stressor_exposure * (congestion_stress_weight * (Traffic_Congestion / reference_congestion) + weather_stress_weight * Weather_Driving_Difficulty + sleep_stress_weight * Lack_of_Sleep + provocation_stress_weight * Perceived_Provocations)
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions add stress. It is the baseline stressor exposure scaled by a weighted index of congestion, adverse weather, fatigue and perceived provocations. The weights sum to one so that at reference conditions the index equals one.

variables.name: baseline stressor exposure
variables.documentation: Stress points added per month when all driving stressors are at their normal reference values.

variables.name: congestion stress weight
variables.documentation: Share of routine stress exposure attributable to traffic congestion.

variables.name: weather stress weight
variables.documentation: Share of routine stress exposure attributable to adverse weather driving difficulty.

variables.name: sleep stress weight
variables.documentation: Share of routine stress exposure attributable to driver fatigue and lack of sleep.

variables.name: provocation stress weight
variables.documentation: Share of routine stress exposure attributable to perceived provocations from other drivers.

variables.name: stress recovery rate
variables.documentation: First order recovery from stress once drivers are off the road. Balancing loop B1: the more stress accumulated, the faster it dissipates, which limits growth and keeps the stock non negative.

variables.name: stress recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated driving stress to dissipate.

variables.name: reference stress level
variables.documentation: Normal level of driver stress used to normalize the stress term in the anger propensity index.

variables.name: Normalized Aggressive Driving
variables.documentation: The learned behaviour stock: the degree to which observing aggressive driving from others has made such behaviour seem normal and acceptable.

variables.name: initial normalized aggression
variables.documentation: Degree of social normalization of aggressive driving at time zero, below the reference level.

variables.name: aggression normalization rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which observed aggressive driving teaches other drivers that aggression is normal. Proportional to the pool of incidents currently being observed.

variables.name: normalization strength from observed aggression
variables.documentation: Normalization points added per observed incident per month; how strongly witnessing aggression teaches imitation.

variables.name: aggression norm decay rate
variables.documentation: First order forgetting of learned aggressive norms as drivers turn over and as aggression stops being observed. Keeps the stock non negative.

variables.name: aggression norm decay time
variables.documentation: Average time for learned aggressive driving norms to fade in the absence of new observed aggression.

variables.name: reference normalization level
variables.documentation: Normal level of social normalization of aggressive driving, used to normalize this term in the anger propensity index.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Vehicles currently queued in the road network. Heavy traffic, delays and stop and go conditions raise stress and impatience.

variables.name: initial traffic congestion
variables.documentation: Vehicles on the congested network at time zero.

variables.name: vehicle entry rate
variables.documentation: Exogenous traffic demand: vehicles entering the congested network each month.

variables.name: base traffic demand
variables.documentation: Exogenous monthly travel demand entering the network.

variables.name: traffic clearing rate
variables.documentation: First order clearing of queued vehicles. Balancing loop B2: more congestion means more vehicles clearing per month, which prevents unbounded congestion and keeps the stock non negative.

variables.name: Effective Clearing Time
variables.documentation: Actual time needed to clear the queue. Lengthened by incident disruption and adverse weather, shortened by adequate road design (wide lanes, clear intersections).

variables.name: normal clearing time
variables.documentation: Time to clear the vehicle queue under normal weather, normal road design and no incident disruption.

variables.name: reference congestion
variables.documentation: Normal congestion level used to normalize the congestion terms in the frustration, impatience and stress formulations.

variables.name: Incident Disruption Multiplier
variables.documentation: Road rage incidents themselves block lanes, cause near misses and collisions, and so lengthen the effective clearing time. Equals one when incidents are at their reference level.

variables.name: incident disruption sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly a proportional rise in incidents lengthens the time needed to clear traffic.

variables.name: Road Design Adequacy
variables.documentation: Quality of road design relative to normal. Values below one represent poor design such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, which slows clearing and worsens congestion.

variables.name: Weather Driving Difficulty
variables.documentation: Difficulty of driving conditions from weather such as heavy rain or snow relative to normal. Values above one slow traffic clearing and add stress.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Index of how often drivers feel cut off, tailgated or honked at. Rises with the circulating pool of incidents relative to a reference level and with the prevalence of distracted driving. Weights sum to one so the index is one at reference conditions.

variables.name: incident provocation weight
variables.documentation: Share of perceived provocation explained by exposure to recent road rage incidents.

variables.name: distraction provocation weight
variables.documentation: Share of perceived provocation explained by distracted driving such as phone use, texting or eating.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Prevalence of phone use, texting and eating while driving relative to normal. Raises near misses and therefore perceived provocation.

variables.name: reference incident level
variables.documentation: Normal size of the circulating incident pool, used to normalize provocation and disruption indices.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Index of feeling blocked or wronged by other drivers. Rises with perceived provocations and with congestion relative to its reference level. Weights sum to one so the index is one at reference conditions.

variables.name: frustration weight provocations
variables.documentation: Share of frustration explained by perceived provocations from other drivers.

variables.name: frustration weight congestion
variables.documentation: Share of frustration explained by being blocked in heavy traffic.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Index of driver impatience. Rises with congestion (delays and stop and go conditions) and with the share of drivers running late, and falls when drivers have a higher tolerance for delays.

variables.name: impatience weight congestion
variables.documentation: Share of impatience explained by traffic delays.

variables.name: impatience weight lateness
variables.documentation: Share of impatience explained by drivers being under time pressure.

variables.name: Share of Drivers Running Late
variables.documentation: Fraction of trips made by drivers who are running late and therefore have little slack for delays.

variables.name: reference share running late
variables.documentation: Normal fraction of trips made under time pressure, used to normalize the lateness term.

variables.name: Tolerance for Delays
variables.documentation: Willingness of drivers to accept delays relative to normal. Higher tolerance damps impatience for the same amount of delay.

variables.name: Hostile and Competitive Personality Traits
variables.documentation: Prevalence of impulsive, hostile and competitive drivers in the population relative to normal. Acts as a direct multiplier on the propensity to translate anger into aggressive acts.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Driver fatigue relative to normal. Fatigue impairs judgement and enters as an anger susceptibility multiplier, and also adds directly to stress accumulation.

variables.name: Anger and Aggression Propensity
variables.documentation: Multiplicative index of how likely an average driving hour is to produce an aggressive act. Combines stress, frustration, impatience, learned normalization, hostile personality prevalence and fatigue. Each normalized term equals one at reference conditions, so the whole index equals one when everything is normal.

variables.name: stress elasticity
variables.documentation: Strength with which relative driver stress raises the propensity for aggression.

variables.name: frustration elasticity
variables.documentation: Strength with which relative frustration raises the propensity for aggression.

variables.name: impatience elasticity
variables.documentation: Strength with which relative impatience raises the propensity for aggression.

variables.name: normalization elasticity
variables.documentation: Strength with which the social normalization of aggressive driving raises the propensity for aggression.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a compact quantitative SD model of the escalation, then run it and use the engine's feedback-loop analysis to ground the explanation.

The CLD renderer is failing on an environment-side API configuration error (temperature/thinking mismatch), so I'll give you the structure in prose. Everything below comes from the built and simulated model.

The model (5 variables, 1765-1775)

Variable Type Equation
American Identity and Anti British Sentiment stock, dmnl, init 1 accumulates Boston Tea Party Defiance
Boston Tea Party Defiance inflow, 1/Year Identity × Taxation / (1 + British Coercion)
Taxation aux, 1/Year French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand × British Coercion
British Coercion from the Boston Massacre and the Intolerable Acts aux, dmnl = American Identity and Anti British Sentiment
French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand constant, 1/Year 0.2

No errors, no unit warnings. The stock has an inflow only and is uniflow, so it cannot go negative. Extreme-condition check: set the repayment demand to zero and Taxation, Defiance and all growth go to zero — nothing revolts spontaneously, which is the correct boundary behavior.

Simulated behavior (run eval-run-1): the identity stock climbs monotonically with an accelerating slope, 1.00 to 3.53. Defiance goes 0.10 to 0.55 per year, Taxation 0.20 to 0.71 per year, Coercion 1.00 to 3.53. Nothing settles.

The three loops the engine found

R1 — Defiance breeds identity (reinforcing). Identity → Boston Tea Party Defiance (+) → Identity (+). Each open act of resistance deepens the shared sense of being American and being wronged, which makes the next act easier. This is the engine of the whole story, and the reason "colonial identity" belongs in the causal explanation rather than in the background.

R2 — Coercion enforces taxation, taxation provokes defiance (reinforcing). Identity → British Coercion (+) → Taxation (+) → Defiance (+) → Identity (+). Britain answers colonial assertiveness with troops and punitive law, and those are the very instruments that press and enforce the revenue demand. The heavier tax then supplies the grievance the next act of defiance targets. The Boston Massacre and the Intolerable Acts sit on this loop not as independent causes but as the coercion side of it firing.

B1 — Coercion suppresses open defiance (balancing). Identity → Coercion (+) → Defiance (−) → Identity (+). Troops in Boston and the closed port genuinely did remove opportunities for open defiance.

Why war, and not a settlement

Collapse the model to the single state S (identity), since Coercion = S and Taxation = 0.2·S:

dS/dt = 0.2 · S² / (1 + S)

Attributing marginal gain to each loop, the reinforcing pair R1 + R2 holds 72 to 80 percent of total loop gain across the entire decade — 80 percent in 1765, still 72 percent in 1775. B1 gains share only slowly, 20 to 28 percent, and never comes close to 50. There is no dominance shift anywhere in the run. The system was in the same regime in 1765 as in 1775.

The reason B1 can never win is structural. Coercion enters defiance as 1/(1 + C), a diminishing-returns suppressor whose elasticity asymptotes at −1. But coercion also multiplies taxation, and that channel has constant elasticity +1, undiminished. So repression buys a fraction of a unit of quiet and delivers a full unit of grievance. Net loop gain stays positive at all times.

This is Escalation welded to Fixes that Fail. Coercion is the short-term fix; its unintended consequence — enforced taxation, martyrs, propaganda — strengthens exactly the thing it was meant to put down.

The second structural fact is what is absent: the identity stock has no outflow. There is no reconciliation, no redress, no forgetting. Sentiment can only accumulate. That asymmetry, more than any single event, is what makes hostilities the terminal state.

What this implies about causes

dS/dt is positive for every S > 0; the only equilibrium is S = 0 and it is unstable. So in this formulation there is no point of no return after 1765 — the commitment was made when Parliament decided the colonies would repay the French and Indian War debt. 1770 and 1773 look like turning points because the growth is quadratic in S at low levels and therefore invisible early. They are symptoms of loop dominance, not causes.

Ranked leverage, if the goal was to avoid war:

  1. Zero the French and Indian War Debt Repayment Demand. The inflow is strictly proportional to it, so this alone flatlines the entire system. No loop is ever energized.
  2. Cut the Coercion → Taxation link: raise revenue by consent and representation rather than by enforcement. Removes roughly 36-40 percent of driving gain.
  3. Restrain coercion alone (no troops, repeal the Intolerable Acts). Not sufficient — R1 survives and still gives pure exponential growth with about a seven-year doubling time. Restraint without addressing revenue only delays war.
  4. Create an outflow from the identity stock — genuine grievance redress. This is the only lever that can drain accumulated sentiment rather than merely slow its growth, and its absence is precisely why this structure has no stabilizing mechanism.

Where I would push back on the model

The "war was structurally inevitable" conclusion is a property of this five-variable boundary. There is no grievance-resolution outflow, taxation is unsaturated, and there is no British political feedback (Parliament responding to lost trade or the cost of occupation). If you want to stress this, the two tests worth running are: add a redress outflow, and add a saturating ceiling on taxation — then see whether B1 can ever be made to take dominance. Want me to run either, or plot the run with dominant-loop shading?

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

The generator produced an incomplete model — only the stock exists, with no flows. Let me check the rest and then repair it.

Specs are correct, but the variable set and relationships are essentially empty. Let me load the editing tools.

No edit_variables tool is registered in this session. Let me retry generation with a more compact prompt — the previous failure looks like truncation.

Now let me verify what was actually built.

Structure is now complete. Let me check relationships and run the model.

Structure and relationships are complete, with no errors or unit warnings reported. Running the simulation.

Variable names need the underscore form used in the model.

Behavior is S-shaped growth to a plateau (200 → 488 incidents), nothing goes negative, and inflow converges to outflow. Now the feedback analysis, which I need before I can say anything about loops.

Exactly 4 loops confirmed by the engine. Let me get the expert analysis.

The model

I built a stock and flow model held to your limits: 5 concept variables and exactly 4 feedback loops (the engine confirmed 4 loops, no more). The two flows are structurally required by the stock, and nine named constants hold the parameters, since the equations may not contain hard-coded values.

Stock: Road Rage Incidents (incidents) — the prevailing level of recent aggressive driving in society, accumulating via road rage incident rate and draining via road rage cooling rate (first-order, stock / persistence time, so it cannot go negative).

Auxiliaries: Traffic Congestion, Driver Stress and Anxiety, Perceived Provocations, Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior — all dimensionless indices equal to 1 under normal conditions, multiplying into the inflow.

The exogenous triggers from your background enter as constants rather than as loop variables: poor road design and adverse weather set baseline congestion from road design and weather; impulsive/hostile/competitive personality traits, lack of sleep and distracted driving set driver impulsivity and fatigue.

The four loops (engine-confirmed)

  • L1 reinforcing — congestion/stress: Road Rage Incidents → Traffic Congestion (+) → Driver Stress and Anxiety (+) → incident rate (+) → Road Rage Incidents
  • L2 reinforcing — social learning: Road Rage Incidents → Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior (+) → incident rate (+) → Road Rage Incidents
  • L3 reinforcing — provocation/retaliation: Road Rage Incidents → Perceived Provocations (+) → incident rate (+) → Road Rage Incidents
  • L4 balancing — cooling off: Road Rage Incidents → road rage cooling rate (+) → Road Rage Incidents (−)

What the simulation actually did

Road Rage Incidents rise from 200 to 488 and plateau; incident rate 177 → 244 per month; cooling rate 100 → 244, converging exactly on the inflow. Most movement happens in the first 10 months, equilibrium by roughly month 20. This is limits to growth, not runaway escalation.

Feedback explanation of how road rage changes over time

Early on, the three reinforcing loops dominate. Each incident feeds back three ways at once: it normalizes aggressive driving for everyone who observes it (L2), it adds stop-and-go delay that raises stress and impatience (L1), and it means more drivers get cut off, tailgated or honked at, provoking retaliation (L3). Inflow exceeds outflow and incidents compound.

Dominance then hands over to the balancing loop. The three reinforcing effects saturate — their marginal strength falls toward zero as incidents rise — while cooling off stays linear in the stock and keeps gaining strength proportionally. Around month 20 the outflow catches the inflow and L4 holds the system steady.

The crucial result: the plateau is high, not a return to baseline. The reinforcing loops do not switch off at equilibrium, they merely stop growing, leaving the multipliers permanently elevated (1.33 × 1.275 × 1.44 ≈ 2.44). Equilibrium is inflow × persistence time = 244 × 2 = 488 incidents, roughly 2.4 times the starting level. Road rage becomes self-sustaining at a worse new normal. The balancing loop caps the problem; it never undoes it.

Leverage. L2, learned aggressive behavior, carries the largest multiplier and the highest sensitivity, making normalization the strongest intervention point. L1 is second and has the advantage of being attackable from outside the loop, by reducing baseline congestion through road design, or by reducing driver impulsivity, fatigue and distraction — both scale the entire inflow. Because the stock has a two-month persistence time, any intervention takes months to register.

Critique

Structurally the model is sound: polarities are consistent, the stock has proper first-order outflow control with no MIN/MAX clamps, units are dimensionally consistent with no engine unit warnings, and inflow converges on outflow as conservation requires. Two honest limitations: the leverage ranking is driven entirely by the assumed sensitivity parameters (0.8, 0.6, 0.5) and the shared half-saturation of 400, which are illustrative rather than estimated; and the five-variable ceiling forced personality traits, sleep and distraction into a single constant rather than giving them their own dynamics.

Worth doing next: a sensitivity analysis on the three sensitivity parameters and the half-saturation level to test whether L2 really is the dominant leverage point, and a plot of Road Rage Incidents with dominant-loop bands overlaid to see the handover visually.

supportingInfo.explanation:
No edit tools registered in this session, so I'll use the documented update_model workflow (edit session file, then push). Three structural defects to fix: the Boston Tea Party never fires, the Intolerable Acts are therefore dead structure, and militia arms before any grievance exists.

Tea Party now fires endogenously in 1773, but as a slow trickle rather than a discrete event, and the garrison implausibly collapses to 85 during the war. Two more fixes:

Behavior now fits the reference mode: taxation begins 1765, the Boston Massacre fires in 1770, grievance plateaus during the quiet years 1771-72, the Boston Tea Party occurs endogenously in 1773, the Intolerable Acts follow, and hostilities crosses 1 in early 1775. No stock goes negative. Now the loop analysis.

71 loops confirmed. Consulting Seldon on dominance and structural critique.

Seldon identified real defects. Applying the five substantive fixes — identity floor, the missing garrison-cost loop, direct occupation grievance, a stronger repression test, and a finer DT.

Occupation grievance is firing from 1754, which wrongly starts the revolution during the French and Indian War. The grievance is about the peacetime army quartered after 1763, not the ordinary garrison.

Timing is now historically accurate — Tea Party at end of 1773, Intolerable Acts through 1774. One last calibration on the readiness normalization so the hostilities index crosses unity at Lexington and Concord rather than a year early.

Excellent reference-mode fit: quiescent to 1765, Stamp Act ignition, Massacre pulse in 1770, grievance plateau 1771-72, Tea Party firing endogenously in late 1773, Intolerable Acts through 1774, and hostilities crossing unity in spring 1775. Refreshing the loop analysis on the final run.

The causal-loop rendering tool is returning a server-side configuration error (temperature may only be set to 1 when thinking is enabled) on every call — that's a fault in the drawing service, not in the loop specification. I'll give you the structure in prose instead.

The model

Eight stocks, 98 variables, simulated 1754-1776 at DT 0.03125:

Stock Units Role
French and Indian War Debt pounds Fills 1754-63, then Britain wants it repaid
Colonial Taxation pounds/year Zero until the Stamp Act year, 1765
Colonial Grievance grievance Memory of taxation without representation, the Massacre, the Acts, occupation
American Identity identity Being American rather than British
British Troops in the Colonies troops The garrison
Colonial Defiance defiance Boycotts, non-importation, committees of correspondence
Intolerable Acts Severity acts Coercive legislation, including closing the port of Boston
Colonial Militia Readiness militia Minutemen, drilling, powder

The Boston Tea Party is not scheduled by date — it fires when Colonial Defiance crosses a threshold, and it self-limits once the 342 chests are gone. The run produces it in late 1773, the Intolerable Acts through 1774, and the hostilities index crossing unity in spring 1775.

The feedback explanation

The engine found 104 loops. Ten carry the story.

R1 — the fiscal-military trap. British Troops in the Colonies → cost of garrisoning the colonies → debt pressure to tax the colonies → Colonial Taxation → Colonial Grievance → Colonial Defiance → more troops. This is the deep irony of the period: the army sent to control the colonies is the expense that justifies taxing them.

R2 — grievance forges identity, identity sharpens grievance. Colonial Grievance → American Identity → grievance sensitivity → Colonial Grievance. A fixed tax does not produce fixed anger. The more colonists thought of themselves as Americans, the more each shilling of stamp duty insulted them.

R3 — acting together makes Americans. American Identity → Colonial Defiance → American Identity. Boycotting is the manufacturing process for the shared political self that sustains the next boycott.

R4 — Boston Massacre propaganda. Colonial Defiance → British Troops in the Colonies → Boston Massacre casualties → Colonial Grievance → Colonial Defiance. Five deaths, converted by engravings and orations into a permanent step increase in the grievance stock. In the run, grievance jumps from 86 to 128 across 1770-71.

R5 — Tea Party to Intolerable Acts. Colonial Defiance → Boston Tea Party → Intolerable Acts Severity → Colonial Grievance → Colonial Defiance. Punishing one town radicalised all thirteen. The coercive relaxation time is ten years, which is exactly why one night in Boston harbour became a permanent grievance.

R6 — the arms race. British Troops in the Colonies → Colonial Militia Readiness → British perception of colonial defiance → more troops. This loop needs no tax, no statute and no martyr to keep turning, and it dominates the final years.

R7 — occupation breeds resistance. Troops → grievance at quartering → defiance → more troops. Reinforcing a garrison to restore order enlarged the disorder it was sent to suppress.

Against these, three balancing loops — and each fails in a different, instructive way:

B1 — boycott forces repeal. Defiance made taxes uncollectable and forced repeal, which genuinely bent Colonial Taxation downward. But grievance is a stock: repealing the tax does not refund the anger already banked.

B2 — repression. Troops suppressed visible defiance, and you can see it working — defiance decelerates and tops out near 76 while militia readiness multiplies past 25,000. It succeeded at what it measured and failed at what mattered. It also has a perverse arm: quieting protest removes the very pressure that had been producing repeals.

B3 — debt relief. Revenue was supposed to retire the war debt and end the need for taxes. Peak collection was about £173,000 a year against a £90,000,000 debt. Over twenty-two years the debt falls by under 1 percent. This loop is arithmetically dead — which means fiscal pressure was effectively permanent.

The answer to your question

Hostilities broke out because dominance relayed between reinforcing loops while every restraint acted too slowly or on the wrong variable. Taxation opened the sequence in 1765; the Massacre added a permanent step in 1770; repeal and fading anger produced a genuine lull in 1771-72 (visible in the run as a flattening of grievance growth); the Tea Party and Intolerable Acts destroyed that lull in 1773-74; and by 1775 the arms race had become self-sustaining and needed no fresh grievance at all. The tea channel saturates and coercive severity levels off — but the military loops keep growing, which is why the crisis ended in arms rather than settlement.

The highest-leverage intervention Seldon identified is not repealing taxes but not garrisoning in response to political defiance — because troop presence feeds R1, R4, R6 and R7 simultaneously, and hostilities is the product of militia and troops. The second is timing: because the state lives in stocks with 5-10 year decay times, the same concession in 1765 is worth far more than in 1774. By then grievance and identity were already accumulated, and nothing in the structure reverses them.

Caveats worth knowing

  • The Boston Massacre is date-gated to 1770 and conditional on troops being present, so it is a triggered event, not a fully endogenous one. Its consequences are endogenous.
  • The hostilities index has no outbound links — the model explains the build-up to first blood, not the war that followed.
  • Repression gain was deliberately set high (1.5) to give the balancing loop a fair chance; escalation survives it, so the outbreak is structural rather than a parameterisation artefact.
  • The engine reported no unit warnings.

I'd suggest next either a sensitivity analysis on the identity gains and repression gain, or a set of counterfactual policy runs — no Intolerable Acts, colonial representation in Parliament, or no reinforcement after 1768 — to see which one actually averts 1775.

variables.name: French and Indian War Debt
inflows: war borrowing from the French and Indian War
variables.documentation: Accumulated British national debt incurred defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-1763). Starts at zero in 1754 and accumulates war borrowing; it is drawn down only by revenue actually collected from the colonies. It is the ultimate driver of British fiscal pressure to tax America.

variables.name: war borrowing from the French and Indian War
variables.documentation: Borrowing to finance the war, active only during the war years as determined by the time switch built from the named war start year and war end year parameters.

variables.name: debt repayment from colonial taxation
variables.documentation: Retirement of war debt out of revenue actually collected in America. The MIN with a first-order drain on the remaining debt guarantees the debt stock can never be driven below zero.

variables.name: Colonial Taxation
variables.documentation: The standing annual level of taxes Parliament imposes on the colonies, beginning with the Stamp Act of 1765 (stamp duties on legal documents, newspapers and playing cards) and continuing with later duties. Zero before 1765.

variables.name: new tax impositions
variables.documentation: Rate at which Parliament legislates new taxes. Gated to zero before the named Stamp Act year and thereafter proportional to the fiscal pressure created by the war debt.

variables.name: tax repeals
variables.documentation: First-order repeal of standing taxes (as with the Stamp Act repeal and the partial Townshend repeal), amplified when colonial defiance makes a tax unenforceable.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial anger at taxation without representation, at the Boston Massacre, and at the Intolerable Acts. It is a memory stock: grievances persist and compound rather than resetting each year.

variables.name: grievance accumulation
variables.documentation: Total rate at which new grievance is generated, summing taxation without representation, the Boston Massacre, the Intolerable Acts, and the standing military occupation.

variables.name: grievance fading
variables.documentation: First-order fading of anger over time when no new provocations occur, so grievance can never go negative.

variables.name: American Identity
variables.documentation: The distinct colonial sense of being American rather than British subjects. Begins small in 1754 and is built up by shared grievance and by acting together in defiance.

variables.name: identity formation
variables.documentation: Formation of a common American identity from ordinary shared colonial experience, from shared suffering (grievance), and from shared collective action (defiance such as boycotts and committees of correspondence). The baseline term prevents identity from decaying to nothing during the quiet pre-1765 years.

variables.name: identity erosion
variables.documentation: Slow first-order fading of distinct identity in the absence of reinforcing experience.

variables.name: British Troops in the Colonies
variables.documentation: Regular British soldiers stationed in America (the garrison left after 1763 and the later Boston quartering). Their presence is what makes an incident like the Boston Massacre possible.

variables.name: troop deployment
variables.documentation: Rate of sending regiments to America. A standing peacetime garrison is continually replaced as tours end, and reinforcements above that are sent in proportion to how defiant London perceives the colonies to be.

variables.name: troop withdrawal
variables.documentation: First-order rotation and withdrawal of the garrison, guaranteeing troop numbers stay non-negative.

variables.name: Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: The standing level of organized resistance: boycotts, non-importation agreements, the Boston Tea Party, and the committees of correspondence.

variables.name: defiance mobilization
variables.documentation: Rate at which colonists organize resistance, driven by accumulated grievance and multiplied by the strength of American identity, which makes joint action possible.

variables.name: defiance demobilization
variables.documentation: First-order decay of organized resistance as boycotts lapse, accelerated by the repressive effect of the troop presence.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Severity
variables.documentation: Accumulated coercive legislation the colonists called the Intolerable Acts, including closing the port of Boston until the ruined tea was paid for.

variables.name: coercive legislation
variables.documentation: Passage of punitive laws. Driven mainly by the burst of tea destruction in the Boston Tea Party - the direct provocation for closing the port of Boston until the ruined tea was paid for - and secondarily by standing defiance above London's tolerance threshold.

variables.name: coercive relaxation
variables.documentation: Slow first-order lapse or softening of coercive statutes.

variables.name: Colonial Militia Readiness
variables.documentation: Armed colonial preparation: minutemen, drilling, stockpiling of powder and arms.

variables.name: militia mobilization
variables.documentation: Rate of arming and drilling. Requires accumulated grievance - colonists do not arm against their own government without cause - and then scales with American identity, with the severity of the Intolerable Acts, and with the size of the British garrison.

variables.name: militia demobilization
variables.documentation: First-order lapse of armed readiness when men return to farms, keeping readiness non-negative.

variables.name: war time switch
variables.documentation: Dimensionless switch equal to one only between the named war start year and war end year, turning war borrowing on and off.

variables.name: war start year
variables.documentation: Year the French and Indian War began.

variables.name: war end year
variables.documentation: Year the French and Indian War ended.

variables.name: war borrowing rate
variables.documentation: Annual borrowing to finance the war while it lasts.

variables.name: reference debt
variables.documentation: Scale of debt at which British fiscal pressure to tax America is considered normal (index of one).

variables.name: minimum debt repayment time
variables.documentation: Shortest time in which the remaining debt could physically be paid off, used to keep the debt stock non-negative.

variables.name: fraction of revenue to debt repayment
variables.documentation: Share of colonial revenue actually applied to retiring war debt rather than to current administration.

variables.name: debt pressure to tax the colonies
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of how strongly British finances push Parliament to raise revenue in America. Combines the inherited French and Indian War Debt with the recurring cost of the garrison now stationed in the colonies.

variables.name: Stamp Act switch
variables.documentation: Dimensionless gate that is zero before the named Stamp Act year and one thereafter, so no colonial taxation exists before 1765.

variables.name: Stamp Act year
variables.documentation: Year of the Stamp Act, the first direct internal tax on the colonies.

variables.name: tax imposition responsiveness
variables.documentation: How much new annual taxation Parliament legislates per year for each unit of debt pressure.

variables.name: fractional repeal rate
variables.documentation: Baseline fraction of standing taxes repealed per year.

variables.name: repeal amplification from defiance
variables.documentation: Multiplier greater than one showing that boycotts and non-importation make taxes uncollectable and force repeal faster.

variables.name: repeal gain from defiance
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of the repeal rate to normalized colonial defiance.

variables.name: reference tax level
variables.documentation: Level of annual colonial taxation regarded as the normal reference for judging the burden.

variables.name: taxation without representation grievance
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of the perceived injustice of being taxed by a Parliament in which the colonies have no representatives; it scales with the standing tax burden.

variables.name: grievance generation rate from taxation
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per year at the normal reference level of unrepresented taxation.

variables.name: grievance from taxation without representation
variables.documentation: Annual grievance produced by unrepresented taxation, amplified by how strongly colonists already see themselves as Americans with rights.

variables.name: grievance sensitivity from identity
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing that a stronger American identity makes every British action feel more offensive. Closes the grievance-identity reinforcing loop.

variables.name: identity grievance sensitivity gain

variables.name: reference identity
variables.documentation: Level of American identity treated as normal for normalization.

variables.name: reference grievance

variables.name: reference defiance
variables.documentation: Level of organized colonial defiance treated as normal for normalization.

variables.name: grievance decay time

variables.name: Boston Massacre year

variables.name: Boston Massacre event duration

variables.name: Boston Massacre casualties

variables.name: propaganda effect per casualty

variables.name: Boston Massacre propaganda effect

variables.name: grievance from the Boston Massacre
variables.documentation: Contribution of the massacre to grievance accumulation, amplified by existing American identity.

variables.name: grievance per coercive act
variables.documentation: Anger generated per year by each unit of coercive legislation such as closing the port of Boston.

variables.name: grievance from the Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Contribution of the Intolerable Acts to grievance accumulation, closing the coercion-grievance reinforcing loop.

variables.name: identity formation rate
variables.documentation: Identity created per year per unit of normalized shared grievance or shared defiance.

variables.name: identity decay time
variables.documentation: Average time over which a distinct American self-conception would fade without reinforcement.

variables.name: identity effect on mobilization
variables.documentation: Multiplier by which a shared American identity makes intercolonial organizing (committees of correspondence, congresses) easier.

variables.name: identity mobilization gain
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of defiance mobilization to normalized American identity.

variables.name: defiance mobilization rate
variables.documentation: Defiance organized per year at normal grievance and normal identity.

variables.name: defiance decay time
variables.documentation: Average time over which boycotts and associations lapse without renewal.

variables.name: repression effect on defiance
variables.documentation: Multiplier greater than one by which the garrison suppresses open resistance, closing the balancing repression loop.

variables.name: repression gain
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of defiance demobilization to the normalized size of the British garrison. Set deliberately high so the balancing repression loop is given a genuine chance to contain the escalation.

variables.name: reference troop level
variables.documentation: Garrison size treated as normal for normalization.

variables.name: reference militia
variables.documentation: Level of armed colonial readiness across all the colonies treated as normal for normalization. Calibrated so the hostilities index reaches one at the point armed conflict actually broke out in spring 1775.

variables.name: militia weight in perception
variables.documentation: Weight London gives to colonial arming, relative to political defiance, when judging the state of the colonies.

variables.name: British perception of colonial defiance
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of how rebellious London believes the colonies to be, based on organized resistance and on visible arming. Drives troop deployment and hence the arms race.

variables.name: normal troop deployment rate
variables.documentation: Troops sent per year when perceived defiance is at its normal index of one.

variables.name: troop withdrawal time
variables.documentation: Average tour length before regiments are rotated home.

variables.name: tea party defiance threshold
variables.documentation: Level of organized defiance above which resistance escalates from boycott to the open destruction of property. Calibrated so the Boston Tea Party emerges endogenously in 1773 rather than being imposed by date.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party
variables.documentation: Discrete switch: once organized defiance crosses the property-destruction threshold, resistance escalates from boycott to throwing the tea into Boston harbour. Zero before the threshold is crossed, one after.

variables.name: tea per tea party event
variables.documentation: Chests of tea destroyed in a full Boston Tea Party.

variables.name: tea destroyed by the Boston Tea Party
inflows: tea destruction in the Boston Tea Party
variables.documentation: Chests of tea actually thrown into Boston harbour and ruined - the tea Parliament demanded the colonists pay for, closing the port of Boston until they did. As a stock it fills once and then stops, so the Boston Tea Party is a single historical event rather than a permanent condition.

variables.name: reference tea destruction rate
variables.documentation: Rate of tea destruction corresponding to a full Boston Tea Party, used to normalize that provocation to an index of one.

variables.name: British tolerance threshold
variables.documentation: Named level of standing colonial defiance London will tolerate before resorting to coercive legislation. Set above the Tea Party threshold so the destruction of the tea, not routine defiance, is what first triggers the Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: coercive legislation rate
variables.documentation: Coercive acts passed per year per unit of normalized provocation. Sized so a full Boston Tea Party yields the handful of statutes the colonists called the Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: coercive relaxation time
variables.documentation: Average time before punitive statutes lapse or are softened.

variables.name: reference intolerable acts severity
variables.documentation: Severity of coercive legislation treated as normal for normalization.

variables.name: militia mobilization rate
variables.documentation: Militia readiness created per year per unit of normalized identity, coercion or troop presence.

variables.name: militia decay time
variables.documentation: Average time over which armed readiness lapses without reinforcement.

variables.name: boycott sensitivity
variables.documentation: Sensitivity of tax collection failure to normalized defiance (smuggling, intimidation of stamp distributors, non-importation).

variables.name: tax collection effectiveness
variables.documentation: Fraction of the nominal tax that can actually be collected; falls toward zero as boycotts and resistance rise.

variables.name: colonial tax revenue collected
variables.documentation: Money Britain actually receives from America; it falls as defiance and boycott rise, which both starves debt relief and forces repeals.

variables.name: hostilities
variables.documentation: Outbreak indicator: armed colonists and armed regulars in the same space. It rises multiplicatively, marking the point at which a Lexington and Concord becomes likely.

variables.name: tea party duration
variables.documentation: Time over which the tea is destroyed and the news reaches and is acted upon by Parliament.

variables.name: tea destruction in the Boston Tea Party
variables.documentation: Rate at which tea is thrown into the harbour once defiance crosses the property-destruction threshold. Self-limiting: it approaches the chests in a full Boston Tea Party and then falls to zero, so the provocation is a burst rather than a standing condition, and the stock can never exceed the tea available.

variables.name: baseline garrison
variables.documentation: Standing peacetime garrison Britain maintains in America regardless of colonial behaviour; reinforcement in response to defiance is added on top of this floor.

variables.name: baseline shared colonial experience
variables.documentation: Ongoing sense of common colonial life - shared language, an intercolonial press, coastal trade and travel - that sustains a baseline American self-conception even in the absence of grievance or defiance.

variables.name: annual cost per soldier
variables.documentation: Annual cost to the Treasury of maintaining one soldier in America.

variables.name: cost of garrisoning the colonies
variables.documentation: Standing annual charge of the American garrison. Britain's insistence that the colonies contribute to the cost of their own defence is what converts troop presence back into fiscal pressure to tax them.

variables.name: reference annual military cost
variables.documentation: Annual military charge in America treated as normal, used to normalize garrison cost into the fiscal-pressure index.

variables.name: grievance per normalized troop presence
variables.documentation: Anger generated per year by a normal-sized garrison quartered among civilians, independent of any particular incident.

variables.name: grievance from the British military occupation
variables.documentation: Standing anger at reinforcements quartered among civilians over and above the ordinary peacetime garrison, amplified by American identity. Only troops sent in response to colonial defiance count as an occupation; the customary garrison does not. Distinct from the one-off Boston Massacre.
