variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Dimensionless congestion index (0..1) representing heavy traffic, delays and stop-and-go conditions. Initial value 0.4. It changes only through its single net biflow, which is a first-order goal-seeking adjustment toward an indicated congestion level, so the stock can never go negative and never exceed 1.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index (0..1) of drivers feeling frustrated and blocked by other drivers. Initial value 0.3. Accumulates through one net biflow that closes the gap between current frustration and the frustration indicated by impatience, perceived provocations and stress.

variables.name: Learned Behavior
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index (0..1) of how normalized aggressive driving has become in society through observing it in other drivers. Initial value 0.2. It is a slow social memory: it accumulates when incidents are common and decays when they are rare.

variables.name: change in Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Net biflow into Traffic Congestion. First-order goal-seeking: the gap between an indicated congestion level and current congestion is closed over a congestion adjustment time embedded numerically as 4 Weeks. Indicated congestion is a weighted average (weights sum to 1) of poor Road Design, adverse Weather Conditions, Distracted Driving (crashes and slow reactions block lanes) and Road Rage Incidents (incidents block lanes, normalized by Personality Traits so the term is dimensionless). MIN/MAX bound only the goal expression, keeping it in 0..1; the stock itself is never clamped. Negative values simply mean congestion is clearing (loop B2).

variables.name: change in Frustration
variables.documentation: Net biflow into Frustration. First-order goal-seeking toward an indicated frustration formed as a weighted average (weights sum to 1) of Impatience, Perceived Provocations and Stress and Anxiety, with the frustration adjustment time embedded numerically as 2 Weeks. The dependence on the Frustration stock itself with a negative sign is the balancing cooling-off loop B1.

variables.name: change in Learned Behavior
variables.documentation: Net biflow into Learned Behavior. Aggressive driving observed on the road (proportional to Road Rage Incidents, normalized by Personality Traits to stay dimensionless) pulls the normalization of aggression up, while the term in Learned Behavior pulls it back down when incidents are rare (extinction loop B3). The normalization/extinction time is embedded numerically as 26 Weeks, reflecting that social norms change slowly (about half a year).

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The central output of the model: the rate of aggressive driving behaviour caused by anger and frustration. It rises with Frustration (anger in the moment) and with Learned Behavior (aggression that has been normalized by observing others), combined as a weighted average whose weights sum to 1. Personality Traits is the unit-bearing baseline propensity that scales the index into incidents per week, making the equation dimensionally consistent.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of being cut off, tailgated or honked at. Other drivers' aggression is exactly what one perceives as provocation, so it rises with Road Rage Incidents (divided by Personality Traits so the units cancel and the result is dimensionless); congestion creates more close interactions, and distracted drivers behave erratically. Weights sum to 1 to keep the index in a sensible 0..1 range.

variables.name: Stress and Anxiety
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of driver stress. High stress makes drivers irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. It rises with accumulated Frustration, with Lack of Sleep (fatigue impairs coping) and with adverse Weather Conditions (harder, tenser driving). Weighted average with weights summing to 1.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of low tolerance for delay and the feeling of running late. Congestion directly makes drivers late, and fatigue lowers tolerance for delay. Weighted average with weights summing to 1.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of phone use, texting and eating while driving. Stressed drivers seek distraction and multitask, and fatigued drivers lose attentional control. Weighted average with weights summing to 1.

variables.name: Personality Traits
variables.documentation: The population's baseline propensity for impulsive, hostile and competitive aggressive response. It is the only unit-bearing constant in the model and converts the dimensionless anger indexes into incidents per week. Value 1.

variables.name: Road Design
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0..1 index of POOR road design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections) that contributes to congestion and frustration. Value 0.4.

variables.name: Weather Conditions
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0..1 index of ADVERSE weather (heavy rain, snow) that slows traffic and raises driver stress. Value 0.3.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0..1 index of driver fatigue impairing judgement, raising stress, impatience and distraction. Value 0.35.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include the variables "Taxation", "Anti British Sentiment" and "Colonial Identity".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of the escalation dynamics. Let me start by loading the tools I need.

Empty session. Building the escalation model now.

Behavior does not match the reference mode — Hostilities stays at zero. Let me check available edit tools.

No dedicated edit tool in this session — update_model is the designated path (edit session file, then push). Applying targeted recalibration and one structural fix (identity spread needs saturation, not pure exponential).

Names are stored with spaces (equations use underscores) — the three required names are exact. Applying edits.

Hostilities break out too early (1772.5), before the Tea Party. Structural cause: coercive legislation accumulates from ordinary protest. Britain tolerated routine protest and legislated punitively only against conspicuous defiance — adding that threshold.

Reference mode is now reproduced: Hostilities exactly zero until 1773, then accelerating. No unit warnings reported by the engine. Now running feedback analysis.

16 loops identified. Getting the LTM dominance narrative and expert analysis.

Seldon flags three real defects: Hostilities is a dead-end stock, there is no mobilisation delay (war starts 1773.5, two years early), and the coercion side has no cost feedback. Fixing all three.

Coercion loop stalls: defiance settles exactly at British tolerance, so the Intolerable Acts decay and mobilisation never crosses. Retuning the tolerance and mobilisation thresholds.

Reference mode now matches: Hostilities exactly zero until 1775.0, first shots 1775.25. Running Seldon's DT robustness test.

DT sensitivity persists — caused by the zero-width pulses. Replacing them with finite-duration events so results are DT-independent.

The loop list contains a stale link (Readiness directly to Outbreak) left from the pre-mobilisation structure. Checking and cleaning.

Clean loop set: 23 loops (15 reinforcing, 8 balancing). Generating the final dominance narrative and the explanatory diagram.

The diagram tool is failing on a server-side configuration error, so I'll give the explanation in prose. Pulling the final numbers.

Model built and validated

I built a 15-stock-and-flow SFD covering 1763 to 1776 (DT 0.0625, Euler), simulated as eval-run-11. Six accumulations carry the story: French and Indian War Debt, Taxation, Anti British Sentiment, Colonial Identity, Intolerable Acts, Colonial Military Mobilization, and Hostilities.

Reference-mode fit from the actual output: Taxation rises from zero and peaks at 2.12 tax acts in 1772, then falls to 1.71 by 1776. Anti British Sentiment climbs from 0.50 to 10.93 grievance, with a visible step at the 1770 Boston Massacre (3.53 to 4.79 within a year). Colonial Identity traces an S-curve from 0.10 to 0.96. Intolerable Acts are exactly zero until the Boston Tea Party in 1773, then jump to 1.13 coercive acts. Hostilities are exactly zero for eleven years and first become positive at 1774.94 — the spring of 1775. No stock goes negative anywhere.

The feedback explanation

The engine identified 23 feedback loops: 15 reinforcing, 8 balancing. Dominance shifts across four distinct phases.

1763–1769, the fiscal loops smolder. Four reinforcing loops share one mechanism. Unpaid war debt from the French and Indian War and a persistent revenue shortfall keep the perceived need for colonial revenue high, so Parliament imposes duties like the Stamp Act. Taxation generates grievance — amplified by an explicit multiplier for having no representatives in Parliament — which accumulates as Anti British Sentiment. Sentiment produces acts of defiance; defiance collapses tax compliance through smuggling and non-importation; collections fall; the shortfall widens; Parliament taxes harder. Britain taxed more precisely because its taxes were being resisted. This is a classic fixes-that-fail escalation. It is slow because three balancing loops oppose it — sentiment cooling, revenue-shortfall correction, and debt retirement.

1770, the propaganda loop takes over. The massacre matters in this model not as a shock but as a renewable asset. Dominance passes to a reinforcing loop in which sentiment builds Colonial Identity, and a stronger identity makes the massacre propaganda more effective, which manufactures fresh grievance, which raises sentiment again. The causal centre of gravity shifts here: before 1770 grievance came from Parliament, after 1770 a substantial share is produced internally.

1771–1772, the decisive structural insight. The balancing repeal loops win on the fiscal front — resistance raises repeal pressure, shortens the effective repeal time, and turns Taxation down after 1772. By any Treasury measure the crisis is resolving. Yet Anti British Sentiment keeps climbing, because dominance now rests with identity self-propagation and massacre propaganda, neither of which needs any new British action. Repealing a tax removes a flow, not a stock. The accumulated sentiment and identity remain, and they have acquired their own means of self-renewal.

1773–1775, the coercion regime and the delay. The Tea Party pushes defiance past what Britain will tolerate, and coercive legislation passes — including closing the port of Boston until the ruined tea was paid for. Dominance transfers to the coercion loops, which have no fiscal brake: taxes at least raised revenue, whereas coercion produces only grievance. Worse, enforcing coercion adds to the war debt, quietly reviving the revenue pressure that started the quarrel. But Hostilities remain exactly zero through 1774, because armed conflict does not begin when people are angry enough — it begins when enough are simultaneously under arms, and Colonial Military Mobilization is a stock that must be filled against militia going home. That accumulation is what puts Lexington in 1775 rather than 1773.

Once mobilization crosses, the war loops close: bloodshed generates grievance, grievance sustains defiance, defiance sustains coercion, coercion sustains mobilization. The conflict becomes self-sustaining and no tax repeal can reach back to undo it.

The roles invert completely. Taxation started the process and was irrelevant by the end. Anti British Sentiment stored it. Colonial Identity amplified it and finally armed it.

Validation performed

Seldon's critique caught three real defects in my first version, all fixed: Hostilities was a dead-end stock with no outflow of causality (bloodshed now radicalises opinion); there was no mobilisation delay, so war started in 1773.5, two years early; and coercion had no cost, so the enforcement-cost loop was missing. I also replaced zero-width pulses with finite-duration events after a DT convergence test at 0.25, 0.125 and 0.0625 showed the instantaneous spikes were creating artifacts. The regime shift is robust across all three step sizes; onset varies by about a quarter-year.

Limitations worth flagging. The multiplicative readiness gate makes coercion a logically necessary condition, so the model cannot test whether war could have come from taxation and identity alone. There is no loyalist counter-mobilisation opposing identity growth, no balancing loop by which Britain conciliates rather than hardens, and repeal is routed directly from colonial anger rather than through the British merchants whose losses actually drove it. Troop presence is absent, so the Boston Massacre is exogenous rather than an endogenous product of soldiers among civilians.

The causal loop diagram tool is returning a server-side configuration error, so I could not render the visual. Two things I would suggest next: a stacked feedback-dominance chart confirming the loop handoffs quantitatively, or a policy experiment — if Britain had never passed the Intolerable Acts, does this structure still produce a war?

variables.name: French and Indian War Debt
variables.documentation: The British national debt incurred defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-63). Britain wanted the colonies to help repay it, so this stock is the ultimate driver of the perceived need for colonial revenue. It can only fall through repayment.

variables.name: Debt Repayment from Colonial Revenue
variables.documentation: Debt retired using revenue actually collected in the colonies. The MIN with a first-order drain term guarantees the debt stock can never be driven negative.

variables.name: Initial War Debt
variables.documentation: Approximate British national debt at the close of the French and Indian War in 1763.

variables.name: Reference War Debt
variables.documentation: Normalizing value for the debt so that the debt pressure index equals 1 at the 1763 level.

variables.name: Minimum Debt Repayment Time
variables.documentation: Shortest time over which the remaining debt could conceivably be retired; provides the structural non-negativity limit on repayment.

variables.name: Debt Ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of outstanding war debt relative to its 1763 reference level.

variables.name: Taxation
variables.documentation: Cumulative burden of British revenue acts in force in the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act of 1765 taxing legal documents, newspapers and playing cards, Townshend duties, Tea Act). Starts at zero in 1763 before the new revenue programme began.

variables.name: Imposition of New Taxes
variables.documentation: Rate at which Parliament legislates new colonial taxes, proportional to how strongly it perceives a need for colonial revenue.

variables.name: Repeal of Taxes
variables.documentation: First-order repeal of standing tax acts (as with the Stamp Act repeal of 1766). Because it is proportional to the stock, Taxation can never become negative.

variables.name: Normal Tax Imposition Rate
variables.documentation: Number of new revenue acts Parliament passes per year when the perceived need for colonial revenue is at its reference level of 1.

variables.name: Tax Repeal Time
variables.documentation: Average life of a tax act in the absence of colonial pressure.

variables.name: Effective Tax Repeal Time
variables.documentation: Life of a tax act after colonial resistance is taken into account; boycotts and petitions shorten it.

variables.name: Repeal Pressure from Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier (1 at reference sentiment) by which colonial agitation accelerates repeal of taxes. This closes the balancing loop that repealed the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties.

variables.name: Perceived Need for Colonial Revenue
variables.documentation: How strongly Parliament feels it must raise money in America. Rises with remaining war debt and with the shortfall between target and actual colonial revenue.

variables.name: Debt Pressure Weight
variables.documentation: Weight given to outstanding war debt in forming the perceived need for colonial revenue.

variables.name: Shortfall Pressure Weight
variables.documentation: Weight given to the current revenue shortfall in forming the perceived need for colonial revenue.

variables.name: Target Colonial Revenue
variables.documentation: Annual revenue Britain intended to raise in America toward imperial defence and debt service.

variables.name: Revenue Shortfall
variables.documentation: Gap between what Britain wanted from the colonies and what it actually collected. Every boycott widened this gap and provoked yet more taxes.

variables.name: Shortfall Ratio
variables.documentation: Fractional revenue shortfall, a dimensionless pressure between 0 and 1.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Revenue Collected
variables.documentation: Money actually collected: the number of tax acts times the yield of a typical act times the fraction of the tax that colonists actually pay.

variables.name: Revenue per Tax Act
variables.documentation: Annual yield of a typical revenue act under full compliance.

variables.name: Tax Compliance Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of the nominal tax that is actually paid. Smuggling, non-importation agreements and boycotts drive it down as defiance rises.

variables.name: Normal Tax Compliance Fraction
variables.documentation: Compliance fraction at the reference level of colonial defiance.

variables.name: Effect of Defiance on Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier (1 at reference defiance) showing how boycotts and non-importation collapse tax collection.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial grievance against British rule. It accumulates from taxation without representation, from the propaganda memory of the Boston Massacre and from the Intolerable Acts, and it decays slowly as tempers cool.

variables.name: Initial Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Low residual resentment in 1763, when most colonists still regarded themselves as loyal Britons.

variables.name: Grievance from Taxation
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per year by standing tax acts. The constitutional objection that the colonists had no representatives in Parliament multiplies the anger produced by each act.

variables.name: Grievance per Tax Act
variables.documentation: Grievance generated each year by one standing tax act before the representation multiplier.

variables.name: No Taxation Without Representation Effect
variables.documentation: Amplification of tax grievance caused by the absence of colonial representation in Parliament: the same tax provokes far more anger when it is seen as unconstitutional.

variables.name: Grievance from Boston Massacre Propaganda
variables.documentation: Grievance produced by the remembered and publicised killing of five colonists by British soldiers in 1770.

variables.name: Grievance per Propaganda Unit
variables.documentation: Grievance created by one unit of circulating massacre propaganda.

variables.name: Grievance from Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Grievance produced each year by coercive legislation in force, such as the act closing the port of Boston until the ruined tea was paid for.

variables.name: Grievance per Coercive Act
variables.documentation: Annual grievance generated by one coercive act in force. Coercion is far more inflammatory per act than taxation.

variables.name: Grievance per Hostility
variables.documentation: Grievance generated each year by blood already shed. Killing destroys the loyalist middle ground and makes reconciliation harder.

variables.name: Grievance from Bloodshed
variables.documentation: Grievance produced by the fighting itself. Once blood is shed the conflict feeds on itself: casualties radicalise opinion, which drives further defiance, coercion and fighting.

variables.name: Cooling of Sentiment
variables.documentation: First-order fading of anger when no fresh provocation occurs, as in the quiet years 1770-1773. Proportional drainage keeps the stock non-negative.

variables.name: Sentiment Cooling Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which colonial anger subsides absent new provocation.

variables.name: Reference Sentiment
variables.documentation: Normalizing level of grievance used to build dimensionless effect multipliers, set near the mid-range of grievance reached during the imperial crisis.

variables.name: Sentiment Ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of anti-British feeling relative to its reference level.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The shared sense of being American rather than British, carried by committees of correspondence, intercolonial congresses and a common press. Small but positive in 1763.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak but non-zero intercolonial identity in 1763; it must be positive for the self-reinforcing spread of identity to be able to start.

variables.name: Growth of American Identity
variables.documentation: Identity spreads contagiously: the more colonists already share an American self-image, the faster it spreads through committees of correspondence and a common press, and shared grievance against Britain accelerates that spread. Growth saturates as identity approaches its ceiling in the colonial population.

variables.name: Identity Spread Rate
variables.documentation: Fractional rate at which existing American identity reproduces itself at reference sentiment.

variables.name: Maximum Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Ceiling on how far a shared American identity can spread through the colonial population. Identity spreads contagiously into a finite population, so its growth must saturate rather than grow without bound.

variables.name: Effect of Sentiment on Identity Growth
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier (1 at reference sentiment) capturing how shared grievance against Britain welds separate colonies into one people.

variables.name: Erosion of American Identity
variables.documentation: Slow decay of common identity through provincial rivalry and loyalist attachment to Britain. First-order, so identity cannot become negative.

variables.name: Identity Erosion Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which a shared identity fades if nothing sustains it.

variables.name: Reference Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Normalizing level of American identity used to build dimensionless multipliers.

variables.name: Identity Ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of American identity relative to its reference level.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Time
variables.documentation: Year in which British soldiers fired on a Boston crowd and killed five colonists.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Intensity
variables.documentation: Size of the propaganda shock released by the massacre.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Duration
variables.documentation: Period over which news of the killings spread through the colonial press and the engravings circulated. Giving the event a finite duration rather than an instantaneous spike makes the result independent of the simulation time step.

variables.name: Boston Massacre
variables.equation: Boston_Massacre_Intensity / Boston_Massacre_Duration * (STEP(1, Boston_Massacre_Time) - STEP(1, Boston_Massacre_Time + Boston_Massacre_Duration))
variables.documentation: The killing of five colonists by British soldiers in 1770, released as a finite burst of propaganda material spread over the months in which the story circulated.

variables.name: Propaganda Memory Time
variables.documentation: Time constant over which the memory of the massacre, kept alive by engravings, sermons and annual commemorations, fades.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Propaganda Effect
variables.documentation: Circulating massacre propaganda. The smooth gives the event a persistent memory rather than a one-instant shock, and a stronger American identity amplifies how effectively the story is spread.

variables.name: Effect of Identity on Propaganda
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier (1 at reference identity) for how far a shared American identity and its network of presses and committees amplify massacre propaganda.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Time
variables.documentation: Year of the destruction of the East India Company tea in Boston harbour.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Intensity
variables.documentation: Magnitude of the single most conspicuous act of colonial defiance, which showed Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Duration
variables.documentation: Period over which the destruction of the tea and the wave of imitation it inspired played out. A finite duration rather than an instantaneous spike keeps the result independent of the simulation time step.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party
variables.equation: Boston_Tea_Party_Intensity / Boston_Tea_Party_Duration * (STEP(1, Boston_Tea_Party_Time) - STEP(1, Boston_Tea_Party_Time + Boston_Tea_Party_Duration))
variables.documentation: The destruction of the East India Company tea in Boston harbour, a finite burst of conspicuous defiance showing that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.

variables.name: Acts of Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: Riots, boycotts, non-importation agreements, tarring of customs officers and the Tea Party. Defiance requires both anger and enough shared identity to act collectively, hence the product form.

variables.name: Normal Defiance Rate
variables.documentation: Rate of defiant acts when both sentiment and identity are at their reference levels.

variables.name: Reference Defiance Rate
variables.documentation: Normalizing rate of defiance used to build the dimensionless compliance effect.

variables.name: Defiance Ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of colonial defiance relative to its reference level.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Coercive legislation in force, such as the Boston Port Act which closed the port until the ruined tea was paid for, the Massachusetts Government Act and the Quartering Act. Zero in 1763.

variables.name: Passage of Coercive Legislation
variables.documentation: Britain answers defiance with punishment, but only once defiance exceeds what it is willing to tolerate. Ordinary protest is absorbed; conspicuous defiance such as the destruction of the tea brings harsh laws, one of which closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.

variables.name: Coercive Acts per Defiance Act
variables.documentation: Severity of the British legislative response per act of colonial defiance.

variables.name: Cost per Coercive Act
variables.documentation: Annual cost of garrisoning, blockading and administering the colonies under each coercive act. Punishing America was not free.

variables.name: Enforcement Cost of Coercion
variables.documentation: Cost of enforcing coercive legislation, added to the debt Britain was trying to make the colonies repay. Coercion therefore deepens the very fiscal hole that motivated colonial taxation in the first place.

variables.name: British Tolerance for Defiance
variables.documentation: Level of colonial defiance Britain was prepared to absorb through ordinary law and customs enforcement. Routine riots, petitions and smuggling provoked no coercive legislation; only conspicuous defiance beyond this tolerance brought punitive statutes such as the Boston Port Act.

variables.name: Relaxation of Coercive Legislation
variables.documentation: Slow lapse or suspension of coercive laws. First-order, so the stock cannot go negative.

variables.name: Coercion Relaxation Time
variables.documentation: Average time a coercive act stays in force. Britain was very slow to repeal the Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: Reference Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Normalizing level of coercive legislation used to build the dimensionless readiness index.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of coercion in force relative to its reference level.

variables.name: Readiness for Armed Resistance
variables.documentation: Multiplicative combination of anger, common identity and coercion. All three are necessary: anger without organisation is a riot, organisation without coercion is a petition. Only when all three are high does armed resistance become possible.

variables.name: Threshold for Armed Resistance
variables.documentation: Level of readiness that must be exceeded before militias muster and shots are fired. Keeps hostilities essentially at zero through the 1760s.

variables.name: Colonial Military Mobilization
variables.documentation: Militia companies mustered, powder and arms stored, and committees of safety standing ready. Armed conflict cannot begin the instant colonists become willing to fight; the means of fighting must first be accumulated. This stock supplies that delay.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Military Mobilization
variables.documentation: No organised colonial military force stood against the Crown in 1763.

variables.name: Militia Mustering Rate
variables.documentation: Militia companies raised per year for each unit of readiness above the threshold at which colonists begin to arm.

variables.name: Mustering of Militia
variables.documentation: Colonists arm and drill once grievance, shared identity and coercion together push readiness past the point at which petitioning seems futile.

variables.name: Demobilization Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which mustered companies disperse if no further provocation sustains them.

variables.name: Demobilization of Militia
variables.documentation: Militia disperse back to their farms absent fresh provocation. First-order, so the mobilization stock cannot go negative.

variables.name: Mobilization Needed for Armed Conflict
variables.documentation: Armed force that must be standing before a confrontation with regular troops turns into shooting rather than dispersal.

variables.name: Hostility Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which mustered armed force beyond the minimum needed converts into actual fighting.

variables.name: Outbreak of Armed Conflict
variables.documentation: Fighting begins only when enough armed force has actually been mustered. The accumulation in the mobilization stock is what delays the outbreak by roughly two years after readiness first crosses its threshold.

variables.name: Hostilities
variables.documentation: Cumulative armed conflict between Crown and colonies. The outcome variable: essentially zero until the early 1770s, then rising sharply as Lexington and Concord approach in 1775.

testParams.name: include requested variables for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include the variables "Traffic Congestion", "Driver Stress" and "Accidents".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of road rage dynamics from the background information you provided. Let me start by loading the model tools.

Empty model. I'll build the SFD directly from your background information.

Model built as specified — 86 variables, 5 stocks, no errors or warnings reported. Running it.

Algebraic loop: Perceived Provocations → Frustration → Anger → Aggressive Driving Behavior → back to Perceived Provocations, with no state in between. Let me check for edit tools.

No edit_variables tool in this session. I'll regenerate with the algebraic loop broken structurally — making Perceived Provocations a state with a perception/decay delay, which is also the more defensible formulation (retaliation lags the provocation that triggers it).

Structure is clean — 6 stocks, all with first-order outflow control, every variable has units and documentation, no errors or warnings reported. Running.

Only 3 of 10 variables came back. Requesting the rest.

Multi-word names appear to need underscores. Retrying.

No negative stocks, conservation holds. But two structural problems: the run starts far from equilibrium (a 20-week initialization transient), and Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior pegs at its ceiling of 1.0 by week ~50, which kills the contagion feedback for 80% of the horizon. Let me solve for a properly initialized, unsaturated parameterization offline before changing the model.

My replica tracks the engine. Now solving for a self-consistent fixed point where the reference constants equal the t=0 operating point.

Fixed point found: starts in equilibrium, no saturation, all stocks positive, clean escalation. Applying the corrected initialization and reference constants.

All nine constants applied, structure intact, no errors or warnings. Running.

Engine matches my replica to 4 decimals. Running extreme-condition tests and pulling the loop analysis.

All extreme-condition tests pass — no negatives anywhere, and freezing the distracted-driving trend (X6) holds every stock at its initial value, confirming true equilibrium initialization. Now the loop analysis.

16 loops: 9 reinforcing, 7 balancing. Let me get the LTM narrative and Seldon's expert read.

Model built, validated, and analyzed. Here is what it says.

What the model is

A 6-stock SFD in weeks over a 5-year horizon. The accumulations are Traffic Congestion, Driver Stress, Accidents, Road Rage Incidents, Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior, and Perceived Provocations. Every stock drains through a first-order control, so none can go negative.

Your background factors enter where they belong: Road Design Quality and Weather Conditions Severity push congestion buildup; Lack of Sleep enters both as Fatigue Judgment Impairment and as accident risk; Impulsive Hostile Competitive Personality Prevalence acts as a multiplier on anger, not a source of it; Frustration and Impatience are separated (blocked movement versus schedule pressure) because they enter anger independently; Distracted Driving is the one exogenous condition that trends over time, from 0.20 to 0.46.

Perceived Provocations had to be a stock, not an auxiliary. As an auxiliary it created a simultaneous algebraic loop that crashed the solver. Making it a state is also the better formulation — retaliation lags the provoking act.

Validation

Two real defects were found and fixed. The model was initialized far from equilibrium, so the first 20 weeks were numerical settling, not behavior. And Reference Road Rage Incidents was low enough that Observed Aggressive Driving Exposure hit its ceiling of 1.0 by week 50 — silently severing the social-learning feedback for 80 percent of the run. Both corrected; exposure now stays at 0.50 to 0.53 throughout.

Extreme-condition tests pass. Freezing the distracted-driving trend holds every stock flat at its initial value, confirming genuine equilibrium initialization. Under maximally adverse conditions Aggressive Driving Behavior reaches 0.925 and stops — the saturating response holds. No stock goes negative in any scenario.

The feedback explanation

The engine found 16 loops: 9 reinforcing, 7 balancing. They fall into three families.

Congestion and crashes feeding each other. Congestion Crash Risk Cycle is the fastest reinforcing structure in the model and requires no behavioral change at all — crashes create congestion, and congested conditions mechanically raise crash risk. Running alongside it, Congestion Frustration Cascade and Congestion Impatience Cascade convert queue length into felt obstruction and time pressure, while Crash-Congestion Stress Spiral and Crash Anxiety Contagion route the same disturbance through the slower stress accumulation. Accidents sits at the junction where all of these close, which is why it moves most.

Aggression provoking aggression. Tit-for-Tat Provocation is the fast one — aggressive driving creates provocations, provocations raise frustration, frustration produces more aggressive driving. Provocation Stress Escalation is its slow twin, running the same exchange through Driver Stress, so a provocation leaves a residue of tension rather than just a moment of anger.

Aggression teaching aggression. Aggression Imitation Spread makes incidents self-propagating: visible road rage normalizes road rage, which amplifies anger, which produces more incidents. Aggression Habit Retention makes the norm sticky by slowing forgetting whenever aggression is visible.

Against these, the balancing loops — Traffic Dispersal, Accident Clearance, Stress Recovery, Provocation Memory Fading, Incident Resolution, Aggression Habit Decay, Normalization Saturation — do not stop the growth. They shape its character, converting what would be an accelerating takeoff into a steady climb.

What happens to road rage in the future

Over 260 weeks, driven only by rising distraction: Accidents up 35.8 percent, Traffic Congestion up 25.4 percent, Driver Stress up 17.1 percent, Road Rage Incidents up 5.5 percent.

The ordering is the finding. Road rage rises least in percentage terms, and that is not reassuring — it is the signature of how the system works. Road Rage Incidents sits far downstream, buffered by the recovery and fading loops on stress and provocations, and drained continuously by Incident Resolution. The physical damage arrives first and largest; the behavioral response is the compressed, late-arriving tail of it.

The model's answer to "what causes road rage" is therefore that road rage is largely a derived condition. Nobody in this model becomes angry spontaneously. Distraction raises crashes, crashes and congestion amplify each other, congestion and crashes generate frustration and impatience and chronic stress — and only then does aggression appear, after which it sustains itself through retaliation and imitation.

Where the leverage is

Cutting the accident-to-congestion link is the single strongest lever tested: Traffic Congestion collapses 77 percent and Road Rage Incidents fall 29 percent. Removing the learned-behavior amplification cuts incidents 18 percent. Removing aggressive personalities cuts them only 8 percent — personality amplifies the system but does not drive it.

This is the counterintuitive result worth sitting with. The high-leverage interventions are upstream and unglamorous — faster incident clearance, road design, distraction reduction — not driver-directed anger management, which acts on a multiplier rather than on a source.

Caveats

Two boundary choices matter. There is no enforcement or policing structure, because your background did not mention one, so the model cannot represent deterrence. And the "all benign" test still leaves 118 incidents, meaning a floor of road rage persists from baseline traffic and provocation alone that no environmental intervention here can remove.

I can draw the causal loop diagram of this structure, chart the trajectories with dominant-loop shading, or test specific policies — say, distraction enforcement against accident clearance capacity — if any of those would be useful.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Index of heavy traffic, delays and stop-and-go conditions on the road network. Now initialized at its t=0 equilibrium value so the run starts in balance rather than with a startup transient.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion builds from baseline traffic pressure, amplified by poor road design and adverse weather, plus congestion created by accidents blocking lanes.

variables.name: Congestion Dissipation
variables.documentation: First-order clearing of congestion as traffic flows through the network; guarantees congestion can never go negative.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress and anxiety in the driving population; high stress makes drivers irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. Initialized at its t=0 equilibrium value.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions (congestion, weather, provocations, fatigue, accidents) add to accumulated driver stress.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: First-order relaxation of accumulated driver stress through rest and time away from driving.

variables.name: Accidents
variables.documentation: Accidents on the road network that have not yet been cleared. Initialized at its t=0 equilibrium value.

variables.name: Accident Occurrence
variables.documentation: Rate of new accidents: a baseline rate scaled by risk factors such as distraction, aggression, weather, fatigue and congestion.

variables.name: Accident Clearance
variables.documentation: First-order clearing of accidents from the road network by emergency and recovery services.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Active and recently observed incidents of aggressive driving caused by anger and frustration. Initialized at its t=0 equilibrium value.

variables.name: Road Rage Incident Occurrence
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents occur, proportional to the prevailing fraction of aggressive driving behavior.

variables.name: Road Rage Incident Resolution
variables.documentation: First-order resolution of road rage incidents as they end or fade from public visibility.

variables.name: Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.documentation: Degree to which aggressive driving has been normalized by drivers observing it in others. Initialized to match the t=0 observed exposure so neither the normalization inflow nor the fading outflow is active at the start.

variables.name: Aggression Normalization
variables.documentation: Rate at which observed aggressive driving becomes socially normalized when exposure exceeds the current learned norm.

variables.name: Aggression Norm Fading
variables.documentation: Slow erosion of the aggressive driving norm when observed exposure falls below the learned norm.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Accumulated recent experience of being cut off, tailgated or honked at, which provokes anger and retaliatory behavior. Perception builds and fades with a delay, so retaliation lags the provoking act. Making this a stock inserts the state needed to break the otherwise simultaneous algebraic loop through frustration, anger and aggressive driving. Initialized at its t=0 equilibrium value.

variables.name: Provocation Exposure
variables.documentation: Rate at which aggressive drivers generate newly perceived provocations for other drivers.

variables.name: Provocation Fading
variables.documentation: First-order decay of the memory of provocations, so that a driver's sense of being provoked fades over time.

variables.name: Normalized Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Traffic congestion expressed relative to a reference level so it can be combined with other dimensionless drivers. The reference is now set at the equilibrium congestion level so the normalized value starts near one.

variables.name: Normalized Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Driver stress expressed relative to a reference level so it can be combined with other dimensionless drivers.

variables.name: Normalized Accidents
variables.documentation: Accidents expressed relative to a reference level so they can be combined with other dimensionless stress drivers. The reference is now set at the equilibrium accident level.

variables.name: Observed Aggressive Driving Exposure
variables.documentation: Fraction of drivers effectively exposed to visible aggressive driving, capped at one. The reference incident level is now high enough that this term stays below its ceiling across the whole 260 week horizon, keeping the learned-behavior feedback loop active.

variables.name: Accident Congestion Impact
variables.documentation: Additional congestion pressure created by accidents blocking lanes on the network.

variables.name: Poor Road Design
variables.documentation: Complement of road design quality, representing the degree of narrow lanes and confusing intersections in the network.

variables.name: Road Design Effect on Congestion
variables.documentation: Multiplier on congestion buildup from road design; equals one when design is perfect and rises as design worsens.

variables.name: Weather Effect on Congestion
variables.documentation: Multiplier on congestion buildup from adverse weather such as heavy rain or snow.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Sense of being blocked by other drivers plus the effect of accumulated perceived provocations, both of which lead to anger.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Impatience of drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays under congested conditions.

variables.name: Anger and Frustration Pressure
variables.equation: Frustration_Weight_on_Anger * Frustration + Impatience_Weight_on_Anger * Impatience + Stress_Weight_on_Anger * Normalized_Driver_Stress
variables.documentation: Combined psychological pressure toward anger from frustration, impatience and accumulated stress.

variables.name: Personality Amplification
variables.documentation: Amplification of anger into aggression due to the prevalence of impulsive, hostile or competitive personalities.

variables.name: Fatigue Judgment Impairment
variables.documentation: Amplification of anger into aggression because fatigue impairs judgment and self-control.

variables.name: Learned Behavior Amplification
variables.documentation: Amplification of anger into aggression because aggressive driving has been normalized by observing others.

variables.name: Effective Anger Pressure
variables.documentation: Anger pressure after amplification by personality, fatigue and learned norms; the driving force for aggressive behavior.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.documentation: Saturating response of aggressive driving to effective anger pressure, bounded between zero and one; safe division avoids divide-by-zero.

variables.name: Accident Risk Multiplier
variables.equation: (1 + Distraction_Impact_on_Accidents * Distracted_Driving) * (1 + Aggression_Impact_on_Accidents * Aggressive_Driving_Behavior) * (1 + Weather_Impact_on_Accidents * Weather_Conditions_Severity) * (1 + Fatigue_Impact_on_Accidents * Lack_of_Sleep) * (1 + Congestion_Impact_on_Accidents * Normalized_Traffic_Congestion)
variables.documentation: Multiplicative increase in accident risk from distraction, aggression, weather, fatigue and congestion relative to baseline conditions.

variables.name: Total Stress Pressure
variables.equation: Congestion_Stress_Weight * Normalized_Traffic_Congestion + Weather_Stress_Weight * Weather_Conditions_Severity + Provocation_Stress_Weight * Perceived_Provocations + Fatigue_Stress_Weight * Lack_of_Sleep + Accident_Stress_Weight * Normalized_Accidents
variables.documentation: Weighted sum of the conditions that generate stress for drivers: congestion, weather, provocations, fatigue and accidents.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Prevalence of phone use, texting and eating while driving, trending upward over the horizon toward a saturation ceiling. This is the exogenous driver that pushes the equilibrated system away from its initial balance.

variables.name: Initial Road Rage Incidents

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and equations.

Let me run the model as-given to establish baseline behavior before I change anything.

Baseline confirms a serious pathology. Note Exposed_population climbs monotonically to 2833 while its outflow Total_incubation is only 66/week against an inflow of 167/week — the Exposed stock is a trap. Effective residence time in Exposed is 2833/66.4 ≈ 42 weeks, not the intended 3 days. The epidemic never ignites (25 deaths in 60 weeks against 17M susceptible).

Let me examine the culprit equation precisely.

The style pattern is now unambiguous. Every stock's outflow in this model is DELAY3(<that stock's inflow(s)>, <that stage's residence time>):

Stock Outflow driver Delay time
Presymptomatic DELAY3(Incubation + Influx, ...) Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week
Asymptomatic DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, ...) Avg_period_asymptomatic/Days_per_week
Symptomatic DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, ...) Avg_length_symptomatic_period
Recovered DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, ...) Average_immunity_period
Exposed DELAY3(Exposed_population/.../..., ...) Avg_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week

Total_incubation is the sole variable that breaks the pattern. Applying the fix:

Equation is updated. The reported unit warning is stale (generated at the last simulation). Let me re-run to refresh the engine's unit check and verify behavior.

The model now produces a genuine epidemic wave, and no stock goes negative. Let me verify conservation of population rigorously.

Conservation holds to 0.2 people out of 17 million. Let me sanity-check the exogenous influx driver, since my hand-estimate of its integral disagreed.

The influx equals TIME exactly — the graphical function is not being applied. Let me check the other graphical-function variable.

Both findings need verification. First, let me determine whether the persisting unit warning is live or cached, using a controlled probe.

The probe produced no new warning. Let me run the model to see whether a simulation refreshes the unit checker.

Confirmed: a blatant dimensional error (Infectious_population = sum of Person stocks, labeled "Week") produced no warning even after a full run. The unitWarnings field is frozen from the original model load, so the persisting Total incubation entry is a cached diagnostic of the old equation. Reverting my probe:

Probe reverted cleanly. Now let me check whether the causal-link metadata tracked my equation change.

Relationship metadata did not auto-sync. Let me re-run to leave the model in a clean, freshly-simulated state and do final validation.

The model is now validated. Here is my analysis.

Formulation error found and fixed

Total_incubation — the outflow governing exit from the Exposed stock

Before:

DELAY3(Exposed_population/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week)

After:

DELAY3(Infection, Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week)

This single variable contained three compounding defects.

1. Mixed delay paradigms — an exponential drain nested inside a pipeline delay. The inner expression Exposed_population/time is a first-order (exponential) drain of the stock. That was then wrapped in DELAY3, a third-order pipeline delay — so the cohort was delayed twice, by two different mechanisms. Every other stage transition in this model uses one consistent idiom: a pipeline delay applied to the stock's inflow, over that stage's residence time.

Stock Outflow driver Residence time
Presymptomatic DELAY3(Incubation + Influx, ...) Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week
Asymptomatic DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, ...) Avg_period_asymptomatic/Days_per_week
Symptomatic DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, ...) Average_length_of_symptomatic_period
Recovered DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, ...) Average_immunity_period
Exposed was a stock drain inside a DELAY3 —

Exposed was the only stock breaking the pattern. The fix makes it DELAY3 of Infection, which is that stock's sole inflow — matching the other four exactly.

2. Wrong time parameter. The drain used Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections (6 days — the recovery period for asymptomatic infectives, already correctly used by Recovery_without_symptoms). Exit from Exposed is incubation, which is governed by Average_COVID_incubation_time. A parameter belonging to a downstream stage was controlling an upstream one.

3. Broken unit conversion — the source of the engine's unit warning. The chained division X / Average_period / Days_per_week divides by Day/Week where it needed to multiply. Dimensionally: Person/Day divided by Day/Week gives Person·Week/Day², exactly the People*Weeks/Days^2 the unit checker reported against a declared Person/Week.

Measured impact. These defects made the effective residence time in Exposed roughly 42 weeks instead of 3 days — about 98 times too slow. Exposed acted as a trap: at the end of the original run, inflow was 167 people/week against an outflow of only 66/week, and the stock was still climbing monotonically.

Original Corrected
Effective residence in Exposed ~42 weeks 0.41 weeks (target 3/7 = 0.4286)
Peak symptomatic infectious 91 1,427,668 at week 19
Cumulative deaths at week 60 25 69,451
Susceptible depletion 0.02% 81.1% peak

The original model simply never produced an epidemic in a population of 17 million.

Validation performed: all seven stocks stay non-negative; Incubation + Asymptomatic_incubation equals Total_incubation to zero deviation; and population conservation closes to 0.2 people out of 17 million (initial 17,000,000 plus cumulative influx minus cumulative deaths matches the sum of the six living stocks).

Three things I did not change, but you should know about

The unitWarnings field is stale — it is not reporting a live problem. It still shows the Total incubation warning, but the dimensions it cites match the old equation character-for-character. I verified this is a caching artifact: I deliberately relabeled Infectious_population (a sum of Person stocks) as "Week", ran the model, and no warning appeared for it. The checker has not re-run since the model was loaded. I reverted that probe. Re-open the model in your client to get a fresh check; the corrected equation is dimensionally clean (Person/Week delayed by Week yields Person/Week).

The engine ignores the x-coordinates of your graphical functions and spreads the points evenly. Social_distancing_measures is being evaluated with its 19 points spaced uniformly across the range 0 to 104 rather than at the x-values you specified. I confirmed this to four decimal places: at t=7.23 the model returns 0.02516 and even spacing predicts 0.02510; at t=9.65 it returns 0.06700 against a predicted 0.06700; at t=31.36 it returns 0.5283 against 0.5280. The practical consequence is that your first lockdown, encoded to begin at week 9, actually ramps from week 5.8 to week 34.7. Your intervention timeline is stretched by roughly a factor of three. I have not resampled this curve because that means rewriting your policy data, which should be your call.

The graphical function on Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad is not applied at all. That variable evaluates to TIME verbatim — it returns 0.305 at t=0.305 and 60 at t=60, a straight identity line, instead of the seeding pulse peaking at 2000 people/week around week 8. The discriminator is variable type, not point spacing: Social_distancing_measures is a variable and its lookup is applied, while this one is a flow and its lookup is dropped. So resampling the points to uniform spacing will not fix this one. Your epidemic is currently being seeded by a linear ramp, which is why the outbreak takes until week 19 to peak. Fixing it requires attaching the lookup differently in your client, and every route I can see involves either a new variable or a new relationship, both of which you ruled out.

One consequence of the fix worth flagging

The relationships section did not auto-sync with my equation change. It still carries Exposed population -> Total incubation and Average period of asymptomatic infections -> Total incubation, both artifacts of the erroneous equation, and it lacks Infection -> Total incubation. I left that section untouched, since correcting it would mean adding a relationship record and you ruled that out unconditionally.

To be explicit about what the equation change did structurally: it re-routes one existing input rather than introducing new structure. The causal path from infection through incubation to the presymptomatic and asymptomatic stages is preserved and no new pathway was created — it now bypasses the Exposed stock in exactly the way the other four stage transitions bypass theirs. The Exposed stock still correctly accumulates everyone in transit, which is why conservation holds. If your client regenerates arrows from equations you can ignore this; if not, you will want to repoint that one arrow by hand.

errorExplanations.name: developing_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use the flows 'Incubation + Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad' as input to DELAY3, not the stock 'Presymptomatic infectious' divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

Now let me examine the one flagged unit warning and the formulation style across the model. Making the fix:

The equation is updated; the reported unit warning appears to be stale from the pre-edit run. Let me run the model to force the engine to re-check.

Model runs clean — no negative stocks, and population conservation checks out (17,000,000 minus 69,450 cumulative deaths equals the final total). Let me verify whether the unit warning is stale by forcing a re-validation:

The run confirms the fix is active: peak Presymptomatic_infectious (6.41e5) equals peak Developing_symptoms (1.477e6/wk) times the 3/7-week presymptomatic residence time — exactly what a 3/7-week pipeline should produce.

Formulation Error Found and Fixed

Error 1: Developing symptoms — wrong delay input, wrong time constant, wrong unit conversion

Original equation:

DELAY3(Presymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)

Fixed equation:

DELAY3(Incubation + Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad,
       Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)

This single variable contained three compounding defects:

1a. Style inconsistency — a stock-drain expression stuffed inside a pipeline delay. Every other stock outflow in this model is a pure third-order pipeline delay of that stock's inflows, not a fractional drain of the stock itself:

Stock Outflow formulation
Exposed Total_incubation = DELAY3(Infection, ...)
Asymptomatic infectious Recovery_without_symptoms = DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, ...)
Symptomatic infectious Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious = DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, ...)
Recovered Losing_immunity = DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, ...)
Presymptomatic infectious was DELAY3(Stock/time/time, ...) — the odd one out

The original mixed paradigms: it took a first-order exponential drain (Stock/time_constant) and then passed that through a third-order pipeline delay. That is not a coherent delay of either type — it is an exponential outflow whose output is then delayed again, which double-counts the residence time and does not conserve the cohort. The fix routes the presymptomatic stock's own inflows (domestic Incubation plus imported Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad) through the pipeline, matching the model's established style.

1b. Wrong parameter — asymptomatic period used for the presymptomatic stage. The drain used Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections (6 days), which governs how long people stay in the Asymptomatic infectious stock and is already correctly used in Recovery without symptoms. The residence time of the Presymptomatic infectious stock is Presymptomatic_period (3 days). Note the original equation used Presymptomatic_period only as the delay-time argument while using the asymptomatic period as the drain rate — the two disagreed, so the variable had two conflicting residence times at once.

1c. Dimensional error — division instead of multiplication by Days per week. Presymptomatic_infectious / Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections / Days_per_week evaluates dimensionally to Person / Day / (Day/Week) = Person*Week/Day², not Person/Week. This is exactly the engine's warning: "Developing symptoms" has units: "Person/Week (People/Weeks)" but the equation suggests units: "PeopleWeeks/Days²"*. To convert a per-day rate into a per-week rate you multiply by days per week; dividing inverts the conversion. In the corrected equation the conversion appears only where it belongs — in the delay-time argument, Presymptomatic_period / Days_per_week = Day / (Day/Week) = Week — and the delayed quantity is already Person/Week, so the whole expression is Person/Week.

Numerical severity. The erroneous drain rate was Stock/6/7 per week — an effective 42-week residence time in a stage that should last 3 days, roughly a 100-fold under-drain. Imported cases in particular would have been trapped: with the outflow no longer tied to the stock's inflows, people arriving from abroad had no properly-scaled exit path from the presymptomatic stage.

Post-fix validation

  • Unit consistency: the corrected expression resolves to Person/Week throughout. I must flag transparently that the engine's unitWarnings field still reports the original People*Weeks/Days^2 message verbatim after the edit, the re-run, and a forced re-validation. That message describes the old equation, which no longer exists in the model — the current equation has no dimensional path to Days^2. This appears to be a cached warning the client has not refreshed rather than a live finding, but I am reporting it rather than suppressing it, since the engine is authoritative on unit consistency and I will not overrule it.
  • Non-negativity: all stocks have min = 0 across the run; nothing goes negative. The pipeline formulation guarantees this structurally, since the outflow is a delayed copy of the inflow — no MIN/MAX clamps were needed.
  • Conservation: final Total population = 16,930,550 = 17,000,000 initial − 69,450 Cumulative COVID deaths. Mass balance holds exactly; deaths are correctly excluded from Total population (and therefore from the contact-mixing denominator) while being accumulated separately.
  • Reference mode: epidemic seeded entirely by imported cases, growing through weeks 5–15, peaking around week 19–20 as social distancing reaches 0.7, then collapsing — followed by slow susceptible replenishment via Losing immunity and a low-level resurgence toward week 60. Behaviorally plausible for the structure.

Variables I checked and found correct

Infection (dimensionally clean at Person × 1/Week × Dmnl × Dmnl), Total incubation, Incubation / Asymptomatic incubation (the two shares sum to 1, conserving the exposed outflow), Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious, Recovery / Dying of COVID (CFR split sums to 1), Losing immunity (correctly uses no Days per week conversion, since Average immunity period is already in weeks), Total population, Infectious population, Contacts per person per week, and both graphical functions.

One item requiring your decision

The corrected equation now references Incubation and Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad, but the relationships section still carries the arrows generated from the erroneous equation: Presymptomatic infectious → Developing symptoms and Average period of asymptomatic infections → Developing symptoms. Bringing the causal arrows in line with the corrected equation would mean adding relationship entries, which you explicitly prohibited, so I have left the relationships section completely untouched. No new relationships, variables, or feedback loops were introduced, and no variable was renamed. If you want the diagram arrows to match the equations, say so and I will repoint those two arrows — it is bookkeeping to match the fix, not new structure.

errorExplanations.name: recovery_without_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Asymptomatic incubation' flow as input, not the 'Asymptomatic infectious' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model inspection tools and retrieving the current model.

Let me run the model as-is to capture baseline behavior before changing anything.

Confirmed a serious behavioral defect: Asymptomatic_infectious balloons to 7.8M and is still holding 4.6M people (27% of the population) at week 60, because its outflow is roughly 49x too small. Now let me apply the fixes.

The equations are in. The unit warning text still describes the old equation, so it's stale from the previous run. Let me re-run to refresh the engine's unit check.

Let me test whether the checker is mishandling my nested parentheses by using an algebraically equivalent flat form.

Behavior is now correct — the drain is exactly Asymptomatic × 7/6 (error 0.0). Let me verify conservation of people, accounting for the influx from abroad.

Conservation holds exactly (17,000,000 to within 0.2 people over 60 weeks, accounting for immigration). Now let me determine definitively whether that persistent unit warning is live or cached, by probing the checker with a deliberately different units string.

Definitive: I set the units to Person/Day, yet the warning still reports has units: "Person/Week". The checker is not re-reading the model — that warning is a cached artifact of the original broken equation. Reverting my probe:

Reverted correctly. Final run to leave the model in a clean simulated state:

All checks pass. Final state is clean.

Analysis complete: one substantive formulation error found and fixed

Error 1 (critical): Recovery without symptoms — double delay plus an inverted day-to-week conversion

Original:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

Fixed:

Asymptomatic_infectious*Days_per_week/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections

This single equation contained two compounding defects:

1a. The delay was applied twice. The first argument, Asymptomatic_infectious/period, is already a complete drain formulation — a stock divided by a residence time. Wrapping that in DELAY3 imposes a second, independent third-order delay on a flow that the stock's own accumulation had already delayed. Note the contrast with the model's other chain exits: Total_incubation, Developing_symptoms, Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious and Losing_immunity all apply DELAY3 to the inflow rate of their stock, never to a level-based drain. Mixing the two idioms in one equation delays the same cohort twice.

1b. The Day-to-Week conversion was upside down, and unparenthesized. A/period/Days_per_week parses as A/(period × Days_per_week) = A/42. The intended residence time is period/Days_per_week = 6/7 = 0.857 week, giving A/0.857 = A × 1.1667. The written form made the outflow 49 times too small, and produced the dimensions Person·Week/Day² rather than Person/Week — exactly the mismatch the engine's unit checker flagged.

Why it mattered behaviorally. I ran the model before and after. Originally the asymptomatic stock ballooned to 7.8 million and was still holding 4.58 million people — 27 percent of the entire population — permanently trapped in a supposedly 6-day infectious state at week 60. After the fix it peaks at 1.03 million and clears to 40. The outflow is now exactly Asymptomatic × 7/6 (verified to 0.0 absolute error against the simulated series).

Error 2 (minor, declaration): missing delayVariable sub-type

Total_incubation and Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious are plain variables whose equations use DELAY3, but neither declared subType: "delayVariable". Set on both so the delay state is declared consistently with the model's own conventions.

I also set uniflow: true on Recovery without symptoms and added documentation to the three variables I touched.

Important caveat on the choice of fix

The relationships section records exactly three inputs to this flow: Asymptomatic infectious, Average period of asymptomatic infections, and Days per week — precisely the inputs of a first-order drain, with no arrow from Asymptomatic incubation. Since you instructed me not to add relationships, I fixed it as a first-order drain, which preserves the causal structure exactly.

Be aware of the tradeoff: the model's other four chain exits use third-order DELAY3, so this branch now has an exponential (first-order) dwell-time distribution while the others are Erlang-3. Epidemiologically, DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, period/Days_per_week) would be more realistic and stylistically uniform — but it swaps the Asymptomatic infectious arrow for an Asymptomatic incubation one, changing the causal structure. Say the word if you want that instead.

Verification performed

  • No stock goes negative (all minima exactly 0; Susceptible bottoms at 3.83M).
  • Conservation holds: Total population + Cumulative deaths − cumulative influx from abroad stays at 17,000,000 to within 0.2 people over 60 weeks.
  • Chain ordering is physically sensible: Exposed peaks week 19.0, Presymptomatic 19.6, Asymptomatic 19.9, Symptomatic 20.2.
  • I checked all 34 variables for dimensional consistency by hand; no other mismatches.

One thing to know about the engine's unit warning

The engine still emits: "Recovery without symptoms" has units "Person/Week" but the equation suggests units "People*Weeks/Days^2". This warning is stale, not real. I verified this directly: I temporarily set the variable's units to Person/Day, and the checker still reported has units: "Person/Week" — it is not re-reading the model. The message text describes the original broken equation verbatim. I reverted the probe; units are back to Person/Week. The warning should clear when the model is reloaded in your client. I flag it explicitly because I do not want you to dismiss a future genuine warning as this cached one.

Not changed (flagging, not fixing)

  • Most variables still have no documentation field. Not a formulation error, but worth filling in.
  • Chance of contact with an susceptible person uses plain / rather than safe //. Harmless here since Total population cannot reach zero, but // would be more defensive.

Next I would suggest a get_feedback_information run to confirm the corrected asymptomatic branch now carries its intended share of transmission, and extreme-condition tests (social distancing pinned at 0 and at 1).
