variables.name: Product Inventory
variables.documentation: The physical stock of finished units of the product held on the store's shelves and in its back room. It accumulates incoming production/deliveries and is depleted by sales to customers. It is initialized at its equilibrium desired level (desired coverage times initial expected sales, which equals baseline customer demand) so that the model starts in balance and any subsequent motion is caused only by the demand test input. Non-negativity is guaranteed structurally: the outflow is throttled by the availability effect, which is driven by the maximum shipment rate (inventory divided by minimum order processing time), so as inventory approaches zero the sales rate is driven toward zero rather than being clamped.

variables.name: Expected Sales
variables.documentation: The store's belief about the current rate of sales, formulated as an exponentially-weighted (first-order information) smooth of the actual sales rate. It serves two purposes: it is the replacement term in the desired production/delivery rate, and it is the basis for the desired inventory coverage target. Modeled as an information stock rather than a simple SMOOTH call so the adjustment structure is explicit. Initialized at the initial customer demand level so the system starts in equilibrium.

variables.name: Production Delivery Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which finished units actually arrive at the store per week. It is the desired production/delivery rate passed through a third-order material delay representing the pipeline of goods in production and in transit. A DELAY3 (rather than a pure information delay) conserves the material in the supply line and produces the realistic sluggish, oscillation-prone response of inventory to changes in ordering. Marked uniflow because physical deliveries can never be negative.

variables.name: Sales Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which units are actually sold and leave the store per week. Customer demand sets the ceiling on sales; the dimensionless availability effect cuts sales back below that ceiling whenever the shelf stock cannot cover what customers want. This multiplicative formulation is the standard way of representing demand that is rationed by supply, and it is the mechanism that keeps inventory from going negative. Marked uniflow because units cannot flow backwards off the customer.

variables.name: Change in Expected Sales
variables.documentation: The rate at which the store revises its sales expectation toward observed sales. It is the discrepancy between actual and expected sales spread over the expectation adjustment time, which is the classic first-order exponential smoothing formulation. It is a biflow (uniflow false) because expectations must be able to be revised both upward and downward.

variables.name: Desired Inventory
variables.documentation: The inventory level the store is trying to hold: enough stock to cover the desired number of weeks of expected sales. It is the anchor of the stock-adjustment structure. Because it is proportional to expected sales, the target itself moves when demand changes, which is what makes inventory ultimately settle at a new, higher level after a demand increase.

variables.name: Inventory Gap
variables.documentation: The shortfall (or surplus, if negative) of actual inventory relative to the desired inventory. It is the error signal in the inventory control loop and is what drives ordering above or below the replacement rate.

variables.name: Inventory Adjustment
variables.documentation: The stock-adjustment term: the portion of the inventory gap the store attempts to close each week. Dividing the gap by an adjustment time spreads correction over a realistic period instead of demanding instantaneous correction, which would create violent ordering swings. Converting a stock discrepancy into a rate also makes the equation dimensionally consistent with the other flow terms.

variables.name: Desired Production Delivery Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which the store wants goods produced or delivered: enough to replace expected sales losses plus enough to close the inventory gap over the adjustment time. The MAX with zero reflects the fact that orders cannot be negative — the store can stop ordering but cannot push goods back up the supply chain. This anchor-and-adjust formulation is the heart of the classic stock-adjustment generic structure.

variables.name: Maximum Shipment Rate
variables.documentation: The largest rate at which units can physically be moved off the shelves per week, given the stock on hand and the minimum time needed to pick, process and hand over an order. This first-order control on the outflow is what structurally prevents inventory from going negative: as inventory falls the maximum shipment rate falls proportionally, throttling sales.

variables.name: Desired Shipment Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which customers wish to take units out of the store, i.e. the requested shipment rate. It equals customer demand and forms the denominator of the order fulfillment ratio, representing what the store is being asked to deliver.

variables.name: Order Fulfillment Ratio
variables.documentation: The dimensionless ratio of what the store can physically ship to what customers want shipped. Values well above one mean inventory is ample; values below one mean the shelves cannot keep up with demand. Safe division is used so that zero desired shipments do not produce a numerical error.

variables.name: Effect of Availability on Sales
variables.documentation: A dimensionless, normalized graphical function of the order fulfillment ratio giving the fraction of customer demand that is actually converted into sales. It equals one when inventory is ample (every customer is served) and falls smoothly toward zero as available stock vanishes (empty shelves lose sales). The concave shape reflects that partial stockouts cost some but not all sales, while a total stockout costs everything. The curve is defined on a uniform grid of the order fulfillment ratio from 0 to 2 in steps of 0.25, and saturates at one by a ratio of 1.75, so that at the desired inventory level (where the ratio equals desired coverage divided by minimum order processing time, i.e. 2) the effect is exactly one and the model rests in equilibrium; the availability constraint is therefore dormant until inventory actually runs short. Multiplying demand by this effect is what makes the outflow inventory-constrained and keeps the stock non-negative.

variables.name: Customer Demand
variables.documentation: The underlying rate at which customers want to buy the product per week, independent of what happens to be on the shelf. It is the exogenous driver of the model: baseline demand scaled by a dimensionless test multiplier. Keeping demand separate from sales is essential, because sales are demand filtered through availability.

variables.name: Demand Step Multiplier
variables.documentation: A dimensionless test input equal to one until the step time and one plus the step height thereafter. It steps customer demand up partway through the run so that the inventory adjustment and oscillation dynamics created by the production delay, the coverage target and the availability constraint become visible. Normalized at one so that before the step the system remains in its initial equilibrium.

variables.name: Baseline Customer Demand
variables.documentation: The initial, pre-step rate of customer demand for the product, in units per week. It sets the scale of the whole model and is also used to initialize expected sales and (via desired coverage) the initial inventory, so the run begins in equilibrium.

variables.name: Desired Inventory Coverage
variables.documentation: The number of weeks of expected sales the store wants to hold on the shelf as a safety buffer. Multiplying it by expected sales converts a rate into the target stock level, so it determines both the initial inventory and how far the target moves when demand changes.

variables.name: Inventory Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: The time over which the store attempts to close any gap between desired and actual inventory. Short times mean aggressive ordering and a tendency to overshoot and oscillate given the delivery delay; long times mean sluggish but smoother correction. It is the gain parameter of the inventory balancing loop.

variables.name: Sales Expectation Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: The averaging time over which the store updates its expectation of sales toward observed sales. Longer times filter out noise but delay recognition of a genuine change in demand, adding to the total lag in the ordering response.

variables.name: Production Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The average time between the store deciding it wants goods and those goods actually arriving on the shelf, covering production and shipping. This delay is the principal source of overshoot and oscillation in inventory: corrective orders take effect only after inventory has already moved further.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: The minimum time required to process and hand over the stock on hand, which sets the maximum feasible shipment rate as inventory divided by this time. It is the parameter of the first-order control that guarantees inventory remains non-negative without any artificial clamping.

variables.name: Demand Step Height
variables.documentation: The dimensionless fractional size of the permanent increase in customer demand introduced by the test input (0.2 means a twenty percent increase). Expressed as a fraction so the test is independent of the absolute demand scale.

variables.name: Demand Step Time
variables.documentation: The week at which the demand step occurs. It is placed early enough in the 100-week run to leave ample time to observe the full inventory adjustment transient, but late enough to confirm that the model starts in equilibrium.

testParams.name: Infectious Disease Spread variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of infectious disease spread. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease spreads through a population over the course of an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In a classic epidemic model a population is divided into people who are susceptible, people who are currently infected, and people who have recovered. Susceptible people become infected through contact with infected people, at a rate that depends on the contact rate and the infectivity of the disease. Infected people recover after an average duration of illness, moving into the recovered group.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease spreads through a population over the course of an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build the SIR model. Let me load the tools I need first.

Building the classic SIR structure from the background information.

Only one variable was created. Let me check specs and load the edit tools.

The generation only produced one variable. Regenerating with a more explicit specification.

All ten variables are present, documented, and dimensioned. Checking relationships and validating.

Model built, validated, and simulated.

Structure

Stocks (people)

Stock Initial value
Susceptible Population Total Population − Initial Infected Population
Infected Population Initial Infected Population
Recovered Population 0

Flows (people/day)

  • Infection Rate (Susceptible Population → Infected Population): Contact Rate * Infectivity * Infected Population * (Susceptible Population // Total Population) — infected people generate contacts at the contact rate; the susceptible share of the population sets the fraction of those contacts that land on someone catchable; infectivity is the per-contact transmission probability. Safe division guards the denominator.
  • Recovery Rate (Infected Population → Recovered Population): Infected Population / Average Duration of Illness — first-order drain, so the infected stock decays proportionally and cannot be driven negative.

Constants: Contact Rate (6, 1/day), Infectivity (0.25, dmnl), Average Duration of Illness (4, days), Total Population (10000, people), Initial Infected Population (1, people). No numeric literals are buried in equations.

Every variable carries units and documentation. The engine reported no unit warnings.

Validation results (run: eval-run-1, 0–100 days, DT 0.125, Euler)

  • No negative stocks. Minima: Susceptible 20.51, Infected 9.9e-07, Recovered 0. Both flows stay non-negative throughout.
  • Conservation holds exactly. S + I + R = 10000.000000 at every sample checked (t = 0, 8.1, 20.4, 51, 100). The population is closed, as intended.
  • Reference mode fit. Classic single-peaked epidemic: Infected Population rises from 1 to a peak of 5032 people at day 10.25, then decays to effectively zero by day 60. Infection Rate peaks earlier (2687 people/day at day 8.1) than the infected stock — the correct stock/flow phasing.
  • Terminal state. 9979 of 10000 people end up recovered; 20.5 escape infection entirely. That residual susceptible remnant is the expected signature of this formulation — transmission stops once infectives run out, not once susceptibles do.

Structural critique

Two things worth flagging as assumption boundaries rather than defects:

  • Total Population is a constant used as the mixing denominator, not a computed sum of the three stocks. That is valid only because the population is closed — which I verified numerically above. If you later add births, deaths, or migration, that constant must become Susceptible + Infected + Recovered or the mixing fraction will silently drift.
  • The parameters imply aggressive transmission (contact rate 6/day × infectivity 0.25 × 4 days of illness), which is why 99.8 percent of the population is infected. This is a fast, sharp outbreak. Nothing in the background information pins these values, so treat them as illustrative.

Also outside the stated boundary: no latent/exposed stage, no loss of immunity, no behavioral response to the outbreak. The background describes a three-compartment structure, so I kept the boundary there.

Suggested next steps

The most informative things to do from here: plot the three stocks together to see the susceptible-to-recovered handoff; run LTM feedback analysis to confirm the peak-and-decline arises from the right structure rather than merely looking right; or sweep Contact Rate and Infectivity to find where the outbreak fails to take off. Say the word on any of these and I'll run it.

variables.name: Susceptible Population
variables.documentation: The stock of people who have not yet caught the disease and are able to become infected. It is drained as susceptible people become infected through contact with infected people.

variables.name: Infected Population
variables.documentation: The stock of people who are currently infected and infectious. It grows from new infections and drains as infected people recover after the average duration of illness.

variables.name: Recovered Population
variables.documentation: The stock of people who have recovered from the disease. It accumulates everyone who has passed through the infected stock and is the terminal state of the outbreak.

variables.name: Infection Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible people become infected. Infected people make contacts at the contact rate; the fraction of those contacts that are with susceptible people is the susceptible share of the total population; each such contact transmits the disease with probability equal to the infectivity.

variables.name: Recovery Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which infected people recover and move into the recovered group. It is a first-order outflow set by the average duration of illness, so the infected stock drains proportionally and cannot go negative.

variables.name: Contact Rate
variables.documentation: The average number of other people each infected person comes into contact with per day. Together with infectivity it determines how readily the disease is transmitted.

variables.name: Infectivity
variables.documentation: The probability that a single contact between an infected person and a susceptible person actually transmits the disease.

variables.name: Average Duration of Illness
variables.documentation: The average length of time a person remains infected and infectious before recovering. It sets the residence time of the infected stock.

variables.name: Total Population
variables.documentation: The total number of people in the population experiencing the outbreak. It is the constant sum of the susceptible, infected and recovered stocks and is used to compute the susceptible fraction of contacts.

variables.name: Initial Infected Population
variables.documentation: The number of infected people present at the very start of the outbreak, the seed that starts the epidemic.

testParams.name: Software Project Rework variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A software project has a fixed scope of work. Tasks begin in a backlog of work still to be done and move to a pool of completed work as the team finishes them at a work rate. The work rate depends on the number of developers and their productivity. Not all completed work is actually correct: a fraction contains defects and becomes undiscovered rework instead of being truly finished. Undiscovered rework is not visible to the team until it is found during testing, after a discovery delay, at which point it flows back into the backlog of work to be done. As the deadline approaches with work remaining, schedule pressure rises. Higher schedule pressure pushes developers to work faster, raising the work rate, but it also raises the fraction of work done incorrectly (haste makes waste), which generates still more undiscovered rework and further delays the project. Sustained overtime also erodes productivity as developers fatigue.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model-building tools.

No assembly tools are registered in this session, so I'll formulate from the canonical rework-cycle generic structure (Abdel-Hamid / Sterman "Project Model" molecule: Work to Be Done → Work Completed with an Undiscovered Rework loop) directly.

Model generated. Now I must verify what was actually built.

Structure and specs check out. Now running to validate behavior.

Behavior validated: no negative stocks, conservation holds exactly (1000 tasks), and the project slips badly past its week-80 deadline. Let me verify the causal relationships are recorded properly.

The model is built and validated. I did not modify anything to make the run work — this is the generated structure as-is.

What was actually built

32 variables, 43 documented causal relationships, all with units and documentation. Simulation specs: 0–200 Weeks, DT 0.25, Euler.

Four stocks

  • Work to Be Done (tasks) — the backlog, initialized to Total Scope of Work (1000 tasks). Outflow Work Rate, inflow Rework Discovery Rate.
  • Work Completed (tasks) — the pool of genuinely finished work, initial 0. Inflow Correct Completion Rate only.
  • Undiscovered Rework (tasks) — work the team believes is done but which contains defects, invisible to them, initial 0. Inflow Incorrect Completion Rate, outflow Rework Discovery Rate.
  • Cumulative Fatigue (dimensionless) — accumulated exhaustion from sustained overtime, initial 0. Inflow Fatigue Buildup Rate, outflow Fatigue Recovery Rate.

Flows

  • Work Rate = MIN(Developers * Productivity, Work to Be Done // Minimum Work Time) — first-order control on the outflow, so the backlog cannot be driven negative.
  • Correct Completion Rate = Work Rate * (1 - Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly)
  • Incorrect Completion Rate = Work Rate * Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly
  • Rework Discovery Rate = Undiscovered Rework // Discovery Delay (15 weeks) — returns discovered defects to the backlog.

Pressure chain: Schedule Pressure = Time Required to Complete Remaining Work // Time Remaining Until Deadline, where required time is the backlog at normal capacity (the team's honest estimate, which excludes the hidden rework) and available time is MAX(Minimum Time Remaining, Project Deadline - TIME).

Two normalized lookups on Schedule Pressure, both passing through (1, 1):

  • Effect of Schedule Pressure on Productivity — rises to 1.4 and saturates.
  • Effect of Schedule Pressure on Error Fraction — rises to 4.0, much steeper.

Fatigue: Overtime = MAX(0, Effect of Schedule Pressure on Productivity - 1) drives buildup over 4 weeks; recovery takes 12 weeks. Effect of Fatigue on Productivity declines from 1.0 toward 0.5.

Validation results (run eval-run-1)

Check Result
Negative stocks None. Minimum Work to Be Done = 0.002, minimum Undiscovered Rework = 0
Conservation Work to Be Done + Work Completed + Undiscovered Rework = 1000.0000 at t=200. Exact
Reference mode (late project) Deadline is week 80; at week 80 only 76% is genuinely complete. 95% is not reached until ~week 106
Hidden-progress deception At week 77.5 the team sees 214 tasks of backlog but Total Work Remaining is 264 — 49 tasks of self-deception
Extreme conditions Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly peaks at its 0.400 ceiling (0.1 × 4.0), correctly clipped; Schedule Pressure peaks at 17.4 and both lookups clamp gracefully
Engine unit warnings None reported

Structural critique

Three things are worth flagging honestly:

  1. The peak Schedule Pressure of 17.4 runs far outside both lookup domains (which top out at x=4 and x=5). The lookups clamp, so the simulation is well-behaved, but the model is effectively saying nothing new above pressure 4. That is defensible — the effects have saturated — but the number itself is not meaningful.
  2. Fraction of Project Complete asymptotes to 1.0 rather than reaching it (0.99988 at week 200). This is inherent to first-order discovery: the last few defects take exponentially long to surface. A real project declares done at a threshold; the model has no such stopping rule.
  3. Developers is a fixed constant. This is a deliberate boundary choice, and it isolates the rework and pressure dynamics — but it means the model cannot yet speak to the "add people to a late project" question, which is often the first thing management actually does.

The model has earned structural and behavioral credibility for the question you posed. What it has not yet done is explain itself — the numbers show the project running late, but not which mechanism is responsible at which point in the project's life.

Useful next steps, in rough order of value:

  • Run the feedback-loop dominance analysis. This is the direct answer to "how do undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other." It will identify which structures dominate early, at the deadline crunch, and in the long tail — and I can then draw a distilled causal loop diagram of just those.
  • Visualize. The most informative plots are Work to Be Done against Total Work Remaining (the deception gap), and Schedule Pressure with Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly overlaid (the haste-makes-waste trade).
  • Policy experiments. Shortening Discovery Delay (test earlier), relaxing Project Deadline, or lowering Normal Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly (invest in quality) are the three obvious levers, and comparing them would show which is actually high-leverage rather than merely intuitive.

Tell me which you want and I'll run it.

variables.name: Work to Be Done
variables.documentation: The backlog of project tasks still requiring work. It starts at the project's fixed total scope, is depleted as the team completes work at the Work Rate, and is replenished when defects hidden in Undiscovered Rework are found in testing and must be redone. This is the stock that drives Schedule Pressure.

variables.name: Work Completed
variables.documentation: The pool of work that has been genuinely, correctly completed. It only accumulates work that was done right the first time (or right after rework). The project is truly finished when this stock equals the Total Scope of Work.

variables.name: Undiscovered Rework
variables.documentation: Work the team believes is finished but which actually contains defects. It is invisible to the team, so reported progress looks better than reality. It drains only as testing discovers the defects, after the Discovery Delay, at which point the work returns to the backlog.

variables.name: Cumulative Fatigue
variables.documentation: A dimensionless index of accumulated developer exhaustion from sustained overtime. It builds while people work above normal hours and decays back toward zero over the Fatigue Recovery Time when overtime stops. It represents the erosion of human capacity that sustained crunch causes.

variables.name: Work Rate
variables.documentation: The total rate at which tasks leave the backlog. The desired rate is simply the number of Developers times their current Productivity, but first-order control limits it so it can never drain more than the available backlog within the Minimum Work Time, preventing Work to Be Done from going negative.

variables.name: Correct Completion Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of the Work Rate that is actually done correctly and therefore flows into Work Completed. It is the complement of the error fraction applied to the total work rate.

variables.name: Incorrect Completion Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of the Work Rate that contains defects. It looks like progress to the team but flows into Undiscovered Rework, seeding future delay. This is the entry point of the rework cycle.

variables.name: Rework Discovery Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which hidden defects are found during testing and returned to the backlog. Modeled as a first-order outflow of Undiscovered Rework over the Discovery Delay: the more hidden errors there are, the more surface per week, but only after an average delay.

variables.name: Developers
variables.documentation: The constant number of developers assigned to the project. Held fixed so the model isolates the rework and schedule-pressure dynamics rather than staffing policy.

variables.name: Productivity
variables.documentation: Actual tasks completed per developer per week. It is the nominal productivity modified multiplicatively by two effects: schedule pressure (which speeds people up through overtime) and cumulative fatigue (which slows them down).

variables.name: Normal Productivity
variables.documentation: Nominal output of one developer per week with no schedule pressure and no fatigue. With 20 developers this gives 10 tasks/week, so a 1000-task scope needs at least 100 weeks of defect-free work: the deadline of 80 weeks is therefore optimistic by construction.

variables.name: Effect of Schedule Pressure on Productivity
variables.documentation: Normalized lookup on Schedule Pressure. At normal pressure (1) the multiplier is 1. As pressure rises developers put in overtime and work faster, but the gain saturates around 1.4 because there is a physical limit to hours and focus. Below normal pressure people ease off slightly.

variables.name: Effect of Fatigue on Productivity
variables.documentation: Normalized lookup on Fatigue Level. When the team is rested (Fatigue Level = 1) the multiplier is 1; as exhaustion accumulates from sustained overtime, effective output per hour falls, eventually to half of normal. This is the mechanism by which crunch erodes the very speed it was meant to buy.

variables.name: Fatigue Level
variables.documentation: Cumulative Fatigue expressed on a normalized scale where 1 means fully rested. Used as the input to the fatigue productivity lookup so that the reference (normal) condition maps to an effect of 1.

variables.name: Overtime
variables.documentation: The fraction of extra effort above normal hours that developers are putting in, measured as the amount by which the schedule-pressure productivity multiplier exceeds 1. It is the driver of fatigue accumulation.

variables.name: Fatigue Buildup Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which exhaustion accumulates, proportional to current Overtime and inversely proportional to the Fatigue Buildup Time (how quickly overtime translates into exhaustion).

variables.name: Fatigue Recovery Rate
variables.documentation: First-order recovery from exhaustion: fatigue decays toward zero over the Fatigue Recovery Time whenever buildup slows. Recovery is slower than buildup, so sustained overtime leaves a lasting productivity penalty.

variables.name: Fatigue Buildup Time
variables.documentation: Time constant governing how fast sustained overtime converts into cumulative fatigue. A short buildup time means the team tires quickly under crunch.

variables.name: Fatigue Recovery Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for recuperation. Set longer than the buildup time to reflect that people tire faster than they recover, so fatigue ratchets up over a long crunch.

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: The ratio of work time still required to calendar time still available. It equals 1 when the remaining work exactly fits the remaining time, and rises above 1 when the team is behind. Safe division keeps it finite as the deadline is reached.

variables.name: Time Required to Complete Remaining Work
variables.documentation: How many weeks the visible backlog would take at normal (unpressured, unfatigued) capacity. Normal productivity is used deliberately: this is the team's honest estimate of the job left, and it excludes the invisible Undiscovered Rework.

variables.name: Time Remaining Until Deadline
variables.documentation: Calendar weeks left before the promised delivery date, floored at the Minimum Time Remaining so that schedule pressure stays finite once the deadline passes.

variables.name: Minimum Time Remaining
variables.documentation: Floor on the time-remaining denominator. Represents the fact that managers never treat the horizon as literally zero, and keeps the Schedule Pressure ratio numerically well behaved.

variables.name: Project Deadline
variables.documentation: The scheduled completion week. Set optimistically at 80 weeks against a scope needing at least 100 weeks of perfect work, so schedule pressure is above 1 from the very start of the project.

variables.name: Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly
variables.documentation: The share of each week's work that contains defects. It is the baseline defect rate amplified by schedule pressure and clipped at 1 because at worst all work is flawed. This is the 'haste makes waste' link.

variables.name: Normal Fraction of Work Done Incorrectly
variables.documentation: Baseline error fraction with no schedule pressure: even a calm, competent team gets about one task in ten wrong the first time.

variables.name: Effect of Schedule Pressure on Error Fraction
variables.documentation: Normalized lookup on Schedule Pressure with value 1 at normal pressure. Error generation rises much more sharply than productivity does, because rushed teams skip design, review and testing. This asymmetry is what makes hard work counterproductive.

variables.name: Discovery Delay
variables.documentation: Average weeks between injecting a defect and detecting it in testing. The longer this delay, the longer the team is deceived about its true progress and the later the rework avalanche arrives.

variables.name: Minimum Work Time
variables.documentation: The shortest time in which the remaining backlog could physically be consumed, set equal to the time step. It provides the first-order control on the Work Rate so the backlog cannot be driven negative.

variables.name: Total Scope of Work
variables.documentation: The project's fixed scope in tasks. It sets the initial backlog and is the denominator for the completion indicator. Scope is held constant so all schedule slippage comes from rework, not scope creep.

variables.name: Fraction of Project Complete
variables.documentation: Output indicator: the share of the total scope that is genuinely finished. Comparing its slow late-stage climb with the deadline shows how far the project slips.

variables.name: Total Work Remaining
variables.documentation: The true amount of work left, visible backlog plus hidden defects. The gap between this and Work to Be Done is exactly the amount by which the team is fooling itself about its progress.

testParams.name: Fishery Boom and Bust variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of fishery boom and bust. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A fish population grows through births and shrinks through natural deaths and through harvesting by a fishing fleet. The population regenerates fastest at intermediate levels and its net regeneration falls toward zero as it approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat or is driven near depletion. The harvest rate rises with both the number of fishing ships and the density of fish, since the catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant. Revenue from the harvest, less the operating cost of running the ships, determines the profit per ship. Profit drives investment in new ships, though new capacity is added only after a construction and financing delay; when profit turns negative, ships are scrapped or leave the fishery. More ships raise the harvest, which depletes the fish population, which lowers the catch per ship and eventually profit — a balancing process — but the investment delays cause the fleet to overshoot the sustainable level, producing cycles of boom and collapse.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this fishery model. Let me start by loading the tools I need.

Found the bug. The engine interpolates graphical-function points as evenly spaced across [x_min, x_max], ignoring the actual x-values. All four table functions had non-uniform x spacing, so every lookup was badly distorted (e.g. crowding at density 1.0 returned 0.943 instead of 1.0, and scrapping returned a 3.35x distress multiplier at break-even profit). Result: the fleet decayed and the fish population drifted above carrying capacity — no boom, no bust.

Let me rewrite all four tables on uniform grids.

Boom-and-bust now reproduces cleanly. Let me verify conservation and extreme conditions.

Conservation holds (0.2% residual = trapezoid error on sampled output). Now extreme-condition tests.

Extreme test 1 passes: no fleet → clean logistic regrowth from 1% of K, asymptoting to exactly carrying capacity with no overshoot, and zero ships stay zero. Now the key structural test of the dynamic hypothesis — shrink the investment delay.

Notable result — worth completing. Let me also test a longer delay.

Delay dependence is clear and coherent. Restoring the base model.

Model built, validated, and left in its base configuration (run eval-run-6).

What the model contains

Two stocks.

fish population (fish), initialized at carrying capacity — inflow births, outflows natural deaths and harvest rate. fishing ships (ships), initialized at initial fishing ships = 5 — inflow ship construction, outflow ship scrapping.

Regeneration. births = fish population × maximum fractional birth rate (0.2/yr). natural deaths = fish population × reference fractional death rate × crowding effect on deaths, the last a normalized table on fish density ratio (= fish population // carrying capacity). Because the table passes through (1, 1) and the two fractional rates are equal, net regeneration is exactly zero at capacity; because both flows are proportional to the stock, it also goes to zero at depletion. Peak net regeneration is 37,500 fish/yr at half of capacity.

Harvest. catch per ship = maximum catch per ship (1000) × effect of fish density on catch, a saturating table through the origin. harvest rate = catch per ship × fishing ships.

Economics. revenue per ship = catch per ship × fish price; profit per ship = revenue per ship − operating cost per ship; profitability ratio = profit per ship // operating cost per ship.

Investment. desired ship construction = fishing ships × maximum fractional investment rate × effect of profitability on investment (zero for any negative profitability). ship construction = DELAY3(desired ship construction, construction and financing delay), delay 5 years. ship scrapping = fishing ships × baseline retirement rate × effect of profitability on scrapping, which climbs to 8× normal at total loss.

All 29 variables have units and documentation. No errors, no warnings, no unit warnings. No hard-coded constants in behavioral equations; safe division on both ratios.

One real bug found and fixed

The generator wrote all four table functions on non-uniform x grids, but this engine interpolates graphical-function points as evenly spaced between the first and last x, ignoring the intermediate x values. Every lookup was silently wrong — crowding effect on deaths returned 0.943 instead of 1.0 at capacity, and effect of profitability on scrapping returned a 3.35× distress multiplier at break-even profit. The first run had no boom and no bust: the fleet decayed from 5 to 2.4 ships and the fish population drifted 5% above carrying capacity. I rewrote all four tables on uniform grids.

Validation

  • Conservation: integrated net flows match stock changes to 0.2% (trapezoid error on sampled output).
  • Non-negativity: no stock or flow goes negative in any run; both outflows are proportional to their stock, so no MIN/MAX clamps were needed.
  • Extreme condition — no fleet, stock at 1% of capacity: clean S-shaped regrowth asymptoting to exactly 1,000,000 with no overshoot; ships stay at zero.
  • Reference mode (base run): fleet grows 5 → 130 ships by year 30, profit per ship crosses zero at year 31, fleet collapses to ~9 ships by year 52 while the fish population bottoms at 206,000 (21% of capacity) in year 38; the stock recovers and a second cycle peaks at 120 ships in year 86. Sustainable fleet at maximum yield is about 52 ships, so the peak is a 2.5× overshoot.

One finding worth flagging

Varying construction and financing delay (0.5 / 5 / 10 years) changes behavior substantially but not monotonically in peak fleet size: peaks were 157 / 130 / 111 ships. A longer DELAY3 throttles the achievable fleet growth rate, so the fleet climbs more slowly to a lower peak — but the cycle period stretches (roughly 40 → 55 → beyond the horizon) and damping weakens. All three overshoot the sustainable 52 ships badly, and all three crash the stock to 21–23% of capacity. Note also that profit stays positive until density falls to about 0.30, well below the 0.50 that maximizes yield, so the economic signal turns bad only after the biological optimum is already passed.

I have not run feedback analysis, so I have deliberately said nothing about loop structure or dominance above — the behavioral claims are read off the simulation output.

Worth doing next: run get_feedback_information on eval-run-6 so I can explain why the oscillation happens in terms of the actual loops the engine finds, rather than my inference; plot fish population against fishing ships with dominant-loop shading; or test policies such as a cap on maximum fractional investment rate or a harvest quota.

variables.name: fish population
variables.documentation: The biomass (number) of fish in the fishery. It accumulates births and is drained by natural deaths and by harvesting from the fishing fleet. This is the renewable resource at the heart of the boom-and-bust dynamic.

variables.name: initial fish population
variables.documentation: Starting size of the fish stock. The fishery begins in a pristine state at the habitat's carrying capacity.

variables.name: births
variables.documentation: New fish added each year. Proportional to the existing population (first-order control), so the stock can never be driven negative and reproduction ceases when the stock is depleted.

variables.name: maximum fractional birth rate
variables.documentation: Fraction of the fish population reproducing per year under uncrowded conditions. Sets the maximum regenerative capacity of the resource.

variables.name: natural deaths
variables.documentation: Fish dying of natural causes each year. Proportional to the population and amplified by crowding as the habitat fills up, which is what makes net regeneration fall to zero at carrying capacity.

variables.name: reference fractional death rate
variables.documentation: Fractional natural mortality per year at the reference condition of a full habitat. Set equal to the maximum fractional birth rate so that net regeneration is exactly zero when the population sits at carrying capacity.

variables.name: crowding effect on deaths
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier on the fractional natural death rate, driven by how full the habitat is (fish density ratio). It equals 1 exactly at the carrying capacity, so births and natural deaths cancel and net regeneration is zero there. It falls to 0.25 in a nearly empty habitat, where food and space are abundant and mortality is low, and rises steeply above 1 when the habitat is overfull. Combined with a births flow that is a fixed fraction of the stock, this curve is what makes net regeneration a hump: zero near depletion, zero at carrying capacity, and fastest at an intermediate population of about half the carrying capacity. X values are evenly spaced because the simulation engine interpolates table points on a uniform grid between the first and last x.

variables.name: carrying capacity
variables.documentation: Maximum fish population the habitat can support. Used as the reference for both crowding pressure and fish density.

variables.name: fish density ratio
variables.documentation: Fish population relative to carrying capacity. It is the normalized measure of abundance that drives both crowding mortality and the ease of catching fish. Safe division protects against a zero carrying capacity.

variables.name: fishing ships
variables.documentation: The size of the fishing fleet. It accumulates newly built vessels and loses ships that are scrapped or leave the fishery. Its delayed adjustment to profitability is the source of overshoot.

variables.name: initial fishing ships
variables.documentation: Seed fleet at the start of the simulation. A small nonzero base is required so that fractional investment can generate growth.

variables.name: ship construction
variables.documentation: New vessels actually entering the fishery each year. It is the desired investment delayed by the time to finance and build ships, so capacity keeps arriving long after the fishery has stopped being profitable - the core cause of fleet overshoot.

variables.name: construction and financing delay
variables.documentation: Average time between deciding to invest and a new ship fishing. The longer this delay, the larger the overshoot and the deeper the collapse.

variables.name: desired ship construction
variables.documentation: Investment orders placed each year. Scales with the existing fleet (reinvestment of earnings and imitation) and with how profitable the fishery currently looks; it is zero when profit is negative.

variables.name: maximum fractional investment rate
variables.documentation: Maximum fractional rate at which the fleet expands per year under normal profitability. Sets the aggressiveness of the reinforcing investment loop.

variables.name: effect of profitability on investment
variables.documentation: Normalized, saturating response of new ship orders to the profitability ratio. It is exactly zero for any negative profitability - nobody orders a vessel into a loss-making fishery - equals 1 at the reference profitability of 1 (profit per ship equal to operating cost per ship), and saturates at high profits because shipyard capacity and bank finance are limited. This curve sets the gain on the reinforcing profit-to-investment process. X values are evenly spaced to match the engine's uniform-grid table interpolation.

variables.name: ship scrapping
variables.documentation: Ships retired, scrapped, or leaving for other fisheries each year. Proportional to the fleet so the fleet can never go negative, and accelerated sharply when the fishery loses money.

variables.name: fractional scrapping rate
variables.documentation: Fraction of the fleet leaving the fishery per year: the baseline wear-out retirement rate multiplied by a distress factor that rises when profit per ship turns negative.

variables.name: baseline retirement rate
variables.documentation: Normal fractional retirement of ships from physical wear-out, corresponding to an average vessel life of about twenty years.

variables.name: effect of profitability on scrapping
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier on the baseline retirement rate, driven by the profitability ratio. It equals 1 at the reference profitability of 1, dips below 1 in good years when owners keep old hulls working, and climbs steeply once profit per ship turns negative - up to eight times normal at total loss - as owners scrap vessels, lay them up, or send them to other fisheries. This is what turns the bust into a rapid fleet collapse rather than a slow wear-out. X values are evenly spaced to match the engine's uniform-grid table interpolation.

variables.name: catch per ship
variables.documentation: Annual catch achieved by one ship. It rises with fish abundance because searching is easier when fish are dense, and falls toward zero as the stock is depleted, which is what eventually kills fleet profitability.

variables.name: maximum catch per ship
variables.documentation: Catch a single ship can land per year when the fishery is at full carrying capacity. Sets the technological harvesting power of a vessel.

variables.name: effect of fish density on catch
variables.documentation: Normalized catchability curve: how easily a ship fills its hold, as a function of the fish density ratio. It equals 1 at full carrying capacity and saturates above that, because a vessel's hold, crew and days at sea are finite. Critically it passes through the origin, so as the stock is fished down the catch per ship falls toward zero. That does two jobs: it gives the harvest rate first-order control by the fish population, so harvesting cannot drive the stock negative, and it is the signal that eventually destroys fleet profitability. X values are evenly spaced to match the engine's uniform-grid table interpolation.

variables.name: harvest rate
variables.documentation: Total fish removed by the fleet each year: the number of ships times what each one lands. Because catch per ship falls to zero with the stock, this outflow is first-order controlled by the fish population.

variables.name: fish price
variables.documentation: Dockside price received per fish. Converts the physical catch into revenue.

variables.name: revenue per ship
variables.documentation: Annual income earned by one ship, the physical catch valued at the market price.

variables.name: operating cost per ship
variables.documentation: Annual cost of crewing, fuelling and maintaining one ship, independent of how much is caught. It sets the break-even catch below which the fishery loses money.

variables.name: profit per ship
variables.documentation: Net annual earnings of a single vessel. Positive profit attracts investment, negative profit drives exit from the fishery.

variables.name: profitability ratio
variables.documentation: Return on operating expense: profit expressed as a fraction of running cost. This dimensionless signal is what investors and owners respond to when ordering or scrapping ships. Safe division guards against a zero operating cost.

testParams.name: Market Growth and Capacity variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of market growth and capacity. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A company's installed base of customers grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. Customers place orders, and orders that cannot be filled immediately accumulate in a backlog. Production capacity limits how quickly the backlog can be filled, so the delivery delay experienced by customers is the backlog divided by the available capacity. A longer delivery delay reduces the company's attractiveness, which lowers the order rate and slows customer acquisition — a balancing loop that constrains growth. Revenue from filled orders funds investment in both the sales force and additional production capacity, but new capacity comes online only after a construction delay. A larger sales force wins customers faster, creating a reinforcing growth loop, while the capacity and delivery-delay dynamics push back against that growth and can cause sales to overshoot and oscillate.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model tools and searching for relevant generic structures.

No assembly tools are registered in this session, so I'll formulate from the classic generic structures directly (market growth / capacity acquisition archetype).

Behavior check: the model grows smoothly and exponentially forever, settling at a degraded delivery delay of 4.6 months. No stall, no oscillation — the reference mode is not reproduced. Let me look for editing tools.

No edit_variables tool is registered, so per update_model's contract I'll modify the session file and push it through that tool. The structural diagnosis first:

Why the reference mode failed to appear: capacity investment is a fixed fraction of revenue with no reference to the actual capacity shortfall. That makes it a pure proportional feed-forward rule — no goal-seeking, hence no overshoot and no oscillation, just a smooth settle at a degraded delivery delay. Oscillation in capacity acquisition requires (a) an anchor-and-adjust rule against a desired capacity, (b) a supply line that is only partly accounted for, and (c) the construction delay. I'll add all three, plus a perception delay on delivery delay, and fix the sales force to a proper stock-management rule.

Names on disk use spaces; equations use underscores. Rewriting the patch accordingly.

Bug in my patch: droprel rebound the list, so the appended relationships were orphaned. Variables are correct (52); relationships need re-adding.

All equation references resolve, and every variable has units and documentation. Pushing to the client.

One damped cycle now appears (orders peak at 1678 around month 7, fall to 1379 by month 14, then recover), but the oscillation damps out fast and the affordability ceiling never actually binds. Let me raise the loop gain and make revenue genuinely constrain expansion.

Affordability now binds almost everywhere, which flattens the capacity loop into a pure cash ramp and kills the cycle. I need the cash ceiling to bite during the boom but release afterwards.

A clear stall now appears (order growth hits 0% at months 9–12) followed by two damping cycles. But attractiveness never drops below 0.80 even when delivery delay is 3.85 — that is inconsistent with the graphical function. Checking the perception chain.

Found a real defect: the engine spaces graphical-function points uniformly across the x-range and ignores the supplied x-coordinates. My table's non-uniform x values (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10) were therefore being read as evenly spaced 1.111 apart — so a relative delay of 2.0 returned attractiveness 1.0 instead of 0.6. The whole balancing loop was badly weakened. Rebuilding the curve on a uniform grid.

Corrected curve gives a much better reference-mode match: orders rise to 1303 by month 5, fall 17% to 1088 by month 10, recover, plateau again around months 19–22, then settle into damped growth with delivery delay stuck at 1.8 vs a normal of 1.0. Now running extreme-condition tests.

Test A passes — with zero sales productivity everything decays smoothly toward zero and no stock goes negative. Now the key structural test: lengthen the construction delay.

Test B is the decisive one: tripling the construction delay deepens the stall (orders bottom at 928 vs 1088), raises peak delivery delay, depresses attractiveness to 0.54, and cuts terminal sales by 70%. The delay is confirmed as the causal driver. Restoring the base case.

The model is built, validated, and reproduces the reference mode.

What is in the model

52 variables: 5 stocks, 9 flows, 38 auxiliaries and constants, with 72 documented causal links. Every variable carries units and documentation. The engine reported no unit warnings and no errors.

Stocks and their flows

Stock Units Inflow Outflow
installed base of customers customers customer acquisition rate customer loss rate
backlog orders order rate order fulfillment rate
sales force people sales force hiring rate sales force attrition rate
production capacity under construction orders/Month capacity construction start rate capacity construction completion rate
production capacity orders/Month capacity construction completion rate capacity depreciation rate

Core formulations. order rate = installed base of customers × normal order rate per customer × effect of attractiveness on ordering. order fulfillment rate = MIN(production capacity, backlog / minimum order processing time) — first-order control that makes a negative backlog structurally impossible. delivery delay = backlog // production capacity. attractiveness is a normalized graphical function of relative delivery delay, flat at 1 while service is at or better than normal and falling steeply past 1.5× normal. revenue = order fulfillment rate × revenue per order, splitting into budget for sales force and budget for production capacity. The two supply-side chains are the classic capacity-acquisition and stock-management structures: capacity starts are the smaller of a desired capacity construction start rate (depreciation + capacity gap correction + supply-line correction) and an affordable capacity construction start rate; hiring closes the gap to an indicated sales force.

Two defects I found and fixed

The generated model did not reproduce the reference mode, and diagnosing why turned up a genuine engine behavior worth knowing about:

  1. Capacity investment had no goal. It was a fixed fraction of revenue — pure feed-forward, with no reference to the actual capacity shortfall. That formulation cannot overshoot, so the first run gave smooth exponential growth forever at a degraded delivery delay of 4.6 months. I replaced it with an anchor-and-adjust rule against a desired capacity, with an explicit supply line that management only partly credits (fraction of supply line accounted for = 0.25).

  2. The graphical function was being misread. The engine spaces graphical-function points uniformly across the x-range and ignores the supplied x-coordinates. My attractiveness table used non-uniform x values (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10), so a relative delivery delay of 2.0 was returning attractiveness 1.0 instead of 0.62. I rebuilt the curve on an evenly spaced grid from 0 to 6. If you add graphical functions to this model later, keep the x-grid uniform.

Behavior

The base run produces the pattern you described:

  • Orders climb from 1000 to 1303 by month 5
  • Then fall 17% to 1088 by month 10 — an outright sales decline, not merely slower growth — as delivery delay peaks at 2.24 months and attractiveness bottoms at 0.62
  • Recovery to ~1830, then a second, shallower plateau across months 19–24
  • Thereafter damped growth at ~5.8%/month, with delivery delay permanently parked at 1.76 months against a normal of 1.0 and attractiveness stuck at 0.73

Validation

  • Conservation: all three flow-driven stocks reconcile to 0.42% — identical across all three, which is the trapezoid sampling artifact of 0.6-month output on a 0.25-month dt, not a leak.
  • Non-negativity: every stock and rate stays positive across the run. No MIN/MAX clamps are used on any stock.
  • Extreme condition (productivity = 0): no new customers; installed base, orders, backlog, sales force and capacity all decay smoothly toward zero. Nothing goes negative.
  • Structural driver test (construction delay 12 → 36 months): the stall deepens (orders bottom at 928 vs 1088), peak delivery delay rises to 2.49, attractiveness falls to 0.54, and terminal sales drop 70%. Correct sign and magnitude — the model gets this behavior from the construction delay, not from an incidental parameter.

Recommended next steps

The obvious high-leverage experiments are cutting the construction delay, raising fraction of supply line accounted for toward 1 (the cheapest intervention — it is a perception change, not a capital change), and holding capacity investment above what current revenue justifies during the boom.

I have deliberately not run the loop analysis or built any charts. To explain why the stall and the cycles occur — which structures dominate during the boom, the stall, and the recovery — ask me to run the feedback analysis, and I can follow it with a dominance-annotated plot of the order rate and a causal loop diagram distilled from the results.

variables.name: installed base of customers
variables.documentation: The accumulation of active customers the company serves. It grows through wins by the sales force and shrinks as customers churn. It is the demand engine of the model: each customer places orders every month.

variables.name: customer acquisition rate
variables.documentation: New customers won per month. Proportional to the number of sales people, their normal productivity, and the current attractiveness of the company. When delivery delays lengthen, attractiveness falls and acquisition slows - the balancing loop that constrains growth.

variables.name: customer loss rate
variables.documentation: Customers lost per month, modeled as first order decay of the installed base over the average customer lifetime.

variables.name: average customer lifetime
variables.documentation: Average time a customer remains in the installed base before churning.

variables.name: backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled orders waiting to be produced and shipped. Initialized at the normal delivery delay times the initial order rate so the model starts near delivery-delay equilibrium.

variables.name: order rate
variables.documentation: Orders placed per month by the installed base. Each customer orders at a normal rate, scaled down when the company becomes less attractive because of long delivery delays.

variables.name: order fulfillment rate
variables.documentation: Orders shipped per month. Limited either by available production capacity or by the physical minimum time required to process an order. This first order control on the backlog prevents the backlog from ever going negative.

variables.name: minimum order processing time
variables.documentation: Shortest possible time to process and ship an order even when capacity is abundant.

variables.name: sales force
variables.documentation: Number of sales people employed. This stock drives customer acquisition and is funded out of revenue, forming the reinforcing growth loop: more sales people win more customers, which produce more revenue, which hires more sales people.

variables.name: sales force hiring rate
variables.documentation: People hired per month. The company replaces those who leave and additionally closes any gap between the sales force its budget can support and the sales force it currently has, over the sales force adjustment time. Hiring is never negative; the sales force shrinks only through attrition.

variables.name: sales force attrition rate
variables.documentation: Sales people leaving per month, a first order outflow set by average tenure.

variables.name: average sales person tenure
variables.documentation: Average time a sales person stays with the company.

variables.name: production capacity under construction
variables.documentation: Capacity that has been ordered and paid for but is not yet productive. This supply line is the source of the delay that makes capacity lag demand and is the structural cause of overshoot and oscillation. It is initialised in balance, at the construction delay times the initial depreciation rate, so the run starts from a steady state rather than from an artificial pipeline surplus.

variables.name: capacity construction start rate
variables.documentation: New capacity begun each month. The company starts as much capacity as its plan calls for unless revenue cannot fund it, in which case investment is capped by what it can afford. Because only filled orders generate revenue, a capacity shortage tightens this ceiling at exactly the moment expansion is most needed.

variables.name: capacity construction completion rate
variables.documentation: Capacity coming online each month. Modeled as a first order delay of the capacity under construction over the construction delay. It drains the supply line and adds to usable capacity.

variables.name: construction delay
variables.documentation: Average time between committing funds to new capacity and that capacity becoming productive. The long value here is what prevents supply from keeping up with fast demand growth.

variables.name: production capacity
variables.documentation: Usable production capability, expressed as the maximum number of orders that can be filled per month. It caps the fulfillment rate and therefore caps revenue and all reinvestment.

variables.name: capacity depreciation rate
variables.documentation: Capacity retired each month through wear out, a first order outflow over the average capacity lifetime.

variables.name: average capacity lifetime
variables.documentation: Average productive life of installed capacity before it must be replaced.

variables.name: delivery delay
variables.documentation: Time customers wait for their orders, calculated as the backlog divided by the rate at which capacity can drain it. Safe division protects against zero capacity.

variables.name: normal delivery delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers consider normal or acceptable; used as the reference point for judging service.

variables.name: relative delivery delay
variables.documentation: Dimensionless ratio of the delivery delay the market perceives to the delivery delay it considers normal. A value of one means service is exactly as expected; larger values mean customers believe they are waiting longer than is acceptable. It is the input to the attractiveness curve.

variables.name: attractiveness
variables.documentation: Company attractiveness in the eyes of the market: a normalised graphical function of the relative delivery delay, defined on an evenly spaced grid of relative delay from zero to six. It equals one while service is at or better than normal, so no reward is given for beating the delivery promise, and it falls steeply once the wait stretches past about one and a half times normal, flattening near zero when waits become several times normal. This curve is the pivot of the balancing loop: it is the single place where poor delivery service is converted into lost orders and lost customers.

variables.name: effect of attractiveness on ordering
variables.documentation: Multiplier applied to normal ordering by existing customers. Existing customers cut back orders in the same proportion that the company loses attractiveness.

variables.name: normal order rate per customer
variables.documentation: Orders a satisfied customer places each month when service is normal.

variables.name: normal customer wins per sales person per month
variables.documentation: Productivity of a sales person: customers won per month when the company is fully attractive.

variables.name: revenue
variables.documentation: Money earned per month. Only orders that are actually filled generate cash, so revenue is capped by production capacity - this is why a capacity shortfall starves both growth loops at once.

variables.name: revenue per order
variables.documentation: Average revenue received for each order shipped. Together with the investment fractions and the unit costs it determines how much sales force and how much capacity a given volume of filled orders can pay for.

variables.name: budget for sales force
variables.documentation: Monthly money allocated to expanding the sales force.

variables.name: budget for production capacity
variables.documentation: Monthly money allocated to building new production capacity.

variables.name: fraction of revenue invested in sales force
variables.documentation: Share of revenue the company reinvests in selling effort.

variables.name: fraction of revenue invested in production capacity
variables.documentation: Share of revenue the company reinvests in capacity expansion.

variables.name: cost per sales person per month
variables.documentation: Fully loaded monthly cost of employing one sales person.

variables.name: cost per unit of capacity
variables.documentation: Capital cost of adding one unit of capacity, where a unit of capacity is the ability to fill one more order per month. It converts the capital budget into a construction start rate and so sets the financial speed limit on expansion.

variables.name: time to perceive delivery delay
variables.documentation: How long it takes the market to notice and internalise a change in the delivery delay it is actually experiencing. Customers judge the company on recent experience and word of mouth rather than on today's instantaneous queue, so this perception lag sits between the physical delay and the market's reaction to it.

variables.name: perceived delivery delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay as the market currently believes it to be: a first order exponential smooth of the actual delivery delay. This is the quantity customers actually respond to when judging the company, and the lag it introduces is one of the phase shifts that turns the growth limit into a cycle rather than a smooth ceiling.

variables.name: time to perceive orders
variables.documentation: How long management averages incoming orders over before treating the result as the level of demand to plan capacity against. It filters short term noise out of the order rate but also delays management's recognition of genuine growth.

variables.name: expected order rate
variables.documentation: Management's working estimate of the rate at which orders are arriving, formed as a first order smooth of the actual order rate. It is the demand anchor of the capacity plan.

variables.name: desired backlog
variables.documentation: The backlog the company is content to carry: exactly enough unfilled orders to keep customers waiting the normal delivery delay and no longer. Backlog above this level is read as a service problem to be fixed with capacity.

variables.name: backlog adjustment time
variables.documentation: How aggressively management tries to work an excess backlog back down to the desired backlog. Shorter times make the capacity plan react more sharply to a service shortfall and raise the gain of the capacity loop.

variables.name: backlog correction
variables.documentation: The extra throughput per month the company would need, over and above covering expected orders, to eliminate the excess backlog within the backlog adjustment time. Positive whenever service is worse than normal.

variables.name: desired production capacity
variables.documentation: The capacity management judges it needs: enough to keep pace with expected orders plus enough to work off any excess backlog. This is the goal of the capacity acquisition loop and the reference against which the capacity gap is measured.

variables.name: capacity adjustment time
variables.documentation: How quickly management tries to close the gap between desired and actual production capacity. It sets the gain of the capacity acquisition loop; combined with the construction delay it determines whether capacity settles smoothly on demand or overshoots it and cycles.

variables.name: adjustment for production capacity
variables.documentation: The rate of new construction needed to close the gap between desired and installed production capacity over the capacity adjustment time. This is the main corrective term in the investment rule.

variables.name: desired production capacity under construction
variables.documentation: How much capacity ought to be in the construction pipeline in steady state: enough in flight, across the construction delay, to replace capacity as it wears out. It is the reference level against which the actual supply line is judged.

variables.name: supply line adjustment time
variables.documentation: How quickly management corrects a discrepancy between the capacity actually in the construction pipeline and the pipeline it believes it ought to be carrying.

variables.name: fraction of supply line accounted for
variables.documentation: The degree to which management credits capacity that is already ordered and paid for but not yet completed when deciding how much more to start. One means the pipeline is fully taken into account; zero means capacity on the way is ignored, so the same shortfall is ordered over and over. Values well below one are the classic source of overshoot in capacity acquisition and are what converts the construction delay into a sustained oscillation.

variables.name: adjustment for supply line of production capacity
variables.documentation: The correction applied to construction starts for the state of the pipeline, weighted by how much of the pipeline management actually credits. When more capacity is in flight than the reference level this term is negative and restrains further starts; when management discounts the pipeline that restraint is weak and starts keep piling up.

variables.name: desired capacity construction start rate
variables.documentation: The construction start rate management would like: enough to replace depreciating capacity, plus a correction for the capacity gap, plus a correction for the pipeline. It is held at or above zero because construction already committed cannot be un-started.

variables.name: affordable capacity construction start rate
variables.documentation: The most capacity the company can begin building each month given the share of revenue it devotes to capital investment and the cost of a unit of capacity. This is the financial ceiling on expansion, and because only filled orders earn revenue it tightens precisely when a capacity shortage is starving fulfilment.

variables.name: indicated sales force
variables.documentation: The number of sales people the selling budget can support: the budget divided by the fully loaded monthly cost of one person. It is the target toward which the actual sales force is steered, and it can grow only as fast as revenue from filled orders grows, which is how a capacity shortage throttles the growth engine.

variables.name: sales force adjustment time
variables.documentation: How long it takes the company to recruit and onboard the people needed to close the gap between the sales force its budget indicates and the sales force it actually has.

testParams.name: Population Growth simulates to completion
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of population growth. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll load the model generation tool and build this.

Specs match. Running the model.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure (5 variables, exactly as specified):

Variable Type Equation Units
Population stock initial 1000; inflow births, outflow deaths individuals
births flow (uniflow) Population * fractional_birth_rate individuals/year
deaths flow (uniflow) Population * fractional_death_rate individuals/year
fractional_birth_rate auxiliary 0.03 1/year
fractional_death_rate auxiliary 0.015 1/year

Specs: start 0, stop 100, DT 0.25, time units years, Euler integration.

Validation performed:

  • No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine. All variables carry units and documentation.
  • No hard-coded constants inside flow equations — both fractional rates are named auxiliaries.
  • Both flows are first-order proportional to the stock, so Population cannot go negative structurally; no MIN/MAX clamping needed. Confirmed in the data: minimum Population = 1000, minimum births = 30, minimum deaths = 15, all strictly positive.
  • Conservation check: births - deaths divided by Population equals exactly 0.015 per year at every sampled point, as the formulation requires.
  • Reference-mode check: run eval-run-1 produces smooth exponential growth from 1000 at t=0 to 4469.1 individuals at t=100. The Euler analytic expectation is 1000 × (1 + 0.015 × 0.25)^400 = 4469.1 — an exact match. (The continuous-time solution 1000·e^1.5 = 4481.7 is ~0.3% higher; that gap is the expected Euler discretization error at DT = 0.25, well within tolerance. Reducing DT would shrink it if you want closer agreement with the analytic curve.)

Structural critique: the model is a pure first-order linear system with constant fractional rates — appropriate for the stated problem, but note the boundary excludes anything that would bend the growth curve (density dependence, resource limits, age structure, migration). Over a 100-year horizon the population more than quadruples with no constraint, which is a consequence of that boundary choice, not a defect in the formulation.

Next steps you might want: a time-series plot of Population with births and deaths; a feedback analysis to explain the growth mechanism; or a sensitivity sweep on the two fractional rates.

variables.name: Population
variables.documentation: The stock of individuals in the population. It accumulates births and is depleted by deaths, starting from an initial value of 1000 individuals.

variables.name: births
variables.documentation: The number of individuals added to the population each year, equal to the current population times the fractional birth rate. This is the reinforcing (positive) feedback loop driving growth.

variables.name: deaths
variables.documentation: The number of individuals removed from the population each year, equal to the current population times the fractional death rate. This is a balancing (negative) feedback loop draining the stock.

variables.name: fractional birth rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the population that gives birth each year. Held constant at 0.03 per year so that births scale proportionally with population size.

variables.name: fractional death rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the population that dies each year. Held constant at 0.015 per year so that deaths scale proportionally with population size.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.
