testParams.name: Predator-Prey System with Three Modules
testParams.prompt:
Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.
Make sure to create a model with exactly the specified modules; do not add any additional modules beyond what is specified.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model is built and pushed. Here is what is actually in it.

Structure — exactly three modules: lions, foxes, chickens

Each module uses the specified component names.

lions (apex — no predator, hence no predation rate)

  • lions.count — stock, 20 animals, inflow lions.births, outflow lions.deaths
  • lions.births = birth_rate * count (animals/Year)
  • lions.deaths = death_rate * count (animals/Year)
  • lions.birth rate = 0.5, lions.death rate = 0.5 (1/Year)

foxes

  • foxes.count — stock, 100 animals, inflow foxes.births, outflows foxes.deaths and foxes.predation rate
  • foxes.births = birth_rate * count, foxes.deaths = death_rate * count
  • foxes.predation rate = predation_coefficient * lions_count * count — foxes killed off by their predator, the lions
  • foxes.birth rate = 0.4, foxes.death rate = 0.1, foxes.predation coefficient = 0.015 (1/(animals*Year))
  • foxes.lions count — ghost of lions.count (crossLevelGhostOf = lions.count)

chickens

  • chickens.count — stock, 1000 animals, inflow chickens.births, outflows chickens.deaths and chickens.predation rate
  • chickens.births = birth_rate * count, chickens.deaths = death_rate * count
  • chickens.predation rate = predation_coefficient * foxes_count * count — chickens killed off by their predator, the foxes
  • chickens.birth rate = 1.0, chickens.death rate = 0.1, chickens.predation coefficient = 0.009
  • chickens.foxes count — ghost of foxes.count (crossLevelGhostOf = foxes.count)

Ghost naming follows the stated rule: module prefix preserved with a space replacing the period. Specs: 0–100 Year, DT = 0.0625, Euler. Every variable has units and documentation; no bare numeric constants appear inside equations — all parameters are named variables. get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings.

Formulation notes

Predation is written as predator count times prey count times a coefficient. This makes the loss proportional to the predator population as the background requires, and the additional proportionality to the prey's own stock supplies first-order control, so no population can be driven negative by its outflows (natural deaths are likewise fractional and self-limiting). Parameters are set so each level's gains and losses balance at the initial stock values, which is the only bounded parameterization this structure admits: because births depend on fixed fractional rates rather than on prey consumed, the couplings run strictly one way, lions to foxes to chickens.

Simulation status — blocked by the engine, not the model

run_model fails at model load with Failed to load XMILE model: list index out of range. I isolated the cause with minimal test models pushed through update_model:

  • A flat, non-modular model simulates successfully.
  • A two-module model with no ghost passes the XMILE loader.
  • Any model containing a variable with crossLevelGhostOf set fails with this same index error — including a minimal two-module case, a parent-to-child root-level ghost, an empty-equation ghost, and a dotted ghost name. A stock-typed ghost fails differently ('NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip').

So the failure is in this build's cross-module ghost conversion, and the required structure (predation driven by the predator's count in another module) cannot avoid a ghost. I also confirmed the equation convention this loader wants and used it throughout: module-local unqualified references with underscores for spaces (birth_rate * count), not module-qualified names.

Recommended next steps: if the ghost conversion gets fixed, run and inspect the three count stocks for the equilibrium check and non-negativity, then pull feedback information before any behavioral interpretation. As a diagnostic-only workaround, a flattened single-module copy of the same equations will simulate today and can verify the numerics, but I have not built one since the brief requires exactly the three modules.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model is built and pushed to the client. No errors and no unit warnings are reported.

Structure (as actually built)

Module frimbulators (single module, no parent):

Variable Type Equation Units
frimbulators.count stock 20 (initial), inflow = frimbulators.frimbulator growth frimbulators
frimbulators.frimbulator growth flow (uniflow, inflow only) count * fractional_growth_rate frimbulators/day
frimbulators.fractional growth rate constant 0.02 1/day

Causal relationships extracted from the background information (all three, with polarity):

  1. frimbulators.count → frimbulators.frimbulator growth (+): growth is stated as relative to current size, so the current count drives the daily addition.
  2. frimbulators.fractional growth rate → frimbulators.frimbulator growth (+): the 2 percent per day rate scales how much of the current count is added.
  3. frimbulators.frimbulator growth → frimbulators.count (+): the growth flow is the only inflow accumulating into the count.

Specs: 0 to 100 days, dt 0.25, Euler, time units days.

Formulation notes: the 2 percent is abstracted into a named constant rather than hard-coded in the flow equation; the flow is dimensionally frimbulators/day = frimbulators * (1/day); no outflow exists because the background states none, so the count cannot go negative from an initial value of 20.

Simulation status

The model will not simulate in this environment, and the cause is the engine, not the formulation. I isolated it: a bare stock named frimbulators.count inside module frimbulators, with no flows and no equations referencing anything, fails with 'frimbulators.count not found as model element'; the identical stock with a flat (unqualified) name simulates fine. The local XMILE loader in this session cannot resolve module-qualified variable names. Since you explicitly required one module per object with <module>.count, I kept the modular structure and did not flatten it.

If you want numeric output here, the option is to flatten to unqualified names (count, frimbulator growth, fractional growth rate), which would violate the requested naming convention. Say the word and I will produce that as a throwaway variant for verification while leaving the modular model as the deliverable. Otherwise the analytic behavior is fixed by the structure: pure exponential growth, 20 * exp(0.02 * t) frimbulators, doubling roughly every 35 days.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built and pushed. Structure (module frimbulators, one object type, so no ghosts required):

Variable Type Equation Units
frimbulators.count stock 100 (initial) frimbulators
frimbulators.growth inflow count * fractional_growth_rate frimbulators/week
frimbulators.fractional growth rate constant 0.05 1/week
frimbulators.decline outflow constant_decline frimbulators/week
frimbulators.constant decline constant 5 frimbulators/week

Causal relationships extracted from the background (5 total):

  1. frimbulators.count → frimbulators.growth (+) — growth is 5% relative to current size, so the stock drives its own inflow
  2. frimbulators.fractional growth rate → frimbulators.growth (+)
  3. frimbulators.growth → frimbulators.count (+)
  4. frimbulators.constant decline → frimbulators.decline (+)
  5. frimbulators.decline → frimbulators.count (−)

Sim specs: 0–52 weeks, DT 0.25, Euler. The 5% and the 5 frimbulators/week are abstracted into named constants rather than hard-coded in the flow equations.

Validation notes:

  • get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings.
  • Behavior check: I simulated a structurally identical non-modular copy of this model (run eval-run-7) and inspected the numbers — count holds at exactly 100 for all 52 weeks, with growth = 5 and decline = 5 every week. The stock starts precisely at the knife-edge where 0.05 × 100 equals the constant 5/week, so net accumulation is zero. It never goes negative and no conservation law is violated.
  • The modular version itself will not simulate in this environment: the simulation back end (PySD) flattens module-qualified names, so it reports frimbulators.count not found as model element. This is a name-resolution limitation of the simulation path for modular models, not a defect in the model equations — the identical flat model runs cleanly. I kept the modular form because your naming convention requires it.
  • Structural caveat worth flagging: decline is a level-independent constant drain, exactly as the background states. If count were ever perturbed below 100, the stock would fall and could eventually go negative, since nothing slows the outflow as the stock empties. The background gives no mechanism for that, so I did not add one — say the word if you want a first-order control on the outflow.

Useful next steps: an extreme-conditions test (initial count of 0, or 5% vs. a larger constant decline) to probe the equilibrium's instability, or a plot of count against its two flows.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, the baseline inventory shows one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built as two modules, with every stated cause-effect link represented explicitly.

Structure

Module whatajigs

Variable Type Equation Units
whatajigs.count stock INIT 100 whatajigs
whatajigs.whatajig growth inflow count * whatajig fractional growth rate whatajigs/Years
whatajigs.whatajig fractional growth rate aux 0.05 1/Years
whatajigs.whatajig depletion outflow balacks count * whatajig loss per balack whatajigs/Years
whatajigs.whatajig loss per balack aux 3 (300%/yr) whatajigs/balacks/Years
whatajigs.balacks count ghost of balacks.count balacks.count balacks

Module balacks

Variable Type Equation Units
balacks.count stock INIT 200 balacks
balacks.balack replenishment inflow whatajigs count * balack gain per whatajig balacks/Years
balacks.balack gain per whatajig aux 0.05 (5%/yr) balacks/whatajigs/Years
balacks.balack decay outflow count * balack fractional decay rate balacks/Years
balacks.balack fractional decay rate aux 0.03 (3%/yr) balacks/whatajigs... (1/Years)
balacks.whatajigs count ghost of whatajigs.count whatajigs.count whatajigs

Specs: 0-50 Years, DT 0.125, Euler. 14 relationships recorded, covering the four stated causal statements plus the flow-to-stock accumulations and the two ghost mirrorings:

  1. whatajigs.count → whatajig growth (+), 5% of current size
  2. whatajigs.balacks count → whatajig depletion (+), 300% of available balacks
  3. balacks.whatajigs count → balack replenishment (+), 5% of current whatajigs count
  4. balacks.count → balack decay (+), 3% of current amount

get_current_model reports no errors, no warnings, and no entries in unitWarnings.

Verification note

The modular form does not convert to XMILE in this build — every attempt to simulate a model containing modules fails at load ("list index out of range" / element-lookup failure), including a known-good modular model borrowed from another session and a stripped three-variable modular test. Simulation works only for non-modular name spaces here.

To check the equations behave as written, I ran a temporary flat mirror of the identical structure (run eval-run-13), inspected the data, then restored the modular model as the delivered artifact. Numbers from that mirror: whatajigs starts at 100 with growth of 5/Year against depletion of 600/Year, so whatajigs.count goes negative within the first year (-49 at t=1, -15510 at t=50), while balacks decline slowly from 200 to about 45.

Credibility critique

The negative whatajigs value is a direct consequence of the specification, not an artifact I introduced: a 300%-of-balacks drain (600/Year at t=0) is two orders of magnitude larger than the 5% self-growth (5/Year), and the drain does not depend on whatajig availability. I deliberately added no first-order control on that outflow and no MIN/MAX clamps, since the background states the depletion is driven purely by the balacks count and this is a causal-extraction exercise. If whatajigs are physical and cannot go negative, the missing real-world mechanism is availability-limited depletion (depletion scaling down as whatajigs approach zero) — that is a structural change beyond what the source text says, so I left it out and am flagging it instead.

Options from here: add availability-limited depletion to make whatajigs non-negative, extract loop dominance (would require the modular-simulation blocker to be resolved), or plot the mirror run's trajectories.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this as a three-module SFD. Let me load the model generation tool first.

No edit tool is registered in this session, so I'll regenerate. The taper structure the generator added is unnecessary here — refluppers has net positive flow throughout, so it introduces spurious causal links that would corrupt a causal-discovery reading.

Simulation fails at XMILE load. The most likely culprit is the cross-module ghost's explicit qualified equation. Regenerating with the ghost expressed purely as a ghost reference.

Still failing. Bisecting to isolate whether the cross-module link or the module machinery itself is at fault.

Progress — the XMILE load error is gone, confirming the cross-module ghost caused it. New error now. Let me inspect what was actually built.

The stock's inflow/outflow lists use module-qualified names while in-module equations use unqualified ones. Testing that inconsistency.

Same error. Testing whether the bare name count is the blocker versus modules themselves.

count is not the culprit — the error simply followed the rename. The failure is module-qualified name resolution. Testing a flat baseline to confirm the engine works at all.

Flat model simulates. Confirmed: module-qualified name resolution is broken in this session's engine, not the model structure. Let me validate behavior on the flat equivalent first.

Behavior validated on the structurally identical flat model:

  • marticatenes: flat at 50 (already at equilibrium 10/0.2)
  • exemintes: 120 decaying goal-seeking to 80 (8/0.1), reaching 80.1 by month 60
  • refluppers: rising linearly 75 to 195 (+2/month net), never negative

Now rebuilding in the modular form you specified.

Model delivered. Here is what is actually in it.

Structure: 3 modules, 16 variables, 15 recorded relationships

Module marticatenes

Variable Type Equation Units
marticatenes.count stock 50 marticatenes
marticatenes.new marticatenes arriving flow (in) marticatene arrival rate marticatenes/Month
marticatenes.marticatene arrival rate aux 10 marticatenes/Month
marticatenes.marticatenes leaving flow (out) count * marticatene fractional outflow rate marticatenes/Month
marticatenes.marticatene fractional outflow rate aux 0.2 1/Month

Module refluppers

Variable Type Equation Units

refluppers.marticatenes count ghost of marticatenes.count — marticatenes
refluppers.refluppers gained from marticatenes flow (in) marticatenes count * reflupper gain fraction from marticatenes refluppers/Month
refluppers.reflupper gain fraction from marticatenes aux 0.2 refluppers/(marticatenes*Month)
refluppers.refluppers lost flow (out) reflupper loss rate refluppers/Month
refluppers.reflupper loss rate aux 8 refluppers/Month

Module exemintes

Variable Type Equation Units
exemintes.count stock 120 exemintes
exemintes.new exemintes arriving flow (in) exeminte arrival rate exemintes/Month
exemintes.exeminte arrival rate aux 8 exemintes/Month
exemintes.exemintes depleting flow (out) count * exeminte fractional depletion rate exemintes/Month
exemintes.exeminte fractional depletion rate aux 0.1 1/Month

The single cross-module causal link is marticatenes.count into the refluppers module, carried by the ghost refluppers.marticatenes count, per your convention. Exemintes is fully independent — the background states no connection. Every magnitude is a named constant; no numbers are buried in flow equations. All 16 variables carry units and documentation, and the engine reported no unit warnings.

Important caveat: this model does not simulate in this session

The modular form fails at run_model with Failed to load XMILE model: list index out of range. I bisected this rather than guessing:

  1. Modular + ghost — fails at XMILE load
  2. Ghost rewritten as a pure ghost (empty equation) — still fails at load
  3. Ghost removed entirely, modular — load succeeds, then fails with 'marticatenes.count not found as model element'
  4. Stocks renamed count to inventory count — same error, following the rename, so count is not the problem
  5. Flat model, no modules, identical equations — simulates cleanly

So the fault is module-qualified name resolution in this session's engine, not your naming convention and not the model structure.

Behavior validated on the structurally identical flat model

From run eval-run-7 (0 to 60 months, dt 0.125, Euler), values inspected directly:

  • marticatenes: flat at 50.0 throughout. It starts exactly at its equilibrium, 10 / 0.2 = 50.
  • exemintes: 120 decaying smoothly to 80.10 by month 60, approaching 8 / 0.1 = 80.
  • refluppers: 75 rising linearly to exactly 195 at month 60. Inflow is pinned at 10/month (0.2 x 50) against a constant 8/month outflow, so net +2/month.

No stock goes negative, and none can: both fractional outflows are proportional to their own stock, so they are first-order self-limiting, and refluppers rises monotonically. I deliberately removed a taper/adequacy-ratio guard the generator had initially added around the constant reflupper drain — it was unstated structure that would have injected spurious causal links into a causal-discovery model, and the trajectory confirms it was never needed.

The modular model is what is loaded in your client now. If you would rather have a version that actually runs, say the word and I will swap in the flat equivalent with names like marticatenes count, refluppers count, exemintes count — same 15 causal relationships, dots replaced by spaces.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model is built and pushed to the client. Structure as verified by get_current_model / read_model_section:

Module dominitoxings

  • dominitoxings.count — stock, init 45, units dominitoxings
  • dominitoxings.arriving dominitoxings — inflow = new dominitoxings per day (dominitoxings/day)
  • dominitoxings.new dominitoxings per day — 12 dominitoxings/day
  • dominitoxings.departing dominitoxings — outflow = count * dominitoxing loss fraction
  • dominitoxings.dominitoxing loss fraction — 0.3 1/day

Module povals

  • povals.count — stock, init 35, units povals
  • povals.dominitoxings count — ghost of dominitoxings.count (units dominitoxings)
  • povals.replenishing povals — inflow = dominitoxings count * poval replenishment fraction
  • povals.poval replenishment fraction — 0.3 povals/(dominitoxings*day)
  • povals.losing povals — outflow = count * poval loss fraction
  • povals.poval loss fraction — 0.2 1/day

Module auspongs

  • auspongs.count — stock, init 90, units auspongs
  • auspongs.povals count — ghost of povals.count (units povals)
  • auspongs.replenishing auspongs — inflow = povals count * auspong replenishment fraction
  • auspongs.auspong replenishment fraction — 0.2 auspongs/(povals*day)
  • auspongs.reducing auspongs — outflow = auspong reduction rate
  • auspongs.auspong reduction rate — 12 auspongs/day

17 variables, 3 modules, 16 recorded causal links, all with units and documentation. Every fractional and constant rate is a named converter — no hard-coded numbers inside equations. No unit warnings were reported by the engine. Specs: 0–60 days, DT 0.125, Euler.

Naming conventions are honored exactly: one module per object (pluralized), quantity stored in count, cross-module influences carried by ghosts named povals.dominitoxings count and auspongs.povals count. The two stock-to-ghost links are represented by the ghosts' crossLevelGhostOf fields (the platform derives them there rather than as separate relationship entries — repeated attempts to add them as explicit relationships were dropped by the tool).

Simulation status — unresolved engine limitation. Every attempt to run failed at XMILE load time ("list index out of range"). I isolated the cause with three diagnostic builds:

  • Modules with ghost cross-level references → load fails ("list index out of range").
  • Modules with direct dotted cross-module references in equations (e.g. dominitoxings.count * poval_replenishment_fraction) → the equation parser rejects the dot.
  • Modules with no cross-module coupling at all → XMILE loads, but the run then fails resolving dominitoxings.count as a model element.

So the simulation backend in this environment cannot execute a modularized model with cross-module links, by either supported mechanism. The requested structure is intact and correct in the client; running it will require either a non-modular (flat) variant of the same equations or a fix to the engine's module handling. If you want the flat variant built as a runnable companion, say so and I will produce it — but I have left the modular version in place since that is what you specified.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we start the period with one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock decreases by a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we start the period with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock is reduced through 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory receives new additions of exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock experiences losses of 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built. Three modules, one stock each, every stated cause-and-effect link represented explicitly.

Module pablanksills

  • pablanksills.count — stock, init 110 pablanksills
  • inflow pablanksills.pablanksill replenishment = pablanksill growth fraction * count (pablanksills/quarter)
  • pablanksills.pablanksill growth fraction = 0.06 (1/quarter)
  • outflow pablanksills.pablanksill depletion = pablanksill constant decrease
  • pablanksills.pablanksill constant decrease = 18 (pablanksills/quarter)

Module posistorathers

  • posistorathers.count — stock, init 70 posistorathers
  • inflow posistorathers.posistorather arrivals = new posistorathers per quarter = 25 (posistorathers/quarter)
  • outflow posistorathers.posistorather reduction = posistorather reduction fraction * count
  • posistorathers.posistorather reduction fraction = 0.35 (1/quarter)

Module crypterals

  • crypterals.count — stock, init 95 crypterals
  • inflow crypterals.crypteral additions = new crypterals per quarter = 18 (crypterals/quarter)
  • inflow crypterals.crypteral conversions from posistorathers = posistorather conversion fraction * posistorathers count
  • crypterals.posistorather conversion fraction = 0.35 (1/quarter)
  • crypterals.posistorathers count — ghost of posistorathers.count (crossLevelGhostOf = posistorathers.count), the only cross-module coupling
  • outflow crypterals.crypteral losses = crypteral loss fraction * count
  • crypterals.crypteral loss fraction = 0.22 (1/quarter)

Specs: 0–40 quarters, DT 0.25, Euler. 18 variables, 19 causal links recorded (including posistorathers.count → crypterals.posistorathers count, +). Every rate constant is a named parameter — no numbers embedded in flow equations. The engine reported no unit warnings.

Two things you should know:

  1. Simulation is blocked in this session by a tooling limitation, not by the model. Every attempt to run fails at XMILE load with list index out of range, and I isolated the cause by bisection: the failure appears whenever the cross-module ghost (crossLevelGhostOf) is present, under every variant I tried (ghost as auxiliary, ghost as stock, empty equation, dotted equation, sibling modules, common parent module, nested modules). Removing the ghost lets the model load but then fails at result extraction with pablanksills.count not found as model element, and dotted cross-module references inside equations are rejected by the equation parser outright. I kept the proper ghost, since that is the correct representation of the posistorather-to-crypteral coupling and is what your client expects; a bare cross-module name reference would be an unresolved reference in the module namespace.

  2. Structural note on the pablanksills formulation. As specified, replenishment starts at 6% of 110 = 6.6 per quarter against a fixed drain of 18 per quarter, so the stock declines and, with nothing in the description slowing the constant withdrawal as the inventory empties, it will pass through zero. That is faithful to the background text — it says the decrease is a constant eighteen — but it means the pablanksill stock has no first-order control on its outflow. If you want physically valid behavior, the fix is structural: make the withdrawal taper as the inventory approaches zero (e.g. a desired withdrawal moderated by available inventory), not a MIN/MAX clamp. I have not made that change, since it is not stated in your source material.

Next steps I would recommend: confirm whether your client can simulate the ghosted module structure locally, and tell me whether the pablanksill withdrawal should be hard-constant or inventory-constrained.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we start the period with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory grows through incoming exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock loses 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model delivered: four modules, one per object, in the client.

Structure (modular SFD, weeks, 0–52, DT 0.25, Euler)

proptimatires

  • proptimatires.count — stock, init 40 proptimatires
  • proptimatires.new proptimatires (inflow) = proptimatires arrival rate (5 proptimatires/week)
  • proptimatires.proptimatires losses (outflow) = count * proptimatires loss fraction (0.25 1/week)

ocs

  • ocs.count — stock, init 25 ocs
  • ocs.proptimatires count — ghost of proptimatires.count
  • ocs.oc replenishment (inflow) = proptimatires count * oc replenishment fraction (0.15 ocs/(proptimatires·week))
  • ocs.oc losses (outflow) = oc loss rate (3 ocs/week, constant)

priaries

  • priaries.count — stock, init 80 priaries
  • priaries.proptimatires count — ghost of proptimatires.count
  • priaries.houtals count — ghost of houtals.count
  • priaries.priary replenishment (inflow) = proptimatires count * priary replenishment fraction (0.10 priaries/(proptimatires·week))
  • priaries.priary losses (outflow) = houtals count * priary loss fraction (0.05 priaries/(houtals·week))

houtals

  • houtals.count — stock, init 60 houtals
  • houtals.new houtals (inflow) = houtal arrival rate (7 houtals/week)
  • houtals.houtal losses (outflow) = count * houtal loss fraction (0.08 1/week)

21 causal relationships are recorded with polarities, covering every stated cause and effect: arrival rates and loss fractions into their flows, flows into their stocks (+ inflow, − outflow), stock-to-own-outflow links for proptimatires and houtals, and the three cross-module drivers (proptimatires → oc replenishment, proptimatires → priary replenishment, houtals → priary losses). No units warnings and no model errors are reported.

Validation notes

The simulation engine in this session will not execute the modular form: it fails at XMILE load with cross-module ghosts, and with ghosts removed it fails to resolve module-qualified names ('proptimatires.count not found as model element'). This is an engine/module-handling limitation, not a defect in the structure — variable names, equations, units and links are intact in the delivered model.

To verify the numerics I ran an equation-identical flattened variant (run eval-run-11) and inspected the trajectories:

  • proptimatires: 40 → 20 (arrival 5 / loss fraction 0.25), settled by ~week 20
  • houtals: 60 → 87.1, approaching 7 / 0.08 = 87.5
  • ocs: 25 → 37.0 (replenishment falls from 6 to 3 ocs/week, matching the constant 3 ocs/week loss)
  • priaries: 80 → −18.6, crossing zero around week 45

The priaries stock going negative is a direct consequence of the information as given: its outflow is governed by houtals (0.05 × 87.5 ≈ 4.4 priaries/week at equilibrium) while its inflow is only 0.10 × 20 = 2 priaries/week, and nothing in the description makes priary losses depend on the priaries on hand. I did not add first-order control or MIN/MAX clamping, since that would introduce a causal relationship the background information does not state. If priary losses should in reality be limited by available priaries, that link needs to be supplied explicitly and I will add it.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gains from exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory increases due to 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built: four modules, all causal links extracted

Structure (25 variables, 24 causal relationships, 4 modules, 0–24 Hours, DT 0.25, Euler)

outrances

  • outrances.count — stock, init 150 outrances
  • outrances.new outrances (inflow) = outrance arrival rate (20 outrances/Hours)
  • outrances.outrance decrease (outflow) = count * outrance decrease fraction (0.4/Hours)
  • outrances.outrance diminishment (outflow) = count * outrance diminishment fraction (0.1/Hours)

illigents

  • illigents.count — stock, init 30 illigents
  • illigents.illigent gain (inflow) = illigent gain fraction per outrance (0.4) * illigents.outrances count (ghost of outrances.count)
  • illigents.illigent reduction (outflow) = illigent reduction rate (5 illigents/Hours)

yelbs

  • yelbs.count — stock, init 65 yelbs
  • yelbs.yelb gain (inflow) = yelb gain fraction per outrance (0.1) * yelbs.outrances count (ghost of outrances.count)
  • yelbs.yelb loss (outflow) = yelb loss fraction per traze (0.12) * yelbs.trazes count (ghost of trazes.count)

trazes

  • trazes.count — stock, init 85 trazes
  • trazes.new trazes (inflow) = traze replenishment rate (15 trazes/Hours)
  • trazes.traze outgoing (outflow) = count * traze outflow fraction (0.18/Hours)

Three ghosts carry the cross-module causality, named exactly per your convention: illigents.outrances count, yelbs.outrances count, yelbs.trazes count. Every rate is a named parameter — no numeric constants are embedded in flow equations. All variables carry units and documentation. The model returns no errors and no unit warnings.

Validation status

Structural validation passed. Behavioral validation could not be run: this environment's simulation backend fails to load any modular model — including a two-variable single-module test case I built to isolate it. The engine reports Simulation failed: '<module>.<variable>' not found as model element, and with ghosts present it fails earlier at Failed to load XMILE model: list index out of range. Flattening the same equations into a non-modular model simulates fine, so this is a module-handling limitation in the backend, not a defect in the extracted structure. I kept the modular form because you specified it explicitly.

Structural critique

One issue worth flagging, inherent to the source text rather than the encoding: yelbs.yelb loss is driven by the trazes stock, not by the yelbs stock. Yelbs therefore has no first-order control on its own outflow. Since trazes settles near 83.3 (15/0.18) giving a loss near 10 yelbs/hour, while outrances settles at 40 (20/0.5) giving a gain of only 4 yelbs/hour, yelbs.count declines steadily and will pass below zero within the 24-hour horizon. I did not add a clamp or a self-limiting outflow — the background text specifies no such mechanism, and inventing one would corrupt the causal extraction you asked for.

Recommended next steps: run the model in a client build with working module support to confirm the trajectories, then request feedback-loop analysis to characterize the balancing structure inside outrances and trazes.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built: five modules, one per object

Structure (31 variables, 5 modules, 29 causal relationships) — verified against the model as actually written, not as requested:

Module Stock (init) Inflow Outflow
whatajigs whatajigs.count = 100 growth = whatajigs.count × growth_fraction (0.05/yr) decline = decline_rate (constant 3/yr)
balacks balacks.count = 200 arrivals = balacks.whatajigs count × arrival_fraction (0.05/yr) departures = balacks.count × departure_fraction (0.03/yr)
whoziewhats whoziewhats.count = 200 replenishment = whoziewhats.balacks count × replenishment_fraction (0.05/yr) losses = whoziewhats.count × loss_fraction (0.03/yr)
funkados funkados.count = 12 enhancement = funkados.whoziewhats count × enhancement_fraction (0.05/yr) outgoing = funkados.maxabizers count × outgoing_fraction (0.03/yr)
maxabizers maxabizers.count = 88 replenishment = maxabizers.funkados count × replenishment_fraction (0.05/yr) outgoing = maxabizers.whoziewhats count × outgoing_fraction (0.03/yr)

Ghosts, all created per your convention (crossLevelGhostOf set to the true source):

  • balacks.whatajigs count → whatajigs.count
  • whoziewhats.balacks count → balacks.count
  • funkados.whoziewhats count → whoziewhats.count
  • funkados.maxabizers count → maxabizers.count
  • maxabizers.funkados count → funkados.count
  • maxabizers.whoziewhats count → whoziewhats.count

Note the two cross-links the text specifies that are easy to miss: the funkado outflow is driven by maxabizers, not by funkados; and the maxabizer outflow is driven by whoziewhats, not by maxabizers. Both are represented as ghosts rather than self-referencing decay.

Formulation checks: every percentage and the constant three-per-year loss is its own named parameter with units — no bare constants inside any flow equation. All stocks have initial values and units. The engine reported no unit warnings.

Simulation status

run_model failed twice with Failed to load XMILE model: list index out of range. I traced this end to end through the actual toolchain: the sdjson→XMILE converter emits each module as a separate <model> with access="input" ghost auxes that carry no <eqn>, and the PySD backend's XMILE reader (a) has no grammar rule for module-qualified references such as whatajigs.count, and (b) flattens all <model> sections into a single namespace, which would collapse the five stocks named count into one even if the references parsed. This is a backend limitation with modular models, not a defect in the model — the sdjson itself is well formed and pushed to the client cleanly.

To sanity-check behavioral plausibility without the engine, I hand-integrated the equations offline (Euler, dt 0.25, 0–50 yr). No stock goes negative: whatajigs compounds from 100 to ~540 (5% growth beats the fixed 3/yr loss), balacks dip slightly to ~196 by year 5 then climb to ~417, whoziewhats rise monotonically to ~400, funkados fall briefly then rise to ~537, and maxabizers trough near 44 around year 15 before recovering to ~334. Conservation is not expected here — the text describes open inventories with independent inflow and outflow rules, not transfers between them.

Structural caveat worth recording: funkados.count and maxabizers.count have no first-order control on their outflows (both drains are externally driven), so under different parameters either could be driven below zero. That is faithful to the background text, which states these rules explicitly, so I have not added corrective structure.

Recommended next steps: flatten to a single module if you need this to simulate on the PySD backend (at the cost of the module naming convention you asked for), or open the modular model in a client that supports XMILE modules to run it and then request feedback-loop analysis.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The system is structured as a two-stock coupled feedback model representing whatajigs and balacks.

  1. Whatajigs Dynamics:

    • Governed by a reinforcing feedback loop via whatajigs growth (5% annual self-expansion).
    • Governed by an asymmetric negative coupling outflow whatajigs reduction driven by 300% of the balacks stock.

  2. Balacks Dynamics:

    • Governed by an inflow balacks growth driven by 5% of the whatajigs stock.
    • Governed by a self-limiting balancing feedback loop via balacks reduction (3% annual decay).

  3. Cross-Coupled Feedback:

    • Whatajigs positively influence balack growth, while balacks exert strong downward pressure on whatajigs, forming a predator-prey-like interaction structure.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The facility system consists of three distinct inventory stocks: marticatenes, refluppers, and exemintes.

  1. Marticatenes Subsystem: Represents a classic goal-seeking / balancing feedback loop with a fixed inflow of 10 units per month and a stock-dependent fractional outflow of 20% per month, initial stock 50.
  2. Refluppers Subsystem: Driven exogenously by the marticatenes stock via a gain fraction of 20% per month and drained by a constant outflow rate of 8 units per month, initial stock 75.
  3. Exemintes Subsystem: Operates independently with a constant inflow of 8 units per month and a stock-dependent balancing outflow of 10% per month, initial stock 120.

All numerical parameters have been isolated into clearly named auxiliary variables to adhere strictly to constant handling rules.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, there are initially thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory benefits from 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock suffers depletion of 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock is reduced through a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model represents a multi-echelon inventory dynamic containing three distinct stocks: povals, auspongs, and dominitoxings.

  1. Dominitoxings Subsystem: Dominitoxings behave according to a Goal-Seeking (Balancing) archetype with a constant external inflow (12 units/day) and a first-order fractional outflow (30%/day). At steady state, this inventory approaches 40 units.
  2. Povals Subsystem: Povals receive an inflow proportional to the stock of dominitoxings (30%/day) and lose 20%/day of their own volume via a balancing feedback loop.
  3. Auspongs Subsystem: Auspongs receive an inflow driven by 20%/day of the povals stock, with a constant depletion outflow of 12 units/day.

All constants and fractional parameters have been abstracted into dedicated auxiliary variables to ensure robust parameter exploration and transparent causal tracing.

supportingInfo.explanation:

    • Outflow: crypterals depletion driven by a balancing decay loop with crypterals multiplied by crypterals depletion fraction (0.22).

All parameters and constant values are abstracted into distinct auxiliary variables to comply with modeling standards.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: During operations, there are initially one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gains from 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory benefits from exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: The system represents a multi-stock dynamic network with four core accumulations: outrances, illigents, yelbs, and trazes. Outrances receives an exogenous inflow of 20 per hour and loses material via two distinct fractional rate outflows: 40% per hour transferred into illigents and 10% per hour transferred into yelbs. Illigents accumulates through this 40% inflow from outrances and drains through a fixed loss of 5 units per hour. Yelbs accumulates via the 10% inflow from outrances and experiences an outflow governed by the current stock of trazes (12% of trazes per hour). Trazes has an exogenous inflow of 15 per hour and a standard fractional outflow of 18% per hour. All constants and fractions have been cleanly separated into auxiliary variables to ensure full model transparency and avoid hard-coded numerical values in rate formulations.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we start the period with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Multi-Inventory Interconnected Dynamics

The system consists of five interconnected inventory stocks: whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers.

  1. Whatajigs Subsystem: Displays reinforcing growth based on its current size with a constant balancing reduction flow.
  2. Balacks Subsystem: Driven downstream by whatajigs as an inflow and regulated by self-balancing linear decay.
  3. Whoziewhats Subsystem: Receives inflow from balacks and exhibits first-order linear decay.
  4. Funkados & Maxabizers Coupled Subsystem: Forms a coupled cross-feedback structure where funkados grows from whoziewhats but is reduced by maxabizers, while maxabizers grows from funkados and is reduced by whoziewhats.

All numerical parameters have been isolated into named auxiliary variables following System Dynamics modeling standards.
supportingInfo.title: Interconnected Inventory Stock and Flow Model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation: This model implements a classic Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) epidemic framework augmented with a direct immunization channel through vaccination. The core structure features four state stocks: susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered. Pathogen transmission generates positive reinforcing feedback during early stages as infectious individuals interact with susceptible people via daily contacts, leading to exposure. Balancing feedback loops regulate progression through incubation and recovery delays, as well as the progressive depletion of susceptible hosts via infection and vaccination.
supportingInfo.title: Epidemic SEIR Transmission with Vaccination Dynamics

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the dynamics of hospital capacity during a health crisis by interlinking three core sectors: patient flows, workforce dynamics, and bed capacity management.

  1. Patient Dynamics & Capacity Constraints (Balancing Loop B1): Incoming patient demand fills available hospital beds. As patient numbers approach physical capacity, bed utilization escalates, triggering a nonlinear restriction on admissions to prevent physical overcrowding.

  2. Staff Burnout and Workforce Erosion (Reinforcing Archetype / Eroding Goals R1): As the patient stock grows without immediate staff increases, the patient-to-worker ratio (workload) climbs above normal. Elevated workload drives psychological and physical burnout, which nonlinearly amplifies staff turnover and illness. As healthcare workers depart, the remaining staff experience even greater workload, creating a vicious reinforcing spiral of workforce depletion.

  3. Capacity Surge and Staffing Delays (Balancing Loops B2 & B3): In response to rising patient loads, management initiates hiring and opens surge beds. However, both bed operationalization and staff recruitment involve structural delays. These delays create a transient crisis window where capacity lags behind demand, highlighting why crisis preparedness and rapid surge activation are critical to mitigating healthcare collapse.
supportingInfo.title: Healthcare Capacity and Workforce Burnout Dynamics

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation:
System Archetype and Causal Mechanisms

This model captures the classical Fixes that Fail and Limits to Growth system archetypes governing induced travel demand in transportation planning:

  1. Engineering Balancing Loop (Intended Solution):

    • When congestion exceeds the target congestion level, planning authorities initiate road expansion rate, accumulating road capacity.
    • Increased road capacity reduces congestion and travel time in the short run.

  2. Induced Demand Reinforcing/Balancing Feedback (Unintended Consequence):

    • Reduced travel time increases road attractiveness.
    • Improved attractiveness triggers behavioral shifts (route switching, departure time changes, mode shifts from transit, and newly generated discretionary trips), increasing new traveler adoption.
    • As travelers accumulate on the road, congestion rises back toward or above pre-expansion levels, eroding initial travel-time gains.

  3. Negative Externalities:

    • Because the long-term equilibrium settles at higher total vehicle throughput rather than lower congestion, negative externalities such as pollution and noise externality grow strictly with the expanded traveler volume.
supportingInfo.title: Induced Demand and Urban Road Congestion

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The outbreak of the American Revolution is modeled as an Escalation system archetype driven by two powerful reinforcing feedback loops coupled with an external fiscal driver.

  1. Fiscal Trigger to Initial Grievance: The French and Indian War left Great Britain with significant war debt. Parliament sought to recover costs by imposing taxes (Stamp Act, Townshend Acts) without granting parliamentary representation, initiating the accumulation of Colonial Grievances.

  2. The Escalation Loop: As grievances rose, colonists engaged in organized Colonial Acts of Defiance (such as boycotts and the Boston Tea Party). Parliament perceived this defiance as an intolerable challenge to crown authority and responded with harsher British Coercion and Enforcement (the Intolerable Acts and quartering of troops). A stronger collective identity multiplied colonial capacity for coordinated resistance, driving even larger defiance acts and overpowering balancing dissipation mechanisms until open armed conflict erupted.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model conceptualizes the systemic emergence of road rage through two interacting feedback subsystems: individual emotional accumulation and societal behavioral normalization.

At the operational level, Driver Frustration and Stress accumulates due to situational traffic delays, adverse weather conditions, sleep deprivation, and perceived provocations on the road. This stock is governed by a balancing feedback loop representing natural stress dissipation over time.

At the systemic level, acute frustration translates into observable Road Rage Incident Rate, which triggers social learning (the 'Escalation' and 'Success to the Successful' archetypes). As drivers witness repeated hostility, the Normalized Aggressive Driving Culture grows. This cultural stock exerts two reinforcing feedback influences:

  1. It increases the frequency of hostile driving behaviors, creating more Perceived Provocations for other drivers.
  2. It increases the Aggression Propensity Multiplier, making drivers more reactive to any given delay or stressor.

Together, these feedback mechanisms explain why isolated traffic events can escalate into persistent, self-reinforcing cultural waves of road rage across a transportation network.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The outbreak of the American Revolution is classic example of the Escalation Archetype operating via a strong reinforcing feedback loop.

  1. Underlying Driver: In the aftermath of the French and Indian War, Great Britain exerted Imperial Policy Pressure through taxation (e.g., the Stamp Act) to recover war expenditures.
  2. The Escalation Loop:
    • British enforcement and punitive legislation (British Coercive Measures) accelerated the Grievance Growth Rate among the colonists.
    • This inflow accumulated in the stock of Colonial Grievance, cementing anti-British sentiment and a shared American identity.
    • High grievance motivated organized defiance (Colonial Resistance), such as the Boston Tea Party and boycotts.
    • The British government interpreted resistance not as legitimate protest but as rebellion, retaliating with even harsher policies (the Intolerable Acts and troop deployments), which fed right back into further grievance accumulation.

Without an effective balancing mechanism or political representation to defuse tension, this mutually reinforcing escalation spiral drove the colonies inevitably toward open armed conflict.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:

Taxation

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model articulates the outbreak of the American Revolution using the classical Escalation and Fixes that Fail system archetypes across several interconnected feedback loops:

  1. Taxation & Grievance Escalation Loop (R1 - Reinforcing): British War Debt from the French and Indian War prompts British tax extraction (e.g., Stamp Act). This triggers colonial grievances, which feed into resistance and boycotts, provoking harsher British enforcement that further inflames grievances.
  2. Propaganda & Boston Massacre Loop (R2 - Reinforcing): Deployment of British troops increases urban tension and incident frequency. Clashes such as the Boston Massacre are distributed through patriot communication channels, amplifying outrage and fueling colonial solidarity.
  3. Identity & Solidarity Formation Loop (R3 - Reinforcing): Rising grievances catalyze a distinct American identity and organized defiance networks (Committees of Correspondence, Sons of Liberty), empowering larger collective resistance.
  4. Defiance & Intolerable Acts Coercive Spiral (R4 - Reinforcing): Coordinated defiance (such as the Boston Tea Party) provokes British retaliatory legislation (the Intolerable Acts/Coercive Acts), closing ports and imposing military rule, accelerating the cycle of mutual escalation.
  5. Militia Mobilization & Threat Perception Loop (R5 - Reinforcing): Colonial resistance and militia drills are perceived by the Crown as a direct threat to imperial sovereignty, accelerating preemptive military expeditions (e.g., marching on Concord to seize armaments), which further galvanizes colonial resistance.
  6. Grievance Dissipation Balancing Loop (B1 - Balancing): Colonial grievance naturally dissipates over time in the absence of fresh imperial provocations.
  7. Resistance Attrition Balancing Loop (B2 - Balancing): Colonial mobilization requires continuous energy and resources, experiencing organizational decay if momentum is lost.
  8. Coercive Force Drawdown Balancing Loop (B3 - Balancing): British garrisons and enforcement actions face logistical, financial, and political limits that provide negative feedback toward de-escalation.
  9. Imperial Debt Amortization Balancing Loop (B4 - Balancing): British fiscal strain gradually declines as imperial debt is retired over time.

When the positive feedback loops dominate the balancing mechanisms, mutual escalation inexorably drives the Hostility Breakout Potential past critical thresholds, culminating in open revolutionary warfare at Lexington, Concord, and Bunker Hill.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Feedback-Based Explanation of Road Rage Dynamics

Road rage is an emergent societal and behavioral phenomenon driven by the coupling of individual psychological stress, collective social norms, traffic congestion, and regulatory deterrence. The model contains 8 key feedback loops that govern how road rage unfolds over time:

  1. Reinforcing Loop 1 (Social Normalization / Contagion): road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ social learning rate $\rightarrow$ normalized aggressive behavior $\rightarrow$ driver aggressive propensity $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents. As drivers repeatedly observe hostile driving, tailgating, and rude gesturing, aggressive driving becomes culturally normalized, eroding social inhibitions and increasing baseline aggression.

  2. Reinforcing Loop 2 (Congestion Friction Spiral): road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ road friction from incidents $\rightarrow$ congestion build rate $\rightarrow$ traffic congestion level $\rightarrow$ traffic congestion impact $\rightarrow$ stress generation rate $\rightarrow$ driver stress level $\rightarrow$ driver aggressive propensity $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents. Aggressive maneuvers and brake-checking create stop-and-go shockwaves, worsening regional congestion, which in turn fuels further driver irritation.

  3. Reinforcing Loop 3 (Impatience Delay Escalation): traffic congestion level $\rightarrow$ impatience factor $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ road friction from incidents $\rightarrow$ congestion build rate $\rightarrow$ traffic congestion level. Traffic bottlenecks make drivers fall behind schedule; the resulting urgency and impatience induce hazardous overtaking and rage, which further locks up traffic.

  4. Reinforcing Loop 4 (Retaliatory Tit-for-Tat): road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ retaliatory maneuvers $\rightarrow$ perceived provocations $\rightarrow$ provocation stress multiplier $\rightarrow$ stress generation rate $\rightarrow$ driver stress level $\rightarrow$ driver aggressive propensity $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents. When one driver behaves aggressively, victimized drivers perceive provocation and retaliate, amplifying mutual hostility on the roadway.

  5. Reinforcing Loop 5 (Density Error Generation): traffic congestion level $\rightarrow$ driver errors and cutting off $\rightarrow$ perceived provocations $\rightarrow$ provocation stress multiplier $\rightarrow$ stress generation rate $\rightarrow$ driver stress level $\rightarrow$ driver aggressive propensity $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ road friction from incidents $\rightarrow$ traffic congestion level. Heavy stop-and-go traffic forces tight vehicle spacing, turning routine driver lapses or distracted glances into perceived hostile cutoffs.

  6. Balancing Loop 1 (Law Enforcement Deterrence): road rage incidents $\rightarrow$ enforcement mobilization rate $\rightarrow$ enforcement intensity $\rightarrow$ deterrence factor (decreases) $\rightarrow$ road rage incidents. Rising aggressive incidents trigger public complaints and targeted police crackdowns, restoring deterrence and suppressing reckless driving.

  7. Balancing Loop 2 (Driver Stress Recovery): driver stress level $\rightarrow$ stress relief rate $\rightarrow$ driver stress level. When drivers exit high-friction environments, natural emotional regulation and psychological recovery discharge accumulated frustration.

  8. Balancing Loop 3 (Traffic Network Clearance): traffic congestion level $\rightarrow$ congestion clearance rate $\rightarrow$ traffic congestion level. Natural discharge capacity gradually clears vehicle queues once incoming friction subsides.

Combined with exogenous multipliers—such as adverse weather, confusing roadway geometry, lack of sleep, and distracted driving—these interlocking feedback loops explain why road rage exhibits sudden nonlinear surges, sustained high-aggression equilibria in congested metropolises, and rapid de-escalation when strict enforcement and traffic calming measures take effect.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The outbreak of the American Revolution can be understood through four core feedback loops operating within the classic Escalation Archetype:

  1. Reinforcing Escalation Loop (R1 - Retaliation & Defiance): British attempts to resolve French and Indian War debts via taxation (e.g., Stamp Act) sparked Colonial Grievance. Grievance led to Colonial Acts of Defiance (e.g., Boston Tea Party), which Great Britain met with punitive counteractions (e.g., Intolerable Acts, military garrisoning). This heightened British Coercive Presence, which further accelerated grievance accumulation, locking both sides in a self-reinforcing upward spiral.

  2. Reinforcing Identity Loop (R2 - Shared Resistance & Solidarity): Acts of defiance and shared victimhood (such as the Boston Massacre) galvanized an evolving sense of American identity. As Colonial Identity and Solidarity grew, inter-colonial cooperation expanded, enabling even more organized and widespread defiance.

  3. Balancing Grievance Dissipation Loop (B1): Without continuous provocations, popular grievances naturally diffuse over time.

  4. Balancing De-escalation Loop (B2): British enforcement and military commitments face administrative and political delays that gradually relax coercive measures over time.

Together, the powerful reinforcing loops (R1 and R2) overwhelmed the stabilizing mechanisms, culminating in critical hostility risks that triggered the outbreak of armed conflict in 1775.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the systemic drivers of road rage incidents using four key feedback loops:

  1. Provocation Contagion Loop (Reinforcing Loop R1): Frustrated drivers engage in aggressive driving, creating perceived provocations (e.g., tailgating, cutoff maneuvers) that provoke anger in surrounding drivers, accelerating frustration accumulation and generating even more incidents.

  2. Congestion Disruption Loop (Reinforcing Loop R2): Aggressive driving maneuvers cause micro-delays, sudden braking, and lane disruptions that worsen traffic congestion. Heavier traffic delays exacerbate driver impatience and frustration, fueling further road rage.

  3. Emotional Dissipation Loop (Balancing Loop B1): As the stock of driver frustration builds, natural cooling off and stress relief over time drain frustration back toward baseline levels.

  4. Enforcement Deterrence Loop (Balancing Loop B2): As active road rage incidents proliferate, increased societal attention and police enforcement create a deterrence effect that dampens the translation of anger into aggressive incidents.

These interconnected feedback structures demonstrate that while environmental and psychological factors seed initial road rage, behavioral contagion and traffic disruption can cause self-reinforcing escalations unless checked by social and enforcement counterbalances.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Dynamics of Road Rage Incidents
